Sales and relationship management: how a client is won, and how it is kept

This page explains the two halves of the job. It follows one large client from the first conversation to the years after the contract is signed.

It assumes you have read "Start here". For what a relationship is, who it is with and how trust grows over decades, see the Relationships page.

1. The short answer

  • Sales wins the client. It finds an organisation with a need and persuades it to appoint the firm.
  • Relationship management keeps the promise. It looks after the client once the firm has been appointed.
  • The two overlap. In most teams they sit together and share clients.
  • At junior level the daily work is much the same on both sides.
  • The names differ from firm to firm, so learn the work and treat the labels with care.

What is published about Goldman's labels

  • Goldman's own job titles pair "Client Solutions Group" with the word "Sales". ✔ Verified R1-S04
  • Goldman uses the name "Client Coverage Group" for the people who retain, expand and support existing client relationships. ✔ Verified R1-S11 That definition comes from a Hong Kong advertisement, so it shows the global meaning and says nothing certain about London.
  • A London advertisement for a Client Solutions Group role lists both kinds of work: new business and existing relationships. ✔ Verified R1-S01
  • How the two groups divide the work in London is not published. ∅ Not publicly established
  • The former intern said "CSG is sales and CCG is relationship management". That is one person's account of one team. ? Unverified account

A safe sentence for an interview: "I understand the group both wins clients and looks after them, and that teams split the work in different ways. How does your team divide it?"

2. Two jobs on one client

Read the picture from left to right. The arrow in the middle is the day the client appoints the firm.

Before that day, sales leads. Relationship management helps, mostly with the detailed checks and the set-up plan.

After that day, relationship management leads. Sales stays close and steps forward again when the client might give the firm something new.

The hand-over is gradual. A client who met one person for a year and then never saw them again would feel dropped. Good teams introduce the relationship manager early, well before the win.

3. The sale, step by step

This is how a large UK pension mandate is usually won. The timings are general industry patterns, and they vary a great deal. ≈ Supported inference

Two real, public examples run through the steps.

  • The BAE Systems pension schemes. The trustees appointed Goldman Sachs Asset Management to manage about £23 billion. Goldman announced it on 6 September 2023. ✔ Verified R3-S01
  • The Shell pension entities. Several Shell pension funds and an insurance company owned by Shell appointed Goldman for about $40 billion in September 2025. ✔ Verified R7-S08

Limits and caveats: What the public record does not say

No public source says which Goldman team or which person won either mandate. Announcements name the firm, the client and sometimes a senior spokesperson. Do not credit a win to the London team or to anyone by name.

Step 1. Knowing who might need what

What happens. The team keeps a picture of every organisation it could serve. How big is the scheme? Who advises it? What does it hold today? What is likely to change?

Who leads. Sales.

What the junior person does. Builds and updates the research. Reads the scheme's published reports. Notes changes of trustee, adviser or strategy. Keeps the client database accurate.

How long. It never stops. ≈ Supported inference

How it fails. The research is out of date, so the team approaches a scheme about a problem it solved last year.

Step 2. Getting known before there is a need

What happens. Clients rarely hire a stranger. So the firm works to be known and respected long before any contract is on offer. It publishes research, speaks at events and meets people with nothing to sell.

A large part of this step is the investment consultant. A consultant is a firm that advises the client on which manager to hire. Consultants have research teams that study managers and give each strategy a rating, a formal opinion on its quality. A poor rating, or none, can keep a manager off the list altogether.

Who leads. Sales, with a specialist team for consultants where the firm has one.

What the junior person does. Prepares material for consultant research meetings. Fills in the consultants' data requests accurately and on time.

How long. Years. ≈ Supported inference

How it fails. The firm appears only when it wants something. Or it sends a consultant figures that do not match what it sent last quarter.

Step 3. The first conversation: questions, not a pitch

What happens. Something changes at the client. Its funding improves, a rule changes, or its current manager disappoints. The client or its consultant agrees to talk.

The best first meetings are mostly questions. What are you trying to achieve? What worries you? Who decides, and by when?

Realistic conversation (illustrative): ✎ Illustrative example

Weak opening: "Let me take you through our firm and our forty strategies."

Better opening: "Before I say anything about us, could you tell me what has changed for the scheme this year, and what you would most like to be different in three years?"

Who leads. Sales.

What the junior person does. Writes the briefing note beforehand. Takes notes in the meeting. Records every promise and chases each one afterwards.

How long. Weeks to months. ≈ Supported inference

How it fails. The firm talks about itself, hears nothing, and proposes the wrong thing.

Step 4. The proposal

What happens. The firm turns what it heard into a specific answer. Which strategy, run by whom, under what limits, at what fee, with what reporting.

Who leads. Sales owns the proposal. The portfolio manager, the person who would run the money, owns the investment content.

What the junior person does. Assembles the document. Gathers figures from several teams. Checks every number against its source.

How long. Weeks. ≈ Supported inference

How it fails. The proposal is a standard brochure with the client's name on the cover.

Step 5. The formal tender

What happens. Large clients run a formal competition called a tender. Several managers are invited to bid.

The client sends a request for proposal, often shortened to RFP. It is a long written list of questions. With it comes a due diligence questionnaire, or DDQ, which asks how the firm is run: its controls, its people, its systems, its past problems.

For one type of mandate the competition is the law. UK pension trustees must run a competitive tender, with bids invited from at least three unconnected providers, before appointing a fiduciary manager for 20% or more of the scheme's assets. ✔ Verified W3-S01

Both examples went through a competitive tender.

  • At BAE Systems, the trustees were advised by the consultant Redington and the law firm Travers Smith. The company itself was advised by PwC. ✔ Verified R3-S02
  • At Shell, the consultant Isio oversaw the tender. Each fund set its own criteria and made its own decision. ✔ Verified R7-S08 R7-S12

Notice how many organisations sit around the table. The manager must satisfy the trustees, their consultant, their lawyers and the employer's advisers, all at once.

Who leads. Sales, with a specialist team that writes tender answers where the firm has one.

What the junior person does. A great deal. Drafts answers from the firm's library. Chases experts for the rest. Checks that the same fact is stated the same way in every place.

How long. Often three to nine months. ≈ Supported inference

How it fails. An answer contradicts another answer. A deadline is missed. A weakness is hidden and then found by the consultant.

Step 6. The final presentation

What happens. A short list of two to four managers presents to the trustees in person. The industry nickname is a "beauty parade". Each firm has perhaps an hour.

The trustees are judging two things. Is the answer right for us? And can we work with these people for ten years?

Who leads. The senior sales person, with the portfolio manager and the future relationship manager in the room.

What the junior person does. Builds the presentation. Prepares likely questions and the answers. Usually does not attend.

How long. One day, after weeks of rehearsal. ≈ Supported inference

How it fails. The team cannot answer a question about its own figures. Or the person who will look after the client is absent, so the trustees cannot picture the relationship.

Step 7. Appointment, contract and fee

What happens. The trustees choose. The winner then negotiates the investment management agreement, the contract that sets the rules, the fee and how either side can end it.

The fee is usually agreed in outline during the tender and settled here. Large clients negotiate hard.

Who leads. Sales on the commercial terms. Lawyers on the contract.

What the junior person does. Tracks the open points. Keeps versions of documents in order. Arranges the calls.

How long. One to three months. ≈ Supported inference

How it fails. A term agreed in the room is missing from the contract. Trust takes a knock before the work has begun.

Step 8. Set-up and funding

What happens. Accounts are opened. Identity checks are completed. The client's money and existing investments are moved across. This move is called the transition.

Only when the money arrives does the firm start to earn a fee. An announced mandate is not yet a paying one. At BAE Systems the announcement came in September 2023 and the transition was expected towards the end of that year. ✔ Verified R3-S01

Who leads. Relationship management takes over here, working with the operations teams.

What the junior person does. Runs the checklist. Chases documents. Tells the client, each week, what is done and what is next.

How long. Weeks to months. ≈ Supported inference

How it fails. The client is left guessing. The first report is late or wrong.

4. The whole journey in one picture

The picture groups the eight sales steps above into its first six boxes: research, first talks, proposal, checks, appointment and set-up. Its last two boxes, reviews and the decision to grow, shrink or leave, are what happens next. They go on for as long as the client stays. In the app, the Client lifecycle section lets you step through each stage.

5. After the win: how it is continued

The win starts the clock on a set of promises. Keeping them is the relationship manager's job.

The first 100 days

The client is watching closely. Was the transition smooth? Is the first report clear and correct? Does someone pick up the phone?

A good relationship manager agrees early what the client wants to see, how often, and who to call about what.

The regular rhythm

How often What happens
Every month A short report: value, return, any breach of the rules
Every quarter A full report and often a meeting with the client's investment staff
Once or twice a year A formal review with the trustees, usually with the portfolio manager
At any time Questions from the client, its consultant or its auditors

The relationship manager leads all of this. The junior person builds the reports and packs, checks the numbers, and keeps a log of every question and its answer.

When something goes wrong

Three things go wrong most often: a poor result, an error, or a change of people.

The rule is the same for each. Tell the client quickly, plainly, and before they find out another way. The Relationships page explains why this matters so much.

Money in and money out

A client can add to a mandate, reduce it, or change its rules. Each change alters the fee.

  • A fee review is when the client asks to pay less, often because the mandate has grown or a rival is cheaper. The relationship manager usually hears it first. A senior person decides the response.
  • When the client might want something new, such as a different kind of investment, sales comes back in. This is called cross-selling: offering an existing client a further service.

A good relationship manager only raises a new idea when it fits a need the client has voiced. Pushing products at a client who trusts you spends that trust.

Re-tender or exit

No appointment is permanent. Clients review their managers on a regular cycle, and their consultants keep rating them.

A real example. The Calor Group pension plan had used one fiduciary manager since 2019. In December 2024, after a tender overseen by the consultant Barnett Waddingham, it replaced that firm with Goldman Sachs Asset Management. ✔ Verified R7-S16

That was a win for Goldman. Read it from the other side too. The previous manager lost a client it had held for five years. Every firm that holds a mandate today can be replaced in the same way.

Sometimes the client leaves for a reason that has nothing to do with service. A pension scheme may pass all its money to an insurance company. A good relationship manager helps that happen well.

6. The same two jobs on the wealth route

The second route to clients is Third Party Wealth. Here the team sells funds to other firms, such as private banks and wealth managers, whose advisers then offer them to their own customers.

The two jobs exist here too. They look different.

Sales on the wealth route. The target is the fund selector, the person or team at the bank who decides which outside funds its advisers may use. The selector studies the fund much as a consultant would. If satisfied, the fund goes on the approved list.

After approval. Being on the list is permission to be bought. No money has moved yet. Now the team must reach the bank's advisers, sometimes hundreds of them, and explain when the fund is useful. Money arrives slowly, one customer at a time.

Keeping it there. The selector reviews the list regularly. A fund with weak results or little use can be removed.

So the word "sold" is ambiguous on this route. It could mean approved by the selector. It could mean chosen by an adviser. It could mean money has arrived. Only the last one earns a fee. When someone says a fund has been "sold", ask which they mean.

7. Side by side

Sales Relationship management
The goal A new client, or a new mandate A client who stays and is well served
A typical day Research, first meetings, proposals, tenders Reports, review meetings, questions, problems
Success is measured by New money won Money kept, and how the client rates the service
The pressure Long waits, frequent "no", clear winners and losers Steady deadlines, explaining results you did not choose
You need to be good at Listening, building a case, staying hopeful Reliability, clear explanation, staying calm

These are general patterns across the industry. ≈ Supported inference Real teams blend them.

What is the same

  • Both stand between the client and the people who invest the money.
  • Both depend on colleagues to keep their promises.
  • Both need to understand the investments well enough to explain them.
  • Both rest on the same thing: the client believing what you say.

8. What a junior does on each side

In the first year the two sides feel very alike.

Goldman has published the tasks for a junior London role in this group. They are: prepare and follow up client and prospect meetings, answer day-to-day client questions, work with product specialists and with the marketing, compliance and operations teams, and support the head of the team with market information and presentations. ✔ Verified R1-S01

That list mixes both kinds of work. "Prospect meetings" is sales. "Day-to-day client questions" is relationship management.

On either side you would spend most of your time making documents correct, finding answers inside the firm, and making sure nothing promised is forgotten. The difference grows with seniority, as people begin to own targets or own clients.

9. Pay and prestige

The former intern said analysts are paid £52,000 in sales and £48,000 in relationship management, and that sales is seen as more prestigious. ? Unverified account R1-S41

No public source supports either figure, or the claim about prestige. They are one person's account.

Do not build an answer on them. And do not let a small, unconfirmed pay gap decide which work you say you prefer. An interviewer will ask why, and "it pays more" is a weak reason even when it is true.

10. Which one is for me?

Nobody can answer this for you. These five questions are things to notice about yourself. Nothing more.

  1. When you hear "no" after weeks of effort, how long does it stay with you?
  2. Do you get more energy from starting something new, or from keeping something running well?
  3. Would you prefer a few clear wins and losses a year, or many small things done right every week?
  4. How do you feel about explaining a bad result that was not your decision?
  5. Do you enjoy meeting new people often, or knowing the same people deeply?

Your answers may point one way, both ways or neither. All three are fine at this stage. Many people start on one side and move to the other.

Check your understanding: Can you explain it?

Say these aloud, in your own words.

  1. What does sales lead, and what does relationship management lead?
  2. Name the eight steps of winning a large pension mandate, in order.
  3. Why does an investment consultant matter so much before a tender even starts?
  4. In the BAE Systems tender, who advised the trustees and who advised the company?
  5. Why is an announced mandate not yet a paying one?
  6. On the wealth route, what are the three things "sold" could mean?

Every step in detail

Open a step to see who leads, who supports, what the junior person produces and how it can fail. This describes general industry practice.

A large institutional mandate

1. Research and targeting
In plain English
Working out which organisations might have a need the firm can genuinely meet, before anyone picks up the phone.
What happens
The team maps a market: who the asset owners are, how large they are, who advises them, which managers they use, when contracts or strategy reviews fall due, and which searches are open. Public documents do most of the work: annual reports, statements of investment principles, committee papers, consultant search notices and trade press. Prospects are ranked by fit and timing, and some are deliberately set aside.
Who leads
Sales, with consultant relations where a consultant controls access.
Who supports
Analysts, marketing and data teams; relationship managers who know related organisations.
What the junior person produces
  • One-page prospect briefing with sources and a list of what is not known
  • Tracker of contract end dates, strategy reviews and open searches
  • Map of who advises whom (consultant, independent trustee, actuary)
  • CRM clean-up: correct contacts, roles and meeting history
On the client side
Nobody yet. The prospect does not know it is being researched and owes the firm nothing.
What good execution changes for the client
The client's first conversation is with someone who already understands its structure and constraints and does not waste its time on products that cannot fit.
Failure points
  • Targeting by size alone and ignoring fit
  • Out-of-date information presented as current
  • Pursuing a search where the firm's strategy is not rated by the client's consultant
  • Treating a public document as telling the whole story
Sales versus relationship management (illustrative; varies)
Almost entirely an origination activity. Relationship managers contribute intelligence about clients that share a consultant, sponsor or trustee.
Timing
Continuous background work; intensity rises when a search is announced.
2. First contact and discovery
In plain English
The first conversations, where the aim is to understand the client's problem, not to present a product.
What happens
An introduction is made directly, through a consultant or at an industry event. Early meetings are mostly questions: what the organisation is trying to achieve, what constrains it (liabilities, liquidity needs, governance time, regulation, beliefs), how decisions are made and by whom, and what has disappointed it before. The firm also decides whether it should compete at all.
Who leads
Sales.
Who supports
A product or investment specialist if the conversation turns technical; senior sponsor for very large prospects.
What the junior person produces
  • Question list tailored to the prospect
  • Meeting notes written up the same day, separating what was said from what was inferred
  • Contact map: who decides, who advises, who influences, who operates
  • Follow-up email draft with the material promised
On the client side
Usually an investment officer, pensions manager or chief investment officer; sometimes the consultant alone. They need to know quickly whether this manager is worth further time.
What good execution changes for the client
The client is asked questions that sharpen its own understanding of the problem, and is told honestly if the firm is not a good fit.
Failure points
  • Presenting before listening
  • Speaking only to one contact and mistaking their view for the organisation's
  • Promising follow-up that does not arrive
  • Failing to qualify out: continuing because a meeting was friendly
Sales versus relationship management (illustrative; varies)
Origination. Where the organisation is already a client for another mandate, the relationship manager normally makes the introduction and may lead.
Timing
From a single meeting to many months of intermittent contact.
3. Solution design and proposal
In plain English
Turning what was learned into a specific proposal: which strategy, in what form, on what terms.
What happens
Sales works with portfolio managers, product specialists and sometimes a solutions team to shape a proposal: the strategy or combination of strategies, the vehicle (pooled fund or segregated mandate), benchmark and guidelines, reporting, indicative fees. Pricing outside the standard schedule needs internal approval. The proposal should state what the approach will not do as clearly as what it will.
Who leads
Sales, with the investment or solutions team owning the investment content.
Who supports
Product specialists, pricing or business management, legal for unusual terms, compliance for review.
What the junior person produces
  • First draft of proposal slides from approved content
  • Data tables: performance, risk and peer comparisons reconciled to official records
  • Fee illustration on stated assumptions
  • Version control and compliance-review log
On the client side
Investment staff and consultant. They need a proposal that addresses their stated problem and can be compared fairly with others.
What good execution changes for the client
The client receives a proposal built around its objective and constraints, with trade-offs visible, so it can make an informed comparison.
Failure points
  • A generic pitch with the client's name on the cover
  • Fees or terms quoted without approval
  • Performance shown selectively or for a different vehicle than the one proposed
  • Over-engineering: a complex solution to a simple need
Sales versus relationship management (illustrative; varies)
Origination. For an expansion of an existing mandate the relationship manager often leads because they know the guidelines and history.
Timing
Days for a standard product; months for a bespoke or multi-asset solution.
4. RFP and due diligence
In plain English
The formal written stage: answering the client's questionnaire and proving that what was said is true.
What happens
The client or its consultant issues a request for proposal (RFP) and a due-diligence questionnaire (DDQ) covering organisation, team, process, performance, risk, operations, compliance, responsible investment and fees. Responses are scored. Operational due diligence may include site visits and interviews with risk, compliance and operations staff. For UK occupational schemes appointing a fiduciary manager above the regulatory threshold, a qualifying competitive tender with at least three unconnected providers is required.
Who leads
Sales owns the submission; the RFP team runs the process.
Who supports
Content owners across the firm (portfolio managers, risk, compliance, operations, legal, human resources), each approving the facts in their area.
What the junior person produces
  • Question-by-question tracker with owner, status and deadline
  • First-draft answers from the approved library, updated for the latest quarter
  • Evidence folder: policies, organisation charts, sample reports
  • Consistency check between the RFP, the presentation and the factsheet
On the client side
Consultant's research and operational due-diligence teams, the client's investment staff, sometimes procurement. They need complete, accurate and comparable answers by the deadline.
What good execution changes for the client
The client can rely on the answers when it justifies its decision, and discovers no surprises after appointment.
Failure points
  • Missed deadline or ignored format rules, which can disqualify
  • Stale library answers (old team names, old assets figures)
  • Inconsistency between documents
  • Answering a different question from the one asked
Sales versus relationship management (illustrative; varies)
Origination. In a re-tender the relationship manager is deeply involved because the incumbent's record is part of the evidence.
Timing
Typically weeks, set by the client's timetable.
5. Final presentation and appointment
In plain English
The shortlist meeting, often called a beauty parade, after which the decision-makers choose.
What happens
A small number of shortlisted managers present to the decision-making body, such as a trustee board or investment committee, usually for a fixed time with questions. The consultant normally attends and may score. The team presenting is typically the senior salesperson, the portfolio manager and the person who would manage the relationship. The client then decides, sometimes on the day, and informs managers of the outcome.
Who leads
Senior sales with the portfolio manager.
Who supports
The proposed relationship manager, product specialist, team head for large mandates.
What the junior person produces
  • Rehearsal pack and timed running order
  • Bank of likely questions with agreed answers and who takes each
  • Biographies and leave-behind document
  • Post-pitch record of every question asked and the outcome, including feedback if lost
On the client side
Trustees or committee members, who may be non-specialists with limited time, plus their consultant. They need to understand the proposal, test the people and feel able to defend the choice.
What good execution changes for the client
The decision-makers understand what they are buying and what could go wrong, and meet the people they will actually deal with.
Failure points
  • Talking over the audience's level or under it
  • A portfolio manager who cannot explain simply
  • Presenting a team the client will never see again
  • Not asking for feedback after a loss
Sales versus relationship management (illustrative; varies)
Origination, but this is where the relationship manager should first appear so the handover is not a surprise.
Timing
A single meeting; the decision may follow within days or after the next governance meeting.
6. Legal negotiation and onboarding
In plain English
Agreeing the contract and opening the accounts so the mandate can legally and operationally begin.
What happens
For a segregated mandate an investment management agreement (IMA) is negotiated: guidelines, benchmark, fees, reporting, liability, termination. For a pooled fund the client completes subscription documents. Client due diligence (know-your-customer and anti-money-laundering checks) is completed. Custody links, trading accounts and reporting are set up and tested.
Who leads
Onboarding or client implementation team with legal; the relationship manager coordinates the client side.
Who supports
Sales (to honour what was promised), portfolio manager (to confirm guidelines are workable), operations, compliance, tax.
What the junior person produces
  • Document checklist and status tracker
  • Chasing list for outstanding client and custodian items
  • Comparison of contract terms against the proposal, flagging differences
  • Reporting set-up specification
On the client side
Legal advisers, operations staff, custodian, sometimes the sponsor's treasury. They need a clear list of what is required and prompt answers.
What good execution changes for the client
The mandate starts on the agreed date with guidelines that say what the client intended.
Failure points
  • Promises made in the pitch that the contract does not reflect
  • Guidelines that are ambiguous or cannot be monitored
  • Slow due-diligence document collection delaying funding
  • No single owner between sales and relationship management
Sales versus relationship management (illustrative; varies)
The seam. In a handover model responsibility passes here; in a paired or single-owner model the same people continue.
Timing
Weeks to several months, driven by legal negotiation and document collection.
7. Funding and transition
In plain English
The money or assets actually arrive and the portfolio is built.
What happens
The client transfers cash or existing securities. If assets come from a previous manager, a transition plan sets out how the old portfolio becomes the new one while controlling cost and market exposure; a specialist transition manager may be used. The portfolio manager invests to the target. Fee accrual starts on funded assets. The first report is produced and checked with unusual care.
Who leads
Operations and the portfolio manager, with the relationship manager as the client's single point of contact.
Who supports
Transition specialists, trading, performance and reporting teams.
What the junior person produces
  • Funding timeline with dates and responsible parties
  • Day-one confirmation to the client of what has been received
  • Check of the first report against the contract: benchmark, fee basis, guideline tests
  • Welcome pack: contacts, reporting calendar, escalation route
On the client side
Operations and finance staff, custodian, outgoing manager. They need certainty about dates, amounts and who to call.
What good execution changes for the client
The client's assets are invested as agreed without avoidable cost, and the first report is right.
Failure points
  • Funding later or smaller than announced
  • An error in the first report, which sets the tone
  • Transition costs not explained in advance
  • Performance inception date disputed
Sales versus relationship management (illustrative; varies)
Stewardship begins. An announced mandate is not fee-paying until funded, so sales often stays involved until money arrives.
Timing
Days for cash into a pooled fund; weeks or longer for a complex transition or phased funding.
8. Ongoing reviews and reporting
In plain English
The long middle of the relationship: regular reports, review meetings and answering questions.
What happens
Reports go out on a fixed calendar. Review meetings, typically quarterly to annual, cover performance, positioning, risk, guideline compliance, service and outlook. Between meetings there are ad hoc questions, data requests from the consultant, regulatory reporting needs and operational changes. The relationship manager keeps the internal picture of the client current as people and priorities change.
Who leads
Relationship management.
Who supports
Client service and reporting teams, portfolio managers and product specialists for meetings, consultant relations.
What the junior person produces
  • Draft review pack reconciled to the official performance record
  • Meeting preparation note
  • Minutes and action log within two working days
  • Query log with response times
On the client side
Investment staff, trustees or committee, consultant, operations and finance. They need accurate information on time and plain explanations.
What good execution changes for the client
The client understands what it owns and why it has behaved as it has, and can govern the mandate with confidence.
Failure points
  • Late or wrong reports
  • Meetings that recite a pack and answer no questions
  • Actions that are not followed up
  • Losing touch when the client's staff change
Sales versus relationship management (illustrative; varies)
Stewardship. Sales stays informed because a well-served client is the main source of references and further mandates.
Timing
Years; this stage is most of the relationship.
9. Difficulties
In plain English
Something goes wrong: performance disappoints, an error occurs, or key people leave.
What happens
Common triggers are sustained underperformance, a guideline breach or operational error, the departure of a portfolio manager, a change in the firm's ownership or strategy, or a change on the client's side such as a new consultant. The relationship manager establishes facts, informs the client early, brings the right senior people into the conversation and agrees remedies. Clients may place the manager under formal review or on a watch list.
Who leads
Relationship management, escalating to the team head and senior investment staff.
Who supports
Portfolio manager, risk, compliance and legal for breaches, operations for errors, consultant relations.
What the junior person produces
  • Chronology of facts for an incident
  • Draft holding statement and client note for compliance review
  • Attribution summary of what drove underperformance
  • Tracker of clients affected and who has been contacted
On the client side
Chief investment officer or pensions manager, trustee chair, consultant. They need the truth quickly, a clear account of cause and remedy, and evidence that it will not recur.
What good execution changes for the client
The client hears bad news first from the manager, understands it, and can make a reasoned decision to stay, reduce or leave.
Failure points
  • The client learning of a problem from the press or its consultant
  • Defensive or evasive explanations
  • Predicting a recovery that cannot be promised
  • Compensation or remediation handled slowly
Sales versus relationship management (illustrative; varies)
Stewardship under stress. A badly handled difficulty also damages origination, because consultants remember.
Timing
Unpredictable; a formal review can last several quarters.
10. Additional allocations and cross-sell
In plain English
The client considers giving the manager more money or a second, different mandate.
What happens
A need emerges from the client's changing strategy, for instance moving towards lower-risk assets, adding private markets or consolidating managers. The relationship manager recognises it, tests whether the firm has a suitable capability, and introduces the right colleagues. Even for an existing client a larger or new mandate may need a formal process. Sometimes the right conclusion is that the client should not add.
Who leads
Relationship management or sales, according to the firm's coverage model.
Who supports
Product specialists for the new capability, the original salesperson, pricing for relationship-level fee terms.
What the junior person produces
  • Opportunity note: the client's stated need, evidence and timing
  • Updated client map and exposure summary across all mandates
  • Fee illustration including any breakpoint effect of larger assets
  • Briefing for the specialist who has never met the client
On the client side
Investment staff and consultant. They need a proposal that reflects what the manager already knows about them and respects any limit on exposure to one firm.
What good execution changes for the client
The client gets a relevant idea at the right time from people who understand its situation, and is not pestered with irrelevant ones.
Failure points
  • Pitching while an existing problem is unresolved
  • Proposing a product because it is a firm priority, not because it fits
  • Internal dispute over credit delaying the response
  • Ignoring the client's manager-concentration limits
Sales versus relationship management (illustrative; varies)
The clearest overlap between origination and stewardship. Firms differ on who leads and who is credited.
Timing
Opportunistic; depends on the client's strategy cycle.
11. Formal review or re-tender
In plain English
The client deliberately tests whether the manager should keep the mandate.
What happens
Many asset owners review managers on a fixed cycle or after a trigger. The review may be a desk-based assessment by the consultant, a re-presentation to trustees, or a full re-tender against competitors. Public-sector bodies may be required to re-procure. The incumbent must show its record, how it handled problems, and why it remains the right choice for the client's current needs, which may have changed since appointment.
Who leads
Relationship management, with sales where the review is a competitive tender.
Who supports
Portfolio manager, RFP team, consultant relations, team head.
What the junior person produces
  • Incumbent record: performance, service statistics, incidents and how they were resolved
  • Summary of how the client's needs have changed since appointment
  • Re-tender response using the client's own history, not library text
  • Fee comparison and options for approval
On the client side
Trustees or committee, consultant, sometimes procurement. They need a fair basis for comparison and may want to see the manager challenged.
What good execution changes for the client
The client reaffirms or changes its decision on current evidence, with the incumbent having given an honest account of its record.
Failure points
  • Complacency: treating the review as a formality
  • Defending the original mandate when the client's needs have moved on
  • Fee concessions offered only under threat, which damages trust
  • A new consultant with no history with the firm
Sales versus relationship management (illustrative; varies)
Both. The relationship manager holds the evidence; sales brings competitive discipline.
Timing
Months; the cycle between reviews is typically several years.
12. Renewal or exit
In plain English
The mandate continues on refreshed terms, shrinks, or ends.
What happens
Renewal may bring revised guidelines, fees or reporting. Exit can be full or partial and has many causes: performance, a change in the client's strategy such as a pension scheme buying insurance for its liabilities, consolidation, a merger, or a new decision-maker's preferences. On exit the manager cooperates with the transition: providing data, selling or transferring assets in an orderly way, final reporting and fee reconciliation. How a firm behaves on the way out affects whether it is invited back.
Who leads
Relationship management.
Who supports
Operations, portfolio manager, legal, the incoming transition manager where one is used.
What the junior person produces
  • Transition-out checklist and final reporting schedule
  • Final fee reconciliation support
  • Lessons-learned note recorded in the CRM
  • Updated contact record so the relationship can resume later
On the client side
Investment staff, operations, custodian, incoming manager or insurer. They need a clean, cooperative handover.
What good execution changes for the client
The client leaves or renews with its assets and records in order and without avoidable cost.
Failure points
  • Obstructive or slow cooperation after notice
  • No record of why the client left
  • Treating a rational client decision as a failure to be argued with
  • Losing contact with people who will be decision-makers elsewhere
Sales versus relationship management (illustrative; varies)
Stewardship to the end, then back to origination: a former client is a future prospect.
Timing
Notice periods are set by the contract; transitions take weeks to months.

A fund sold through a bank or wealth manager

1. Gatekeeper research
In plain English
A wealth manager's fund research team studies the fund before anyone is allowed to buy it.
What happens
The fund selector or research analyst screens a peer group, requests data and a questionnaire, meets the portfolio manager and scores the fund against competitors. The asset manager's salesperson supplies information in the selector's format and arranges access to the investment team.
Who leads
Third-party wealth sales.
Who supports
Investment specialist, portfolio manager, marketing and data teams.
What the junior person produces
  • Selector briefing
  • Data in the selector's template, checked to the factsheet
  • Peer-group comparison
  • Meeting notes with open questions
On the client side
Fund selector or research analyst (the gatekeeper), who answers to an investment committee.
What good execution changes for the client
The selector can assess the fund efficiently and accurately against alternatives.
Failure points
  • Data in the wrong format or late
  • A portfolio manager who does not answer the question asked
  • Pitching a fund the firm wants to sell instead of the one the selector is researching
Sales versus relationship management (illustrative; varies)
Origination.
Timing
Weeks to many months; reviews follow the selector's calendar.
2. Buy-list or approved-list decision
In plain English
The intermediary's investment committee decides whether the fund may be used.
What happens
The selector presents a recommendation to an investment committee. If approved, the fund joins a buy list, recommended list or model portfolio universe. Approval is permission to buy; it is not a purchase.
Who leads
The intermediary's committee decides; sales responds to final queries.
Who supports
Legal and product teams for share-class and fee terms.
What the junior person produces
  • Answers to committee follow-up questions
  • Share-class and fee summary
  • Record of the decision and its conditions in the CRM
On the client side
Investment committee, head of research, sometimes compliance.
What good execution changes for the client
The committee decides on complete information and understands where the fund fits and where it does not.
Failure points
  • Assuming approval equals assets
  • Unclear role for the fund in portfolios
  • Share class or fee terms not agreed in time
Sales versus relationship management (illustrative; varies)
Origination, shading into stewardship immediately.
Timing
A committee cycle.
3. Platform availability and set-up
In plain English
The fund must be technically available where advisers actually place trades.
What happens
The right share class is listed on the investment platforms the intermediary uses, with correct identifiers, charges and documents. Distribution agreements are completed. Data feeds to the platform and to research tools are tested.
Who leads
Product and distribution operations, coordinated by the relationship manager or sales.
Who supports
Legal, fund administrator, data vendors.
What the junior person produces
  • Platform availability checklist by share class
  • Document pack: key information, factsheet, prospectus links
  • Data-feed check against official figures
On the client side
Platform operations, the intermediary's operations and compliance staff.
What good execution changes for the client
An adviser who wants to buy the fund can do so without friction, at the correct price.
Failure points
  • Approved fund not available on the platform advisers use
  • Wrong charges displayed
  • Missing documents blocking trades
Sales versus relationship management (illustrative; varies)
Operational seam between the two.
Timing
Days to weeks, depending on the platform.
4. Adviser and portfolio-manager adoption
In plain English
The people who run client portfolios decide, one by one, whether to use the approved fund.
What happens
Advisers, discretionary portfolio managers or the team running model portfolios choose among approved funds. The asset manager supports adoption with briefings, plain-language material and access to specialists. In centrally run model portfolios one decision can move large sums; in adviser-led firms adoption is gradual.
Who leads
Third-party wealth sales, with relationship management for existing holders.
Who supports
Investment specialists, marketing, events.
What the junior person produces
  • Adviser briefing material
  • Event logistics and attendee follow-up
  • Adoption tracker by office or desk
  • Log of objections heard
On the client side
Advisers, discretionary managers, model-portfolio team; behind them, the end investor whose interests the intermediary must serve.
What good execution changes for the client
Advisers understand what the fund is for and can explain it accurately to their own clients.
Failure points
  • Material too technical for adviser conversations
  • No clear reason to choose the fund over an existing holding
  • Coverage spread too thinly across many offices
Sales versus relationship management (illustrative; varies)
Blended.
Timing
Months to years; often never complete.
5. Flows
In plain English
Money arrives, and leaves, in many small transactions.
What happens
Subscriptions and redemptions pass through platforms daily. The manager sees aggregate flows by intermediary, with limited sight of individual end investors. Flows respond to performance, market sentiment, model-portfolio rebalancing and the intermediary's own client growth.
Who leads
No single lead; sales and relationship management both monitor.
Who supports
Data and business-intelligence teams.
What the junior person produces
  • Weekly flow report by intermediary and fund
  • Explanation of unusual movements
  • List of approved-but-unused funds
On the client side
End investors through advisers and platforms.
What good execution changes for the client
The manager notices early when a holder is reducing and can ask why.
Failure points
  • Reading gross sales without redemptions
  • Mistaking a model rebalance for a change of view
  • No follow-up on unexplained outflows
Sales versus relationship management (illustrative; varies)
Blended.
Timing
Continuous.
6. Monitoring and ongoing due diligence
In plain English
The gatekeeper keeps checking that the fund still deserves its place.
What happens
Selectors review held funds on a schedule and after triggers such as underperformance, a manager change or a fund growing too large. The asset manager provides updates, access to the team and prompt notice of changes. For funds reaching retail investors in the UK, the manufacturer and the distributor each carry Consumer Duty obligations, including on fair value, so value assessments and target-market information are part of the exchange.
Who leads
Third-party wealth relationship management.
Who supports
Portfolio managers, product governance, compliance.
What the junior person produces
  • Annual due-diligence update pack
  • Change notifications to all holders
  • Watch-list tracker with decision dates
  • Responses to value and target-market queries
On the client side
Fund research team, investment committee, compliance.
What good execution changes for the client
The intermediary can keep using the fund with confidence, or act promptly if it should not.
Failure points
  • Holders learning of a manager change from the press
  • Slow or incomplete responses to review questions
  • Treating the annual review as routine
Sales versus relationship management (illustrative; varies)
Stewardship.
Timing
Annual cycle plus triggers.
7. Removal or replacement
In plain English
The fund is taken off the list, or the intermediary itself changes.
What happens
A fund may be downgraded, put on hold or removed after poor performance, a team change, a cheaper alternative, list consolidation, or the intermediary being acquired and its lists merged. Removal can trigger rapid redemptions from model portfolios. The manager supports an orderly exit and records the reason.
Who leads
Relationship management.
Who supports
Sales (for alternative funds that may fit), operations, liquidity management within the fund.
What the junior person produces
  • Record of the stated reason and the real one if different
  • Redemption forecast for the portfolio manager
  • Note on whether another capability might genuinely fit
On the client side
Investment committee, selectors, advisers who must explain the change to their clients.
What good execution changes for the client
End investors are moved without avoidable cost and the intermediary remains willing to consider the manager again.
Failure points
  • Arguing with the decision instead of understanding it
  • Immediately pitching a replacement fund
  • No lessons recorded
Sales versus relationship management (illustrative; varies)
Stewardship, then origination begins again.
Timing
Can be sudden.

Teams

Teams and their clients

The group is organised by where the client is and what kind of client it is. Pick a team to see who it serves, what to say about it and what to ask.

Client Solutions Group (CSG)

Umbrella client organisation of Goldman Sachs Asset Management (global) ✔ Verified T-csg

The asset management client business: it develops relationships and delivers investment solutions to institutional and third-party wealth clients worldwide.

Talking points

  • Goldman's own description names two client types, institutional and third-party wealth, across public and private asset classes R1-S10.
  • Its campus titles pair the name with 'Sales', and one London team under the name does both new business and existing relationships R1-S04R1-S01.
  • It has its own management and strategy team running sales budgeting, fundraising projections and Salesforce data governance R1-S13.
  • Matt Gibson is publicly described as head of the group R6-S19.

Questions to ask

  • How does the group divide work between people who win new clients and people who look after existing ones?
  • What does the group measure to know a client relationship is healthy, beyond assets?
  • Which client segment has changed most in the last year, and what did the team do differently?

Watch-outs

  • Do not say 'CSG just means sales' or 'CSG is the sales side and CCG the relationship side': published evidence shows overlap.
  • Do not quote revenue or headcount for the group: none is disclosed R2-S01.
Where the name comes from
Goldman Sachs's own name. Campus and experienced-hire listings use 'Client Solutions Group', 'Global Client Solutions Group', 'Client Solutions Group / Sales' and 'Client Solutions Group (Sales)' R1-S10R1-S04R1-S09R1-S13.
Kind of unit
Umbrella client organisation of Goldman Sachs Asset Management (global)
In one paragraph
The part of Goldman Sachs Asset Management that develops client relationships and delivers investment solutions to institutional and third-party wealth clients worldwide, across public and private asset classes. Goldman's own listings gloss it as 'Sales' and call it 'the sales organization', but at least one London CSG team is also described as managing existing relationships, so it is not new-business-only.
Former intern's account
An umbrella term for everyone who speaks to clients, 'the equivalent of saying sales', covering sales, client relationship management and consultant relations, cut by coverage team, then client type, then sales versus relationship management. He also used 'CSG' for the sales side inside a team. ? Unverified account
What public sources establish
Goldman describes CSG as developing client relationships and delivering investment solutions 'for institutional and third-party wealth clients across the globe' R1-S10. Listing titles equate it with sales R1-S04R1-S09R1-S14. It has a named head (Matt Gibson) R6-S19 and its own management, strategy and finance team that runs sales budgeting, fundraising projections and Salesforce data governance R1-S13R1-S14. A Goldman job advert lists the distribution channels as third party wealth, institutional, consultant, insurance and retirement R4-S09. CSG roles are advertised in London, Frankfurt, Paris, Dubai, Doha, Stockholm, Milan and outside EMEA R1-S05R1-S06R1-S07R1-S08R5-S16R5-S17.
Clients
Institutional investors (pension funds, endowments, foundations, sovereign wealth funds, insurers) and wealth intermediaries (private banks, wealth managers, advisers, platforms, multi-managers) R1-S20R1-S17.
Who decides on the client side
Varies by client type: see each team.
Investment needs
Varies by client type: see each team.
Products and strategies
Goldman lists 'fixed income, equities, liquid alternatives, private equity, private credit, infrastructure and real estate' R1-S10.
Distribution channels
Direct institutional coverage, consultant relations, third-party wealth intermediaries, insurance and retirement channels R4-S09.
Commercial process
Not one process. Institutional business is usually won through consultant-led tenders and long due diligence; wealth business through approval by a gatekeeper and then adoption by advisers. ≈ Supported inference
Specialist dependencies
Portfolio management, product specialists, marketing, compliance, operations, legal, performance measurement and risk, accounting and billing R1-S10R1-S01.
How the business model differs
CSG does not manage money. It is how the investment teams' strategies reach clients and how clients' needs reach the investment teams. Goldman does not disclose revenue, assets, flows or headcount for CSG or for any EMEA client team R2-S01.
Languages (job-description evidence only)
None at group level. Requirements are set team by team in job descriptions.
Recruitment evidence
The 2027 London Summer Analyst listing is filed under this group and contains no team-specific text R1-S02. The 2026 cycle used sub-track titles such as 'Client Solutions Group, UK Institutional Sales' (search result only) R1-S31. An applicant may apply to at most four business and location combinations a year R1-S02.
Unresolved questions
How London applicants are allocated to a team. Whether the Client Coverage Group sits inside CSG or beside it. Whether London teams use 'CSG' to mean the sales side of a team.

Client Coverage Group (CCG)

Function: service and retention of existing clients ✔ Verified T-ccg

A named Goldman group dedicated to retaining, expanding and supporting existing client relationships.

Talking points

  • Goldman's definition: client service, operational support and risk management, 'partnering closely with the sales team' R1-S11.
  • Published tasks include being main point of contact across portfolio management, trading, operations, legal and compliance, and coordinating account openings, restructures and terminations R1-S11.
  • Whether it sits inside or beside the Client Solutions Group in London is not published.

Questions to ask

  • Where does a new mandate pass from the person who won it to the person who looks after it?
  • What makes an onboarding go well from the client's point of view?
  • How much investment knowledge does a client coverage analyst need in the first year?

Watch-outs

  • Do not describe it as administrative: the published tasks need investment and operational knowledge.
  • Do not state how it reports relative to CSG.
Where the name comes from
Goldman Sachs's own name, defined in a Hong Kong advert for 'the global CCG team' R1-S11. London CCG titles were seen in search results only R1-S32. A 'CCG Analyst' title is used for The Hague R5-S14.
Kind of unit
Function: service and retention of existing clients
In one paragraph
The group 'dedicated to retaining, expanding and supporting existing client relationships' through client service, operational support and risk management. It is the nearest public match to what the former intern called the relationship-management side.
Former intern's account
'CCG (Client Coverage Group)' is the label for the relationship-management side of each team: keeps existing clients, analyst base pay £48k against £52k for sales, more seats, sits opposite sales and does much the same work at analyst level. ? Unverified account
What public sources establish
The name and definition are confirmed R1-S11. Official tasks: main point of contact for the client across portfolio management, trading, operations, legal and compliance; client queries; reporting; coordinating account openings, restructures and terminations; questionnaires and audit requests R1-S11. Whether CCG sits inside CSG, and whether every London team has a CCG side, is not established. ∅ Not publicly established The pay figures have no public support. ? Unverified account
Clients
Existing asset-management clients.
Who decides on the client side
The client's investment staff, operations staff and, for reporting, trustees or committees. ≈ Supported inference
Investment needs
Accurate reporting, quick and correct answers, smooth account changes, early warning of problems. ≈ Supported inference
Products and strategies
'Equities, fixed income, and alternative - through various distribution vehicles' R1-S11.
Distribution channels
Existing mandates and fund holdings.
Commercial process
Onboarding, periodic reviews, query handling, account life-cycle events (openings, restructures, terminations), due-diligence questionnaires and audit requests R1-S11.
Specialist dependencies
Strategic Client Services, Client Implementation, portfolio management, trading, operations, controllers, risk, legal, compliance, accounting and billing R1-S11.
How the business model differs
Protects and grows revenue that already exists. Retained revenue is not new revenue, and the official wording itself includes 'expanding', so the sales and relationship-management split is not clean.
Languages (job-description evidence only)

UK Institutional

Client segment within the UK grouping ≈ Supported inference T-uk-inst

Coverage of UK pension schemes, local government funds, endowments, charities and other institutions.

Talking points

  • UK defined benefit schemes are in aggregate surplus (133.7% funded on the PPF measure at end October 2026), so the question is endgame: insure or run on R3-S29.
  • The Pension Schemes Act 2026 eases surplus release and requires defined contribution defaults to reach £25bn by 2030 R3-S20.
  • LGPS pools fell from eight to six and funds must delegate implementation to them R3-S21.
  • Bank Rate rose to 4% on 5 November 2026 R3-S31.
  • In the 2026 cycle a London listing was titled 'Client Solutions Group, UK Institutional Sales' R1-S31.

Questions to ask

  • With schemes in surplus, what are trustees asking the team for that they were not asking three years ago?
  • How does the team work with investment consultants on a strategy that has not yet been rated?
  • How is coverage of LGPS pools different from covering a corporate scheme?

Watch-outs

  • Do not talk about deficits and recovery plans as the main UK pension story.
  • Do not assume every market change is a product opportunity.
  • Do not attribute any public mandate to this team: no source does.
Where the name comes from
The former intern's label. The 2026-cycle London listing was titled 'Client Solutions Group, UK Institutional Sales' (search result only; page expired) R1-S31. Senior public titles: 'head of the UK and Ireland institutional business', then 'co-head of EMEA Institutional Client Coverage' R6-S05R6-S02.
Kind of unit
Client segment within the UK grouping
In one paragraph
Coverage of UK institutional investors. The former intern describes pension funds as dominant, with endowments and foundations and sovereign wealth funds also covered. Public evidence of named UK clients is almost entirely defined benefit pension schemes reached through OCIO or fiduciary mandates, plus older Local Government Pension Scheme mandates.
Former intern's account
His own team, on the sales side. 'The main team' and the one most likely to be hiring. Pension funds dominate; his project was client research on endowments and foundations. ? Unverified account
What public sources establish
Goldman's EMEA institutional marketing defines the institutional business as pension funds, endowments, foundations, sovereign wealth funds and insurers R1-S20. The co-head of EMEA Institutional Client Coverage is quoted in the Shell OCIO announcement R3-S04R6-S02. A head of EMEA defined contribution within CSG was reported appointed in June 2025 (search result only) R6-S26. Public UK mandates outside OCIO are sparse: a Border to Coast emerging-markets equity sleeve (2023) and older local-authority mandates, some later terminated R7-S44R7-S46. No public source names a current head of a 'UK Institutional sales' team. ∅ Not publicly established
Clients
Defined benefit pension schemes, defined contribution master trusts and providers, Local Government Pension Scheme funds and pools, endowments, foundations and charities, and official institutions. Which of these the London team actually covers beyond pension schemes is not publicly established.
Who decides on the client side
Trustee boards and their investment sub-committees, the scheme's in-house investment staff or chief investment officer where one exists, the sponsoring employer on some decisions, and the investment consultant who advises the trustees and often runs the selection. For LGPS assets, increasingly the pool rather than the individual fund R3-S21.
Investment needs
For closed defined benefit schemes: paying pensions as they fall due, hedging interest-rate and inflation risk, generating cash flow, and reaching an endgame (insurer buyout or run-on). Aggregate funding is strong: the PPF 7800 funding ratio was 133.7% at end October 2026 R3-S29. For defined contribution: default-fund design under cost constraints and a push toward private markets R3-S20R3-S23.
Products and strategies
Liability-driven and cashflow-driven investment, credit and fixed income, multi-asset, equity, private markets, and OCIO where the client wants to delegate. Goldman cited about $300bn globally in LDI and CDI in September 2025 R3-S04.
Distribution channels
Direct coverage of schemes and coverage of the consultants who advise them.
Commercial process
Typically: a consultant or trustee identifies a need, a shortlist is drawn, managers answer a request for proposal and due-diligence questionnaire, a final presentation is held, then legal negotiation, onboarding and transition. Cycles are long and the consultant's view of the manager matters throughout. ≈ Supported inference
Specialist dependencies
Consultant relations; the UK LDI and CDI pensions solutions team in fixed income R3-S13; the OCIO and Multi-Asset Solutions teams; product specialists; request-for-proposal and marketing teams; legal and client implementation.
How the business model differs
Few clients, large tickets, slow decisions, formal governance and published advisers. Revenue arrives as a management fee on a mandate or fund holding, at institutional rates. The structural trend (schemes maturing, buying out with insurers, or delegating to OCIO) means the same client may shrink, leave to an insurer, or hand everything to one provider.

No UK institutional job description with a language requirement was read. ∅ Not publicly established

The 2026 London campus track carried the title 'UK Institutional Sales' (search result only) R1-S31. The former intern says it is the team most likely to be hiring. ? Unverified account
Unresolved questions
Current head of UK institutional sales. Whether the team covers endowments, charities, LGPS, DC and sovereign institutions in practice. Whether it is split into sales and relationship management as described.

UK Third Party Wealth (TPW)

Client segment within the UK grouping ✔ Verified T-uk-tpw

Sells Goldman funds, ETFs and alternatives to private banks, wealth managers, advisers and multi-managers, who invest for their own clients.

Talking points

  • Goldman's UK team is 'responsible for new business development' with private banks, wealth managers, financial advisers and multi-managers R1-S17.
  • The reported channel is 'third-party distributed': $714bn of long-term assets at 30 September 2026, globally R2-S02.
  • Thirteen active ETFs were launched in Europe in 2025, and the first evergreen ELTIF 2.0 fund in March 2026 R4-S17R4-S20.
  • The Consumer Duty's price-and-value outcome shapes how buyers judge a fund R4-S31.
  • The EMEA head left in April 2026 with no successor publicly named R6-S06.

Questions to ask

  • After a fund is approved by a wealth manager, what does the team do to help advisers actually use it?
  • How do conversations change when the product is an active ETF or a semi-liquid private-markets fund?
  • Which kind of UK intermediary is hardest to reach, and why?

Watch-outs

  • Do not call the end investor the client.
  • Do not treat an approved-list place as assets won.
  • Do not name an EMEA or UK and Ireland head.
Where the name comes from
Goldman Sachs's own name: a job advert refers to the 'UK Third Party Wealth (TPW) Sales Team' R1-S17; another, seen through an aggregator, to the 'UK & Ireland Third Party Wealth team' R4-S08. A press release names the 'EMEA Third Party Wealth Business' R4-S01.
Kind of unit
Client segment within the UK grouping
In one paragraph
Sells Goldman Sachs Asset Management funds, exchange-traded funds and alternatives to other firms that then use them for their own clients: private banks, wealth managers, financial advisers and multi-managers. The client is an intermediary, not the end investor.
Former intern's account
Sells Goldman funds to other wealth managers and private banks, who offer them to their own private clients. A friend interned on the relationship side. ? Unverified account His named example of a fund sold to another bank's private bank is not publicly established. ∅ Not publicly established
What public sources establish
The UK TPW Sales Team 'is responsible for new business development' with 'private banks, wealth managers, financial advisors and multi-managers' R1-S17. The UK & Ireland team's stated clients are private banks, wealth managers, fund of funds and independent financial advisers, offered traditional and alternative strategies as funds, ETFs or separately managed accounts R4-S08. A UK head of ETF distribution is named publicly R6-S31. The EMEA head from 2021 left in spring 2026 and no successor had been named in the sources found R4-S02. A formal split into sales and relationship management is not publicly established. ∅ Not publicly established
Clients
Private banks, wealth managers and discretionary fund managers, advice networks and independent financial advisers, multi-managers and funds of funds, and the platforms through which they deal.
Who decides on the client side
The fund selector or research team (the gatekeeper), the investment committee that approves the buy list or model portfolio, then individual portfolio managers and advisers who decide whether to use an approved fund. The end investor rarely chooses the fund directly.
Investment needs
Funds that fit a model portfolio or buy list, at a share-class price that passes value assessment, with reliable reporting and someone who can explain performance to advisers. Under the Consumer Duty the distributor must be able to show fair value for retail customers R4-S31.
Products and strategies
UCITS funds, active and index UCITS ETFs (active equity range from April 2025, further fixed-income ETFs in April 2026) R4-S01R4-S17, and evergreen private-markets funds and ELTIFs for eligible investors R4-S19R4-S20. No Goldman Sachs Long-Term Asset Fund or UK model portfolio service was identified. ∅ Not publicly established
Distribution channels
Gatekeeper approval, buy lists and model portfolios, fund platforms, and adviser-facing sales support.
Commercial process
Research and gatekeeper meetings, due diligence, approval, making the share class available on the platforms the firm uses, then adviser-by-adviser adoption and ongoing monitoring. Approval is permission to buy; it does not produce assets by itself. ≈ Supported inference
Specialist dependencies
Product specialists and client portfolio managers, the ETF distribution team, the Third Party Wealth Alternatives team R4-S11, marketing, and compliance for financial promotions.
How the business model differs
Many clients, smaller tickets, flows that build gradually and can reverse quickly. Revenue is the fund's management fee on assets that arrive only when advisers allocate. Buying power is concentrating in model portfolio services and consolidated wealth groups, so fewer decisions move more money.
Languages (job-description evidence only)
'Native English speaker is essential'; no other language required R1-S17.
Recruitment evidence
A UK TPW sales-support analyst advert (closed, undated) R1-S17 and an experienced-hire vice president advert seen through aggregators R4-S08. No campus evidence specific to this team.
Unresolved questions
Head of the UK & Ireland team. Successor to the EMEA head. Whether a separate relationship-management side exists.

OCIO / fiduciary management

Delegated-portfolio business within Multi-Asset Solutions (an investing group); global ✔ Verified T-ocio

Takes delegated responsibility for running all or part of an institution's portfolio; global, and part of Multi-Asset Solutions.

Talking points

  • $480bn of OCIO assets globally at 31 March 2026 R3-S09.
  • BAE Systems (about £23bn, 2023): competitive tender, Redington advising trustees, in-house team transferred R3-S02.
  • Shell (about $40bn, 2025): tender overseen by Isio, each fund deciding for itself R7-S08.
  • UK trustees must tender to at least three providers above 20% of assets R3-S24.
  • UK fiduciary fees fell about 27% in five years R8-S10.

Questions to ask

  • How do coverage teams and the fiduciary management team divide a prospect between them?
  • What do the largest schemes want from an outsourced provider that smaller ones do not?
  • How does the team handle the question of using Goldman's own funds inside a client's portfolio?

Watch-outs

  • Do not say OCIO is UK-only or that it always absorbs the client's team.
  • Do not name the second company from the starting account.
  • Do not quote an OCIO fee: none is public.
Where the name comes from
Goldman Sachs's own names: 'UK fiduciary management business', 'International OCIO and UK Fiduciary Management Team', 'Outsourced Chief Investment Officer business', 'EMEA OCIO Institutional Business' R3-S16R3-S01R3-S10R3-S11.
Kind of unit
Delegated-portfolio business within Multi-Asset Solutions (an investing group); global
In one paragraph
The business that takes delegated responsibility for running all or part of an institution's portfolio. It is global, not UK-only, and it sits in Multi-Asset Solutions, an investment group, not in a regional sales team. Client coverage works alongside it.
Former intern's account
One of three UK sub-teams. 'Pretty sure' it exists only in the UK team. Goldman can bring the client's in-house investment team into the firm. Recently won an award. 'Already over-hired'. ? Unverified account
What public sources establish
Not UK-only: Goldman reported $480bn of OCIO assets under supervision at 31 March 2026 and '$540+ billion' at 30 June 2026, with large US mandates and stated growth in the Netherlands, Germany and Switzerland R3-S09R8-S22R3-S10. ⇄ Conflicting evidence The fiduciary and OCIO teams sit within Multi-Asset Solutions R6-S18R1-S15, supported by a team of more than 300 people that was still growing in November 2025 R3-S07. UK history: a leader hired from a consultant in late 2021 R3-S16, Short Brothers (£1.6bn, 2022) R3-S15, BAE Systems (about £23bn, 2023, in-house team transferred) R3-S01, Shell entities (about $40bn across countries, 2025) R3-S04. Team transfer is reported only in some of the largest deals R7-S04. Fee rates are not disclosed. ∅ Not publicly established 'Over-hired' has no public support. ∅ Not publicly established
Clients
Corporate defined benefit pension schemes of all sizes; also a captive insurer and, in the United States, defined contribution plan advisory. Public UK names include the BAE Systems schemes, Shell UK pension entities, the Short Brothers Common Investment Fund, the Calor plan and the Northern Foods scheme (see the mandates register).
Who decides on the client side
Trustee boards, advised by an independent consultant or evaluator who runs the tender; the sponsoring employer where it bears the cost or its in-house team is affected. In the public UK cases the advisers were Redington, Isio, PwC and Barnett Waddingham R3-S02R3-S04R3-S15.
Investment needs
Governance capacity the trustees do not have in house, faster implementation, access to managers and private markets, integrated liability hedging, and a credible path to the scheme's endgame. Goldman's stated view is that sponsors increasingly ask whether running a pension scheme is core business R3-S07.
Products and strategies
Delegated management: strategy advice (in full fiduciary management), asset allocation, manager selection using internal and external managers, liability hedging and reporting R3-S15R3-S08.
Distribution channels
Competitive tender. UK trust-based schemes must invite bids from at least three unconnected providers before fiduciary managers run 20% or more of assets R3-S24.
Commercial process
Tender run by a third-party evaluator, scored proposals and standardised performance data, trustee decision, then a long transition of assets and, in a few very large cases, of people.
Specialist dependencies
Multi-Asset Solutions portfolio managers, the External Investing Group for manager selection, LDI and CDI specialists, transition management, legal and operations.
How the business model differs
The fee is for running the whole portfolio, usually a low rate on a large base, with underlying managers' fees charged separately. A public UK scheme report (scheme name withheld) shows an asset-based fiduciary fee on the return-seeking and cashflow-driven portfolios with the LDI manager invoicing separately R3-S17. In Goldman's filings, advisory and OCIO alternative accounts averaged 17 basis points in 2025, a firm-wide blend and not a mandate price R2-S01. One appointment can be very large, but each is rare, slow and re-tendered.
Languages (job-description evidence only)
None found for UK roles. The OCIO Insurance advert in The Hague states none in the text read R1-S15.
Recruitment evidence
Senior hiring continued in September 2025 R3-S07. A 'Client Relationship Manager (OCIO)' London title was seen in search results only R1-S33. No analyst-level campus evidence.
Unresolved questions
Goldman's UK-only OCIO assets and market rank. Its OCIO fee rates. Whether CSG summer analysts are placed with OCIO client coverage. Which of two 2026 awards the former intern saw.

Kind of unit
Function: coverage of investment consultants
In one paragraph
Covers the investment consulting firms that advise institutional investors, rate managers and run selections. It does not win mandates directly; it builds the consultants' understanding of the firm so that sales teams are considered.

Consultants' manager-research teams (who rate strategies) and field consultants (who advise specific clients).

Deep, consistent information on strategies, people and process; early notice of changes; access to portfolio managers.

No product of its own. It supports ratings across the firm's strategies.

Research meetings, data submissions to consultant databases, strategy reviews.

Maintain ratings, respond to research requests, brief consultants on changes, and pass intelligence on searches to the sales teams.

Portfolio managers and product specialists for research meetings; the request-for-proposal team for data.
