Liquidity Solutions

Product-line client business (global) ✔ Verified T-liq

Money market funds and short-duration strategies for clients' operating and strategic cash; a global product-line business.

Talking points

  • Liquidity products were $1,051bn of AUS at 30 September 2026, at about 14bp in 2025 R2-S02R2-S01.
  • Clients are financial institutions, hedge funds, institutions, corporates and wealth managers R5-S01.
  • The UK Money Market Funds Regulation is expected to be repealed and replaced by FCA rules R5-S32.
  • Liquidity saw $14bn of net outflows in Q3 2026 while long-term assets grew R2-S02.

Questions to ask

  • What do treasurers ask about first: yield, access or counterparty risk?
  • How are UK rule changes affecting sterling fund clients?
  • How does the team think about tokenised fund shares as collateral?

Watch-outs

  • Do not repeat that everyone speaks French: no public evidence.
  • Do not treat cash balances as sticky: they follow the client's cash needs.
Where the name comes from
Goldman Sachs's own name: 'Liquidity Solutions', with a 'Global Head, Liquidity Solutions Client Business' R5-S01; a London advert refers to an 'EMEA Liquidity Solutions' sales channel (search summary) R5-S09.
Kind of unit
Product-line client business (global)
In one paragraph
A client business organised around a product, not a region: money market funds and short-duration strategies for clients with operating or strategic cash. It has global leadership shared with Insurance Asset Management and an EMEA sales seat in London.
Former intern's account
A product line with its own team 'because the product is strong'. He did not know how it is split. He said an English-only candidate could go there, then said everyone in it speaks French. ? Unverified account
What public sources establish
'Our Liquidity Solutions team oversees $1.2+ trillion in money market and short-term assets' as at 30 September 2026 (global) R5-S01; firm-wide liquidity assets under supervision were $1,051bn at the same date R2-S02. Clients: 'financial institution, hedge fund, institutional, corporate, and wealth management clients' R5-S01. A London 'EMEA Liquidity Solutions Sales (UK Corporates)' seat covers UK corporate and insurance clients (search summary) R5-S09. No evidence that French is required: the one French-speaker advert found belongs to the French sales team. ∅ Not publicly established Its placement inside CSG is the former intern's account; public sources show its own global client-business head.
Clients
Corporate treasurers, financial institutions, hedge funds, private equity and venture firms, public institutions, insurers, pension schemes holding collateral, and wealth clients.
Who decides on the client side
Treasurers and treasury committees working to a board-approved investment policy; chief financial officers; collateral and operations managers at funds and schemes. ≈ Supported inference
Investment needs
Safety of capital first, same-day or next-day access second, yield third. Counterparty diversification, credit ratings and operational ease (portals, cut-off times) often decide the choice. ≈ Supported inference
Products and strategies
Money market funds: GS US$ Liquid Reserves and GS Euro Liquid Reserves (low-volatility net asset value), GS US$ Treasury Liquid Reserves (public debt constant net asset value); short-duration accounts and funds; fixed income ETFs; the Mosaic portal R5-S01.
Distribution channels
Direct treasury coverage and dealing portals.
Commercial process
Onboarding and counterparty approval, then daily subscriptions and redemptions with no sales event attached. The 'mandate' is permission to place cash; the balance moves every day.
Specialist dependencies
Money market portfolio managers and credit analysts; operations and portal support.
How the business model differs
Thin fee on a very large, very mobile balance. The investor earns the portfolio yield net of the fund charge; the manager earns that charge on average balances. Firm-wide, liquidity products earned an average 14 basis points in 2025 R2-S01. Balances can leave in a day for reasons unrelated to service.

Experienced-hire London postings only; no student-programme evidence specific to liquidity.

Insurance

Client vertical (global) ✔ Verified T-ins

Manages insurers' own balance-sheet assets and advises on capital-efficient strategy; a global client vertical.

Talking points

The insurer's chief investment officer and chief financial officer, with actuarial, risk and capital-management teams involved in every decision.
Investment needs
Assets that match liabilities, earn spread, and use regulatory capital efficiently. The rulebook is changing: amended EU Solvency II rules apply from 30 January 2027 R5-S39; the UK regulator has consulted on faster access to matching-adjustment benefits R5-S38. In Goldman's 2026 survey of 434 insurance investment and finance chiefs, 62% planned to increase private-asset allocations R5-S03.

Investment-grade fixed income, private credit and asset-backed finance, and full or partial outsourcing of the general account R5-S02.

Direct coverage by insurance specialists.

Solution design around the insurer's balance sheet, with constraints on capital charges, accounting treatment, book yield and realised gains written into guidelines.
Specialist dependencies
Insurance strategists, the OCIO Insurance team within Multi-Asset Solutions R1-S15, fixed income and private credit teams.
How the business model differs
Large, sticky, low-fee fixed-income mandates where the manager is judged on yield, capital use and accounting outcomes as much as on return against an index.

Facts

Facts and figures worth knowing

A correct number, with its date and what it does not show, is worth more than a confident guess.

Goldman scale

Total assets under supervision (AUS)$4,097bn30 Sep 2026

Everything Goldman manages or advises on for a fee, across asset management and wealth management.

Say it: Goldman reported about $4.1 trillion of assets under supervision at the end of September 2026, which includes wealth management and liquidity assets, so it is wider than the asset management client business I am applying to.

It does not show: It is a firm-wide figure. It is not the Client Solutions Group's assets and it includes $1,051bn of liquidity products.

✔ Verified R2-S02 R2-S03

AUS growth in nine months$3,606bn → $4,097bn31 Dec 2025 to 30 Sep 2026

Supervised assets grew by about $491bn in nine months, through inflows, markets and acquisitions.

Say it: Supervised assets rose from about $3.6 trillion to $4.1 trillion in nine months, and part of that came from markets and acquisitions, not only client decisions.

It does not show: Growth mixes net inflows, market movement and acquired assets such as the $31bn from Innovator.

✔ Verified R2-S01 R2-S02

AWM share of firm net revenues28.6%FY2025

The Asset & Wealth Management segment produced $16,679m of $58,283m firm net revenues.

Say it: Asset & Wealth Management was about 29% of Goldman's net revenues in 2025; the asset management business on its own was closer to 12%.

It does not show: 'About 30%' describes the whole segment including wealth management, not asset management alone and not CSG.

✔ Verified R2-S01

Asset management share of firm net revenues11.6%FY2025

The 'Asset management' business inside AWM earned $6,784m in 2025.

Say it: On Goldman's own segment split, asset management was about $6.8bn of revenue in 2025, under 12% of the firm.

It does not show: Includes incentive fees and investment gains, which are not recurring client fees.

✔ Verified R2-S01

AWM management and other fees$11,538mFY2025

The recurring fee line of the segment: $4,990m from asset management and $6,548m from wealth management.

Say it: Management and other fees were about $11.5bn in 2025, and that recurring line is what the firm points to when it talks about durable revenue.

It does not show: Recurring is not guaranteed: it moves with markets, flows and fee rates.

✔ Verified R2-S01

AWM pre-tax margin and target25% (target about 30%)FY2025; target set in 2026

The segment kept 25 cents of pre-tax profit per dollar of revenue and aims for about 30% within three to five years.

Say it: Goldman has set a public target of roughly a 30% pre-tax margin for Asset & Wealth Management, up from 25% in 2025.

It does not show: A segment target. It says nothing about the profitability of any client team.

✔ Verified R2-S01 R2-S02

Q3 2026 AWM net revenues$5,051mQ3 2026

The latest quarter before the cutoff, 14% above the same quarter a year earlier.

Say it: In the third quarter of 2026 the segment's revenue was about $5.1bn, with management and other fees of about $3.6bn.

It does not show: One quarter; incentive fees of $587m made it unusually strong.

✔ Verified R2-S03 R2-S02

Alternative AUS and 2030 target$491bn (target $750bn)30 Sep 2026; target by end-2030

Supervised alternative assets, and the public growth target.

Say it: Alternatives were $491bn of supervised assets in September 2026, against a stated target of $750bn by the end of 2030.

It does not show: Goldman's marketing figure of 'over $706bn in total alternative assets' uses a wider definition; do not mix the two.

✔ Verified R2-S02

EMEA share of AUS$799bn (19.5%)30 Sep 2026

The only regional cut Goldman publishes.

Say it: Goldman discloses about $800bn of supervised assets for EMEA; it does not publish a UK figure or a split by client channel within the region.

? Unverified account R1-S41

Specific findings from the research. Each says what a quick read gets wrong and how to use it.

The role ✔ Verified

The listing tells you almost nothing

The 2027 London listing carries only programme-wide and division-wide wording: no duties, team, language, deadline or salary R1-S02. On 14 November 2026 it was no longer among the 194 live campus listings, while Frankfurt, Paris, Dubai, Doha and Tokyo CSG listings were R1-S03.

What a quick read gets wrong: Candidates quote the listing as if it described the job; it describes the firm.

Use it: Build your picture of the work from experienced-hire advertisements and say so. Ask: 'The listing is general by design. What does a summer analyst on your team produce in a typical week?'

R1-S02 R1-S03 EDGE-01

The role ✔ Verified

Goldman's own definition of CSG

Goldman describes the Client Solutions Group as the team that develops client relationships and delivers investment solutions for institutional and third-party wealth clients worldwide, across public and private asset classes R1-S10. Its campus titles pair the name with 'Sales' R1-S04.

What a quick read gets wrong: People explain CSG from hearsay when a one-sentence official description exists.

Use it: Open 'what does CSG do?' with Goldman's two client types (institutional and third-party wealth) and two asset worlds (public and private), then add what you understand the junior work to be.

R1-S10 R1-S04 EDGE-02

The role ✔ Verified

The real junior task list is public

A London CSG sales-support advertisement lists the work: prepare and follow up client and prospect meetings, answer day-to-day client queries, work with product specialists, marketing, compliance and operations, and support the country head with market-intelligence and business-development presentations R1-S01.

What a quick read gets wrong: 'I'd support the team' is vague; the actual tasks are written down.

Use it: When asked what you would do as an analyst, name these tasks and connect one to a client outcome, for example a meeting note that makes sure every promise from the last meeting is kept.

R1-S01 EDGE-03

The role ✔ Verified

CSG has its own strategy and data team

The Global Client Solutions Group has a management and strategy team that runs sales budgeting, fundraising projections, weekly business summaries and Salesforce data governance R1-S13R1-S14.

What a quick read gets wrong: Coverage is imagined as conversations only; it is also a measured pipeline.

Use it: Show you understand that call notes and pipeline entries are how a relationship becomes the firm's knowledge. Ask how the team keeps its client records useful.

R1-S13 R1-S14 EDGE-04

Structure ✔ Verified

It is a matrix, mostly outside London

Job advertisements show country teams crossed with channel: Germany and Austria from Frankfurt in German, France from Paris in French, Benelux needing native Dutch even when the seat is in London R1-S05R1-S06R1-S01.

What a quick read gets wrong: A London intern's list of teams looks complete because it lists what is visible from London.

Use it: Describe the structure as geography by client segment by function, and say which parts you know from published advertisements and which from one person's account.

R1-S05 R1-S06 R1-S01 EDGE-05

Structure ✔ Verified

Consultant Relations is a named team

Goldman describes Consultant Relations as the team that works with the investment consultants who advise institutional investors; it works with regional institutional sales teams and builds a pipeline for them R1-S21.

What a quick read gets wrong: The consultant is treated as background when it is often the gatekeeper.

Use it: In any institutional answer, name the consultant's role: rating the strategy, running the tender, advising the trustees.

R1-S21 EDGE-06

Structure ✔ Verified

Distribution channels, in Goldman's words

One Goldman advertisement lists the distribution channels as third party wealth, institutional, consultant, insurance and retirement R4-S09.

What a quick read gets wrong: Candidates divide the world into 'institutional and retail'.

Use it: Use the five-channel list to show you know insurance and retirement are treated as channels in their own right.

R4-S09 EDGE-07

UK Institutional ✔ Verified

The UK endgame question has changed

UK defined benefit schemes had an aggregate funding ratio of 133.7% and a £275.4bn surplus on the PPF measure at end October 2026 R3-S29, and the Pension Schemes Act 2026 makes surplus release easier, with regulations expected in 2027 R3-S20.

What a quick read gets wrong: Preparation written a few years ago still talks about deficits and repair plans.

Use it: Frame UK DB conversations as a choice between insuring the scheme and running it on. A good client question: 'Has the surplus changed how your trustees and sponsor think about buyout versus run-on?'

R3-S29 R3-S20 EDGE-08

UK Institutional ✔ Verified

Rates just moved the other way

Bank Rate was raised to 4% on 5 November 2026, the first increase since August 2023, with the 10-year gilt near 5.15% R3-S31.

What a quick read gets wrong: Anyone working from drafts written earlier in 2026 is still assuming cuts.

Use it: State the date and the direction, then the consequence you are sure of: liability values and hedging collateral move with gilt yields, so pension clients are affected directly.

R3-S31 R8-S49 EDGE-09

UK Institutional ✔ Verified

The buyer is consolidating

LGPS pools fell from eight to six in 2026 and funds must now delegate implementation to their pool R3-S21; defined contribution defaults must reach £25bn by 2030 under the 2026 Act R3-S20.

What a quick read gets wrong: People list client types without noticing there are fewer, larger decision-makers each year.

Use it: Say what follows for coverage: fewer relationships, each worth more, each with a professional investment team that expects institutional-quality answers.

R3-S21 R3-S20 EDGE-10

UK Institutional ✔ Verified

Kipling's title tells you the structure

Goldman's September 2025 announcement titles Chloe Kipling 'co-head of EMEA Institutional Client Coverage'; she was previously head of the UK and Ireland institutional business R6-S02R6-S05. Who leads UK institutional coverage now is not publicly established.

What a quick read gets wrong: Candidates guess at names or use an old title.

Use it: Use the exact title with its date if you mention her, and do not name a UK head. It is reasonable to ask how UK coverage fits within the EMEA institutional business.

R6-S02 R6-S05 EDGE-11

OCIO ⇄ Conflicting evidence

OCIO is global and sits in an investing group

Goldman reported $480bn of OCIO assets at 31 March 2026 R3-S09, and its OCIO teams sit within Multi-Asset Solutions, an investing group, working alongside sales and relationship professionals R1-S15R6-S11.

What a quick read gets wrong: The starting account placed OCIO as a third UK sales team.

Use it: Describe OCIO as an investment business that coverage teams work with. Ask: 'How do UK institutional coverage and the fiduciary management team divide a prospect between them?'

R3-S09 R1-S15 R6-S11 EDGE-12

OCIO ✔ Verified

How the BAE mandate was actually won

The BAE Systems trustees ran a competitive tender, advised by Redington, with Travers Smith as lawyers and PwC advising the sponsor; the schemes' in-house team moved to Goldman R3-S02. In the year to March 2026 the trustee had Gallagher as a separate investment adviser overseeing the arrangement R7-S06.

What a quick read gets wrong: People cite the £23bn and stop.

Use it: Use it to show how a large mandate is decided: tender, adviser, lawyers, sponsor, then continuing independent oversight. Trust did not replace process.

R3-S02 R7-S06 EDGE-13

OCIO ≈ Supported inference

Team transfer is the exception

In-house teams moved in the largest deals (BAE Systems, UPS with 22 people) R7-S21, but nothing of the kind is reported for Short Brothers (£1.6bn) or Calor (£240m), which were ordinary tendered appointments R7-S15R7-S16.

What a quick read gets wrong: The starting account generalised from the most famous deal.

Use it: Say 'in some of the largest mandates the client's team has joined', never 'OCIO means absorbing the team'.

R7-S21 R7-S15 R7-S16 EDGE-14

OCIO ✔ Verified

Two awards fit, and one loss

Goldman won the fiduciary management / OCIO category at the European Pensions Awards (2 July 2026) and the Irish Pensions Awards (4 November 2026) R3-S10R3-S11. It did not win Fiduciary Manager of the Year at the 2026 UK Pensions Awards, which went to Van Lanschot Kempen R3-S14.

What a quick read gets wrong: Naming 'the OCIO award' as a single known fact.

Use it: If awards come up, name the body and date, and add that an award shows a judging panel's view of a submission. It is not evidence of client outcomes.

R3-S10 R3-S11 R3-S14 EDGE-15

OCIO ✔ Verified

Goldman's own account of why big schemes outsource

A Goldman executive said in November 2025 that OCIO has moved from small schemes to large ones with in-house teams, because sponsors question whether running pensions is core business, maturing schemes shift to cashflow and hedging strategies, and chief investment officers are hard to replace R3-S07.

What a quick read gets wrong: Explaining OCIO only as 'small schemes lack resources'.

Use it: Give the three drivers and note they are the provider's view; a trustee might add cost and governance time.

R3-S07 EDGE-16

OCIO ✔ Verified

The filings show OCIO is a low-rate scale business

In 2025 advisory and OCIO alternative accounts averaged $112bn and earned 17 basis points, against 77 on funds and discretionary accounts R2-S01. Goldman discloses no standalone OCIO revenue or fee.

What a quick read gets wrong: Assuming a huge mandate means a huge fee rate.

Use it: Explain that an OCIO provider is paid a low rate on a large base for delegated responsibility, and that the actual fee on any mandate is not public.

R2-S01 EDGE-17

Third Party Wealth ✔ Verified

Third Party Wealth is the official name

A Goldman press release of 28 April 2025 names an 'EMEA Third Party Wealth Business' R4-S01; in the filings the same channel is 'Third-party distributed', $714bn at 30 September 2026 R2-S02.

What a quick read gets wrong: Mixing up team name and reporting line, or calling it 'retail'.

Use it: Use 'Third Party Wealth' for the team and 'third-party distributed' for the reported channel.

R4-S01 R2-S02 EDGE-18

Third Party Wealth ✔ Verified

The EMEA head left in April 2026

Hilary Lopez, head of the EMEA third party wealth business since 2021, was reported on 21 April 2026 to be leaving for a competitor, and no successor had been publicly named by the cutoff R6-S06. Global co-heads Bryon Lake and Padideh Raphael were named that month R6-S08.

What a quick read gets wrong: Quoting a leader from an old article.

Use it: Do not name an EMEA head. If leadership comes up, refer to the global co-heads with the April 2026 date.

R6-S06 R6-S08 EDGE-19

Third Party Wealth ✔ Verified

Who the UK team sells to

Goldman's UK Third Party Wealth sales team is 'responsible for new business development' with private banks, wealth managers, financial advisers and multi-managers R1-S17, and that advertisement asked for a native English speaker and no other language.

What a quick read gets wrong: Thinking the end investor is the client.

Use it: Describe the chain: Goldman sells to a professional buyer who decides for many end clients. Being approved is permission to buy; assets come adviser by adviser.

R1-S17 EDGE-20

Third Party Wealth ✔ Verified

The product push is wrappers and private markets

Goldman launched 13 active ETFs in Europe in 2025 R4-S17 and in March 2026 its first evergreen fund under the revised ELTIF rules, within a G-Series of evergreen private-markets funds R4-S20. No Goldman UK Long-Term Asset Fund or UK model portfolio service was found.

What a quick read gets wrong: Assuming the wealth team sells the same funds as ten years ago.

Use it: Ask how the UK team's conversations change when the product is an active ETF or a semi-liquid private-markets fund, and what suitability questions that raises.

R4-S17 R4-S20 EDGE-21

Third Party Wealth ✔ Verified

Private Wealth as a buyer is only partly supported

Goldman Private Wealth Management publicly describes an open-architecture alternatives platform that includes external managers R4-S27. The specific examples in the starting account are not publicly established.

What a quick read gets wrong: Repeating a named example as fact.

Use it: Say 'Goldman's private wealth business uses external managers on its alternatives platform' and leave it there.

R4-S27 EDGE-22

Liquidity ✔ Verified

A product business with global leadership

Liquidity Solutions has global heads, not regional ones, and serves financial institutions, hedge funds, institutions, corporates and wealth managers R5-S01R5-S04. No public evidence supports a French-language requirement R5-S09.

What a quick read gets wrong: Treating it as another regional sales team.

Use it: Explain the client's problem: cash they may need tomorrow, where safety and access matter more than yield.

R5-S01 R5-S09 EDGE-23

Liquidity ✔ Verified

The rules for sterling money funds are being rewritten

The FCA said on 8 June 2026 that the Government expects to repeal the UK Money Market Funds Regulation by end-2026, with new liquidity guidance of 40% weekly liquid assets for stable-value funds R5-S32. Around 90% of sterling fund assets sit in EU-domiciled funds sold under temporary permissions R5-S34.

What a quick read gets wrong: Not knowing that the funds UK treasurers use are mostly domiciled abroad.

Use it: A client question: 'How are you thinking about the UK rule changes and the equivalence decision for your sterling liquidity funds?'

R5-S32 R5-S34 EDGE-24

Liquidity ✔ Verified

Cash left while long-term money arrived

In Q3 2026 liquidity products had net outflows of $14bn while long-term assets took in $97bn R2-S02.

What a quick read gets wrong: Assuming all assets move together.

Use it: Use it to explain that liquidity balances follow clients' cash needs and rate expectations, so the measure that matters is average balance.

R2-S02 EDGE-25

Insurance ✔ Verified

Insurance is a global vertical

Goldman manages $651bn of insurers' general-account assets R5-S02 and offers partial to full outsourcing plus advice on asset-liability management and capital-efficient strategies R5-S02. Advertisements show London and Frankfurt seats.

What a quick read gets wrong: Filing insurance under 'institutional' with pensions.

Use it: Explain the difference: an insurer is constrained by regulatory capital and accounting, so the same bond can be attractive to a pension fund and expensive for an insurer.

R5-S02 EDGE-26

Insurance ✔ Verified

What 434 insurance investment heads said

Goldman's 15th annual insurance survey (25 March 2026) polled 434 chief investment and finance officers; 62% plan to raise private-asset allocations, with asset-backed finance showing the highest net intended increase R5-S03.

What a quick read gets wrong: Not knowing Goldman publishes its clients' intentions every year.

Use it: Cite the survey as Goldman's own evidence of client demand, then add the limit: stated intentions are not allocations.

R5-S03 EDGE-27

Insurance ✔ Verified

Two rule changes with dates

Amended EU Solvency II rules apply from 30 January 2027 R5-S39; in the UK the regulator consulted on letting insurers add assets to matching-adjustment portfolios before approval, within limits R5-S38.

What a quick read gets wrong: Speaking about 'Solvency II' as static.

Use it: Ask an insurance-facing interviewer which rule change is doing most to alter clients' asset choices.

R5-S39 R5-S38 EDGE-28

Middle East ✔ Verified

Offices opened faster than leadership settled

Goldman opened a Kuwait office in October 2025 and a Riyadh regional headquarters in December 2025 R5-S28R5-S29R5-S30. The head of the Middle East client business left in September 2025, a co-head had stepped down in late 2024, and the current head is not publicly established R6-S14R6-S15.

What a quick read gets wrong: Naming a regional head from an old article.

Use it: Talk about the client base and the office build-out. Do not name a head.

R5-S28 R5-S29 R5-S30 R6-S14 R6-S15 EDGE-29

Middle East ✔ Verified

Sovereign deals are partnerships, read the verbs

Mubadala signed a $1bn separately managed account for Asia Pacific private credit R5-S04; PIF signed a non-binding memorandum with no amount R7-S26; the Qatar Investment Authority 'will target' $25bn of commitments, which one headline reported as 'commits' R7-S28.

What a quick read gets wrong: Adding the headline numbers together.

Use it: Distinguish a funded account, a memorandum and a target. That distinction is itself commercial awareness.

R5-S04 R7-S26 R7-S28 EDGE-30

Do not treat a reported £4k difference as evidence of prestige or role quality.
Sales has fewer seats and is harder to get; relationship management has more.∅ Not publicly establishedNo headcount by function is published. In the public people sample, explicitly sales-titled people outnumber explicitly relationship-titled people, but that reflects which appointments get announced, not staffing R6-S17 R6-S27. R6-S17 R6-S27Do not use. It should not decide which side you say you prefer.
The two sides sit opposite each other, work the same hours and operate as one team; at analyst level the work is basically the same.? Unverified accountNothing public describes seating or hours. It is consistent with the BeNeLux advertisement, where one junior role supports both new business and existing relationships R1-S01. R1-S01Reasonable background for your own expectations. If you refer to it, say a former intern described it that way.
Sales is seen as more prestigious; many relationship people want to move across; internal moves are bureaucratic.? Unverified accountOne person's impression of culture. Nothing public supports or contradicts it. Do not use. Expressing a preference because one side is "more prestigious" would be a weak reason in any case.
A managing director posted about the OCIO award; a partner told him assessment centres are moving in person and will ask more about AI.∅ Not publicly establishedNeither person could be identified from public sources and no identity is suggested here. The Partner Class of 2026 lists Asset & Wealth Management partners in London but does not say which business each works in R1-S27. R1-S27Do not try to name either person.
The first stage is a recorded video interview.✔ VerifiedGoldman's own steps page: "you will be asked to participate in a video interview, which will take approximately 30 minutes to complete", referred to as the HireVue interview R1-S23. R1-S23Prepare for a recorded format.
An associate on the team reviews the recorded video, sometimes at double speed.? Unverified accountNothing public says who reviews recordings or how. The only sensible lesson is general: make the first sentences of an answer clear. Build no tactic on it.
What you say in the recorded interview decides which team you are "drafted" to: region, client type, and sales or relationship management.? Unverified accountThe mechanism is not published. The 2027 London listing names no sub-track while Frankfurt, Paris and Dubai listings do R1-S05 R1-S06 R1-S07, so some allocation must happen after applying, but how is unknown. R1-S05 R1-S06 R1-S07Do not plant keywords to steer allocation. Talk about the client segments that actually interest you and say why.
The assessment centre is three back-to-back interviews with the team and no group task: analyst and associate together, then a vice president or similar, then the managing director who runs the team.? Unverified accountOfficially the final round ("Superday") is "between two and five interviews for campus hires, depending on the division" with "a cross-section of people whom you could possibly work with" R1-S23. Three interviews fits inside that range. The number, order, interviewers and absence of a group task are his experience of one team in one year. "Vice president or similar" fits the fact that Executive Director is the same level as Vice President in EMEA R1-S26. R1-S23 R1-S26Prepare for several one-to-one or two-to-one interviews with team members at different levels; do not rely on the exact sequence.
Assessment centres are now in person and will ask more about AI.∅ Not publicly establishedOfficial pages read are silent on both. Press coverage was not searched because the search allowance ran out, so this is "not investigated" beyond official sources. Recruiters' published guidance says questions are "situational or behavioral" and that they weigh "attitude and aptitude" R1-S24. R1-S24Be ready for either format, and have a considered view on how AI changes client work (see the commercial-awareness chapter). Confirm the format with your recruiter.
Each team hires one analyst per open seat, so a candidate competes only against others drafted to the same team.? Unverified accountNothing public describes seat numbers or how candidates are compared. No hiring probability can be inferred. Do not use.
Each team runs its own hiring timeline, so offers on one team say nothing about another.≈ Supported inferenceGoldman says it evaluates applications throughout the season and that candidates "may hear back regarding different roles at different times" R1-S23. That is about roles, not teams within one listing, so it is consistent with the claim without confirming it. R1-S23Useful for managing your own expectations only.
Asset management is about 30% of Goldman's revenue and valued for stable fee income.⇄ Conflicting evidenceThe figure matches the Asset & Wealth Management segment, which was 28.6% of firmwide net revenues in 2025. The Asset Management business on its own was 11.6% R2-S01. Management and other fees were $11,538m, 69% of the segment, which is the fee income the "stable" point refers to. Fees recur while clients stay and markets hold; they are not guaranteed. Nothing is disclosed for the Client Solutions Group. R2-S01Say "Asset & Wealth Management was about 29% of 2025 net revenues" and name the segment. Do not say asset management alone is 30%.
Goldman recently restricted staff use of Claude Code.≈ Supported inferenceBloomberg reported on 2 November 2026 that Goldman restricted traders and bankers from some AI tools; outlets relaying it say internal guidance limited Claude Code and GitHub's AI coding tools to engineers R2-S10 R2-S08 R2-S09. The Bloomberg article itself could not be read. It is one report, it concerns coding tools for non-engineers, it is not a firm-wide ban on AI, and nothing says how it applies to asset-management client staff. A separate April 2026 report concerned Hong Kong bankers' access to one model R2-S12. R2-S10 R2-S08 R2-S09 R2-S12If AI comes up, describe it accurately as a reported restriction of coding tools to engineers, citing the press. Do not call it a ban on AI.
Details about the former intern's own background, his friend's internship and a candidate he knows.? Unverified accountNot researched, by design. These are private individuals and nothing about them is needed to understand the business. Not relevant. Do not name him or rely on "someone told me" as support for any claim.
An English-only UK candidate is most likely to be sent to the UK team, with the Middle East possible if the answers mention the Middle East.? Unverified accountNo public information on allocation. See IC-36. Do not mention a region you have no real interest in to influence allocation. If the Gulf's sovereign investors do interest you, say why in terms of the clients.

Practise

Practise

Answer aloud first. Then open the reasoning.

The six criteria used here are a proposed practice framework written for this project. Goldman Sachs has not published scoring criteria for this programme, and nobody outside the firm knows what questions will be asked. The questions below are plausible practice material, not predictions. The suggested answers show a way of reasoning; they are not scripts to memorise, and any sentence in square brackets is a slot only you can fill from your own experience.

Why Goldman Sachs?

Why Goldman Sachs IQ-01

Underlying argument
A firm-specific answer has to name a capability, show the evidence, and say why that capability changes the work a junior person in client coverage would do. Three facts carry the argument. First, breadth by channel: long-term assets under supervision at 30 September 2026 were $1,245bn institutional, $1,087bn wealth management and $714bn third-party distributed, so the client business serves both institutions and intermediaries at scale R2-S02. Second, breadth by asset class: $1,405bn fixed income, $1,150bn equity, $491bn alternatives and $1,051bn liquidity R2-S02, which means a client conversation is less likely to be forced toward one product. Third, delegated mandates: Goldman reported $480bn of OCIO assets at 31 March 2026 R3-S09 and was publicly appointed to about £23bn for the BAE Systems schemes after a competitive tender R3-S01. Layer B · interpretation The interpretation is that a coverage analyst here would see whole-portfolio problems, not only single-fund sales. That is an inference from scale, not a disclosed description of the London team's work. The honest limit: the official London listing contains no team-specific duties R1-S02, and breadth is something BlackRock can also claim, so the answer must say why breadth matters to me, not that it is unique.

Depends on: Verified: AUS by channel and asset class (Q3 2026 10-Q); OCIO scale; the BAE Systems appointment. Personal: one honest reason I want to learn across client types rather than specialise early. If I have no such reason, this answer is borrowed. R2-S02 R3-S09 R3-S01 R1-S02 R8-S26

A weak answer, and why it is weak
Goldman Sachs is the most prestigious firm on the street, with a global platform, a strong culture of excellence and the best people. I have always wanted to work here and I know I would learn from the best.

Every clause could be said about any large firm by any candidate. 'Prestigious', 'global platform' and 'best people' are not capabilities, carry no evidence and say nothing about asset management or client coverage. 'I have always wanted to' is a claim nobody can check. It also fails the first follow-up: what would be different at a competitor?

About 30 seconds

Two things, both about the work. The asset management business serves institutions and wealth intermediaries at scale, and it runs public markets, alternatives, liquidity and whole-portfolio OCIO mandates under one roof. For someone starting in client coverage, that should mean the client's problem sets the conversation instead of one product. I can't claim that is unique to Goldman. I can say it is the setting I think I would learn most in, and I'd like to test that.

About 60 to 90 seconds

I'd separate what I can evidence from what I'm inferring. What I can evidence: at the end of September the firm supervised about four trillion dollars, and the long-term part was split fairly evenly between institutional clients, wealth management and third-party distribution. It also has a large delegated business. It was reporting around 480 billion dollars of OCIO assets earlier this year, and the BAE Systems pension schemes appointed it to roughly 23 billion pounds after a competitive tender. What I'm inferring is what that means for a junior person: that a coverage team here deals with whole-portfolio questions, for example a pension scheme deciding how much to delegate, as well as single-strategy searches. I think that is where I would learn fastest, because you have to understand the client's liabilities and governance before any product is relevant. I should be honest about the limit. The published role description doesn't say what the London team does day to day, and other large managers have breadth too. So my reason isn't that Goldman is the only place this exists. It's that the evidence I can find suggests this is a place where the client problem comes first, and that is what I want to be trained in.

Harder follow-ups
  1. BlackRock has more assets and a large fiduciary business too. Why not there?
    Why it is asked: Whether the answer survives 'a competitor could say that too'.
    How to think about it: Concede the overlap: BlackRock states over $400bn of OCIO and fiduciary assets R8-S26. Do not claim uniqueness. Move to the client problem: for which problems is each firm stronger? Passive scale favours BlackRock; then say what you can evidence about Goldman (alternatives fundraising, OCIO team transfers) and that you applied where you could find evidence the work matches what you want to learn.
  2. Would you still want this job if it were at a firm nobody had heard of?
    Why it is asked: Separates interest in the work from interest in the name.
    How to think about it: Answer the counterfactual honestly. If the work is the draw, most of the appeal survives and you can say what would be lost concretely (range of client types, training). If little survives, the motive is the brand, and it is better to discover that now. See the why-tree WT-gs.
  3. What is the weakest part of your reason for choosing us?
    Why it is asked: Self-awareness and honesty under pressure.
    How to think about it: Name it: you are inferring the junior experience from firm-level figures. Say what would confirm or contradict it (what analysts on the team actually spend time on), and ask.

Why Goldman Sachs rather than a competitor with similar products?

Why Goldman Sachs IQ-02

Underlying argument
Start by conceding the premise: at product level, most large managers overlap. Then compare by client problem instead of by league table. For a UK defined benefit scheme considering full delegation, the relevant evidence is delegated-mandate experience: Goldman's publicly announced BAE Systems appointment of about £23bn, where the in-house team transferred R3-S01, and the roughly $40bn Shell OCIO and advisory mandate announced in September 2025 after a tender overseen by Isio R3-S04. For a wealth intermediary the evidence is different: a named Third Party Wealth business and European active ETFs launched from 2025 R4-S01. Layer B · interpretation The defensible claim is narrow: for some client problems there is public evidence that clients running competitive processes chose Goldman. The limits must be said aloud: wins do not show the losing bids were worse, BlackRock won Shell's Dutch fund in 2024 R7-S09, and a client that mainly wants low-cost index exposure is likely better served elsewhere.

Depends on: Verified: BAE Systems and Shell appointments and how they were awarded; the Third Party Wealth name and ETF launches. A clear statement of where a competitor is stronger. No personal story is needed, but a personal reason for preferring problem-led work helps. R3-S01 R3-S04 R4-S01 R7-S09 R7-S06

A weak answer, and why it is weak
Goldman's products are simply better, and its reputation means clients trust it more than competitors. The One Goldman Sachs approach gives clients access to the whole firm, which nobody else can match.

It asserts superiority with no evidence, repeats a slogan, and claims something 'nobody else can match' that the interviewer knows several firms would dispute. It also ignores the question's premise that the products are similar.

About 30 seconds

I'd accept the premise: product by product, the big managers overlap a lot. So I'd compare by client problem. For a large pension scheme thinking about delegating its whole portfolio, there's public evidence that trustees who ran competitive tenders chose Goldman, BAE Systems and Shell being the clearest. That doesn't make Goldman right for everyone. A client who mainly wants cheap index exposure probably belongs elsewhere, and I think saying so is part of the job.

About 60 to 90 seconds

I don't think I can honestly argue the products are better across the board, so I wouldn't try. What I'd say is that 'similar products' hides differences in which client problems a firm has actually been trusted with. Take a UK pension scheme deciding whether to hand over day-to-day investment decisions. Trustees have to run a competitive tender for that. In 2023 the BAE Systems trustees appointed Goldman to about 23 billion pounds, and their in-house investment team moved across. In 2025 Shell's pension entities appointed it to around 40 billion dollars after a consultant-run process. Those are decisions by well-advised clients with alternatives available, and they're the best public evidence I have. There are two limits. First, a win doesn't prove the other bidders were worse, and BlackRock won Shell's Dutch fund the year before. Second, the same evidence says nothing about, say, passive equity, where scale elsewhere is far larger. So my answer is that I'd rather start somewhere with a demonstrated record on the whole-portfolio problems I find most interesting, and be clear with clients about the problems where another firm fits better.

Harder follow-ups
  1. Those are press releases. What do they actually prove?
    Why it is asked: Whether you know the limits of your own evidence.
    How to think about it: They prove an appointment happened, its approximate size and who advised. They do not prove performance, fees, or that the mandate is profitable. Say that, and note that the BAE scheme's own later report still names Goldman as OCIO R7-S06.
  2. Name a client you would tell to go to a competitor.
    Why it is asked: Judgement and honesty when it costs the firm.
    How to think about it: A scheme wanting only low-cost passive exposure; a client whose buyout is months away and needs an insurer, not a manager. Explain that sending them elsewhere protects credibility for the mandates that do fit. See Chapter 7 on when a relationship should end.
  3. If the products really were identical, what would decide it?
    Why it is asked: Whether you understand what coverage adds.
    How to think about it: Then the decision rests on how well the firm understood the client's constraints, the quality of answers in due diligence, reliability during onboarding and price. Those are things coverage teams influence without controlling the investment result.

What do you know about Goldman Sachs Asset Management?

Why Goldman Sachs IQ-03

Underlying argument
Show structure, then scale, then the part relevant to this role, with dates. Asset & Wealth Management is one of the firm's reporting segments and produced $16,679m of the firm's $58,283m net revenues in 2025, 28.6%; the Asset management business inside it was $6,784m, 11.6% R2-S01. Most of the segment's revenue is management and other fees ($11,538m in 2025), which depend on assets under supervision R2-S01. AUS was $4,097bn at 30 September 2026 R2-S02. The Client Solutions Group is described by Goldman as the group that develops client relationships and delivers investment solutions for institutional and third-party wealth clients R1-S10. Layer B · interpretation Be careful with three confusions: AWM is not the same as Asset Management; AUS is Goldman's term and is not identical to another firm's AUM; and no revenue figure is disclosed for the Client Solutions Group.

Depends on: Verified: segment revenue (FY2025 10-K), AUS (Q3 2026 10-Q), Goldman's own description of CSG. No personal evidence needed. R2-S01 R2-S02 R1-S10

A weak answer, and why it is weak
It is one of the largest asset managers in the world with trillions under management, it does everything from equities to alternatives, and asset management is about 30% of Goldman's revenue.

Vague on scale, no dates, and the 30% figure is wrong as stated: about 29% is the whole Asset & Wealth Management segment, and Asset management alone was under 12% in 2025. Confusing the two in front of someone who works there is an avoidable error.

About 30 seconds

It sits inside the Asset and Wealth Management segment, which was about 29 per cent of firm revenue last year. Asset management on its own was nearer 12. Most of that income is management fees on assets under supervision, which were about 4.1 trillion dollars at the end of September. The Client Solutions Group is the part that covers institutional and third-party wealth clients, which is where this role sits.

About 60 to 90 seconds

I'd describe it in three layers. The firm reports an Asset and Wealth Management segment. In 2025 that was about 16.7 billion dollars of net revenue, roughly 29 per cent of the firm, but that includes wealth management and private banking. The asset management business by itself was about 6.8 billion, under 12 per cent. I mention that because I've seen 'asset management is 30 per cent of Goldman' quoted, and it isn't quite right. Second, how it earns money: mostly management fees charged on assets under supervision, which is Goldman's term for client assets it manages or advises on for a fee. That was about 4.1 trillion dollars at the end of September, spread across fixed income, equities, alternatives and about a trillion of liquidity products. The fee rate differs a lot by asset class, so the mix matters as much as the total. Third, the client side. Goldman describes the Client Solutions Group as developing client relationships and delivering investment solutions for institutional and third-party wealth clients. What I can't tell you from public sources is how the London team is organised or what it earns, because that isn't disclosed, and I'd rather say that than guess.

Harder follow-ups
  1. What is the difference between AUS and AUM?
    Why it is asked: Precision with the firm's own vocabulary.
    How to think about it: AUS is Goldman's disclosed measure: assets where it earns a fee for managing or advising, including some advisory assets. Other firms define AUM differently, so cross-firm comparisons need care. See the glossary entry and Chapter 5.
  2. Why does the mix of assets matter?
    Why it is asked: Linking assets to revenue.
    How to think about it: Average effective fees in 2025 were 58bp for alternatives, 54bp equity, 17bp fixed income and 14bp liquidity R2-S01. A dollar moving from equity to liquidity lowers revenue even though AUS is unchanged.
  3. How much revenue does the Client Solutions Group generate?
    Why it is asked: Will you invent a number?
    How to think about it: It is not disclosed. Say so. Add that revenue is jointly produced by investment teams, coverage and operations, so attributing it to one group would be arbitrary anyway.

Where might Goldman Sachs be the wrong choice for a client?

Why Goldman Sachs IQ-04

Underlying argument
A credible candidate can state where the firm they are applying to is less suitable. Three grounded cases. Low-cost index exposure: Goldman itself lists the shift to passive and lower-fee products as a risk to its average effective management fee R2-S01, and BlackRock's scale in index and ETFs is far larger ($15.5tn AUM, $135bn into iShares in one quarter) R8-S02. Conflicts in delegated mandates: an OCIO provider that can place assets with its own funds has a conflict to manage; Goldman's UK mandates can use both internal and external managers R3-S08, which makes transparency about that choice a real diligence point. Past outcomes: Pensioenfonds Vervoer terminated a roughly €7bn Goldman fiduciary mandate in 2010 citing underperformance R7-S48. Layer B · interpretation The point is not criticism for its own sake: knowing the limits is what lets a coverage person qualify a prospect honestly.

Depends on: Verified: the 10-K risk factor on passive; the Vervoer termination; the internal-and-external-manager structure of UK mandates. No personal evidence needed. R2-S01 R8-S02 R3-S08 R7-S48 R7-S35

A weak answer, and why it is weak
I honestly can't think of one. Goldman has the capability to serve any client, and where there are gaps I'm sure the firm is investing to close them.

It reads as either unprepared or unwilling to be honest. An interviewer who works with clients knows the firm loses mandates and is not the cheapest index provider. Refusing the question suggests you would also avoid telling a client an uncomfortable truth.

About 30 seconds

A client who mainly wants cheap index exposure is probably better served by a firm built around passive scale. Goldman's own filings name the shift to lower-fee products as a pressure on its fees. And in a delegated mandate, a client should look hard at how any provider chooses between its own funds and external ones. I'd rather know those limits than discover them in front of a client.

About 60 to 90 seconds

I can think of three situations, and I think knowing them is part of doing the job properly. The first is a client whose need is low-cost index tracking and little else. The largest passive providers have scale Goldman doesn't, and Goldman's own annual report lists clients moving to lower-fee products as a risk to its average fee. The second is about conflicts. In an outsourced mandate the provider can often choose between its own strategies and outside managers. Goldman's UK mandates can use both. That is a strength when the selection is transparent and a weakness if a client can't see why an in-house fund was picked, so I'd expect a good trustee to press on it. The third is simply that delegated mandates sometimes fail. A Dutch transport pension fund ended a seven billion euro mandate with Goldman in 2010 and gave underperformance as the reason. That was a long time ago, and I don't know the detail, but it is a reminder that appointment isn't the end of the story. None of this puts me off. It tells me where a coverage person needs to be most careful about fit before proposing anything.

Harder follow-ups
  1. If you believe that, how would you sell an in-house fund inside an OCIO mandate?
    Why it is asked: Handling a real conflict of interest.
    How to think about it: You would not 'sell' it. The selection case must stand on the same evidence used for external managers, the client should see the comparison, and the decision belongs to the investment team within the agreed guidelines. A junior supports with accurate material; they do not decide.
  2. Isn't it disloyal to talk about a lost mandate from 2010?
    Why it is asked: Whether you confuse loyalty with silence.
    How to think about it: It is public. Clients and consultants know it. Being able to discuss it calmly is more reassuring than pretending it did not happen. Loyalty and honest challenge conflict less often than people fear; see the values section of Chapter 8.
  3. So should Goldman build a bigger passive business?
    Why it is asked: Commercial reasoning beyond the script.
    How to think about it: Give a view with limits: scale economics favour incumbents; Goldman has instead bought into active and outcome ETFs (Innovator, completed April 2026) R7-S35. Say what evidence would change your view.

Why asset management?

Why asset management IQ-05

Underlying argument
The argument has to move from what the industry does to what I would do in it. Asset managers invest other people's money against a stated objective and are paid mainly a percentage of the assets, so income depends on clients choosing to stay, which makes the relationship continuous instead of transactional. For Goldman, management and other fees were $11,538m of the segment's $16,679m in 2025 R2-S01. Layer B · interpretation Three features follow that could be reasons to choose it: the client's problem is long-dated (a pension paid for decades), the manager is judged repeatedly against something measurable, and the work combines investment understanding with people. Each has a cost: fees fall when markets fall, results are partly outside your control, and much junior work is preparation. Layer C · personal fit Whether those features attract me is a personal claim that needs personal evidence.

Depends on: Verified: fee-based revenue model. Personal: [my own example: something long-running I chose to stay with when a shorter, more exciting option existed], or an honest statement that this is a hypothesis I want to test. R2-S01 R8-S38

A weak answer, and why it is weak
I'm passionate about financial markets and I love the idea of managing money for clients. Asset management is a growing industry with great long-term prospects and I want to be part of it.

'Passionate about markets' fits trading or research better than client coverage. 'Growing industry' is a reason to buy the shares, not to do the job. Nothing says what the work is or why this person would like doing it.

About 30 seconds

Because of how it gets paid. An asset manager earns a fee on assets for as long as the client stays, so it has to keep earning the mandate every quarter. I like that the client's problem is long-term, a pension paid over decades, and that you're measured against something concrete. I should say I haven't worked in it yet, so that's a considered reason, not a proven one.

About 60 to 90 seconds

The honest starting point is the business model. An asset manager invests money for a client against an objective they've agreed, and it's mostly paid a percentage of the assets each year. So the income only continues while the client keeps choosing to stay. I find that more interesting than a one-off fee, because it changes what good work looks like: you're judged repeatedly, against a benchmark or a funding target, over years. The second thing is the nature of the client's problem. A pension scheme has to pay people for decades. An insurer has to match its liabilities. Those are real constraints, and understanding them is most of the job before any product is discussed. I should be clear about the downsides, because they're part of the choice. Revenue falls when markets fall, whatever you do. A lot of the result is outside the control of anyone in client coverage. And early on, much of the work is preparation. I think the combination still suits me, and here I'd give [my own example: a long-running responsibility I stuck with and what kept me interested]. If I didn't have that, I'd say this is a reasoned preference I'm applying in order to test.

Harder follow-ups
  1. You said you like long-term problems. What have you actually done that was long-term?
    Why it is asked: Is the motive supported or borrowed?
    How to think about it: Give real evidence or say plainly that you lack it. A small true example beats a large vague one. If you have none, say what you would need to see in an internship to confirm the preference.
  2. Fees are under pressure across the industry. Why join now?
    Why it is asked: Commercial awareness tied to motivation.
    How to think about it: Acknowledge it: BCG puts institutional fee decline at about 3% a year R8-S38. Then reason: pressure raises the value of understanding what clients will still pay for (delegation, private markets, service) and of people who can explain it.
  3. Why not consulting? Consultants also solve long-term client problems.
    Why it is asked: Distinguishing adjacent careers.
    How to think about it: A consultant advises and leaves implementation to others; a manager is accountable for running the money afterwards. Say which accountability you prefer and why. See the comparison table in Chapter 8.

Why asset management rather than investment banking or sales and trading?

Why asset management IQ-06

Underlying argument
Compare the three on what is sold, to whom, how often, and how the firm is paid. Banking advises companies on transactions for a fee per deal; markets intermediates trades for institutional investors and earns spreads and commissions; asset management is hired by the owner of the money to invest it and earns a recurring fee on assets. In Goldman's reporting these sit in different segments: Global Banking & Markets ($41,453m in 2025) and Asset & Wealth Management ($16,679m) R2-S01. Layer B · interpretation The differences that matter for fit: length of the client relationship (years versus a deal or a trade), whose side you are on (the investor's agent versus an adviser to an issuer or a counterparty), and the rhythm of work (steady coverage and reporting versus deal intensity or market hours). None is superior. Layer C · personal fit The choice should rest on which rhythm and which accountability I actually prefer.

Depends on: Verified: segment structure. Personal: any real exposure to the alternatives and what I learned about my own preferences from it. If I have none, say the comparison is from study, not experience. R2-S01

A weak answer, and why it is weak
Investment banking hours are brutal and trading is being automated, so asset management is the smarter long-term choice with a better lifestyle.

It defines the choice by what it avoids. It insults colleagues in other divisions, signals that lifestyle is the main driver, and says nothing positive or specific about asset management.

About 30 seconds

They solve different problems. A banker advises a company on a transaction. A markets salesperson helps an investor execute a trade. An asset manager is hired by the owner of the money to run it for years and is paid only while they stay. I'm drawn to the third because the relationship continues after the decision, so you have to live with what you recommended.

About 60 to 90 seconds

I'd compare them on what the client is buying. In banking the client is usually a company and it's buying advice on a transaction, so the work peaks around the deal and then the team moves on. In markets the client is an investor who wants to trade, and the relationship is frequent but each interaction is short. In asset management the client hands over money to be run against an objective, and the manager is paid a recurring fee for as long as the client keeps it there. What attracts me is that last feature. If a coverage team helps a pension scheme into a mandate, the same team is in the room a year later explaining how it has gone. I think being accountable after the decision makes you more careful before it. I don't want to pretend the others are worse. Banking and markets are larger parts of this firm's revenue, and plenty of people prefer the intensity of a deal or a market. For me it's a question of which accountability I want. I'd add [my own example: any direct exposure to banking or markets work and what it showed me about my preferences], or else be upfront that this is a comparison I've studied, not lived.

Harder follow-ups
  1. Markets sales is also client coverage. What is really different?
    Why it is asked: Precision about adjacent roles.
    How to think about it: In markets the firm is often the client's counterparty or agent for a trade; in asset management it is the client's fiduciary or appointed manager under an investment agreement. The time horizon, the contract and the regulation of the relationship differ. See the adjacent-roles table in Chapter 6.
  2. If the bonus were much bigger in banking, would you switch?
    Why it is asked: The pay counterfactual.
    How to think about it: Answer truthfully. A reasonable answer: pay matters, but the preference stated was about accountability and time horizon, which pay does not change. If pay would change your answer, know that before the interview.
  3. What would you miss by not doing banking?
    Why it is asked: Balance and realism.
    How to think about it: Name real things: deal execution skills, modelling depth, a sharper finish line. Acknowledging a cost makes the preference more believable.

How does an asset manager actually make money?

Why asset management IQ-07

Underlying argument
Revenue is roughly average fee-bearing assets multiplied by the fee rate, plus performance-related fees where they apply. Assets change through client flows and market movement; the rate changes through mix and negotiation. Goldman's own figures show the spread by asset class: average effective management fees in 2025 of 58bp for alternatives, 54bp for equity, 17bp for fixed income, 14bp for liquidity and 31bp overall R2-S01. Incentive fees are recognised only when they are no longer likely to reverse R2-S01. In alternatives a commitment is not fee-earning until it meets the fund's fee terms: of $438bn of commitments raised from 2020 to 2025, $105bn sat in non-fee-earning assets R2-S01. Layer B · interpretation So an announced mandate, a funded mandate and fee revenue are three different things, and recurring does not mean guaranteed. ✎ Illustrative example Illustration: £500m at 20bp for a full year is £1m of gross management fee before any cost.

Depends on: Verified: effective fee rates and commitment data from the 10-K. The worked arithmetic is illustrative. No personal evidence needed. R2-S01 R8-S38

A weak answer, and why it is weak
They charge a management fee, usually around one or two per cent, plus twenty per cent of profits, so the more assets they manage the more money they make.

'Two and twenty' describes some hedge and private funds, not the bulk of institutional assets, where fees are a fraction of one per cent. It ignores mix, flows, markets and timing, and treats assets and revenue as the same thing.

About 30 seconds

Mostly a percentage fee on the assets it manages, so revenue is average assets times the fee rate. Assets move with client flows and with markets. The rate depends heavily on the asset class. At Goldman last year the average was about 31 basis points overall, but nearer 58 for alternatives and 14 for liquidity. So where the money sits matters as much as how much there is.

About 60 to 90 seconds

The core is simple: average fee-bearing assets multiplied by a fee rate. If a client gives you 500 million pounds at 20 basis points, that's a million pounds a year before any costs, and only if it's funded for the whole year. Then three things complicate it. First, the assets move. Clients add and withdraw, and markets move the value even if nobody does anything. Second, the rate varies a lot. Goldman's reported average last year was about 31 basis points, but alternatives were around 58, equities 54, fixed income 17 and liquidity 14. So a shift from equities into cash lowers revenue with assets unchanged. Large mandates also negotiate lower rates. Third, timing. A mandate that's been announced isn't paying until the money arrives, and in private funds a commitment may not earn fees until it's drawn. Goldman's filings show over a hundred billion dollars of commitments that weren't yet fee-earning at the end of last year. On top of that there are performance fees in some strategies, which only count once they can't reverse. The practical lesson for a coverage team is that a win is the start of revenue, not the same thing as revenue, and keeping a client is avoiding a loss, not adding income.

Harder follow-ups
  1. A client doubles their mandate. Does your fee revenue double?
    Why it is asked: Understanding breakpoints.
    How to think about it: Often not. Tiered schedules charge a lower rate on assets above each breakpoint, so the average rate falls as the mandate grows. Try the tiered case in the fee calculator.
  2. Is that £1m profit?
    Why it is asked: Revenue versus profit.
    How to think about it: No. It is gross fee before portfolio management, operations, distribution and overhead costs. Industry margins are roughly 30% on BCG's figures R8-S38, and no single team can claim the whole fee.
  3. Which matters more to the firm this year: winning a new £500m mandate or keeping an existing £1bn one?
    Why it is asked: Thinking in increments.
    How to think about it: Depends on the fee rates and the probability of loss. Keeping £1bn at 15bp protects £1.5m a year; winning £500m at 20bp adds £1m once funded. Neither is 'more important' in the abstract, and both depend on the client's interest being served.

Why the Client Solutions Group?

Why CSG IQ-08

Underlying argument
Goldman describes the Client Solutions Group as developing client relationships and executing investment solutions for institutional and third-party wealth clients R1-S10, and its listings also label it sales R1-S04. A London team advert describes one team doing both new business development and management of existing institutional relationships R1-S01. Layer B · interpretation The reason to choose it over an investing seat is a preference for a particular task: working out what a client needs given its liabilities, governance and constraints, and then being responsible for connecting that to what the firm can actually deliver. The work sits between the client and the portfolio managers and depends on both. Layer C · personal fit Whether I enjoy that position, in the middle, accountable without control, is the personal claim. The answer must name the task I like, not the importance of clients.

Depends on: Verified: Goldman's description of CSG; the BeNeLux advert showing blended responsibilities. Personal: [my own example: a time I had to find out what someone needed before I could help, and what I did]. Without it the answer is a hypothesis. R1-S10 R1-S04 R1-S01

A weak answer, and why it is weak
I'm a people person with strong communication skills and an interest in markets, so client solutions is the perfect combination of the two for me.

Describes a self-image, not the work. 'People person' and 'interest in markets' apply to private wealth, markets sales, consulting and recruitment. No mention of institutional clients, what a solution is, or what the candidate would do.

About 30 seconds

Because the task I think I'd like most is working out what a client actually needs before any product comes into it. A pension scheme's question is rarely 'which fund'. It's 'how do we pay these liabilities with this governance and this risk budget'. The Client Solutions Group is where that question gets translated into something the investment teams can deliver, and I'd like to learn to do that translation well.

About 60 to 90 seconds

I'd start with what the group does, as far as Goldman describes it publicly: it builds client relationships and delivers investment solutions for institutional and third-party wealth clients. One London team advert I read has the same team winning new business and looking after existing relationships. What draws me is a specific part of that. Before anything is proposed, someone has to understand the client: what it owes and when, who makes decisions, what it's allowed to hold, what went wrong last time. Then that has to be turned into a brief the portfolio managers can respond to, and afterwards someone has to stay accountable for whether it was delivered. I like work where you have to understand two sides well enough to translate between them. I should be honest about the uncomfortable part. In that seat you're responsible for outcomes you don't control. You don't run the portfolio, but you're the one explaining a bad quarter. I think I'd find that motivating, not frustrating, and my evidence is [my own example: a time I was accountable for something that depended on other people's work]. If the interviewer pushed me, I'd also say I haven't done this job, so I'm describing what I expect to like and want to find out.

Harder follow-ups
  1. Couldn't you say that about any client-facing job?
    Why it is asked: Specificity. See IQ-09 for the full treatment.
    How to think about it: Concede what is generic, then name what is specific here: institutional clients with liabilities and governance, a fiduciary or contractual relationship lasting years, and a product whose outcome is uncertain and measured.
  2. What is a 'solution' as opposed to a product?
    Why it is asked: Whether the word means anything to you.
    How to think about it: A product is a fund or strategy. A solution starts from the client's objective and constraints and may combine several strategies, external managers, hedging and reporting, or may be 'do nothing'. If the answer is always a product, it was not a solution.
  3. You'd be explaining results you didn't produce. Why would anyone want that?
    Why it is asked: Have you thought about the hard part?
    How to think about it: Because the client still needs an accurate account and a next step, and delivering that well is a skill. Admit it is uncomfortable. See 'The difficult parts' in Chapter 6.

Couldn't you say that about any client-facing job?

Challenge questions IQ-09

Underlying argument
The challenge is fair, so the first move is to concede what is generic: listening, reliability and wanting to be useful apply to any client role. The answer then has to isolate what is different about institutional asset-management coverage. Layer B · interpretation Four differences: (1) the client is an institution with legal duties to other people, so 'the client' is a group of trustees, staff and advisers with different aims; (2) the product is a promise about an uncertain future outcome, measured afterwards against a benchmark; (3) the relationship is contractual and recurring, paid by a fee on assets that the client can withdraw R2-S01; (4) selection is formal, for example UK trustees must run a competitive tender before appointing a fiduciary manager for 20% or more of assets R3-S24. Layer C · personal fit The final step is to say which of those differences I want, since a difference is only a reason if I prefer it.

Depends on: Verified: fee-on-assets revenue model; the UK fiduciary tender requirement. Personal: which of the four differences I can show a preference for. R2-S01 R3-S24

A weak answer, and why it is weak
No, because this role is at Goldman Sachs, working with the most sophisticated clients in the world on the most complex problems.

It answers a question about the job with a statement about the employer, and 'sophisticated' and 'complex' are adjectives without content. It dodges the challenge instead of meeting it.

About 30 seconds

Partly, yes. Wanting to understand people and be reliable applies anywhere. What's specific here is the client and the product. The client is an institution with duties to others, deciding through a committee and a formal process. And what you're offering is an uncertain outcome they'll measure for years while paying a fee they can stop. That's the version of client work I'm choosing.

About 60 to 90 seconds

Some of it, yes, and I'd rather admit that than pretend otherwise. Listening well, following up, being straight with people: that's any client job. What I think is particular to this one comes down to three things. The first is who the client is. It isn't a person spending their own money. It's a board of trustees or an investment committee with legal duties to members, usually advised by a consultant, and each of those people wants something slightly different. The second is what's being offered. It isn't a finished product you can inspect. It's a manager's future behaviour, and the result is uncertain and gets measured against a benchmark every quarter. So honesty about what you don't know matters more than in most sales. The third is the structure. The manager is paid a fee on assets for as long as the client stays, and big decisions go through formal tenders. That makes it a long, repeated relationship, not a transaction. Those three are what I'm choosing. If what I mostly wanted was variety of people or quick wins, I think another client-facing job would suit me better, and I've tried to be honest with myself about that.

Harder follow-ups
  1. Private wealth advisers also deal with long-term money. Why not that?
    Why it is asked: Finer distinction between adjacent roles.
    How to think about it: There the client is an individual or family, the advice covers their whole financial life, and the adviser often chooses among many managers. Here the client is an institution and you represent one manager. Say which you prefer and why; see Chapter 8's comparison.
  2. Which of your three points do you have any evidence you'd enjoy?
    Why it is asked: From argument to personal evidence.
    How to think about it: Pick one and give a real example, or say honestly that it is untested. Do not claim all three.
  3. If I offered you the same work covering retail investors through an app, would you take it?
    Why it is asked: Tests whether 'institutional' is really part of the motive.
    How to think about it: Reason it through: no committee, no liabilities, product-led. If your interest is in institutional constraints, most of the appeal goes. If you would take it anyway, your motive may be distribution in general, which is fine but should be stated.

If you're interested in investing, why not portfolio management or research?

Why CSG IQ-10

Underlying argument
The roles differ in what is decided. A portfolio manager decides what to hold within the client's guidelines; a research analyst forms a view on securities or markets; a coverage professional does neither and instead understands the client, positions the firm's capabilities honestly and stays accountable for the relationship. Layer B · interpretation Coverage needs enough investment knowledge to explain a strategy accurately and to know when to bring in a specialist, but its decision rights stop short of the portfolio. The honest reasons to prefer coverage: I am more interested in why a client needs something than in which security delivers it; I like work that depends on other people; I want breadth across strategies over depth in one. The honest test: if what I enjoy most is forming my own market view and being proved right or wrong, research or portfolio management fits better. Layer C · personal fit This is a preference to evidence, not assert.

Depends on: No Goldman fact is essential. Personal: evidence of which task I gravitate to when given a choice, for example [my own example: a project where I chose the client or stakeholder side over the analysis side, or the reverse].

A weak answer, and why it is weak
I'd love to be a portfolio manager eventually, and client solutions is a great way to learn the business first before moving across to the investment side.

It tells the interviewer the role is a stepping stone to a different job. It also assumes mobility that the candidate has no evidence for, and gives no reason to want the work itself.

About 30 seconds

Because the question I find most interesting is why this client needs this, more than which bond delivers it. A portfolio manager decides what to hold. Coverage has to understand the client well enough to know whether the strategy fits at all. I'd need solid investment knowledge to do that honestly, but I'd be using it to explain and to judge fit, not to pick securities.

About 60 to 90 seconds

I've thought about this, because I do like the investment side. The way I'd put it is that the jobs answer different questions. Research asks what something is worth. Portfolio management asks what to hold, given the mandate. Coverage asks what this client actually needs, whether we have something that genuinely fits, and how to keep the relationship honest once it's running. When I look at what holds my attention, it's the third. I find it more interesting to understand why a pension scheme has the constraints it has than to form a view on a particular credit. I also know coverage isn't a soft option on knowledge. You have to explain a strategy accurately, answer the first layer of technical questions, and know when a question belongs to the portfolio manager. Here I'd give [my own example: a time I chose, or was more absorbed by, the stakeholder side of a piece of work]. I should also say what would change my mind. If I found that what I enjoyed most was building my own market view and being right or wrong on it, then research would suit me better, and I'd want to know that. But on the evidence I have, it's the client question I'd choose.

Harder follow-ups
  1. So you're not good enough at the technical side?
    Why it is asked: Provocation; tests composure and accuracy.
    How to think about it: Do not get defensive. Say the role demands accuracy about investments without owning the decision, and name what you are doing to build the knowledge. Avoid overclaiming skill.
  2. How much investment knowledge does a coverage analyst really need?
    Why it is asked: Realism about the role.
    How to think about it: Enough to explain objective, process, risks and recent performance drivers correctly; to read a client's guidelines; and to recognise the boundary where a specialist must answer. Not enough to advise on security selection.
  3. Would you move to the investment side if offered in three years?
    Why it is asked: The stepping-stone test again.
    How to think about it: Be truthful. A fair answer: I do not know; I would judge it on which work I had found I liked. Do not promise loyalty you cannot know, and do not reveal the role is a means to an end if it is not.

Would you rather work in sales or relationship management?

Sales or RM IQ-11

Underlying argument
First, be accurate about the labels. Goldman's listings equate the Client Solutions Group with sales R1-S04, and a Hong Kong advert defines a Client Coverage Group as dedicated to retaining, expanding and supporting existing relationships R1-S11. But a London Client Solutions Group advert gives one team both new business and existing relationships R1-S01. So the split is real in places and blended in others, and the former intern's account of how London divides is an unverified account. Layer B · interpretation Second, describe the difference in task: sales is weighted to prospecting, qualifying and competing in selection processes, with long uncertain cycles and frequent rejection; relationship management is weighted to reporting, reviews, problem resolution and recognising changing needs. Layer C · personal fit Third, state a preference provisionally, give the reason, and say you would learn either. Do not pick the side you have heard is more prestigious.
