Depends on: Verified: the CSG and CCG wording in Goldman adverts; the blended London advert. Personal: evidence of how I respond to rejection and to repeated maintenance work, for example [my own example]. R1-S04 R1-S11 R1-S01

A weak answer, and why it is weak
Sales, definitely. I'm competitive and target-driven, I love winning, and I know sales is where the real commercial impact is.

It ranks the two by status, implies relationship management lacks commercial impact, and rests on self-description. An interviewer from the relationship side has just been told their job matters less.

About 30 seconds

I'd lean towards the new-business side, but I hold that loosely. From what I've read, the split isn't clean anyway. One London team advert has the same people doing both. What attracts me to sales is the work of understanding a prospect from scratch. What I'd need to test is how I handle long cycles that end in a no. I'd be glad to learn either.

About 60 to 90 seconds

I'll give a preference, but first I'd say I'm cautious about the labels. In Goldman's own adverts the Client Solutions Group is described as sales, and there's a Client Coverage Group described as retaining and expanding existing relationships. But a London advert I read gives one team both jobs, so I don't want to assume a hard line. On the work itself: the new-business side is weighted towards researching prospects, qualifying them and competing in formal selection processes. The cycles are long, and most of them end without a win. The existing-client side is weighted towards reviews, reporting, fixing problems and noticing when a client's needs have changed. I'm drawn more to the first, because I like the work of understanding an organisation I know nothing about. The thing I can't yet prove is how I'd cope with months of effort ending in rejection. My evidence on that is [my own example: a time sustained effort came to nothing and what I did next]. I also think I'd be a better salesperson for having done the servicing side, because that's where you see whether what was promised got delivered. So if I were placed in relationship management I'd treat it as the right place to learn, not second prize.

Harder follow-ups
  1. Which is harder?
    Why it is asked: Invites a ranking; tests nuance.
    How to think about it: They are hard differently: sales carries rejection and uncertainty; relationship management carries explaining disappointing outcomes and sustaining quality when nothing is new. Avoid ranking. See Chapter 6, 'The difficult parts'.
  2. I run the relationship team. Convince me you want to be here.
    Why it is asked: Was the preference real or tactical?
    How to think about it: Do not reverse your answer. Explain what you would specifically value in the relationship seat (seeing delivery, client depth, expansion that follows from service) and why your lean is mild.
  3. Sales pays more. Is that why?
    Why it is asked: The pay claim is an unverified account; tests honesty.
    How to think about it: Say you have heard it but cannot verify it, and that it is not a sound basis for choosing. Pay differences are not publicly established for this team.

What is the difference between sales and relationship management?

Sales or RM IQ-12

Underlying argument
Give the first approximation, then show why it is only an approximation. First approximation: sales brings in new clients and new assets; relationship management keeps and develops existing ones. Goldman's wording supports both ends: CSG labelled as sales R1-S04; a Client Coverage Group 'dedicated to retaining, expanding and supporting existing client relationships' R1-S11. Why it blurs: existing clients are the main source of additional mandates, so relationship managers sell; a salesperson who wins a mandate carries promises into onboarding; and some teams combine both R1-S01. Consultant relations is a third function, covering the investment consultants who advise institutions and building a pipeline for sales R1-S21. Layer B · interpretation The useful distinction is by task and by clock: uncertain, lumpy, competitive work versus recurring, scheduled, cumulative work.

Depends on: Verified: Goldman's CSG, CCG and Consultant Relations wording. No personal evidence needed. R1-S04 R1-S11 R1-S01 R1-S21

A weak answer, and why it is weak
Sales wins the client and relationship management does the admin afterwards, like sending reports and answering emails.

It reduces relationship management to administration, ignores that expansion and retention are commercial outcomes, and misses the overlap. It also suggests the candidate thinks the work after the win is less skilled.

About 30 seconds

As a first cut, sales wins new clients and relationship management keeps and grows existing ones. In practice it blurs. Most additional mandates come from existing clients, so relationship managers sell. And whatever sales promised gets tested in onboarding. Some teams do both. I think the more useful difference is the rhythm: lumpy, competitive and uncertain on one side, scheduled and cumulative on the other.

About 60 to 90 seconds

The simple version is that sales brings in new clients and new money, and relationship management looks after clients once they're in. Goldman's own adverts fit that roughly. The Client Solutions Group gets labelled as sales, and there's a Client Coverage Group described as retaining, expanding and supporting existing relationships. But I think the simple version misleads in three ways. First, a lot of new assets come from existing clients adding a mandate, and that's often led by the person who already knows them. So relationship management is commercial, not administrative. Second, the handover isn't clean. If sales has set expectations about reporting or access to the portfolio manager, someone has to deliver that, and a client who feels oversold is hard to keep. Third, some teams simply don't separate it. A London advert I saw has one team doing both. There's also consultant relations, which covers the advisers who sit between the manager and the client. So I'd describe the difference by the shape of the work. One side is uncertain and competitive: long pursuits, formal tenders, a lot of no's. The other is recurring: quarterly reviews, queries, noticing change early. Both need investment knowledge and both are judged on whether the client was well served.

Harder follow-ups
  1. Who owns the client?
    Why it is asked: A trap: nobody 'owns' a client.
    How to think about it: The relationship belongs to the firm; individuals contribute credibility. Day-to-day responsibility is assigned, and it varies by team. See Chapter 7 on institutional versus personal relationships.
  2. A relationship manager spots that the client needs a new strategy. Who leads?
    Why it is asked: Understanding of coordination.
    How to think about it: It depends on the team's model. Typically the person who knows the client leads the conversation and brings in specialists; where a separate sales team exists, there is a handover. Say you would ask how the team does it.
  3. Where do consultants fit?
    Why it is asked: Do you know the third function?
    How to think about it: Consultants advise trustees on manager selection and often run the search. Consultant relations keeps them informed so strategies are rated and considered. See the principal-agent chain in Chapter 1.

Institutional sales cycles can take over a year and often end in a no. How would you handle that?

Sales or RM IQ-13

Underlying argument
Explain why cycles are long before talking about resilience: decisions go through committees that meet periodically, consultants screen managers, and formal tenders are required in some cases, for example for UK fiduciary management above 20% of assets R3-S24. The BAE Systems and Shell appointments both followed competitive processes R3-S01R3-S04, and for each winner several firms did the same work and lost. Layer B · interpretation Handling it is partly practical: qualify early so effort goes where there is a real chance; treat the work products (research, a clear understanding of the client) as assets the firm keeps; ask for feedback after a loss; keep the relationship because needs change. Layer C · personal fit It is partly temperament, which needs personal evidence, not adjectives.

Depends on: Verified: tender requirement; BAE and Shell processes. Personal: [my own example: sustained effort that ended in rejection, and what I did in the following weeks]. R3-S24 R3-S01 R3-S04

A weak answer, and why it is weak
I'm very resilient and I never give up. I see every no as one step closer to a yes, so rejection really doesn't bother me.

Adjectives and a slogan. 'Rejection doesn't bother me' is not believable and suggests little reflection. 'Never give up' is also wrong: knowing when to stop pursuing a poor-fit prospect is part of the job.

About 30 seconds

I'd expect it to be hard, and I'd try to make the effort worth something even when the answer is no. That means qualifying early, so I'm not spending a year on a client we don't fit. It means asking why we lost. And it means keeping in touch, because a scheme's needs change. On temperament, I'd rather give you an example than an adjective: [my own example].

About 60 to 90 seconds

First I'd want to understand why it takes that long, because it changes how you handle it. An institutional client decides through a committee that might meet four times a year. A consultant usually screens the managers. For some decisions, like appointing a fiduciary manager in the UK, a competitive tender is required. So a year isn't slowness, it's the client doing its job properly. And for every announced win, like BAE Systems or Shell, there were firms that did the same work and lost. Given that, I think there are practical things that help. One is qualifying honestly at the start: is there a real need, do we fit, is there a decision coming? Walking away early from a poor fit is better than a long, polite no. Another is treating what you learn as lasting. The research on that client and the relationships with their advisers don't disappear because one search went elsewhere. A third is asking for feedback and passing it to the people who can use it. As for how I'd cope personally, I don't want to just say I'm resilient. What I can point to is [my own example: sustained effort that ended in rejection, and what I did next]. And if I didn't have one, I'd say that this is one of the things I most need the internship to show me.

Harder follow-ups
  1. When do you stop pursuing a prospect?
    Why it is asked: Judgement over persistence.
    How to think about it: When the need is not real, the fit is poor, or the decision-maker has clearly chosen. Persisting then wastes the client's time and the firm's. Keep a light, useful contact instead.
  2. You lose a tender you worked on for months. What do you do the next morning?
    Why it is asked: Concrete behaviour.
    How to think about it: As a junior: update the pipeline record accurately, help the senior request and record feedback, file the research so it is reusable, and thank the internal specialists. No drama, no blame.
  3. Does a long cycle mean the junior never sees a result?
    Why it is asked: Realism about motivation.
    How to think about it: Often true within a 10-week internship. So the satisfaction has to come from the intermediate work being good. If you need frequent closure, say so and consider whether the relationship side suits you better.

What would you actually do as an analyst?

The role IQ-14

Underlying argument
Be honest about what is and is not known. The official London listing contains no duties specific to the Client Solutions Group R1-S02; the programme is described as nine to ten weeks with training and real responsibilities R1-S22. Team adverts give better clues: a London team role supporting new business and existing institutional relationships R1-S01, and a UK Third Party Wealth sales-support analyst role R1-S17. ≈ Supported inference From those and general industry practice, a junior's work is mostly preparation and follow-through: client and prospect research; meeting briefing notes; pulling performance and positioning data for review packs; first drafts of sections of RFP and due-diligence responses; keeping the CRM and pipeline accurate; coordinating with portfolio specialists, legal and operations; meeting notes and action tracking. What a junior does not do: give investment advice, quote fees, make commitments, or decide what to propose. Layer B · interpretation The value of the junior's work is that seniors walk into a meeting accurately prepared and that promises get kept.

Depends on: Verified: the listing's lack of role detail; programme length; wording of the two team adverts. The task list is a supported inference from adverts and industry practice, and should be labelled as such in the answer. R1-S02 R1-S22 R1-S01 R1-S17

A weak answer, and why it is weak
I'd be building relationships with clients, pitching investment solutions and helping to win new mandates for the firm from day one.

It describes a senior's job. An intern does not pitch to clients or win mandates. It suggests the candidate has not thought about what a junior realistically contributes and may be disappointed by the real work.

About 30 seconds

Mostly preparation and follow-through. Researching a client before a meeting and writing the briefing note. Pulling the numbers for a quarterly review pack and checking them. Drafting parts of a due-diligence response. Keeping the pipeline and client records accurate. Taking notes and chasing actions. I wouldn't be advising clients or quoting anything. The point of the work is that the senior people are properly prepared and what was promised gets done.

About 60 to 90 seconds

I'll be upfront that the published description for this programme doesn't list team duties, so this is my best reading from the team adverts I could find and from how the industry works. I'd expect most of my time to go on four kinds of task. First, research: who is this pension scheme or wealth manager, what do they hold, who advises them, what's changed recently. That becomes a briefing note before a meeting. Second, materials: pulling performance and positioning data for a client review, checking it against the source, and assembling the pack. Third, written responses: first drafts of sections of an RFP or a due-diligence questionnaire, using approved content and flagging what needs a specialist. Fourth, keeping the record straight: client notes, pipeline updates, actions from meetings and who owns them. What I wouldn't do matters as well. I wouldn't give a client a view on what to buy, quote a fee, or agree to anything. Those belong to senior colleagues and the investment teams. I don't see the preparation as lesser work. If a number in a review pack is wrong, the client's trust in everything else drops. And if I had a quiet week, I'd use it to sit in on calls and learn how the seniors handle the difficult questions.

Harder follow-ups
  1. That sounds like a lot of admin. Will you be bored?
    Why it is asked: The motivation test on the real work.
    How to think about it: Do not deny it is repetitive. Say what makes it worthwhile to you (accuracy matters, you learn a client each time) and give evidence that you sustain quality on repeated tasks, or admit it is untested.
  2. You find an error in a pack ten minutes before it goes out. What do you do?
    Why it is asked: Responsiveness versus accuracy.
    How to think about it: Tell the owner immediately with the specific discrepancy and the source. Do not fix silently and do not let it go to protect the deadline. The decision to delay is the senior's. See the values conflicts in Chapter 8.
  3. What would a great intern do that an average one wouldn't?
    Why it is asked: Initiative within realistic limits.
    How to think about it: Checks numbers against source unasked; writes notes someone else could act on; asks why a client is structured as it is; closes loops. Not: cold-calling clients or volunteering opinions in meetings.

What does the Client Solutions Group do, and how is it organised?

The role IQ-15

Underlying argument
Separate three evidence levels. Verified: Goldman describes the group as developing client relationships and executing investment solutions for institutional and third-party wealth clients across public and private asset classes R1-S10; listings label it sales R1-S04; Third Party Wealth is a named business with an EMEA unit R4-S01; a senior title 'co-head of EMEA Institutional Client Coverage' appears in a Goldman press release R7-S08; Consultant Relations works with investment consultants R1-S21; the OCIO team sits within Multi-Asset Solutions, an investing group, and works with sales and relationship professionals R1-S15. Supported inference: coverage is cut by region and by channel, because adverts exist for country teams and for channel teams and several carry language requirements R1-S01. Unverified account: the exact London sub-team structure and the sales-versus-relationship split described by a former intern.

Depends on: Verified sources as cited. The key skill is labelling what is known, inferred and unknown. No personal evidence needed. R1-S10 R1-S04 R4-S01 R7-S08 R1-S21 R1-S15 R1-S01 R3-S09

A weak answer, and why it is weak
It's split into UK, Middle East, Nordics, Switzerland, Benelux, Liquidity and Insurance, and each of those is split into Third Party Wealth, Institutional and OCIO, and then into CSG for sales and CCG for relationship management.

It recites one person's informal account as fact to someone who knows the real structure. Parts are contradicted by public sources: OCIO is not a UK-only sales sub-team, and other European countries are covered from local offices. Confident detail that is wrong is worse than honest outline.

About 30 seconds

Publicly, Goldman describes it as the group that builds client relationships and delivers investment solutions for institutional and third-party wealth clients. From job adverts, coverage looks organised by region and by channel: institutional, third-party wealth, consultants, with insurance and liquidity as their own specialisms. The OCIO investment team sits in Multi-Asset Solutions and works alongside. I don't know the detailed London structure, and I'd like to hear it.

About 60 to 90 seconds

I can tell you what's public and where my knowledge stops. Goldman's own description is that the Client Solutions Group develops client relationships and delivers investment solutions for institutional and third-party wealth clients, across public and private markets. In its job listings it's also simply called sales. From there, the organisation seems to be cut two ways at once. One cut is by channel: institutional clients like pension funds and sovereign investors, and third-party wealth, meaning private banks and wealth managers who put Goldman funds in front of their own clients. There's also a consultant relations function for the advisers who influence institutional decisions. The other cut is by geography. There are adverts for country and regional teams, some needing a local language, and some European markets are covered from local offices, not London. A couple of things sit slightly apart. Insurance and liquidity look like global specialisms. And the people who actually run OCIO portfolios are in Multi-Asset Solutions, which is an investment team that works with coverage. What I can't see from outside is how the London desks divide the work between winning business and servicing it, or the reporting lines. I've heard an informal account, but I haven't been able to verify it, so I'd rather ask.

Harder follow-ups
  1. What is the difference between institutional and third-party wealth clients?
    Why it is asked: Basic channel understanding.
    How to think about it: Institutional: the end owner or its trustees appoint you directly, often by segregated mandate. Third-party wealth: an intermediary selects your fund for its own clients, so approval and flows are separate steps. See IQ-19.
  2. Where does OCIO sit, and is it only in the UK?
    Why it is asked: Corrects a common misconception.
    How to think about it: Not UK-only: Goldman reported $480bn of OCIO assets globally at 31 March 2026 with large US mandates R3-S09. The OCIO investment team sits in Multi-Asset Solutions; coverage works with it.
  3. How did you find this out?
    Why it is asked: Research method and honesty.
    How to think about it: Say exactly: Goldman's careers pages and press releases, filings, trade press, and one informal account you treated as a lead. That is a strength.

Which team or client segment interests you most, and why?

The role IQ-16

Underlying argument
Answer with a client problem, not a team name chosen for tactical reasons. The former intern's claim that video answers determine team allocation is an unverified account, and shaping answers around it would be a keyword tactic built on nothing. Layer B · interpretation A sound answer picks a segment because of a feature of its problem. UK institutional: defined benefit schemes with strong funding (PPF 7800 funding ratio 133.7% at end October 2026) R3-S29 choosing between buyout, running on and delegation. Third-party wealth: an intermediary chain where approval and flows are separate R1-S17. OCIO: whole-portfolio delegation with tenders and team transfers such as BAE Systems R3-S01. The answer should also say honestly which constraints apply: several regional teams require a language R1-S01.

Depends on: Verified: funding data; BAE appointment; language requirements in adverts. Personal: why that problem interests me, with [my own example] if I have one; otherwise framed as curiosity. R3-S29 R1-S17 R3-S01 R1-S01 R3-S27

A weak answer, and why it is weak
I'd love to join the Middle East team because sovereign wealth funds are the most exciting clients and the region is growing fast.

If chosen because of a rumour that mentioning a region gets you placed there, it is a tactic, not a preference, and it collapses under one follow-up about what a sovereign fund needs. 'Exciting' and 'growing fast' are not reasons.

About 30 seconds

UK institutional, because of the problem those clients have right now. Many defined benefit schemes are well funded, so the question has changed from closing a deficit to choosing an endgame: sell to an insurer, run on, or delegate. I find that a more interesting conversation than a single product search. I'm open on team, though, and I only speak English, which I realise rules some regional desks out.

About 60 to 90 seconds

I'd answer by the client problem I find most interesting, and I'm open about where that leads. Right now that's UK pension schemes. A few years ago most of them were trying to repair deficits. Today, on the Pension Protection Fund's numbers, the universe as a whole is well over a hundred per cent funded. That changes the question trustees are asking. It's now which endgame: buy out with an insurer, run the scheme on and possibly release surplus, or hand the portfolio to a fiduciary manager. Each of those leads to a different relationship with an asset manager, and one of them, buyout, means the assets leave. I think that's an unusually interesting moment to be learning client coverage, because you can't have a sensible conversation without understanding the scheme's whole position. The BAE Systems appointment is the kind of case I'd want to understand from the inside. I'm also curious about third-party wealth, because the chain between the fund and the end investor is so different. I should be realistic too. I speak only English, and I can see some regional teams need Dutch or German. And I haven't worked with any of these clients, so this is where my curiosity points, not a fixed view.

Harder follow-ups
  1. What does buyout mean for an asset manager?
    Why it is asked: Depth behind the chosen example.
    How to think about it: The scheme pays an insurer to take on the liabilities; assets transfer to the insurer, so the manager's mandate ends, unless the insurer is itself a client. 2025 saw a record 370 buy-ins worth about £38bn R3-S27.
  2. If we placed you on a different team, would you be disappointed?
    Why it is asked: Flexibility and sincerity.
    How to think about it: Say what you would look for in any team (a client problem to understand, people to learn from). Avoid sounding indifferent or sounding like the preference was a performance.
  3. Why not the Middle East?
    Why it is asked: May probe whether you are gaming allocation.
    How to think about it: Answer on substance: say what you know and do not know about sovereign investors' needs, and that you would not claim an interest you cannot support.

What does a UK defined benefit pension scheme need from an asset manager today?

Clients IQ-17

Underlying argument
Start from the scheme's position. A defined benefit scheme owes fixed pensions; trustees must invest to pay them. Funding has improved sharply: the PPF 7800 universe showed a £275.4bn surplus and a 133.7% funding ratio at end October 2026 R3-S29. Gilt yields are high, with the 10-year around 5.15% when Bank Rate rose to 4% on 5 November 2026 R3-S31. Layer B · interpretation Needs follow from the endgame chosen. Buyout: portfolios that insurers will accept, liquidity, low volatility against insurer pricing, then termination. Run-on: cashflow-matching credit, liability hedging, and governance for any surplus release, a route the Pension Schemes Act 2026 addresses R3-S20. Delegation: a fiduciary manager, appointed by tender R3-S24. Across all: accurate reporting, collateral and liquidity resilience, and a manager who will say when its product is not needed. The limit: schemes differ, and an aggregate surplus hides underfunded ones.

Depends on: Verified: PPF funding data; Bank Rate and gilt yield; Royal Assent date; tender rule. Interpretation of needs is Layer B. No personal evidence needed. R3-S29 R3-S31 R3-S20 R3-S24

A weak answer, and why it is weak
They need high returns to pay their pensioners, so they want the best-performing equity and alternatives funds to grow their assets as much as possible.

It gets the client backwards. A well-funded closed scheme wants certainty of paying liabilities, not maximum growth. The answer shows no awareness of liabilities, funding levels or endgames.

About 30 seconds

It depends on the endgame, because most schemes are now well funded. If they're heading to buyout, they need a portfolio an insurer will take, and then the mandate ends. If they're running on, they need assets that pay the pensions as they fall due and hedge rates and inflation. If they're delegating, they need a fiduciary manager. In all three they need accurate reporting and a manager honest about fit.

About 60 to 90 seconds

I'd begin with where schemes are, because it's changed. A defined benefit scheme has promised fixed pensions, and the trustees' job is to make sure they're paid. For years the problem was deficits. Now the Pension Protection Fund's index shows the universe at about 134 per cent funded on its measure, with gilt yields around five per cent. So for many schemes the question is no longer how to grow but how to finish. I think there are three routes, and the need differs for each. One is buyout: pay an insurer to take the liabilities. Then the scheme needs liquid, low-risk assets the insurer will accept, and the asset manager's mandate ends. Another is running on. Then it needs credit that produces cash when pensions are due, hedging against rates and inflation, and a framework for what happens to any surplus, which this year's Pension Schemes Act deals with. The third is delegating to a fiduciary manager, which has to go through a competitive tender. What's common to all of them is unglamorous: reporting they can rely on, enough liquidity to meet collateral calls, and a manager that tells them when they don't need its product. I'd add a caution. That funding figure is an aggregate, and some schemes are still in deficit, so I wouldn't assume any of this about a particular client before understanding its position.

Harder follow-ups
  1. Bank Rate just went up. Is that good or bad for these schemes?
    Why it is asked: Mechanism, not headline.
    How to think about it: Higher yields reduce the present value of liabilities; a hedged scheme sees assets fall with them, so the net effect depends on the hedge ratio. Rapid moves also mean collateral calls on LDI. Avoid 'good' or 'bad' without the hedging point.
  2. If the best outcome is buyout, why would you tell them?
    Why it is asked: Client interest against firm revenue.
    How to think about it: Because trustees and their advisers will reach that conclusion anyway, and a manager that obstructs it loses credibility with the consultant and with every other scheme. See 'When would the client be right to leave?'.
  3. Who actually decides?
    Why it is asked: Governance.
    How to think about it: The trustee board, advised by an investment consultant and a scheme actuary, with the sponsoring employer consulted. Not one person. See Chapter 7, 'Who the client actually is'.

What is OCIO, and why would a pension scheme use it?

Clients IQ-18

Underlying argument
OCIO, outsourced chief investment officer, means the client delegates day-to-day investment decisions on all or much of its portfolio to a provider within an agreed strategy. Goldman says the terms OCIO and fiduciary management are used interchangeably in the UK R3-S08 and defines OCIO accounts as those where it is the outsourced CIO of its clients R2-S01. Scale: $480bn at 31 March 2026 R3-S09. Why delegate: Goldman's stated view is that sponsors question whether running pensions is core, schemes are maturing, and CIO succession is hard R3-S07. Mechanics: portfolios can use internal and external managers R3-S08; a public UK scheme report shows an asset-based fiduciary fee with the LDI manager charging separately R3-S17; UK trustees must tender R3-S24. Not universal: in BAE Systems the in-house team transferred R3-S01, but that is a feature of the largest deals. Layer B · interpretation Risks: conflicts over in-house funds, concentration on one provider, and harder-to-compare performance.

Depends on: Verified as cited. No personal evidence needed. Avoid saying OCIO is UK-only or that teams always transfer. R3-S08 R2-S01 R3-S09 R3-S07 R3-S17 R3-S24 R3-S01 R3-S02 R8-S10

A weak answer, and why it is weak
OCIO is when a company outsources its whole investment team to Goldman, which takes over all the staff and manages everything. It's a product only the UK team offers.

Two factual errors: team transfers happen in some of the largest deals, not as a rule, and Goldman's OCIO business is global with major US mandates. It also describes the form without the reason a client would choose it.

About 30 seconds

It's when a client hands day-to-day investment decisions on its portfolio to a provider, inside a strategy the client still sets. In the UK it's also called fiduciary management. A scheme does it when running investments in-house is no longer core or practical, for governance, cost or succession reasons. Trustees keep responsibility and have to appoint by competitive tender. Sometimes the in-house team moves across, as with BAE Systems, but that's not the norm.

About 60 to 90 seconds

OCIO stands for outsourced chief investment officer. The client, say a pension scheme, keeps setting the objectives and the overall strategy, and remains legally responsible. What it hands over is the day-to-day implementation: choosing and changing managers, running the hedging, rebalancing. In the UK the same thing is usually called fiduciary management. Why would trustees do it? Goldman's own explanation is that sponsors are asking whether running a pension portfolio is really their business, that mature schemes need more specialised cashflow and hedging work, and that replacing an in-house CIO is hard. I'd add speed: a delegated manager can act between trustee meetings. On how it works, the provider typically charges a fee on the assets it oversees, and it can use its own funds and outside managers. Trustees have to run a competitive tender before delegating a large share. In the biggest cases, like BAE Systems, the scheme's own investment team transferred to Goldman, but I wouldn't generalise from that. And there are real risks a client should weigh. The provider has a conflict if it favours its own products. The scheme becomes dependent on one firm. And comparing results across providers is difficult. Goldman reported around 480 billion dollars of these assets globally in the spring, so it's a large business and not only a UK one.

Harder follow-ups
  1. How is that different from just hiring Goldman to run a bond mandate?
    Why it is asked: Product versus delegation.
    How to think about it: A bond mandate is one slice against one benchmark. OCIO is responsibility for the whole portfolio's implementation, including which other managers are used. The fee, the governance and the accountability differ.
  2. How should trustees control the conflict of interest?
    Why it is asked: Thinking from the client's side.
    How to think about it: Transparency on in-house versus external allocations and their fees, independent oversight (the BAE trustees retained Redington) R3-S02, clear guidelines, and periodic review or re-tender.
  3. Is the UK fiduciary market growing?
    Why it is asked: Current awareness.
    How to think about it: Assets are up, driven by a few very large schemes; mandate numbers fell and fees are down about 27% over five years on IC Select's data R8-S10. Growth and fee pressure together.

How is distributing through a wealth manager different from covering an institutional investor?

Clients IQ-19

Underlying argument
In institutional coverage the manager is appointed by the asset owner or its trustees, often into a segregated mandate. In third-party wealth the buyer is an intermediary choosing funds for its own clients. Goldman uses the name Third Party Wealth; its UK sales team's clients are described as private banks, wealth managers and similar firms R1-S17, and the firm reports a 'third-party distributed' channel of $714bn of long-term AUS R2-S02. Layer B · interpretation The chain has several gates: a fund research team or gatekeeper puts a fund on an approved list; an investment committee or model-portfolio team decides whether to hold it; platforms must carry the share class; advisers or discretionary managers then allocate client by client. So approval is permission, not purchase, and flows arrive gradually and can reverse the same way. The product is usually a pooled fund or ETF with a published charge, not a negotiated mandate. The end investor is never met.

Depends on: Verified: the Third Party Wealth name and client types; the channel figure. The chain is general industry practice (Layer B). No personal evidence needed. R1-S17 R2-S02 R4-S01

A weak answer, and why it is weak
It's basically the same, you're just selling funds to a different type of client, and wealth managers are less sophisticated so the conversations are simpler.

It misses the structural difference (intermediary versus owner), and 'less sophisticated' is both wrong and insulting to professional fund selectors. It shows no grasp of why approved-list status does not equal assets.

About 30 seconds

The institutional client owns the money, or is its trustee, and appoints you directly. A wealth manager is an intermediary picking funds for its own clients. So there are more gates. A research team approves the fund. A committee or model portfolio decides to use it. The platform has to carry it. Then advisers allocate client by client. Getting on the list is permission to be bought, not a sale.

About 60 to 90 seconds

The main difference is who you're dealing with and what they do with your product. With a pension scheme, the people across the table are responsible for the money, and if they appoint you it's usually a mandate with its own agreement and guidelines. With third-party wealth, which is Goldman's name for it, the client is a private bank or wealth manager choosing funds to use for its own customers. You never meet the end investor. That creates a chain. First a fund research team has to approve the fund. Then whoever builds portfolios has to decide to hold it, often inside a model portfolio. The fund has to be available on the platforms they use. And then money arrives as individual advisers or portfolio managers allocate, one client at a time. Two things follow. Being added to an approved list is a real achievement, but it produces nothing by itself. The work after that is helping the people who allocate understand when the fund is useful and when it isn't. And the product is different: a pooled fund or ETF with a published charge, where price and share class matter, not a negotiated mandate. I'd also expect it to be faster-moving in both directions, since a model portfolio change can add or remove a fund across many clients at once.

Harder follow-ups
  1. A fund gets approved but no money comes in. What might be wrong?
    Why it is asked: Diagnosing the chain.
    How to think about it: Check each gate: is it on the platform and in the right share class; is it in any model portfolio; do advisers know what it is for; is it priced competitively against the incumbent; did the champion who approved it leave?
  2. Why has Goldman launched active ETFs in Europe?
    Why it is asked: Linking product to channel.
    How to think about it: Wealth intermediaries increasingly build portfolios with ETFs for cost and ease of trading; Goldman entered European active ETFs in 2025 R4-S01. Present it as a response to how this channel buys, with the caveat that active ETF adoption in Europe is still developing.
  3. Who is your client's client, and do you owe them anything?
    Why it is asked: Conduct awareness.
    How to think about it: The end investor. You do not advise them, but UK rules such as the Consumer Duty put obligations on firms in the distribution chain about fair value and clear information. Material must be accurate for the audience that will ultimately rely on it.

When we say 'the client' in an institutional relationship, who do we actually mean?

Clients IQ-20

Underlying argument
A client is an institution acting through several people with different duties and incentives. For a UK pension scheme: the trustee board holds legal responsibility; an investment sub-committee does the detailed work; the sponsor's finance team cares about cost and balance-sheet effect; an investment consultant advises and often runs manager searches; in-house investment staff, where they exist, monitor managers; operations, legal and procurement control onboarding. The BAE Systems appointment shows the cast: trustees decided, Redington advised them, Travers Smith acted as lawyers and PwC advised the sponsor R3-S02. In the Shell process each fund made its own decision with Isio overseeing the tender R7-S08. Layer B · interpretation Implications for coverage: there is no single decision-maker to persuade; different people need different information; the consultant is both audience and gatekeeper; and the relationship must survive individuals leaving.

Depends on: Verified: the parties named in the BAE and Shell announcements. The role descriptions are general UK pensions practice. No personal evidence needed. R3-S02 R7-S08

A weak answer, and why it is weak
The client is the Chief Investment Officer, because they make the investment decisions, so that is who you need to build the relationship with.

Many schemes have no CIO, and where one exists they recommend while trustees decide. Building one relationship leaves the firm exposed when that person leaves and ignores the consultant, who may control the shortlist.

About 30 seconds

Several people with different jobs. For a pension scheme, the trustees are legally responsible and make the decision. A consultant advises them and often runs the search. The sponsoring company cares about cost. There may be in-house investment staff, and there are legal and operations people who control onboarding. With BAE Systems you can see it in the announcement: trustees, their adviser, their lawyers and the sponsor's adviser were all named.

About 60 to 90 seconds

I think the mistake is to picture one person. Take a UK pension scheme. The trustee board is legally responsible for the money and takes the decision, usually on a recommendation from an investment committee. They're often part-time, so they rely heavily on an investment consultant, who advises on strategy and frequently runs the search and scores the managers. The sponsoring employer isn't the decision-maker but cares a great deal, because it stands behind the scheme. If there's an in-house team, they monitor the managers day to day. And then there are lawyers and operations staff, who don't choose the manager but can certainly delay an onboarding. You can see this in real appointments. When the BAE Systems trustees appointed Goldman, the announcement named the trustees' strategic adviser, their law firm and the sponsor's adviser. In the Shell case each pension fund made its own decision through a process a consultant oversaw. For coverage, a few things follow. Different people need different things: a trustee wants clarity, a consultant wants evidence, operations wants accurate documents. You can't rely on one champion, because people move on. And the consultant is both someone you inform and someone who may decide whether you're considered at all.

Harder follow-ups
  1. The consultant and the trustees disagree about your strategy. What do you do?
    Why it is asked: Navigating a multi-party client.
    How to think about it: As a junior, nothing unilateral: record it accurately and tell your senior. In principle, do not play one off against the other; give both the same accurate information and let the client's governance resolve it.
  2. Your main contact leaves. What happens to the relationship?
    Why it is asked: Institutional versus personal relationship.
    How to think about it: If the knowledge is in the CRM and several people on both sides know each other, little is lost. If it lived in one person's head, a lot is. See Chapter 7 on relationship knowledge as organisational knowledge.
  3. Who is the client in third-party wealth?
    Why it is asked: Transfer of the idea.
    How to think about it: The intermediary firm, acting through fund selectors, a committee and advisers, with an end investor you never meet. Same principle: several roles, different needs.

Tell me about a recent development that matters to our clients.

Commercial awareness IQ-21

Underlying argument
Choose one event and follow the chain: what happened, how it reaches the client, what decision changes, what it means for existing investments, what a manager might usefully do, and the counterargument. Example: on 5 November 2026 the Bank of England raised Bank Rate to 4% by an 8 to 1 vote, the first rise since August 2023, with the 10-year gilt yield around 5.15% that day R3-S31 and CPI at 3.5% in September R8-S49. For a UK defined benefit scheme, higher yields lower the present value of liabilities; a hedged scheme's matching assets fall too, and leveraged hedges call for collateral. Funding was already strong: 133.7% on the PPF 7800 measure at end October R3-S29. Layer B · interpretation Decisions that may change: whether to lock in funding by de-risking, whether buyout pricing has become more attractive, whether liquidity buffers are adequate. A manager's useful response is to help the client check collateral headroom and review the endgame plan, not to push a product. Counterargument: one rate move rarely changes a long-term strategy, and schemes hedged close to 100% are largely indifferent.

Depends on: Verified: the Bank Rate decision, gilt yield, CPI and PPF funding figures. The mechanism and implications are Layer B. A personal view is welcome if labelled as a view. R3-S31 R8-S49 R3-S29

A weak answer, and why it is weak
Interest rates have gone up recently, which is making markets volatile, so clients are nervous and looking for safe investments. That's a great opportunity for Goldman to offer its fixed income products.

No date, no number, no mechanism. It does not say which clients or why they would be affected, and it jumps to a product sale. It would not survive 'how exactly does a rate rise affect a pension scheme?'.

About 30 seconds

The Bank of England raised Bank Rate to four per cent on the fifth of November, its first rise since 2023. For a UK pension scheme, higher gilt yields shrink the value of its liabilities. If it's hedged, its matching assets fall as well and it may have to post collateral. So the practical questions are whether the liquidity buffer is big enough and whether it's a moment to lock in a strong funding position.

About 60 to 90 seconds

I'd pick the Bank of England's decision on the fifth of November to raise Bank Rate to four per cent. It was the first increase since 2023, and ten-year gilt yields were a little above five per cent. Here's why I think it matters to a UK pension client. A scheme's liabilities are valued using gilt yields, so when yields go up, the liabilities get smaller. Most schemes hedge that, which means the assets they hold for hedging fall in value too. Where the hedge uses leverage, the scheme has to post more collateral, sometimes quickly. So the first question for a client isn't about returns at all. It's whether there's enough liquid collateral if yields move further. The second is strategic. Schemes are already well funded in aggregate, around 134 per cent on the Pension Protection Fund's measure. Higher yields can make insurer pricing more attractive, so some trustees will ask whether to bring a buyout forward. What a manager can usefully do is help the client stress-test its collateral and revisit its plan, and that may or may not involve anything new. I'd add the counterpoint. A scheme that's almost fully hedged is largely unaffected, and one rate decision shouldn't rewrite a long-term strategy. I'd want to know the client's hedge ratio before saying anything specific.

Harder follow-ups
  1. Why does a higher yield reduce liabilities?
    Why it is asked: Do you understand the mechanism or just the headline?
    How to think about it: Liabilities are future payments discounted to today. A higher discount rate makes each future pound worth less now, so the total present value falls. Long-dated payments are most sensitive. See duration in Chapter 1.
  2. So what would you sell them?
    Why it is asked: The product-push trap.
    How to think about it: Possibly nothing. Start with what they need to check. If a need emerges (collateral, cashflow-matching credit), specialists propose. Say plainly that not every market change is a reason to sell.
  3. What would change your view?
    Why it is asked: Thinking in scenarios.
    How to think about it: If inflation fell quickly and the Bank reversed, urgency would fade. If yields rose sharply, collateral stress would dominate. Name the indicators: CPI prints, the MPC vote split, gilt auction demand.

What is the biggest challenge facing active asset managers?

Commercial awareness IQ-22

Underlying argument
Fee pressure from low-cost alternatives combined with costs that grow faster than revenue. Evidence: BCG reports institutional fees falling about 3% a year, margins near 30%, and from 2010 to 2025 revenues growing 5.1% a year against costs at 5.4% R8-S38. Goldman lists the move to passive and lower-fee products as a risk to its average effective management fee R2-S01. BlackRock took $135bn into iShares ETFs in one quarter of 2026 R8-S02. In UK fiduciary management fees fell about 27% over five years R8-S10. Layer B · interpretation Responses visible in public: move toward areas where clients still pay for scarcity or responsibility (alternatives at 58bp against 17bp for fixed income at Goldman R2-S01; OCIO; active ETFs), and consolidate for scale (Nuveen completed its acquisition of Schroders in October 2026) R8-S08. Limits: alternatives carry liquidity and valuation risk, private-credit redemption limits are a live concern, and scale deals often disappoint. For coverage, the consequence is that price is discussed in more conversations and 'what are we paying for?' needs a concrete answer.

Depends on: Verified: BCG data, the 10-K risk factor, Goldman's effective fee rates, iShares flows, the Schroders acquisition. The interpretation is Layer B. No personal evidence needed. R8-S38 R2-S01 R8-S02 R8-S10 R8-S08

A weak answer, and why it is weak
Market volatility and geopolitical uncertainty make it very hard for active managers to outperform, but that also creates opportunities for skilled stock pickers like Goldman.

Volatility is a condition, not a structural challenge, and the answer has no evidence. It ends with an unsupported compliment. It misses the fee and cost dynamic the interviewer deals with daily.

About 30 seconds

Getting paid. Clients can buy market exposure for almost nothing, so they question every active fee, and costs have been rising faster than revenue across the industry. Goldman's own filings name the shift to lower-fee products as a risk. The response you can see is managers moving towards things clients still pay for, private markets and delegated mandates, and merging for scale. Each of those has its own risks.

About 60 to 90 seconds

I'd say it's the squeeze between falling fees and rising costs. On the fee side, a client can now buy broad market exposure through an index fund or ETF for a few basis points, so any active fee has to be justified. Consultancy data puts institutional fee declines at around three per cent a year, and in UK fiduciary management fees have dropped by roughly a quarter in five years. Goldman says in its annual report that if clients keep moving to lower-fee products, its average fee will fall further. On the cost side, the same data shows industry costs growing slightly faster than revenues for fifteen years: technology, regulation, data. What are firms doing about it? Two things stand out. One is shifting towards areas where the client is paying for something scarce or for responsibility. At Goldman, alternatives earn around 58 basis points against 17 for fixed income, and OCIO is growing. The other is scale through mergers. Schroders became part of Nuveen last month. I wouldn't call either a solution. Private assets are illiquid and harder to value, and there are already concerns about redemption limits in some private credit funds. For someone in client coverage, the practical effect is that price comes up more often, and you need a specific answer to the question of what the client is getting for the fee.

Harder follow-ups
  1. So is active management dying?
    Why it is asked: Resisting an extreme.
    How to think about it: No evidence for that. Active assets remain very large; the pressure is on undifferentiated active at high fees. Distinguish segments, and say what evidence would shift your view (sustained outflows across active fixed income, for instance).
  2. A client says your fee is double a passive fund's. What do you say?
    Why it is asked: Applying the theme to a conversation.
    How to think about it: As a junior you would not negotiate. In principle: be clear what the strategy does that an index cannot, show net-of-fee results honestly, and accept that if the client only needs the exposure, passive may be right. See practice case PC-02.
  3. Why are private markets the answer if they're risky?
    Why it is asked: Counterargument awareness.
    How to think about it: They are a response, not 'the answer'. Higher fees reflect illiquidity, complexity and capacity limits. Suitability depends on the client's horizon and liquidity needs; for a scheme near buyout they are usually unhelpful.

How will AI change this job?

Commercial awareness IQ-23

Underlying argument
Analyse tasks, not the whole role, and separate what is observed from what is forecast. Observed: Cerulli finds 81% of institutional sales and service teams use AI to generate and refine RFP content and 77% for meeting notes and summaries R8-S41; Isio finds 85% of fiduciary management firms use AI, mainly for efficiency tasks such as drafting reports and emails and not for investment decisions R8-S10. Layer B · interpretation So first drafts of RFP answers, meeting summaries, routine report commentary and research collation are already being automated. Tasks that need supervision: anything sent to a client must be checked against source and approved, since firms remain accountable for accuracy. Uncertain: whether clients will accept AI-mediated service for complex questions; how junior training changes when the drafting that taught the basics is done by a tool. Do not claim human relationships are automatically irreplaceable: for standard queries, speed and consistency may make a tool better. Where a person adds measurable value: judging fit, handling exceptions and bad news, and being accountable.

Depends on: Verified: Cerulli and Isio survey findings. Forecasts must be labelled as forecasts. Personal: honest description of how I use such tools and check their output, if asked. R8-S41 R8-S10

A weak answer, and why it is weak
AI will automate the boring tasks, but it can never replace the human touch. Relationships are built on trust and that will always need people, so this job is safe.

A comforting slogan with no evidence and no task detail. 'Never' and 'always' are unprovable. It ignores that the 'boring tasks' are most of a junior's work and how juniors learn.

About 30 seconds

I'd look at it task by task. Drafting is already changing: survey data says most institutional sales teams use AI for RFP content and meeting notes. That's much of what a junior does. What it doesn't remove is checking that every figure is right, judging whether something fits this client, and being accountable for what was said. I wouldn't claim people are irreplaceable. For routine queries a tool may simply be better.

About 60 to 90 seconds

I think the honest way to answer is by task, and to keep apart what's already happened from what's a guess. What's already happened: one industry survey this year found about four in five institutional sales and service teams use AI to produce RFP content, and nearly as many for meeting notes. A survey of UK fiduciary managers found most use it for drafting reports and emails, but not for investment decisions. So the first draft of a questionnaire response or a meeting summary, which is classic junior work, is increasingly done by a tool. What still needs a person, at least for now, is the checking and the judgement. Anything that goes to a client has to be accurate and approved, and the firm is accountable for it. Someone has to notice that a standard answer doesn't fit this client's situation. And difficult conversations, a bad quarter or a mistake, need someone who can be held to what they say. What I'm less sure about is two things. Whether clients come to prefer a fast, consistent tool for routine questions. I suspect many will. And how juniors learn the basics if they stop writing first drafts. My own approach would be to use the tools, verify everything against source, and deliberately learn the content, not just pass it along.

Harder follow-ups
  1. If the drafting is automated, why do we need you?
    Why it is asked: Blunt version of the same question.
    How to think about it: For verification, context and follow-through now; and because the firm needs people who will grow into the judgement roles. Do not oversell. Acknowledge fewer juniors may be needed per team.
  2. Did you use AI to prepare for this interview?
    Why it is asked: Honesty, and whether your understanding is your own.
    How to think about it: Answer truthfully. If yes: say how you checked facts against primary sources and that the views you are giving are ones you can defend unaided. Never use it during a live or recorded interview.
  3. Where could AI serve clients better than a person?
    Why it is asked: Willingness to concede the point.
    How to think about it: Instant answers to factual queries, consistent reporting commentary, searching long documents, out-of-hours availability. Say so; it shows you are analysing, not defending.

I'm the trustee chair of a mid-sized pension scheme. What should we be talking about?

Commercial awareness IQ-24

Underlying argument
This is a discovery test disguised as a pitch request. The right response is a small number of well-chosen questions and then a view conditional on the answers, because the relevant topic depends on facts not yet known: funding level, hedge ratio, endgame target and governance capacity. Context that makes the questions pointed: aggregate funding is strong (133.7% PPF 7800 at end October 2026) R3-S29; yields are high and rates have just risen R3-S31; the Pension Schemes Act 2026 received Royal Assent in April R3-S20; buy-in volumes by number hit a record in 2025, mostly small deals R3-S27. Layer B · interpretation A mid-sized scheme's live topics are likely to be: endgame choice and timing; collateral and liquidity resilience; whether the governance burden justifies delegation; cost. A junior would not lead this conversation, so the answer should show the thinking, not role-play seniority.

Depends on: Verified: funding, rates, Act and buy-in data. The topic list is Layer B. No personal evidence needed. R3-S29 R3-S31 R3-S20 R3-S27

A weak answer, and why it is weak
I'd talk to you about our private credit fund. It offers attractive yields with low volatility, and many pension schemes are increasing their allocations, so it could be a great fit for your portfolio.

It proposes a product before learning anything about the scheme. An illiquid fund may be exactly wrong for a scheme two years from buyout. It is the behaviour that makes trustees distrust salespeople.

About 30 seconds

Before suggesting anything I'd want to ask three things. How well funded are you, and how much of your rate and inflation risk is hedged? What's your target: buyout, running on, or undecided? And how much time does your board have for investment decisions? Depending on the answers, the useful conversation might be about collateral, about preparing for an insurer, or about delegation. It might also be that you need nothing new from us.

About 60 to 90 seconds

If I may, I'd start by asking you some questions, because I don't think I can say anything useful without them. First, where is the scheme on funding, and how much of the interest rate and inflation risk is hedged? I ask because schemes in aggregate are well funded at the moment, and the Bank of England has just raised rates, so the issues are very different for a fully hedged scheme and one that isn't. Second, what are the trustees aiming for? If it's a buyout in the next few years, the conversation is about getting the portfolio into a shape an insurer will accept, and about liquidity. If you're considering running on, it's about assets that pay the pensions as they fall due, and about the new legislation on surplus. Third, how is the board's time? For a mid-sized scheme, the governance load is often the real constraint, and that's where delegation to a fiduciary manager sometimes makes sense, through a proper tender. I'd be cautious about anything illiquid until I knew your timeline. And I should be straightforward that, in reality, a senior colleague would lead this conversation and I'd be preparing for it. But that's the order I'd want the questions asked in.

Harder follow-ups
  1. We're 105% funded, 90% hedged, targeting buyout in three years. Now what?
    Why it is asked: Can you reason from the answers?
    How to think about it: Priorities: protect the funding position, close the remaining hedge gap if affordable, move toward assets insurers accept, keep liquidity, avoid new illiquid commitments, and get data and benefits cleaned up. Much of this is not an asset-management sale.
  2. You haven't recommended anything. Isn't that a wasted meeting?
    Why it is asked: Pressure to push product.
    How to think about it: A first meeting that establishes the client's position accurately is the basis for any later proposal. Recommending without it risks an unsuitable suggestion. Offer a concrete next step instead.
  3. What would make you bring up private markets?
    Why it is asked: Conditions for suitability.
    How to think about it: A long horizon (run-on), tolerance for illiquidity, governance capacity to oversee it, and a cashflow need the assets fit. Absent those, do not raise it.

What does it mean to build trust with a client?

Trust and relationships IQ-25

Underlying argument
Trust is the client's justified expectation about how you will behave when they cannot check. It has to be translated into components and observable behaviour: competence (what you say about a strategy is correct), reliability (you do what you said, when you said), honesty (you report bad news and limits unprompted), and putting the client's interest ahead of a short-term sale (you say when something does not fit). Layer B · interpretation It is built in small, checkable acts: a number in a pack that matches the source; a call returned on the day promised; 'I don't know, I'll confirm by Thursday' followed by an answer on Thursday. It is not friendliness, and it does not replace verification: UK trustees must still tender before appointing a fiduciary manager R3-S24 and clients run due diligence regardless of rapport. Trust reduces the client's cost of monitoring; it does not remove their duty to monitor. Layer C · personal fit A junior builds it mainly through accuracy and follow-through.

Depends on: Verified: the tender requirement as an example of process continuing regardless of trust. Personal: [my own example: a time someone relied on me because I had been accurate or had told them something unwelcome]. R3-S24

A weak answer, and why it is weak
Building trust is about forming a genuine personal connection, being friendly and approachable, and always being there for the client so they feel valued.

It describes rapport. A client can like someone and still not rely on their numbers. Nothing here is observable or testable, and it ignores honesty about limits, which is where trust is actually won or lost.

About 30 seconds

I'd define it as the client being able to rely on what you say when they can't check it themselves. In practice that's small things. The figures you send are right. You do what you said by when you said. You tell them bad news before they find it. And you say when something of ours doesn't fit. It isn't the same as being liked, and it doesn't replace their own due diligence.

About 60 to 90 seconds

I think the word gets used loosely, so I'd pin it down. Trust is a client being willing to rely on you where they can't easily verify. For that to be justified, a few things have to be true, and each one shows up in behaviour. Competence: when you explain how a strategy works, you're right, and you know where your knowledge ends. Reliability: if you said the report would arrive Tuesday, it arrives Tuesday. Honesty: when performance is poor or there's been an error, they hear it from you first, with the facts. And a willingness to put their interest first in the moment, which mostly means being prepared to say 'I don't think this is right for you'. For a junior, I think nearly all of it comes down to accuracy and follow-through. One wrong number in a quarterly pack makes a client wonder about the rest. I'd add two cautions. It isn't friendliness. A client can enjoy your company and still double-check everything you send. And it doesn't replace process. Trustees still have to run tenders and due diligence however good the relationship is, and they should. What trust changes is how much effort the client has to spend watching you. My own evidence for valuing this is [my own example: a time someone relied on me because I'd been accurate or told them something unwelcome].

Harder follow-ups
  1. Give me an example of when being trustworthy would cost you a sale.
    Why it is asked: Is the principle real when it is expensive?
    How to think about it: A prospect asks whether your strategy suits a three-year horizon and it does not. Saying so loses the sale and usually wins a better conversation later. A junior flags the mismatch to the senior; they do not decide alone.
  2. How is trust different from a good relationship?
    Why it is asked: Precision.
    How to think about it: A relationship can be warm and still not relied on. Trust is specific: trusted to do what, by whom? See the five meanings of 'relationship' in Chapter 7.
  3. If the client trusts you, why do they need a 200-question DDQ?
    Why it is asked: Trust versus controls.
    How to think about it: Because their duty is to their members, not to you, and individuals change. Formal checks protect both sides. Trust makes the process smoother; it is not a substitute.

When would the client be right to leave?

Trust and relationships IQ-26

Underlying argument
Retention is not automatically a good outcome. A client is right to leave when staying no longer serves its objective. Layer B · interpretation Cases: (1) the need has ended, for example a defined benefit scheme insuring its liabilities; there were a record 370 UK buy-in transactions in 2025 R3-S27; (2) the strategy has persistently failed to do what it was hired to do after a fair period, as when Pensioenfonds Vervoer terminated a roughly €7bn Goldman mandate in 2010 citing underperformance R7-S48; (3) the people or process that were hired have changed materially; (4) the same exposure is available at materially lower cost and the client needs nothing more; (5) a breach of guidelines, a serious error or loss of confidence in the manager's candour. Cases where leaving may be wrong: short-term underperformance consistent with the stated style, or switching into last year's winner. The coverage professional's part: give accurate information so the decision is well made, do not obstruct, run a clean exit, and keep the relationship. Revenue is lost either way if the fit has gone; credibility is lost only if the firm behaves badly.

Depends on: Verified: UK buy-in volumes; the Vervoer termination. The framework is Layer B. Personal: optional example of advising someone against my own interest. R3-S27 R7-S48

A weak answer, and why it is weak
If we're doing our job properly the client should never need to leave. I'd work hard to understand any concerns and do whatever it takes to keep them.

It treats retention as the goal and the client's departure as a failure to be prevented. 'Whatever it takes' is alarming to anyone who has seen a manager obstruct a justified exit. It never answers the question.

About 30 seconds

When staying no longer serves what they hired us for. If a pension scheme reaches buyout, the assets should go to the insurer. If a strategy has failed over a fair period to do what it was appointed to do, or the team that was hired has gone, or they can get the same thing much cheaper and need nothing more. In those cases the job is to make the exit clean and stay credible.

About 60 to 90 seconds

I think there are several situations, and it's worth being specific, because 'never' is the wrong answer. The clearest is when the need has gone. A pension scheme that insures its liabilities hands assets to the insurer, and that can be the right result for its members. There were hundreds of those transactions in the UK last year. Second, when the strategy hasn't done its job over a reasonable period. That happens to every firm. A Dutch pension fund ended a large mandate with Goldman back in 2010 and cited underperformance. Third, when what the client hired has changed: the portfolio manager leaves, or the process drifts. Fourth, when they can get the same exposure for a lot less and aren't using anything beyond it. And fifth, if there's been a serious error or they've stopped believing what they're told. There are also times when leaving would be a mistake, like selling a manager after one bad year that's entirely in line with its style. In that case the right thing is to explain clearly and let them decide. In all of this, I think the coverage person's job is the same: give the client accurate information, don't get in the way of a good decision, and make any exit smooth. The fee is lost either way. Whether the firm is trusted with the next mandate depends on how it behaved.

Harder follow-ups
  1. Your bonus depends on retention. Still the same answer?
    Why it is asked: Incentive conflict made personal.
    How to think about it: Acknowledge the conflict exists. Then: a retained client who should have left becomes a worse problem later, consultants remember, and the firm's conduct rules require acting with integrity. Say you would raise a concern internally if pressured.
  2. How do you tell a justified exit from an overreaction?
    Why it is asked: Judgement.
    How to think about it: Compare the outcome with what was promised and the stated style, over the agreed horizon. Has anything structural changed? Is the client reacting to one period? Give them the evidence either way.
  3. What do you actually do during an exit?
    Why it is asked: Concrete behaviour at junior level.
    How to think about it: Help coordinate the transition timetable with operations and the client's transition manager, make sure final reporting is accurate and prompt, record the reasons in the CRM, and stay courteous. People move to other schemes.

Clients buy performance, not relationships. So why does coverage matter?

Trust and relationships IQ-27

Underlying argument
Partly concede: over time, a strategy that fails its objective will lose the mandate however good the service, as public terminations show R7-S48. Then show what performance alone cannot do. Layer B · interpretation (1) Before appointment, performance is a track record, which is evidence about the past; the client is buying future behaviour and needs to understand process, people and fit, which is what due diligence and the formal tender test R3-S24. (2) Fit: a strategy with strong returns can be wrong for a client's liabilities or liquidity. (3) During the mandate, the client needs to know why results are what they are, in time to act; unexplained underperformance gets a manager fired faster than explained underperformance. (4) Needs change, and someone has to notice. (5) In delegated mandates, the client is buying responsibility and service as much as returns: BAE Systems transferred its team R3-S01. Limit: coverage cannot rescue a bad product for long, and where a client only needs cheap exposure, coverage adds little.

Depends on: Verified: the tender requirement, the BAE appointment and the Vervoer termination as bookends. Layer B reasoning. No personal evidence needed. R7-S48 R3-S24 R3-S01

A weak answer, and why it is weak
I disagree. People buy from people, and at the end of the day it's all about relationships. If clients like and trust you they'll stay with you even through bad performance.

It replaces one slogan with another. 'They'll stay through bad performance because they like you' describes inertia, which is not something to be proud of, and institutional clients have duties that prevent it.

About 30 seconds

There's truth in it. No relationship keeps a mandate that fails for long. But performance is only known afterwards. Before they appoint you, the client is judging process and fit. During the mandate they need to understand why results are what they are, early enough to act. And their needs change. Coverage is how those things happen. Where a client just wants cheap market exposure, I'd agree it matters much less.

About 60 to 90 seconds

I'd agree with half of that. If a strategy keeps failing to do what it was hired for, no amount of service saves it, and it shouldn't. Clients do terminate large mandates for underperformance. But I think 'they buy performance' skips some steps. At the point of hiring, nobody can buy future performance. They have a track record, and what they're really assessing is whether the process and the people are likely to repeat it, and whether the strategy fits their particular liabilities and constraints. That's what a tender and due diligence are for, and the coverage team is who the client deals with through it. A strategy with great numbers can still be wrong for a scheme that needs liquidity in two years. Then, once the money is invested, results arrive with noise. A client who understands why a quarter was poor, and whether it's consistent with the approach, makes a better decision than one who's left guessing. And needs change. Someone has to notice that a scheme has moved closer to buyout and the mandate should shrink. In delegated mandates it goes further: the client is buying responsibility and reporting, not only return. Where I'd concede the point fully is commoditised exposure. If all a client wants is an index at the lowest cost, coverage adds very little, and it would be dishonest to pretend otherwise.

Harder follow-ups
  1. So is coverage just explaining away bad results?
    Why it is asked: Cynical reading.
    How to think about it: No: an explanation has to be accurate and include what would make the manager wrong. If results are inconsistent with the stated process, coverage should say that internally and expect the client to act. Spin destroys the trust it is trying to protect.
  2. Can you measure the value coverage adds?
    Why it is asked: Rigour.
    How to think about it: Imperfectly: retention against comparable mandates, share of existing clients adding assets, consultant ratings, client surveys, errors and complaints. Attribution is shared with investment teams, so be modest.
  3. Would clients be better off dealing directly with portfolio managers?
    Why it is asked: Is the middle role needed?
    How to think about it: Sometimes they do, and coverage arranges it. But a manager spending days on client queries is not managing money, and the client needs someone accountable across strategies, contracts and service.

A client asks you a technical question and you don't know the answer. What do you do?

Difficult conversations IQ-28

Underlying argument
Layer B · interpretation The costs are asymmetric: saying 'I don't know' costs a moment of discomfort; a confident wrong answer can lead to a wrong decision and, once discovered, casts doubt on everything else you have said. Communications with clients must be fair, clear and not misleading, which a guess presented as fact is not. The behaviour: say plainly that you do not know or are not certain; repeat the question back to make sure you have it exactly; say who will answer and by when; write it down; follow up on time, even if only to say the answer needs another day. If you know part of it, say which part you are sure of. A junior should also know which questions they must never answer themselves: views on what to buy, fees, legal terms, forward-looking performance. Layer C · personal fit Personal evidence helps here: a real occasion of admitting a gap.

Depends on: No Goldman fact needed. Personal: [my own example: a time I said I did not know, what I did next, and what happened].

A weak answer, and why it is weak
I'd use my general knowledge to give the best answer I could and keep the conversation flowing, because it's important to always appear confident and knowledgeable in front of clients.

It recommends bluffing. In a regulated business where clients act on what they are told, appearing knowledgeable matters far less than being right. It is the answer most likely to worry an interviewer.

About 30 seconds

I'd say I don't know. Something like: 'I'm not certain, and I'd rather not guess. Let me check I've understood the question. I'll come back to you by tomorrow afternoon with an answer from the portfolio team.' Then I'd write it down, get the answer from the right person, and reply when I said I would. A wrong answer given confidently does far more damage than a short delay.

About 60 to 90 seconds

I'd tell them I don't know, and I'd try to do it in a way that's useful. The words would be something like: 'I don't want to give you an answer I'm not sure of. Can I check I've got the question right?' Then I'd repeat it back, because half the time the question is more specific than it first sounded. Then: 'I'll take that to the portfolio specialist and come back to you by tomorrow afternoon.' After the call I'd write the question down exactly, take it to the right person, and make sure the reply goes out by the time I gave. If the answer isn't ready, I'd still get in touch then to say so. If I knew part of it, I'd say which part I was confident of and which I wasn't. The reasoning is simple. The client may act on what I say. If I guess and I'm wrong, the best case is embarrassment and the worst is a bad decision. And once a client catches one confident mistake, they recheck everything else. There's also a category of question I shouldn't answer even if I think I know: whether they should buy something, what the fee would be, anything legal. Those go to the people responsible. My own example of this is [my own example: a time I admitted not knowing and what I did next].

Harder follow-ups
  1. The senior on the call looks at you to answer. Still say you don't know?
    Why it is asked: Social pressure.
    How to think about it: Yes, briefly and without drama, and offer what you do know. The senior would much prefer that to a wrong figure they later have to correct with the client.
  2. What if you're 90% sure?
    Why it is asked: Calibrating confidence.
    How to think about it: Say so: 'I believe it is X, but let me confirm.' State the answer and the uncertainty together, then confirm in writing. Never round 90% up to certain.
  3. How do you stop it happening again?
    Why it is asked: Learning.
    How to think about it: Learn the answer properly, not just relay it. Keep a list of questions you could not answer. After a few weeks it shows exactly what to study.

A strategy has underperformed its benchmark for three quarters. How should that be explained to the client?

Difficult conversations IQ-29

Underlying argument
Layer B · interpretation The client needs four things: the facts stated plainly and early (how much, over what period, net of fees); the causes, separated into what was a deliberate position and what was a mistake or bad luck; whether the result is within what the strategy was described as capable of; and what, if anything, is changing. The explanation belongs to the portfolio team; coverage ensures it reaches the client promptly, in a form they can use, with the same message for trustees and consultant. What must not happen: burying the number, cherry-picking periods, blaming 'the market' when the benchmark is the market, or reassurance without reasons. The client may conclude the strategy no longer fits, and that is their right. A junior's part: accurate attribution data in the pack, checked to source; a briefing note anticipating questions; a clear record of what was said and promised.
