Client Solutions Group

Level 1 · First principles

What it is. The part of the asset manager that finds clients, proposes how the firm could manage their money, and looks after them once they have appointed it. Why it exists. Portfolio managers are employed to invest. Someone else has to understand each client's situation, bring the right specialists to the conversation and keep the relationship working. Who uses it. Pension schemes, insurers, sovereign funds, endowments, and the wealth firms that choose funds for their own customers.

Level 2 · Institutional mechanics

Two levels of meaning. The name is used for the whole global organisation ("Global Client Solutions Group") and, more loosely, as a synonym for sales. ✔ Verified R1-S13 R1-S09 Not new business only. The London-based BeNeLux advertisement says "The BeNeLux Client Solutions Group is responsible for new business development and managing existing institutional client relationships". ✔ Verified R1-S01 Labels move. A mirror of that same advertisement dated 12 October 2026 calls the team "The BeNeLux Institutional Sales Team" and keeps an earlier title, "Institutional Sales Support (Dutch Speaking)". The live official page now says "Client Solutions Group". ✔ Verified R1-S19 One team, two labels, within weeks.

Client Coverage Group

Level 1 · First principles

What it is. A named group focused on clients the firm already has. Its job is to make sure an existing client is served accurately and on time, and that problems reach the right internal team. What actually happens. Queries are answered, reports are delivered, new accounts are set up, accounts are restructured or closed, and questionnaires and audit requests are completed.

Level 2 · Institutional mechanics

Goldman's definition continues: "by ensuring exceptional client service, operational support, and risk management. This involves partnering closely with the sales team, keeping them abreast of recent interactions with clients". The advertisement makes the holder the main point of contact across "Portfolio Management, Trading, Operations, Legal, and Compliance", and its own name for the job is "Client Experience Manager". ✔ Verified R1-S11 That advertisement is for Hong Kong. For London, the label appears only in search-result titles: a "CCG Client Relationship Manager" at Vice President level and a "Client Coverage Group Analyst", with a snippet saying the role is "responsible for the management and retention of our existing client relationships". Those pages had expired. ≈ Supported inference R1-S32 A "CCG Analyst" title has also been seen for The Hague. ≈ Supported inference R5-S14

Institutional sales and client relationship management

Level 1 · First principles

Institutional sales means winning mandates from large organisations that invest on behalf of others. Client relationship management means looking after those organisations once they are clients: explaining results, handling changes, and noticing when their needs shift. In plain terms, one side opens the door and the other keeps the house in order. Chapter 6 explains why that neat division is only a first approximation.

Level 2 · Institutional mechanics

Layer B · interpretation The public evidence does not show a single way of dividing these two jobs. The BeNeLux team does both under one name. R1-S01 The Hong Kong definition gives the coverage group "expanding" as well as "retaining", which is commercial work, and has it "partnering closely with the sales team". R1-S11 A relationship manager who grows an existing mandate is doing something a salesperson would recognise. Expect the split to depend on the team, the client segment and the seniority of the people involved.

Third-party wealth distribution

Level 1 · First principles

What it is. Selling funds to firms that then place them with their own customers: private banks, wealth managers, financial advisers and multi-managers. Why it exists. An asset manager cannot reach thousands of individual savers one by one. The wealth firm already has them. What can go wrong. A fund can be approved by the wealth firm and then never bought, because approval only makes a purchase possible.

Level 2 · Institutional mechanics

"Third Party Wealth" is a real public name, not the former intern's shorthand: a Goldman press release names an "EMEA Third Party Wealth Business". ✔ Verified R4-S01 Third Party Wealth appears as a named CSG sub-track in the 2027 Paris and Dubai listings. ✔ Verified R1-S06 R1-S07 A London-based analyst has been hired to support the "TPW Switzerland team", so at least some support for continental clients sits in London. ✔ Verified R1-S18 The firm's filings report the channel firmwide as "third-party distributed" and give no UK figure.

Consultant relations

Level 1 · First principles

What it is. A team that deals with investment consultants, the advisory firms that help pension trustees decide which managers to hire. Why it exists. In many institutional searches the consultant draws up the shortlist. If the consultant's researchers do not know and rate a strategy, the manager may never be invited to compete. How value moves. The consultant is paid by the client, not by the manager. The team's work produces no fee directly; it "creates a pipeline of business for the sales teams".

Level 2 · Institutional mechanics

The older advertisement says the team should "work closely with the regional institutional sales teams" and project-manages "operational due diligence requests across all GSAM products". ✔ Verified R1-S21 It describes the past: the page is undated and uses the older "GSAM" abbreviation. A snippet for a newer "Global Consultant Relations" Vice President role in London mentions covering "over 100 investment consultant firms worldwide", but that page could not be read. ≈ Supported inference R1-S34

Product specialists, client service and RFP support

Level 1 · First principles

Three supporting functions are easy to confuse with the coverage role.

  • A product specialist, also called an investment specialist or client portfolio manager, sits close to one investment team and explains its strategy to clients in depth. They speak for the strategy. They do not usually decide what it buys.
  • Client service handles reporting, account set-up and day-to-day operational requests.
  • RFP support writes the formal answers when a prospect issues a request for proposal (RFP) or a due-diligence questionnaire (DDQ).

Level 2 · Institutional mechanics

Layer A · verified fact What Goldman's advertisements show: the junior London sales-support role is told to "partner with product specialists on a wide range of Goldman Sachs Asset Management products". ✔ Verified R1-S01 The coverage-group advertisement lists "Strategic Client Services" and "Client Implementation" as separate teams. ✔ Verified R1-S11 RFP work is shared with investment teams: the OCIO insurance role includes responses to "RFIs, RFPs and site-visits". ✔ Verified R1-S15 Client portfolio manager titles appear in the site's search for the United States and India. No London client-portfolio-manager or RFP-team advertisement was live on the research date, so how those functions are organised in London is ∅ Not publicly established.

Testing "CSG means sales, CCG means relationship management"

The former intern said that within each team the sales side is called CSG and the relationship side is called CCG. Parts of that hold and parts do not.

Part of the claim What the advertisements show Status
CSG is an umbrella that roughly means "sales" Goldman's own titles say so ✔ Verified R1-S04 R1-S09
"CCG" stands for Client Coverage Group Yes, and it is a real group name ✔ Verified R1-S11
CCG is the existing-client side The official definition matches, and adds "expanding" ✔ Verified for Hong Kong; London wording seen in snippets only
CSG means winning new clients only Contradicted: a London CSG team also manages existing relationships ⇄ Conflicting evidence R1-S01
Inside each London team, "CSG" labels sales and "CCG" labels relationships No public source read shows this ∅ Not publicly established
CCG sits inside the CSG umbrella Not shown; the definition says "within Asset Management" ∅ Not publicly established

Layer B · interpretation A defensible working view: "CSG" names the whole sales organisation and is also used loosely to mean sales. "CCG" is a separate, named group that looks after existing clients and works alongside sales. How the line is drawn inside any one London team is team-dependent until someone on that team says otherwise. In an interview, describe the two kinds of work and ask how the team you are meeting divides them. Do not assert the acronyms as a fact about their desk.

What a Summer Analyst can realistically contribute

Level 1 · First principles

A summer analyst is there for about ten weeks, has no client relationships of their own and is not authorised to speak for the firm. What they can do is make the people who do hold those relationships better prepared and faster. That is real work. A meeting goes differently when the senior person has read an accurate one-page summary of the client's latest annual report than when they have not.

Layer A · verified fact Goldman publishes nothing about what a London CSG summer analyst does. ∅ Not publicly established R1-S22 The nearest official proxy is the task list in the two junior London advertisements, which are full-time roles at a higher level. ✔ Verified R1-S01 R1-S17 Their tasks are:

  • preparing for and following up client and prospect meetings;
  • answering day-to-day client queries on products and services;
  • working with product specialists, marketing, compliance and operations;
  • supporting the country head with "presentations focusing on market intelligence, business development, financial analysis and planning".

Layer B · interpretation A summer analyst would plausibly help with parts of these under supervision. The table below sets out who decides what. It describes general industry practice and is an inference, not a Goldman job architecture. ≈ Supported inference

Level Can do alone Can recommend Needs approval or belongs to others
Summer Analyst Research from public documents; first drafts; data checks; meeting notes Which facts matter for a meeting; a question worth asking Anything sent to a client; any statement about a product; all commercial terms
Analyst Maintain pipeline and client records; assemble meeting packs; route queries Who to target; what to include in a pitch Client-facing material goes through review and compliance; pricing belongs to seniors
Associate Run parts of a tender response; handle routine client contact Proposal structure; follow-up strategy Fee proposals; non-standard terms; investment content belongs to the investment team
Senior coverage professional Lead meetings; own the relationship day to day Fee concessions; resourcing; whether to bid Portfolio decisions belong to portfolio managers; legal terms to legal; large concessions to the team head

Level 2 · Institutional mechanics

Three boundaries that apply at every level.

  1. Investment decisions belong to the investment team. A coverage professional can explain why a portfolio manager bought something. They cannot promise that the manager will buy or sell anything. In an OCIO mandate, the delegated decisions sit with Multi-Asset Solutions, not with sales. R1-S15
  2. What a client is told is controlled. UK rules require communications to clients to be fair, clear and not misleading, so material is reviewed before it goes out. Chapter 6 covers the detail in its regulatory guardrails section.
  3. Suitability is the client's decision, taken with its advisers. Institutional clients have trustees, investment committees and consultants. The coverage team proposes; the client's governance disposes.

The app's Role comparison view puts any two or three of these roles side by side, including the functional roles (institutional sales, relationship management, third-party wealth, consultant relations, product specialist, client service and RFP).

How titles work

Level 1 · First principles

The ladder visible in Goldman's own listings and announcements runs: Summer Analyst, Analyst, Associate, Vice President, Managing Director, Partner. ✔ Verified R1-S26 R1-S27 R1-S29 Two points catch people out.

  • Executive Director is the same level as Vice President. Outside the United States, people at Vice President level are commonly called Executive Director. It is one rung with two names, not two rungs.
  • Partner is not the next automatic step after Managing Director. People are invited into a partner class.

Level 2 · Institutional mechanics

The evidence: listings titled "Executive Director" in London and Singapore carry the corporate title "Vice President", and the firm announces a single "Vice President and Executive Director Class". ✔ Verified R1-S10 R1-S26 The Partner Class of 2026 is "a group of 109 individuals who have been invited to become partners of Goldman Sachs as of January 1, 2027". ✔ Verified R1-S27 That release lists name, division and office only, so nobody can be placed in the Client Solutions Group from it. Several advertisements are titled "Analyst/Associate" or "Associate/Executive Director", which means one seat can be filled at more than one level. ✔ Verified R1-S01 R1-S29

For the interview format this means the people the former intern said you would meet (an analyst and associate, then a vice president "or similar", then a managing director) are plausible as levels, and "or similar" is very likely Executive Director. The sequence itself is his account only. ? Unverified account

What this job is not: boundaries with adjacent careers

Chapter 6 has a compact table of adjacent roles (Adjacent roles: what this job is not). This section explains where each one overlaps with client coverage and where the boundary falls, with one example each. All examples are fictional. ✎ Illustrative example

Investment banking. Overlap: both involve senior client relationships and pitching. Boundary: a banker advises a company on a transaction and is paid once when it completes. A coverage professional asks a client to delegate money for years and the firm is paid for as long as the money stays. Example: a water company's finance director hires a bank to arrange a bond issue. The trustees of that company's pension scheme, a legally separate body, hire an asset manager to run a credit portfolio. Same company name, different client, different decision-makers, different fee.

Markets sales and trading. Overlap: the word "sales", and knowledge of the same securities. Boundary: markets sales helps a client execute a trade today and the bank earns a spread. Asset management sales never executes anything; the product is ongoing management. Example: an insurer's dealing desk rings a bank's sales desk to buy £50 million of gilts. The same insurer's chief investment officer meets an asset manager's coverage team to decide whether to outsource a private credit allocation. The first conversation takes minutes, the second can take a year.

Portfolio management. Overlap: both need to understand the strategy and markets. Boundary: the portfolio manager decides what the fund owns and is accountable for performance. The coverage professional explains those decisions and carries the client's reaction back. Example: a fund lags its benchmark for three quarters. The portfolio manager decides whether to change positions. The relationship manager decides how and when the client hears about it, and who should be in the room.

Investment research. Overlap: reading, analysis, forming a view. Boundary: a research analyst studies securities or economies to inform investment decisions. A coverage analyst studies clients: their liabilities, governance, advisers and existing managers. Example: a research analyst models a utility's cash flows. A coverage analyst reads a pension scheme's annual report to find its funding level, its consultant and when its manager arrangements were last reviewed.

Private wealth advice. Overlap: long relationships built on confidence. Boundary: a private wealth adviser advises an individual on that individual's whole financial position. A coverage professional represents one manager to a professional client that has its own advisers. Example: a family's adviser recommends how to split the family's money across asset classes and managers. An asset manager's third-party wealth salesperson tries to get one fund onto that advisory firm's approved list. The adviser is the salesperson's client, and the family is the adviser's.

Fund operations. Overlap: onboarding, reporting and query handling touch both. Boundary: operations makes sure trades settle, assets are valued and records are correct. Coverage owns the client conversation about those things. Example: a client's custodian reports a different holding from the manager's report. Operations finds and fixes the break. The relationship side tells the client what happened and by when it will be resolved.

Investment consulting. Overlap: both spend their days with trustees and investment committees. Boundary: the consultant is paid by the client to be impartial between managers. The coverage professional is paid by one manager. Example: trustees ask their consultant which three managers should pitch for a mandate. The consultant-relations team at one of those managers spent the previous year making sure the consultant's researchers understood the strategy. Being open about which side you are on is part of being believed.

Four junior work products, and what each one changes

Chapter 6 shows a meeting preparation note, a pipeline update, a questionnaire extract, a performance-review outline and a follow-up plan. The four below are different documents, chosen because a junior person can plausibly draft them and because each links to a client outcome and a commercial consequence. The client, people and figures are invented. ✎ Illustrative example

Sample work product (fictional): 1. Client profile from public documents

Prospect: Halden Water Pension Scheme (fictional). Prepared for: coverage lead, before a first meeting. Sources: scheme annual report, statement of investment principles, implementation statement.

  • Size and type: £1.4bn, closed defined benefit scheme. Funding: 104% on the scheme's own measure at the last valuation.
  • Stated objective: reach a position to buy out with an insurer "within five to eight years".
  • Advisers: investment consultant named in the report; a professional independent trustee chairs the investment sub-committee.
  • Current managers: five, of which two run credit. Manager arrangements "last reviewed" three years ago.
  • Not stated: fees paid; whether a review is planned; views on illiquid assets. Do not assume.
  • Two questions worth asking: How does the buy-out timetable limit what the scheme can hold? Who leads on manager review, the sub-committee or the consultant?

Client outcome: the meeting starts from the scheme's own stated aims, so the trustees do not spend twenty minutes explaining what they have already published. Commercial consequence: the team can decide early whether it has anything relevant to offer. Finding out that it does not is also a result: it saves months of effort on both sides.

Sample work product (fictional): 2. Contact report after a meeting

Client: Halden Water Pension Scheme. Attendees: chair of trustees, pensions manager, consultant; coverage lead, product specialist, analyst (notes).

  • What they said: the buy-out target is firm. Illiquid assets are "a problem to be run off, not added to". The credit managers will be reviewed next spring.
  • What we said: outlined the short-dated credit capability. Did not discuss fees.
  • Commitments made by us: send the credit team's approach to buy-out-ready portfolios by Friday (owner: product specialist). Confirm whether weekly liquidity is available (owner: analyst to obtain answer from the investment team; not yet known).
  • Commitments made by them: the consultant will share the review timetable.
  • Next contact: after the timetable arrives.

Client outcome: every promise made in the room has an owner and a date, so nothing depends on memory. Commercial consequence: the record sits in the client system where the next person can read it. If the coverage lead moves on, the firm still knows what was said. Chapter 7 explains why knowledge trapped with one person is a risk to the relationship.

Sample work product (fictional): 3. Query log entry for an existing client

Client: Northmoor Endowment (fictional). Query received: Tuesday, from the finance officer. "The quarterly report shows a different year-to-date return from the figure your colleague quoted at the meeting."

  • Checked: the report shows the return after fees; the figure quoted in the meeting was before fees. Both are correct on their own basis. Difference: 0.3 percentage points.
  • Confirmed with: performance team (owner of the numbers).
  • Draft reply for the relationship manager to review: two sentences stating both figures, which basis each uses, and that future meeting materials will show both side by side.
  • Root cause noted: the meeting slide did not label the basis.

Client outcome: the finance officer gets an accurate answer within two days and can report to the investment committee without a discrepancy hanging over it. Commercial consequence: small unexplained differences are how confidence erodes. Fixing the label removes a recurring source of doubt. The analyst drafted the reply but did not send it: client communications are reviewed first.

Sample work product (fictional): 4. Fund comparison for a wealth gatekeeper

Intermediary: Castlebrook Wealth (fictional), fund research team. Request: "How does your global bond fund differ from the two we already hold?"

Our fund Fund A Fund B
Benchmark Global aggregate, hedged Same Unconstrained
Typical number of issuers From factsheet From factsheet From factsheet
Ongoing charge From factsheet From factsheet From factsheet
Largest loss in the last five years From factsheet From factsheet From factsheet
  • Where ours is weaker: higher ongoing charge than Fund A.
  • What only the investment team can answer: why duration was cut last year. Routed to the product specialist.
  • Compliance status: draft; not for distribution until reviewed.

Client outcome: the gatekeeper gets a like-for-like comparison built from public documents, including the point that counts against the fund, which they would have found anyway. Commercial consequence: a fund gets onto an approved list when the research team can defend the choice to its own investment committee. A comparison that hides the weak point makes that harder, not easier.

What remains unknown

These points were searched for and not found in public sources. They are open questions to ask, not gaps to fill with a guess.

  • Which London team a 2027 summer analyst joins, and how that is decided. ∅ Not publicly established
  • Whether London teams literally call their sales side "CSG" and their relationship side "CCG", and whether the Client Coverage Group sits inside or beside the Client Solutions Group. ∅ Not publicly established
  • How London organises product specialists, client service and RFP support. ∅ Not publicly established
  • London analyst pay. The figures in the former intern's account have no public support and no conclusion about role quality should be drawn from them. ? Unverified account
  • Whether final-round interviews are now in person. Official pages are silent. ∅ Not publicly established

Check your understanding

  1. The 2027 London listing contains no duties. Where, then, does any description of the summer analyst's work come from, and how should you word it?
  2. Give one piece of evidence that CSG means "sales" and one piece of evidence that a CSG team also manages existing clients.
  3. A client asks a relationship manager whether the fund will sell a holding that has fallen sharply. Who decides, and what can the relationship manager properly say?
  4. Why is the investment consultant not the asset manager's client, and why does the manager still have a team devoted to consultants?
  5. An "Executive Director" and a "Vice President" interview you on the same day. Which is more senior?
  6. In work product 1, which finding would lead the team to conclude it should not pursue the prospect, and why is that a useful outcome?

Teams and business structure

This chapter reconstructs how Goldman Sachs Asset Management's client business is organised in Europe, the Middle East and Africa (EMEA), and what each part of it actually sells to whom. It starts from the former intern's account, tests each piece against public sources, and keeps the two apart.

Three warnings before the detail.

  • Goldman Sachs does not publish an organisation chart for this business, and it discloses no revenue, assets, flows or headcount for the Client Solutions Group, for any EMEA client team or for the UK R2-S01. ✔ Verified Everything below is assembled from job adverts, press releases, trade press and one first-hand account.
  • A team name in a job advert shows that the name was in use on that date. It does not show who reports to whom.
  • Where the only source is the call with the former intern, the statement carries the badge ? Unverified account. Treat those as leads you could ask about, not as facts you could assert.

1. Why a single hierarchy misleads

Level 1 · First principles

Imagine a shop that sells to schools, to restaurants and to other shops, in nine countries, and has one product so different from the rest (say, ice) that it needs its own delivery vans. You could draw that business by country, by type of customer, or by product. Each drawing would be true and each would hide something. The people in it would also tell you they do one of two jobs: finding new customers, or looking after the ones the shop already has.

Goldman Sachs Asset Management's client business is like that. It can be cut four ways:

  1. By where the client is. UK and Ireland, Benelux, the Nordics, Germany and Austria, the Middle East and so on.
  2. By what kind of client it is. An institution investing its own pool of money, or an intermediary choosing funds for other people's money.
  3. By product line. Some products (cash funds, and whole-portfolio outsourcing) are different enough to have their own specialists.
  4. By job. Winning new business, or serving and keeping existing clients.

The analogy stops being accurate in one important place. A shop's customers buy goods and leave. An asset manager's clients hand over money that stays, under a contract, for years, and can be withdrawn. So "looking after existing customers" is not after-sales service. It is where most of the revenue sits.

Level 2 · Institutional mechanics

The former intern described a clean tree: coverage team (mostly regional), then client type inside each team, then sales versus relationship management inside each client type. ? Unverified account Public evidence supports all four cuts but not the tree.

  • Geography and channel cross each other. Job adverts show country or region teams (Benelux, Nordics, Germany and Austria, France, Italy, Switzerland) crossed with channel (Institutional, Third Party Wealth, Insurance, Liquidity) R1-S01R1-S05R1-S06R1-S18. ≈ Supported inference At the same time there are channel leaders above the countries: a co-head of EMEA Institutional Client Coverage R6-S02 and, until spring 2026, a head of the EMEA Third Party Wealth Business R4-S01R4-S02. ✔ Verified A UK institutional salesperson therefore sits in a geography and in a channel at once.
  • Some businesses are global verticals. Liquidity Solutions and Insurance each have named global heads R5-S01R5-S02. ✔ Verified They are not regions.
  • One "team" is not in the client organisation at all. The outsourced chief investment officer (OCIO) business sits within Multi-Asset Solutions, an investing group R6-S18R1-S15. ✔ Verified
  • The job split is real in name but blurred in practice. Goldman defines a Client Coverage Group "dedicated to retaining, expanding and supporting existing client relationships" R1-S11 ✔ Verified, yet a London Client Solutions Group team is described as "responsible for new business development and managing existing institutional client relationships" R1-S01. ✔ Verified

A matrix states this honestly. A tree would have to invent reporting lines to look complete.

3. What sits in London and what sits in local offices

Level 1 · First principles

London is the regional hub, but it is not where every European client is covered. The rule of thumb the evidence supports: the closer a role is to the client and the more it depends on the client's language, the more likely it sits in the client's country. The more it is support, product or UK-facing, the more likely it sits in London.

4. UK Institutional

Profile: UK Institutional.

Level 1 · First principles

An institutional client is an organisation investing a large pool of money that belongs to, or is owed to, other people: a pension scheme, a charity's endowment, a state investment fund. It buys investment management in big pieces, under a negotiated contract, after a formal selection. The team that covers UK institutions spends its time understanding what a small number of such organisations need, getting Goldman's strategies considered when they choose a manager, and keeping the organisations that have already hired it well served.

What is established about the team

The label "UK Institutional" is the former intern's. ? Unverified account The nearest public anchors are a 2026-cycle London campus listing titled "Client Solutions Group, UK Institutional Sales", seen only in a search result after the page expired R1-S31 ≈ Supported inference, and the senior title "head of the UK and Ireland institutional business", held by the person who is now co-head of EMEA Institutional Client Coverage R6-S05R6-S02. ✔ Verified Goldman's EMEA institutional marketing defines the institutional business as pension funds, endowments, foundations, sovereign wealth funds and insurers R1-S20. ✔ Verified A head of EMEA defined contribution within the Client Solutions Group was reported in June 2025 R6-S26. ≈ Supported inference

Not established: the current head of UK institutional sales, the size of the team, whether it is formally split into sales and relationship management, and which client types beyond pension schemes it covers day to day. ∅ Not publicly established

The clients, one type at a time

Chapter 1 explains defined benefit and defined contribution pensions, liability-driven investment and the chain from beneficiary to manager. This section adds what each client is trying to do in November 2026 and how it buys.

Level 2 · Institutional mechanics

Corporate defined benefit (DB) schemes. The scheme has promised pensions linked to salary and service. The promise is the liability. Trustees hold the assets and must invest in the best interests of members W2-S01; before investing they must obtain and consider proper advice W2-S02; they may delegate investment decisions to a fund manager W2-S03. ✔ Verified The sponsoring employer stands behind any shortfall.

  • Objective. Pay every pension, with as little reliance on the employer as possible.
  • Liabilities. Long, and sensitive to interest rates and inflation, which is why schemes hedge with liability-driven investment (LDI).
  • Liquidity. Rising. Most schemes are closed, so pensions paid out exceed contributions coming in, and LDI collateral calls need cash at short notice.
  • Position today. Strong. The 4,838 schemes in the Pension Protection Fund's index had an aggregate surplus of £275.4bn and a funding ratio of 133.7% at the end of October 2026 R3-S29R3-S30. ✔ Verified
  • The decision that follows. With a surplus, the question is the endgame: sell the liabilities to an insurer (a buy-in or buyout), or run the scheme on and use the surplus. 2025 saw a record 370 buy-ins but lower total premium, about £38bn R3-S27R3-S28. ✔ Verified The Pension Schemes Act 2026 makes it easier for trustees to release surplus to sponsors, with regulations expected in force in 2027 R3-S20. ✔ Verified
  • Governance. A trustee board, often with an investment sub-committee, meeting quarterly. Some lay trustees, some professional. Advised by an investment consultant.

Defined contribution (DC) master trusts and providers. Here there is no promise. Members' pots are invested in a default fund chosen by the provider.

  • Objective. Good member outcomes at a cost low enough to win employers.
  • Constraint. Price. Defaults are built to tight fee budgets, which limits what an active or private-markets manager can charge.
  • What is changing. Scale and private assets. Under the 2026 Act, master trust and group personal pension defaults must reach at least £25bn by 2030 or be on track by 2035 R3-S20. ✔ Verified Seventeen providers signed the voluntary Mansion House Accord in May 2025, aiming for 10% of default funds in private markets by 2030, at least half of it in the UK R3-S23. ✔ Verified
  • Governance. A small number of professional investment teams. Fewer, larger buyers every year.

The Local Government Pension Scheme (LGPS). Funded public-sector DB schemes run by local authorities.

  • Objective. Pay pensions while keeping employer (taxpayer) contributions stable. Open to new members, so the horizon is very long.
  • What has changed. Who chooses managers. From 30 June 2026 funds must delegate implementation of their investment strategy to their pool and take principal investment advice from it; the number of pools has fallen from eight to six R3-S21R3-S22. ✔ Verified
  • Consequence. Layer B · interpretation A manager now sells to six pools' investment teams, not to dozens of council committees. A mandate can be won or lost at pool level in one decision. The public record shows both for Goldman: an emerging-markets equity sleeve at Border to Coast in 2023 and a later change in another of its funds (M-R7-21, M-R7-22).

Endowments, foundations and charities. A pool meant to fund a purpose indefinitely.

  • Objective. Spend a steady amount each year while keeping the real value of the capital. There is no dated liability; there is a spending rule.
  • Liquidity. Low need, which is why this group can hold more private and illiquid assets than a mature pension scheme.
  • Governance. Trustees and an investment committee, often volunteers with senior investment backgrounds, usually advised by a consultant or an outsourced provider.
  • Caveat. This paragraph is general industry knowledge. ≈ Supported inference The research did not reach primary sources on UK charity investment rules before the search allowance ran out, and no public Goldman mandate from a UK endowment or charity was found. ∅ Not publicly established The former intern's project on endowments and foundations suggests the team researches them; it does not show they are clients. ? Unverified account

Sovereign and official institutions. Covered under the Middle East heading below, since that is where the public evidence sits.

How the selection actually runs

Level 1 · First principles

An institution rarely picks a manager by itself. It pays an investment consultant to advise it, and the consultant usually organises the search: writes the brief, draws up a list of managers it rates, sends out a long questionnaire, scores the answers and invites three or four managers to present in person. People in the industry call that last meeting a "beauty parade". The trustees decide; the consultant shapes what they see.

Level 2 · Institutional mechanics

This is why coverage has two audiences. The scheme (trustees, and the in-house investment staff where there are any) is the client. The consultant is the gatekeeper. A strategy with no consultant rating may never be shortlisted, whatever the relationship with the scheme. Consultant Relations exists for that second audience: Goldman's own description is that it works with the regional institutional sales teams and builds a pipeline for them R1-S21. ✔ Verified

In the public UK cases a named adviser ran or supported every selection: Redington for the BAE Systems trustees, Isio for Shell, PwC for Short Brothers, Barnett Waddingham for Calor R3-S02R3-S04R3-S15R7-S16. ✔ Verified The consulting sector is itself consolidating into larger groups R3-S34 ≈ Supported inference, which concentrates that gatekeeping in fewer firms (see D-R3-08).

Layer B · interpretation What the evidence suggests about the work. Almost every publicly named UK institutional relationship of Goldman's is a pension scheme, and most of the recent ones are OCIO appointments. That does not mean the institutional team only sells OCIO. Single-strategy mandates are rarely announced, so the public record is biased toward the large delegations that produce press releases. It does suggest that the most visible UK growth has come from schemes delegating more, which makes the boundary between "institutional sales" and "OCIO" a working relationship, not a wall.

5. UK Third Party Wealth

Profile: UK Third Party Wealth.

Level 1 · First principles

"Third party" means the wealth firm is someone else's, not Goldman's. A private bank or wealth manager looks after its own clients' money and needs funds to put it in. Goldman's Third Party Wealth team tries to get Goldman funds chosen by those firms. The team's client is the firm. The person whose savings end up in the fund is the firm's client, and the team will usually never meet them.

What is established about the team

"Third Party Wealth" is Goldman's own name. A press release names the "EMEA Third Party Wealth Business" R4-S01 and a job advert names the "UK Third Party Wealth (TPW) Sales Team", "responsible for new business development" with "private banks, wealth managers, financial advisors and multi-managers" R1-S17. ✔ Verified A second advert, seen through an aggregator, calls it the "UK & Ireland Third Party Wealth team" and adds funds of funds and independent financial advisers to the client list R4-S08. ≈ Supported inference Globally the business has two co-heads R6-S08 ✔ Verified; the EMEA head since 2021 left in spring 2026 and no successor had been named in the sources found R4-S02 (see D-R4-11). In Goldman's results the nearest reported channel is "Third-party distributed", $714bn of long-term assets under supervision at 30 September 2026 R2-S02 ✔ Verified, a firm-wide figure that is not proven to match the Third Party Wealth business in scope and says nothing about the UK.

Not established: the head of the UK and Ireland team, and whether it has a separate relationship-management side. The advert describes only new business development. ∅ Not publicly established

The intermediary chain

Level 2 · Institutional mechanics

Five different parties stand between the fund and the saver. Each can say no.

Link Who it is What it decides What it needs from the manager
Gatekeeper A fund selector or research analyst at the wealth firm Whether a fund is good enough to recommend internally Process, people, performance and risk evidence; access to the portfolio manager
Investment committee Senior investment staff Whether the fund goes on the approved (buy) list or into a model portfolio A clear role for the fund and a price that passes the firm's value test
Platform The administration system the firm deals and holds assets through Whether the right share class is available to buy Operational set-up, share-class terms, data feeds
Adviser or portfolio manager The person running client portfolios Whether to actually use an approved fund A reason to pick it over the other approved funds; updates they can pass on
End investor The private client Whether to invest at all, and to stay Nothing directly from the manager

Why being on the approved list does not guarantee assets. Layer B · interpretation Approval is permission, not a purchase. After it, separate people decide whether to allocate; the platform must carry the share class; and clients must have new money or be willing to switch. Each step can stall for reasons that have nothing to do with the fund. A buy list may hold several funds for the same slot, so approval can mean "one of four options". And firms increasingly run central model portfolios, where one committee's choice moves every client's money at once: the UK model portfolio market was reported at about £190bn R4-S37. ≈ Supported inference That raises the prize for being chosen and the cost of being removed. The fee calculator's two wealth cases show the arithmetic: the listing looks identical on day one whether advisers adopt the fund or ignore it.

The rules that shape the conversation. Platforms have been restricted in taking payments from fund providers since rules that took effect in April 2014 R4-S33, so shelf space cannot simply be bought. UK fund managers must assess the value of their funds at least annually R4-S32, and under the Consumer Duty, which has four outcomes including price and value R4-S31, distributors must be able to show their retail customers get fair value. ✔ Verified Most of Goldman's European funds are domiciled outside the UK, so the Overseas Funds Regime, under which EEA UCITS can be recognised for sale to UK retail investors, matters to what can be offered R4-S30. ✔ Verified The commercial effect is that price and evidence of value are part of every listing discussion (see D-R4-06).

What the team has to sell

Recent product moves are aimed squarely at this channel. Goldman entered European active exchange-traded funds in 2025 and said in April 2026 that it had launched 13 active ETFs in 2025 R4-S01R4-S17. ✔ Verified Its G-Series evergreen private-markets funds are sold through its own Private Wealth Management business and "select third-party distributors" R4-S19, and in March 2026 it added its first evergreen fund under the revised European long-term investment fund rules R4-S20. ✔ Verified A separate "Third Party Wealth Alternatives" team in EMEA specialises in these products R4-S11. ≈ Supported inference No Goldman Long-Term Asset Fund (the UK vehicle) and no UK model portfolio service were found. ∅ Not publicly established

One related point from the call checks out in part. Goldman's own Private Wealth Management describes an open-architecture alternatives platform that includes external managers R4-S27 ✔ Verified, so it is a buyer of other firms' products as well as a channel for Goldman's. The specific examples the former intern gave are not publicly established. ∅ Not publicly established

6. OCIO and fiduciary management

Profile: OCIO / fiduciary management. This is the area where the former intern's account needed the most correction, so it is treated at length.

Level 1 · First principles

Most pension trustees are not full-time investors. Running a multi-billion-pound portfolio means choosing an asset mix, hiring and firing a dozen specialist managers, hedging the liabilities, moving money between them and reporting on all of it. An outsourced chief investment officer is a firm the trustees hire to do that job for them. The trustees keep the big decisions (how much risk, what the goal is). The provider makes the day-to-day ones.

It is a different sale from "please hire us to run a bond portfolio". The client is handing over the keys, not buying one product.

Two names for nearly the same thing

Goldman uses "OCIO" and "fiduciary management" for this business and says the terms are used interchangeably and mean different things in different places R3-S08. ✔ Verified Its own working distinction is useful:

OCIO (Goldman's usage) Fiduciary management (Goldman's usage)
Who sets strategy Trustees, usually with a third-party adviser The manager advises, trustees approve
What is delegated Carrying out the agreed policy "All remaining functions", including asset allocation, reporting and analytics
Typical user, in Goldman's view Larger schemes with experienced in-house staff Smaller schemes with limited resources
Oversight Scheme staff or a third party Goldman suggests a separate strategic adviser

Source for the table: R3-S08. ✔ Verified It is one provider's framing, not an industry standard.

Scope: not UK-only

The former intern was "pretty sure" OCIO exists only in the UK team. ? Unverified account As a statement about Goldman Sachs it is contradicted. ⇄ Conflicting evidence

  • Goldman reported $480bn of OCIO assets under supervision at 31 March 2026 R3-S09, and its product page states "$540+ billion" at 30 June 2026, citing rankings by a research firm as the largest OCIO provider in the United States and second largest globally on 2024 assets R8-S22. ✔ Verified The two figures come from different pages and dates and were not reconciled.
  • The largest mandates are American: UPS's US and Canadian plans in 2024 R7-S21 and Verizon and Lockheed Martin in July 2026 R3-S09. ✔ Verified
  • Goldman cites growth in the Netherlands, Germany and Switzerland R3-S10, and a "Head of EMEA OCIO Institutional Business" title exists R3-S11. ✔ Verified An OCIO Insurance team works from The Hague, with London and New York R1-S15. ✔ Verified

Layer B · interpretation A charitable reading of what he meant: among the London coverage teams he could see, only the UK one had an OCIO sub-team. That may be true and is not public. Either way, do not repeat "OCIO is UK-only" in an interview.

Where it sits

The fiduciary and OCIO teams sit within Multi-Asset Solutions, an investment group R6-S18R1-S15 ✔ Verified, supported by more than 300 people as at November 2025, a number described then as still growing R3-S07. ✔ Verified So OCIO is not a client-coverage team in the way UK Institutional is. Client coverage works alongside it: the co-head of EMEA Institutional Client Coverage is quoted in the Shell announcement R6-S02, a head of sales and distribution for UK fiduciary management was reported in 2022 R6-S27 ≈ Supported inference, and a "Client Relationship Manager (OCIO)" title has been advertised in London (search result only) R1-S33. ≈ Supported inference The remark that the team is "already over-hired" has no public support; the public evidence is of continued senior hiring in 2025 R3-S07. ∅ Not publicly established

What the provider is responsible for

Level 2 · Institutional mechanics

From the public descriptions of Goldman's UK mandates R3-S15R3-S07R3-S08 ✔ Verified:

  • Asset allocation within the risk budget the trustees set (and, in full fiduciary management, advice on the budget itself).
  • Manager selection, using "strategies run by both internal and external managers". The use of external managers matters: the provider is not simply filling the portfolio with its own funds, and trustees will ask how it handles the conflict when it does choose its own.
  • Liability hedging tailored to the scheme.
  • Implementation and transition: moving the assets from the old arrangement to the new.
  • Reporting to trustees.

What it does not take over: the trustees' legal responsibility for the scheme, the funding agreement with the employer, and the decision on the endgame. Arrangements range "from fully delegated fiduciary models to hybrid structures involving consultants and/or independent oversight providers" R3-S07. At BAE Systems the trustees' strategic adviser stayed on to oversee implementation R3-S02. ✔ Verified

The tender rule

UK trust-based schemes must run a competitive tender, inviting bids from at least three unconnected providers, before fiduciary managers manage 20% or more of scheme assets R3-S24. ✔ Verified The duty came from a competition inquiry and has sat in pensions regulations since 1 October 2022. Its practical effect on the sale is large: there is always a formal process, usually run by an independent evaluator, with scored proposals and standardised performance data (see D-R3-07). A warm relationship with the trustees gets a provider invited. It does not get it appointed.

Fees, as far as they are public

Goldman's OCIO fee rates are not disclosed. ∅ Not publicly established Three pieces of public evidence show the structure.

  • A UK scheme's annual report (scheme name withheld) describes "a fiduciary fee based on the asset value" of the return-seeking and cashflow-driven portfolios, with the fiduciary manager able to negotiate fees with the underlying managers and the LDI manager invoicing separately R3-S17. ✔ Verified That is another provider's arrangement and shows the shape, not Goldman's price.
  • In Goldman's own filings, alternative-asset accounts classed as "advisory and OCIO" averaged $112bn in 2025 and earned an average 17 basis points, against much higher rates for funds and discretionary accounts R2-S01. ✔ Verified That is a firm-wide blend for one asset class, reported together with advisory accounts, and cannot be read as a mandate price.
  • Across the UK market, fiduciary fees fell about 27% over five years, with the sharpest competition for mandates above £500m R8-S10. ✔ Verified

Layer B · interpretation The shape is therefore a low rate on a very large base, charged for responsibility, with the underlying managers' fees on top. The calculator's OCIO case uses invented numbers to show it.

Taking on the client's team

The former intern said Goldman "can bring the client's in-house investment team into the firm". ? Unverified account That is true of some mandates and not of the model.

  • Where it happened. BAE Systems' in-house investment team joined Goldman as part of the 2023 mandate R3-S01R3-S02. ✔ Verified A 22-person UPS investment team joined in September 2024 R7-S21. ✔ Verified Trade press describes these, with an earlier Canadian case, as "liftouts" and part of how the business was built, alongside acquisitions of US outsourcing firms between 2015 and 2018 R7-S04R3-S03. ✔ Verified
  • Where it did not. No transfer is reported for the smaller UK appointments, which are ordinary tendered mandates R3-S15R7-S16. ≈ Supported inference

Layer B · interpretation A team transfer happens when a scheme large enough to employ its own investment staff decides to stop doing so. It solves the sponsor's problem (those staff need somewhere to go) and gives the provider people who know the portfolio. Most schemes have no in-house team to transfer.

The award

The former intern saw a managing director's post about an OCIO award. ? Unverified account Two 2026 awards fit, and which he saw is not established R3-S10R3-S11. ≈ Supported inference

Award Date What Goldman states
European Pensions Awards, Fiduciary Management / OCIO 2 July 2026 Award received R3-S10 ✔ Verified
Irish Pensions Awards, Fiduciary Management / OCIO of the Year 4 November 2026 Award received R3-S11 ✔ Verified

For balance: Goldman was Fiduciary Management Firm of the Year at the Pensions Age Awards 2024 R3-S12, and did not win the fiduciary category at the 2026 UK Pensions Awards, which went to another firm R3-S14. ✔ Verified

What an award establishes. These are trade-publication awards decided by a judging panel on written entries, weighted to the previous 12 to 18 months. They show that a panel preferred that entry in that category in that year. They are not a performance ranking, a client survey or a measure of market share. In an interview, "they won an award" is weak evidence; "they were appointed after competitive tenders run by four different independent advisers" is stronger and is also on the public record.

The market it sits in

UK fiduciary management covered about £241bn across 832 mandates in one 2025 survey, the first fall in the number of mandates since 2008, with OCIO-type partial mandates making up 53% of assets R3-S25. ✔ Verified About 18% of UK schemes used some form of it on an earlier survey that Goldman itself cites R3-S08. ✔ Verified Goldman's stated reading is that outsourcing has moved from small schemes to large ones with in-house teams, as sponsors question whether running a pension scheme is core business and as maturing schemes shift to cashflow-driven strategies R3-S07. ✔ Verified Its UK-only assets and market rank are not published. ∅ Not publicly established Cards D-R3-06 and D-R8-07 follow the consequences.

8. Liquidity Solutions and Insurance: two different business models

The former intern listed these beside the regions. They are not regions, and they do not work like the regional teams.

Liquidity Solutions

Profile: Liquidity Solutions.

Level 1 · First principles

Every large organisation has cash it will need soon: next month's payroll, a tax bill, money waiting to be invested. Leaving it all in one bank is risky and earns little. A money market fund spreads it across many very short, very safe loans and lets the organisation take it back the same day. Liquidity Solutions is the business that runs those funds and looks after the organisations that use them.

The client is usually a treasurer. Their order of priorities is fixed: do not lose the money, be able to get it today, and only then earn something on it.

Level 2 · Institutional mechanics

What is established. "Our Liquidity Solutions team oversees $1.2+ trillion in money market and short-term assets" as at 30 September 2026, a global figure R5-S01; firm-wide liquidity assets under supervision were $1,051bn on the same date R2-S02. ✔ Verified Its stated clients are "financial institution, hedge fund, institutional, corporate, and wealth management clients" R5-S01. ✔ Verified It has a global head of its client business and shares a global head with Insurance Asset Management R5-S01R5-S02. ✔ Verified A London "EMEA Liquidity Solutions Sales (UK Corporates)" seat has been advertised (search summary) R5-S09. ≈ Supported inference The products on the UK page are money market funds in dollars and euros, short-duration strategies, fixed income ETFs and a dealing portal R5-S01. ✔ Verified

Client constraints that make it its own business.

  • An investment policy, not a preference. A corporate treasurer invests under a board-approved policy that lists permitted instruments, minimum credit ratings and a maximum share of any one fund. The sale is getting onto that list, and staying inside its limits.
  • The balance moves every day. There is no funding event. Cash arrives before payroll and leaves on payday. The fee calculator's liquidity case shows why average balance, not opening balance, is what matters.
  • Structure matters as much as yield. Chapter 1 explains the fund types. The stable-priced "low volatility" type may only round its price while the true value stays within 20 basis points of it W1-S06 ✔ Verified, so clients care how much room a fund has.
  • Regulation is live. The UK regulator said in June 2026 that the UK money market fund regulation is expected to be repealed by the end of 2026, with new rules expecting stable-priced funds to hold 40% in assets maturing within a week R5-S32. ✔ Verified Funds domiciled in the EU, which hold roughly 90% of sterling money market assets, are sold in the UK under a temporary regime that is being extended R5-S34. ✔ Verified See D-R5-02.
  • Operations sell. Cut-off times, portal integration and reporting decide many choices between similar funds.

How the money works. The investor receives the portfolio's yield less the fund's charge. The manager's revenue is that charge on average balances. Firm-wide, Goldman's liquidity products earned an average 14 basis points in 2025, against 54 for equity R2-S01. ✔ Verified So this is a scale business: very large balances, thin margin, and a fee that managers across the industry have at times waived in part when interest rates were near zero. ≈ Supported inference No Goldman fund fee or waiver figure was read, and none should be quoted.

The French question. The former intern said both that an English-only candidate could work here and that everyone in the team speaks French. ? Unverified account No job description supports a French requirement; the one French-speaker advert found is for the French sales team R5-S10. ∅ Not publicly established

Insurance

Profile: Insurance.

Level 1 · First principles

An insurance company collects premiums today and pays claims later, sometimes decades later. In between, it invests the money. Unlike a pension scheme, the insurer is a regulated company that must hold capital against every risk it takes, and reports profits to shareholders every quarter. So it does not ask "what will earn the most?" It asks "what will pay my claims, earn a steady income, and cost me the least capital?"

Level 2 · Institutional mechanics

What is established. Goldman Sachs Asset Management states it manages "$651 billion in general account assets on behalf of insurance clients" as at 31 December 2025 R5-S02. ✔ Verified ("General account" means the insurer's own balance-sheet assets backing its policies, as opposed to policyholders' unit-linked funds.) The offer runs from partial to full outsourcing across fixed income, alternatives and equities, with advice on asset-liability management, strategic asset allocation and capital-efficient strategies R5-S02. ✔ Verified "Insurance Client Solutions Group" seats have been advertised in London and Frankfurt (search summaries) R5-S22R5-S21 ≈ Supported inference, and a Goldman advert lists insurance beside institutional and third-party wealth as a peer channel R5-S42. ≈ Supported inference Whether EMEA insurance staff report to the region or to the global vertical is not established. ∅ Not publicly established

Client constraints that make it its own business.

  • Capital rules. Under Solvency II in the EU and its UK equivalent, each asset carries a capital charge, so two bonds with the same yield can have very different value to an insurer. Amended EU rules take effect on 30 January 2027 R5-S39. ✔ Verified
  • Matching. UK annuity writers can get a regulatory benefit (the matching adjustment) for holding assets whose cash flows match their liabilities. The UK regulator consulted in 2025 on letting insurers add some assets to those portfolios before formal approval, within limits R5-S38. ✔ Verified The final policy was not read.
  • Accounting. Realising a gain or loss changes reported profit, so an insurer may not want a bond sold even when a total-return investor would sell it. Guidelines often limit turnover and realised gains.
  • Income. The measure is frequently the yield at which assets were bought (book yield), not performance against an index.

What clients say they are doing. In Goldman's fifteenth annual insurance survey, published 25 March 2026, 434 chief investment and finance officers were polled; 62% planned to increase private-asset allocations R5-S03. ✔ Verified A provider's survey of its own client base is a view, not a census (see D-R5-05).

The link to UK pensions. Layer B · interpretation When a UK pension scheme buys out with an insurer, its assets move from the trustees to the insurer's balance sheet. The pension client disappears and an insurance client grows. A firm with both an institutional pensions team and an insurance team sees both sides of that transfer, which is one reason the two businesses cannot be understood separately.

9. Six clients compared

The same firm, the same investment teams, six very different conversations.

Client Whose money, and what for Who decides What usually decides it
UK DB pension scheme Members' promised pensions Trustees, advised by a consultant Consultant rating, a formal tender, fit with the endgame plan
Gulf sovereign investor A state's long-term wealth A small senior investment team and committee Senior relationship, tailored partnership terms, private-markets access
Swiss private bank Its private clients' portfolios A fund selector, then each banker Approval, share class and price, then adviser adoption
Nordic pension institution Members' savings, run by professionals A large in-house investment team A specialist capability the team does not have, at an institutional fee
Insurer Its own balance sheet backing policies Chief investment and finance officers with actuaries Capital efficiency, cash-flow matching, book yield
Corporate treasury The company's operating cash The treasurer, under a board policy Safety, same-day access, operational ease
Client Size and pace Liquidity need How the manager is paid Typical way it ends
UK DB pension scheme Large, slow, formal Rising as the scheme matures Fee on a mandate, or one fee for the whole portfolio in OCIO Buyout with an insurer, re-tender, or consolidation
Gulf sovereign investor Very large, very few, long courtship Low Bespoke: account fees and private-fund terms Strategy change or the investor builds the capability itself
Swiss private bank Many small holdings that add up Daily dealing Fund management fee on whatever advisers allocate Removal from the approved list
Nordic pension institution Large, direct, price-aware Moderate Institutional mandate fee, hard negotiated Taken in-house or re-tendered
Insurer Large, sticky, rule-bound Matched to claims Low fee on big fixed-income mandates Regulatory or strategy change; merger
Corporate treasury Balances that swing daily Same day Thin fund charge on the average balance Cash is needed, or a policy limit is hit

Limits and caveats

These tables are interpretation. Layer B · interpretation ≈ Supported inference They compress general industry practice into one line per client and are not statements about Goldman's clients. The Gulf, Swiss and Nordic rows in particular rest on general knowledge and thin sourcing; no primary source on how those client types select managers was read. Use them to organise your thinking, then test each cell against a real case before relying on it.

How to read the comparison. Layer B · interpretation

  • The client is not always the owner of the money. A pension trustee, a private bank and a treasurer are all acting for someone else, under rules. Much of what looks like caution or slowness is that duty at work. The sovereign investor and the insurer are closer to principals, which is partly why their terms are more bespoke.
  • "Winning" means different things. For a pension scheme it is an appointment after a tender. For a private bank it is approval, which may be followed by nothing. For a treasurer it is a place on a permitted list, after which the balance does whatever the company's cash flow does. Quoting a "win" without saying which kind is a common way to overstate.
  • What ends the relationship is often nothing to do with service. A scheme buys out. A treasurer needs the cash. A bank is acquired and its buy list is merged. Good coverage sees these coming and helps the client through them even when the assets leave.
  • The specialist dependency changes. UK pensions coverage leans on liability and credit specialists; Gulf coverage on the private-markets business; wealth on product specialists who can talk to advisers; insurance on people who understand capital rules; liquidity on portfolio managers and operations. The coverage professional's skill is knowing which specialist the client needs and getting them into the room, not being all of them.

10. What this means for the London summer programme

Layer B · interpretation Reasoning from the evidence, with its limits stated.

  • The official listing does not name a team. The 2027 London listing contains only programme-wide and division-wide wording R1-S02. ✔ Verified How applicants are allocated is unpublished. The former intern's account (that recorded-interview answers decide the team, and that each team hires one analyst per seat) is one person's experience from an earlier cycle. ? Unverified account
  • UK-facing work is the most likely exposure for an English-only candidate, on the language evidence in section 3. That covers three quite different businesses: winning and serving institutional mandates, getting funds used by wealth intermediaries, and supporting whole-portfolio delegation. Be ready to explain all three and to say honestly which you understand best.
  • Do not present the intern's tree as fact. Safer and more accurate: "My understanding is that the group is organised by client region and by channel, with Third Party Wealth and Institutional as the main channels and businesses like Insurance and Liquidity run as global verticals. I would like to understand how the London teams divide new business and existing-client work." That is supported by public sources and invites correction.
  • Open questions worth asking a team member, because no public source answers them: how the UK institutional team divides work between new business and existing clients; how coverage works with the OCIO team on a large delegation; who covers consultants day to day; and what a summer analyst's project typically looks like.

Check your understanding

  1. Draw the business three ways: by geography, by client segment and by job. What does each drawing hide?
  2. Why is OCIO shown outside the Client Solutions Group on the map, and what evidence puts it there?
  3. A fund is added to a private bank's approved list in January. Give three separate reasons it might hold no assets from that bank in December.
  4. A UK pension scheme with a surplus is choosing between an insurer buyout and running on. For each choice, what happens to its asset manager's mandate?
  5. The former intern said OCIO is UK-only and that Goldman can absorb a client's team. Which part of each statement survives the evidence?
  6. Why does a treasurer care more about a money market fund's structure than about a few basis points of yield?
  7. Which rows of the six-client table are best supported by sources in this chapter, and which are mostly general knowledge?

Unresolved after this research

  • Current heads of UK institutional sales, UK and Ireland Third Party Wealth, the EMEA Third Party Wealth Business, Middle East coverage, and EMEA liquidity and insurance coverage.
  • Whether the Client Coverage Group sits inside the Client Solutions Group, and whether each London team has both sides.
  • Goldman's UK-only OCIO assets, its fee rates, and which 2026 award the former intern saw.
  • Whether Middle East coverage is still partly London-based after the 2025 departures.
  • Swiss, French and Italian institutional coverage; the structure in Iberia.
  • Any UK endowment, charity, DC master trust or recent Nordic mandate.

Each is recorded in the coverage register with whether it was searched for and not found, or not yet investigated.

People, staffing and recruitment

This chapter answers four questions. Who, according to public sources, leads the parts of Goldman Sachs Asset Management (GSAM) that a London Client Solutions Group (CSG) summer analyst might join? What do public sources show about the balance between sales and relationship management? Which languages do real job descriptions ask for? And how much of the former intern's account of recruitment survives a check against what Goldman Sachs publishes?

Three rules apply throughout. The public title is what the source says, word for word. The function (sales, relationship management, leadership, specialist) is our interpretation and is labelled as such. Every sighting carries an evidence date, because people move and a title seen in 2024 may not be current in November 2026. The full directory, with one entry per person, is in the People directory of the application and Appendix B of the PDF.

Limits and caveats: What this chapter cannot do

It cannot tell you who will interview you, how many people work in any team, or how likely an offer is. It is a sample of people the trade press chose to write about, checked against a small number of official pages. Treat names as context for understanding the business, not as a contact list.

1. Method and its limits

What was searched

Layer A · verified fact The people research used four kinds of public source:

  • Official Goldman Sachs material: press releases, GSAM insight pages that carry an author's title, the careers site's listing titles, and class announcements for partners and for vice presidents and executive directors.
  • Trade press: Professional Pensions, Investment Week, Funds Europe, Funds Society, Citywire-type move stories, and national outlets such as finews.ch (Switzerland), FundResearch (Germany), Realtid (Sweden) and Investment Officer (Netherlands).
  • Conference and author biographies: speaker pages for industry events, and writer profiles on distributor websites.
  • Search-result snippets: the short text a search engine shows for a page that could not be opened. These are recorded as "snippet only" and never rated above Supported inference.

The exact query strings are listed at the end of the chapter so the work can be repeated or extended.

Why the directory is thinner than planned

Three constraints shaped the result, and each is a limit on the evidence, not a finding about Goldman Sachs.

  1. The search allowance ran out. The people stream ran 28 searches before a shared limit was reached. Junior and mid-level profiles, managing-director class lists, conference programmes and publicly indexed professional-profile snippets were not investigated. That is different from "searched and not found".
  2. Goldman's own sites could not be read by the fetch tool. Pages on the firm's main site and careers site returned an error or needed a browser to render. No workaround was used for the people stream. Where an official page is cited from its search snippet, the source is marked "snippet only".
  3. Paywalls. Investment Week, Investment Officer, IPE and Global Trading showed a headline or first sentences only.

Why snippets and biographies go stale

  • A speaker biography is written by the speaker and is true on the day it was submitted. It is rarely taken down when the person moves.
  • Search engines sometimes attach today's date to an old article because the site prints the current date in its banner. Two such cases were caught on opening the page: a Nordic team article that reads as recent is from May 2020 R6-S17, and a "senior team shake-up" story is from January 2022 R6-S37.
  • Trade press reports arrivals far more often than departures, and reports heads of teams far more often than their staff. The directory therefore over-represents senior people and new hires.

Note: How to read "still in post at the cutoff?"

Yes means a source dated 2026 shows the person in the role. Likely means the latest sighting is recent and nothing reports a move. Unknown means the sighting is old or undated. No means a departure or move has been reported. None of these is a confirmation from Goldman Sachs.

  • It can support a narrow observation: publicly reported hiring in 2021 to 2026 was concentrated in OCIO and fiduciary management, in Third Party Wealth country leadership, and in new channel heads (defined contribution, exchange-traded funds, alternatives for wealth).   • It cannot support any statement about net headcount, about junior hiring, or about which team "is hiring" this cycle. A press-reported senior hire says nothing about analyst seats.
  • It does show that several regional leadership posts changed hands or became unclear in 2025 and 2026 (EMEA Third Party Wealth, the Middle East). A sensible candidate does not name a regional head in an interview without checking the date.

5. How titles work

Level 1 · First principles

A bank's "corporate title" is a rank, such as Analyst or Managing Director. A "role title" says what the person does, such as "head of UK ETF distribution". The same person has both, and public sources often give only one. Two people with the same rank can do very different jobs.

Layer A · verified fact What Goldman Sachs's own material shows:

  • The ranks visible in official listings and announcements are Summer Analyst, Analyst, Associate, Vice President or Executive Director, Managing Director and Partner R1-S26R1-S27R1-S29. ✔ Verified
  • Executive Director and Vice President are the same level. Listings titled "Executive Director" in London carry the corporate title "Vice President", and the firm announces a single "Vice President and Executive Director Class" each year R1-S26R1-S29R1-S10. ✔ Verified "Executive Director" is the working title used outside the United States. It is not the step after Vice President.
  • Partner is a selected class, not simply the next rung. People are "invited to become partners"; the class announced on 5 November 2026 has 109 people, effective 1 January 2027 R1-S27. ✔ Verified Matt Gibson's biography records managing director in 2008 and partner in 2010 as separate events R6-S19. A partner is also a managing director; most managing directors are not partners.
  • A role can be filled at more than one rank. Several listings are titled "Analyst/Associate" or "Associate/Executive Director" R1-S29. ✔ Verified

Level 2 · Institutional mechanics

For the directory this has three consequences. First, the "title class" field is left as Unclear for 23 of 42 people, because the source gave a role title ("head of…") and no rank. We did not infer rank from seniority of role. Second, the partner-class release lists name, division and office only, so it cannot place anyone in the Client Solutions Group. Third, a generic title such as "Asset Management Analyst" says nothing about team, so no one was assigned to a team on that basis.

6. The sales versus relationship-management balance

Observed public-profile sample, not headcount

The directory holds 42 people found in public sources. Of these, 6 are classified as sales, 0 as relationship management and 36 as blended, leadership, specialist or unclear. Numerator and denominator are both this sample. Senior and externally visible people are over-represented, and titles rarely state the function, so this says nothing reliable about the real sales-to-relationship-management ratio, team sizes or hiring odds.

By function (interpretation)

  • Leadership: 27
  • Sales: 6
  • Unclear: 4
  • Product/Investment specialist: 4
  • Both/blended: 1

By client segment

  • Multiple: 16
  • Third Party Wealth: 9
  • OCIO/Fiduciary: 5
  • Institutional: 4
  • Unclear: 4
  • Consultant Relations: 3
  • Liquidity: 1

Layer A · verified fact The box above is calculated from the directory each time the project is built. At the time of writing the directory holds 42 people. Six have a title that states a sales, distribution or capital-formation role. None has a title that states relationship management. One is blended, four are product or investment specialists, and the remaining 31 are heads of teams or cannot be classified from the title.

Limits and caveats: Why no ratio is offered

  • Numerator and denominator. Six explicit sales titles and zero explicit relationship-management titles, out of 42 public profiles. Thirty-one of the 42 cannot be placed on either side.
  • Selection bias. Trade press announces heads of sales and new hires. It almost never announces a relationship manager. The zero reflects what gets reported, not who is employed.
  • Missing layer. The junior and mid-level profiles that would show the real mix were not investigated.
  • Conclusion. The sample cannot support a sales-to-relationship-management ratio, a team size, a conversion rate from internship to offer, or any estimate of how competitive a seat is. None is given.

What job descriptions add, which is better evidence than the people sample:

  • A named relationship-side group exists. Goldman defines the Client Coverage Group (CCG) as "dedicated to retaining, expanding and supporting existing client relationships", partnering "closely with the sales team" R1-S11. ✔ Verified for the global definition, from a Hong Kong listing. London titles using "CCG" and "Client Coverage Group" were seen in search snippets only R1-S32. ≈ Supported inference
  • Some teams do both jobs. The London-based BeNeLux Client Solutions Group listing says the team "is responsible for new business development and managing existing institutional client relationships" R1-S01. ✔ Verified A Nordics sales-support listing describes that team in similar terms R5-S08. ≈ Supported inference
  • The former intern's statements that every team has a sales side and a relationship side sitting opposite each other, and that sales has fewer seats, are an ? Unverified account. Nothing public confirms or contradicts the seating or the seat count.

Layer B · interpretation The defensible position: both functions exist at Goldman Sachs and have names; how they are divided varies by team; and no public source lets anyone count them.
