  • The firm's job is to make the relationship survive the person. That means more than one point of contact on each side, senior and junior coverage, direct links between operations teams and between the portfolio manager and the client's investment staff.
  • The individual's job is to make themselves replaceable in the file and valuable in the room. These are compatible. The person who documents everything is the one a firm can safely promote, because their clients can be handed on.

6.5 Relationship knowledge as organisational knowledge

What a coverage team learns about a client is an asset only if someone else can use it. In practice this means a customer relationship management (CRM) system holding contacts, call notes, meeting records, open actions and the history of decisions, with access controlled so that confidential client information reaches only those who need it.

Sample work product (fictional): A call note that turns a conversation into organisational knowledge ✎ Illustrative example

Client: hypothetical DB scheme. Date: 12 March. Attendees: in-house investment manager (client); coverage lead, analyst (manager).

  • Facts stated by the client: sub-committee meets 14 May; papers due 5 May. Consultant is reviewing all credit managers in the third quarter. Sponsor has asked trustees for an indicative buy-in timetable by year end.
  • Client's concerns, in their words: "The chair does not want another quarter like the last one explained in jargon."
  • What we committed to: one-page plain-English attribution summary by 28 April (owner: analyst to draft, portfolio manager to approve). Climate methodology note by 5 May (owner: product specialist).
  • What we do not know: whether the buy-in timetable would cover the whole scheme or the pensioner section only. To ask at the May meeting.
  • Judgement, labelled as such: coverage lead's view is that the mandate is secure through the consultant review if the plain-English reporting improves. This is an opinion, not something the client said.
  • Sensitivity: the buy-in timetable is not public. Restricted to the coverage team and the portfolio manager.

Notice the separations: fact from opinion, the client's words from the manager's interpretation, known from unknown, and who may see it. A note like this lets a successor take the next call without asking the client to repeat themselves.

What happens when the knowledge stays in one head. Layer B · interpretation

  • The client has to re-explain its situation to each new contact, and reasonably concludes the firm does not listen.
  • Promises made verbally are missed because nobody else knew they existed.
  • The firm repeats a proposal the client rejected two years ago for a reason nobody recorded.
  • Sensitivities are lost: the new person raises the subject the previous person knew to avoid.
  • The firm cannot tell whether a departing employee's clients are at risk, because it does not know what those relationships consisted of.
  • From the client's side, their own institutional memory of the manager is also lost if their contact kept nothing, which is why careful clients minute manager meetings.

There is a tension here too. Recording everything takes time away from clients, and people are sometimes reluctant to write down the knowledge that makes them valuable. A firm that wants the notes written has to make them useful to the writer and has to reward handing clients on well.

7. Where a junior fits

A summer analyst will not own a relationship, lead a review meeting or negotiate a fee. It is still possible to say precisely how junior work connects to everything above. Layer B · interpretation

Junior task Trust component it supports Client outcome Commercial consequence
Checking every figure in a review pack against source Competence, consistency The committee decides on correct numbers No public correction; the consultant's file stays clean
Maintaining the action tracker after meetings Reliability Promised items arrive No minutable service complaint
Drafting a same-day holding reply for approval Responsiveness The client's deadline is protected The manager is easy to deal with
Writing the call note Institutional continuity The client is not asked twice The relationship survives staff changes
Researching a prospect's published accounts and governance before a first meeting Competence The meeting starts from the client's actual situation Fewer wasted meetings; better-fitted proposals
Flagging a slide that says more than the DDQ supports Honesty, consistency The client is not misled A problem is caught before a researcher finds it

What a junior does not do: state house investment views as their own, commit the firm to dates, prices or terms without approval, share one client's information with another, or decide what a client is told about performance. Knowing these limits, and asking when unsure, is itself part of being trustworthy.

8. Translation table: from abstract words to observable facts

Use this to test any sentence you write or say about this subject. If a claim cannot be moved from the first column to the second, it is not yet saying anything.

Abstract word Observable action The difficult choice it involves Concrete consequence
"Trust" The client asks your view before deciding and accepts "I will check" Admitting you do not know versus sounding fluent Fewer re-checks by the client; earlier sight of new decisions
"Relationship" More than one person on each side knows the history, and it is written down Time spent documenting versus time spent with clients The mandate survives when either contact leaves
"Understanding the client" You can state who proposes, advises, decides, vetoes and implements, and what each is worried about this year Asking basic questions versus assuming Proposals arrive at the right time, to the right people, in a form they can approve
"Adding value" The client changed, delayed or avoided a decision because of something you supplied, and can say so Supplying information that argues against your own product Demonstrable in a re-tender; survives a fee challenge
"Honesty" Bad news delivered first, by you, with cause separated from excuse Defending the firm's position versus obscuring it An informed keep-or-leave decision; a fair reference either way
"Service" Requests acknowledged the same day with an owner and a time; deadlines met or renegotiated before they pass Speed versus checked accuracy The client stops chasing; no service complaint on the minutes
"Partnership" You proposed something that reduced your own fees because it fitted the client's objective Revenue now versus suitability Sometimes later mandates and references; sometimes simply lower revenue
"Loyalty" The client would choose you again in an open, informed competition Welcoming a re-tender versus making one feel difficult Retention that reflects merit, not inertia
"Long-term" Conduct during an exit is as careful as during a pitch Effort for a client who is leaving versus effort for prospects What the consultant and trustees say about you at their next organisation
"Passion for clients" You read the scheme's annual report before the meeting and found the question nobody had asked Preparation that may never be noticed versus visible activity Occasionally, the insight that changes the meeting. Often, nothing visible at all

  1. Name the five layers of a relationship and give one way each can fail while the others hold.
  2. For a UK DB scheme, who proposes, who advises, who decides and who implements a change of manager? Which statutory duties shape that process? Cite two.
  3. Give two things a relationship reveals that no factsheet can, and two things formal due diligence must establish however good the relationship is.
  4. A client asks a question you cannot answer. Say, in your own words, what you would say. What must your answer contain besides "I don't know"?
  5. Explain why a trustee who trusts a manager completely must still monitor it. Which provision makes their protection conditional on doing so?
  6. Take any two of the eight trust components and describe a situation where they pull against each other.
  7. Use the re-tender test to distinguish retention that reflects value from retention that reflects inertia. Why did the CMA intervene in fiduciary management?
  8. A scheme decides to insure its liabilities and your mandate will end in three years. Describe the best and worst responses and say honestly what the best response does and does not guarantee.
  9. A relationship ended in year 7 of the scenario even though performance and service were good. Why? What does that tell you about who "the client" is?
  10. What must a call note separate, and what goes wrong for the client when relationship knowledge is trapped with one person?
  11. Why is "relationships build trust and trust creates loyalty" an inadequate interview answer? Rewrite it as three observable statements.
  12. Which parts of this chapter describe things you think you would enjoy doing, and which describe things you think are merely important? What evidence do you have for the difference?

Limits and caveats: Limits of this chapter

  • It describes general industry mechanics and UK rules. It does not describe Goldman Sachs's internal practices, incentives, contracts or client arrangements, which are not public. ∅ Not publicly established
  • The statutory and regulatory citations were read on the dates shown in the source register. Regulation 4 and the tendering guidance may have been amended since their last-updated dates; one FCA rule could not be read on the primary page and is marked ≈ Supported inference.
  • The economic lenses are simplifications. Each is labelled with what it assumes.
  • Every dialogue, scenario, fee and outcome is illustrative. Real conversations are messier, and real outcomes depend on facts no example can include.
  • The chapter argues that candour and good exits tend to be rewarded over time. That is a reasoned view Layer B · interpretation, not a measured result, and the chapter gives cases where they are not.

Commercial awareness, competitors and the future of the work

This chapter turns current events into client questions. It covers what has changed for each team's clients up to 14 November 2026, how Goldman Sachs Asset Management (GSAM) compares with rivals on specific client problems, and how the job itself is changing.

Three rules apply throughout.

  • Every development is walked through the same chain: what happened, how it affects the client, what decision changes, what it means for money already invested, a possible GSAM response, what sales would do, what relationship management would do, and the counterarguments.
  • "Possible GSAM response" is always Layer B · interpretation interpretation. It is what a reasonable outsider would expect a manager to do. It is not a statement of what Goldman Sachs is doing or selling.
  • A forecast is labelled as a forecast. No probabilities are given, because none could be defended.

Each development has a card in the commercial-awareness view with the full chain, the sources and the dates. The links in this chapter open those cards.

1. How to read a development

Level 1 · First principles

Commercial awareness is not knowing the news. It is being able to say what a piece of news changes for one particular client.

A headline such as "interest rates rose" means nothing to a client until it is translated. A pension scheme hears "our promised pensions just became cheaper to fund". A company treasurer hears "our cash earns more". A wealth manager hears "clients will ask why they should hold anything riskier than cash". The same event creates three different conversations.

The chain used in this chapter forces that translation:

  1. What happened, with the date it happened and the date it was published.
  2. How it affects the client. Which client, and through what mechanism.
  3. What decision changes. If no decision changes, it is background, not an opportunity.
  4. What it means for existing investments. The client already owns things. Those come first.
  5. A possible response from the manager.
  6. What the sales person is responsible for.
  7. What the relationship manager is responsible for.
  8. Risks and counterarguments. Why the obvious conclusion might be wrong.

Level 2 · Institutional mechanics

Two tests keep the chain honest.

The "so what, for whom" test. If step 2 cannot name a type of client and a mechanism (funding level, capital charge, charge cap, liquidity rule, governance requirement), the analysis is still at headline level.

The "who benefits from my conclusion" test. A manager's view of a market change usually ends with the client needing something the manager sells. That does not make the view wrong, but it is a reason to state the counterargument before the client does. Several sources used here are produced by firms with something to sell: GSAM's own insurance survey, a competing manager's commentary on Dutch hedging, surveys by consultants that also run fiduciary businesses. They are cited for facts and flagged where they are opinion.

Limits and caveats: Not every development is a reason to sell something

Some developments call for explaining to existing clients what happened to their own portfolio. Some call for doing nothing. One card in the set, the departure of the head of GSAM's EMEA Third Party Wealth business in spring 2026 (card), is a fact about the team and not a client topic at all. Each team section below says which developments fall into which group.

2. The backdrop every team shares: rates are rising again

Layer A · verified fact On 5 November 2026 the Bank of England raised Bank Rate from 3.75% to 4% on an 8 to 1 vote. It was the first increase since August 2023. Consumer price inflation was 3.5% and the Bank projected it near 5% by mid-2027. The 10-year gilt yield was about 5.15% that day. ✔ Verified R3-S31R3-S32R3-S33R8-S49 The US Federal Reserve held its range at 3.75% to 4.00% on 28 October 2026 with two members voting for an increase, and the European Central Bank held its deposit rate at 2.50% on 29 October after raising it in September. ✔ Verified R8-S50R8-S51

Limits and caveats: Stale assumption to drop

Preparation material written earlier in 2026 often assumed rates were falling. As at the research date that is wrong for the UK and the euro area. An answer built on "now that rates are coming down" would be dated. Check the latest decision before any interview: the next one may reverse this.

The same event reaches each team's clients differently. Cards: rates backdrop and Bank Rate and gilt yields for UK schemes.

Client Mechanism Likely conversation
UK defined benefit (DB) pension scheme Higher gilt yields lower the present value of promised pensions. Hedged schemes see assets and liabilities fall together. Leveraged hedges need collateral. Hedge ratio, collateral headroom, endgame timing
Insurer New money can be invested at higher yields. Existing bonds show unrealised losses. Reinvestment yield, asset and liability matching
Corporate treasurer Cash and money market funds pay more. Where to hold operating cash, and how much
Wealth manager Cash looks attractive against bonds and against semi-liquid private funds. What risk assets must deliver to earn a place
Sovereign investor Financing costs for private assets rise. Pacing of private-market commitments

Layer B · interpretation The most useful thing a junior person can do with a rate decision is not to predict the next one. It is to know, client by client, which of these mechanisms applies and to have the client's own numbers ready.

Check your understanding

  • Explain to a non-specialist why a rise in gilt yields can improve a pension scheme's funding position while reducing the value of its bonds.
  • Name two clients for whom the November 2026 decision is good news and say why.
  • What would you check on the morning of an interview to make sure this section is still current?

3. UK Institutional: pension schemes, local government funds and other institutions

This section covers the clients the former intern described as the UK Institutional team's main work: pension funds first, then endowments, foundations and official institutions. ? Unverified account Public sources confirm that GSAM uses the title "EMEA Institutional Client Coverage"; a separate UK-only institutional head was not established.

3.1 Defined benefit schemes: surplus and the endgame choice

Level 1 · First principles

A defined benefit (DB) scheme promises a pension based on salary and service. For most of the last twenty years the typical scheme did not have enough assets to cover its promises, and the trustees' main job was closing that gap.

That has changed. Most schemes now have more assets than they need on the standard regulatory measure. The question for trustees is no longer "how do we repair the deficit?" It is "how does this end?" There are two main answers. The scheme can pay an insurer to take over the promises, called a buy-in followed by a buyout. Or it can keep running, called run-on, and decide what to do with any surplus.

For an asset manager these two answers have opposite effects. A buyout ends the mandate: the assets go to the insurer. Run-on keeps the scheme invested for decades.

Layer A · verified fact The Pension Protection Fund's 7800 index showed an aggregate surplus of £275.4bn and a funding ratio of 133.7% at the end of October 2026, across 4,838 schemes. ✔ Verified R3-S29R3-S30 In 2025 a record 370 buy-ins completed, but total premium fell to about £38bn from £47.8bn in 2024, with growth almost entirely in deals under £100m. ✔ Verified R3-S27R3-S28 The Pension Schemes Act 2026 received Royal Assent on 29 April 2026. It makes it easier for trustees of private-sector DB schemes to release surplus to the sponsoring employer, with regulations expected in force in 2027. ✔ Verified R3-S20

Cards: DB surplus and the buy-in market, surplus release and superfunds.

Step Surplus, buy-ins and the new Act
What happened Aggregate surplus of £275.4bn at end October 2026 (published November 2026). Record number of buy-ins in 2025, lower total value. Act passed 29 April 2026; surplus rules expected 2027.
Client effect Trustees are choosing an endgame, not repairing a deficit. Sponsors can now see a route to sharing surplus without winding the scheme up.
Decision that changes Buyout or run-on. If run-on: what protections members get before any surplus is released.
Existing investments Buyout-bound schemes move towards assets an insurer will accept. Run-on schemes need portfolios that pay pensions from income for decades.
Possible GSAM response Layer B · interpretation For buyout-bound clients, an orderly transition. For run-on clients, cashflow-matching credit portfolios and delegated management. For the insurers receiving the assets, insurance asset management.
Sales responsibility Find out which endgame a prospect has chosen before proposing anything. A scheme two years from buyout is not a prospect for a ten-year strategy.
Relationship management responsibility Help an existing client reach its chosen endgame well, including when that endgame removes the assets.
Risks and counterarguments The index uses a measure that is less demanding than insurer pricing, so a surplus on it does not mean a scheme can afford buyout. Surplus-release rules were not in force at the cutoff. A fall in yields could remove a surplus after it has been paid out.

Client question: "Is your target buyout, run-on or still open, and which of your current holdings would be hardest to hand to an insurer?"

When this is not a reason to sell. When a well-funded scheme with a weak sponsor has decided to buy out. The right outcome for members reduces the manager's assets. Chapter 7 covers why helping that happen well is part of the job.

3.2 Defined contribution: scale and private markets

Level 1 · First principles

In a defined contribution (DC) pension each member has a pot. The employer picks a provider, and most members stay in the provider's default fund. The provider, not the member, chooses the managers inside that default.

The government wants fewer, larger providers that invest more in private companies and infrastructure. That makes each remaining provider a very large buyer with a tight cost budget.

Layer A · verified fact Under the Pension Schemes Act 2026, master trust and group personal pension default arrangements must reach at least £25bn by 2030, or be on track for it by 2035. The requirement cannot start before 1 January 2030. The Act also creates a reserve power to require minimum private-market and UK allocations. ✔ Verified R3-S20 Separately, seventeen workplace pension providers signed the voluntary Mansion House Accord on 13 May 2025, aiming for 10% of default funds in private markets by 2030, with at least half of that in the UK. ✔ Verified R3-S23

Card: DC scale and private markets.

Step DC scale and private markets
What happened Scale test legislated April 2026. Voluntary 10% private-markets pledge signed May 2025.
Client effect Providers below scale must grow or merge. Survivors need private-market exposure that works inside a daily-priced default fund.
Decision that changes Which managers supply private-market components, in what vehicle, at what cost.
Existing investments Defaults are mostly low-cost index funds today. Private assets are added in small slices alongside them.
Possible GSAM response Layer B · interpretation Offer private-market and multi-asset building blocks designed for DC. Whether GSAM holds UK DC default mandates was not established in this research. ∅ Not publicly established
Sales responsibility Treat each large provider as a single sophisticated account with a long decision cycle and a cost ceiling.
Relationship management responsibility Supply the evidence the provider needs for its own value-for-money reporting.
Risks and counterarguments The Accord is voluntary and conditional. The reserve power had not been used at the cutoff. Private assets cost more and must justify it. Incumbents with index scale are better placed for the core of a default.

Client question: "How will you reach your private-market target inside your charge budget, and what would make you remove a manager from the default?"

3.3 Local government pension funds: six buyers instead of many

Layer A · verified fact The Local Government Pension Scheme (LGPS) in England and Wales invests through pools. The number of pools fell from eight to six after two pools' proposals were not accepted. Regulations in force from 30 June 2026 require each council fund to delegate implementation of its investment strategy to its pool and to take its principal investment advice from the pool. ✔ Verified R3-S21R3-S22

Card: LGPS reform.

Step LGPS pooling
What happened Eight pools became six during 2026. Delegation to pools became mandatory from 30 June 2026.
Client effect The council fund still sets strategy. The pool company now chooses and manages investments.
Decision that changes The buyer of external management is the pool, and pools are building teams to manage more themselves.
Existing investments Mandates held directly by council funds move into pools and are consolidated or ended.
Possible GSAM response Layer B · interpretation Cover six pools as a small number of large accounts and offer what a pool cannot easily run in-house.
Sales responsibility Understand each pool's plan for internal management before proposing a strategy it intends to build itself.
Relationship management responsibility Manage transitions from fund-level to pool-level mandates without service failures.
Risks and counterarguments Internal management shrinks the opportunity. The public mandate register shows GSAM both winning and losing LGPS-related sleeves (an emerging-markets sleeve, a later removal), both at ≈ Supported inference standard.

3.4 Thesis for UK Institutional

Element View (forecasts labelled)
Base case (forecast) Buy-in numbers stay high and small. More large, well-funded DB schemes compare run-on with buyout. DC money concentrates in a few very large providers. LGPS buying concentrates in six pools.
Plausible alternatives Insurer pricing improves and large schemes buy out quickly, shrinking the DB asset pool. Or yields fall and endgame decisions are postponed. Or the DC reserve power is used and allocation becomes a compliance exercise.
Indicators to watch PPF 7800 funding ratio. Half-year bulk annuity volumes by deal size. The surplus-release regulations. Progress against the Mansion House Accord. Pool business plans.
Evidence that would change the view Several consecutive months of falling funding ratios. Trustees declining to use surplus release once rules exist. A provider meeting the DC scale test without adding private assets.

Check your understanding

  • Why does a rise in DB funding levels reduce the number of mandates in the long run?
  • A scheme is 110% funded on a buyout basis with a weak sponsor. What would you expect its trustees to do, and what does that mean for its asset manager?
  • Who is the buyer of investment management in the LGPS after June 2026?

4. OCIO and fiduciary management

Level 1 · First principles

In an outsourced chief investment officer (OCIO) arrangement, called fiduciary management in the UK, trustees keep the big decisions (the objective, how much risk, the endgame) and hand day-to-day investment decisions to one provider. The provider chooses the underlying managers, runs the liability hedge and reports back.

The client is not buying a fund. It is delegating responsibility. That changes the sale (a regulated tender, usually run by an independent adviser), the fee (a low rate on the whole portfolio) and the relationship (the provider is accountable for the total outcome).

Layer A · verified fact GSAM uses "OCIO" and "fiduciary management" for the same business in the UK. ✔ Verified R3-S08R3-S01 Its OCIO page states more than $540bn of OCIO assets under supervision at 30 June 2026. ✔ Verified R8-S22 A July 2026 press release gives $480bn at 31 March 2026. ✔ Verified R3-S09 The two figures come from different Goldman Sachs pages and dates and were not reconciled here. The business is global: US appointments by Verizon and Lockheed Martin were announced in July 2026. ✔ Verified R3-S09 The former intern's belief that OCIO exists only in the UK team is not supported as a description of Goldman Sachs. ⇄ Conflicting evidence

Layer A · verified fact Two large UK-related appointments are public. Goldman Sachs announced on 6 September 2023 that the trustees of the BAE Systems pension schemes had appointed GSAM for about £23bn of assets, with the schemes' in-house investment team joining GSAM (card). ✔ Verified R3-S01R3-S02 In September 2025 GSAM was appointed by pension entities and a captive insurer related to Shell for about $40bn across several countries (card). ✔ Verified R3-S04R3-S05 No transfer of an in-house team was reported for Shell, so staff transfer is a feature of some very large deals and not of the model. ≈ Supported inference

Full OCIO-style mandates were about 6% of mandates by number and 53% of assets. Fees fell about 27% over five years, driven by competition above £500m, while fees for mandates under £50m rose. ✔ Verified R8-S10R8-S09 Since 1 October 2022 trustees must run a competitive tender with at least three unconnected providers before fiduciary managers run 20% or more of scheme assets. ✔ Verified R3-S24

Step OCIO moves to large schemes while the market consolidates
What happened Multi-billion appointments in 2023 and 2025. Mandate numbers fell for the first time (year to June 2025; published late 2025 and spring 2026). Fees fell at the top end. Providers merged or left.
Client effect Large sponsors ask whether running an in-house pension investment team is core business. Large schemes have many bidders and pricing power. Small schemes have fewer bidders.
Decision that changes Which decisions to delegate, to whom, on what fee, and how to get them back.
Existing investments On appointment the whole portfolio is transitioned. On buyout the mandate ends.
Possible GSAM response Layer B · interpretation Compete where bespoke capability matters, be explicit about the endgame path, and say what happens to the fee when the scheme buys out.
Sales responsibility Win a regulated tender judged by an independent evaluator. The pitch is to the trustees, the sponsor and the adviser at once.
Relationship management responsibility Report against the trustees' objectives, not against a product benchmark, and manage the conflict when the provider's own funds are used.
Risks and counterarguments The pool of schemes shrinks as they buy out. A few clients are a large share of assets. GSAM's UK market share and fee rates are not public. ∅ Not publicly established Other providers also win: BlackRock was appointed to the £8bn British Coal Staff Superannuation Scheme on 1 July 2026. ✔ Verified R8-S26

Awards, precisely. GSAM received the fiduciary management and OCIO award at the European Pensions Awards on 2 July 2026 and at the Irish Pensions Awards on 4 November 2026. ✔ Verified R3-S10R3-S11 It did not win the fiduciary manager category at the 2026 UK Pensions Awards. ✔ Verified R3-S14 An award shows that a judging panel rated a submission. It does not establish market share, performance or client satisfaction.

Client question: "Which decisions do you want to keep, which do you want to delegate, and how would you get them back if you changed your mind?"

When this is not a reason to sell. A scheme that expects to buy out within two or three years gains little from a full delegation that takes a year to tender and transition. The honest advice may be to simplify the existing portfolio and prepare it for an insurer.

Element View (forecasts labelled)
Base case (forecast) Assets grow, mandate numbers shrink, fee pressure stays concentrated in the largest mandates, and providers continue to consolidate.
Plausible alternatives Surplus-release rules make run-on attractive and extend mandate lives. Or faster buyouts shrink the market in assets as well as number.
Indicators to watch The next Isio and IC Select surveys. New multi-billion appointments and who wins them. Regulator attention to in-house fund use.
Evidence that would change the view Mandate numbers rising again. Fee surveys showing stabilisation above £500m. A large scheme taking delegated assets back in-house.

5. Third Party Wealth

Level 1 · First principles

Third Party Wealth sells to firms that invest other people's money: private banks, wealth managers, model-portfolio providers, fund-of-funds teams and adviser networks. The buyer is a professional selector. The money belongs to that firm's clients.

Two features shape everything. First, a chain of people stands between the manager and the end investor, and each link can say no. Second, getting onto a buy list is permission to be bought, not a purchase.

Layer A · verified fact "Third Party Wealth" is a public Goldman Sachs name, including an "EMEA Third Party Wealth Business". ✔ Verified R4-S01 In Goldman Sachs's filings the channel is called "third-party distributed". Long-term assets under supervision (AUS) in that channel were $714bn at 30 September 2026, and it took $97bn of long-term net inflows in the first nine months of 2026. ✔ Verified R2-S02 Those are firm-wide figures. No EMEA or UK figure for the channel is disclosed. ∅ Not publicly established

5.1 Wrappers: active ETFs and public-private products

Layer A · verified fact GSAM launched its first European active exchange-traded funds (ETFs) in January 2025 and an active equity range from 28 April 2025. On 24 April 2026 it added two more active fixed-income ETFs and said it had launched 13 active ETFs in 2025, with about $90bn of ETF assets globally. ✔ Verified R4-S01R4-S17R4-S38 Europe-domiciled active ETF assets were about €117bn at the end of the third quarter of 2026, with J.P. Morgan Asset Management holding about 41%. Passive ETFs took about 57% of European fund flows in that quarter. ≈ Supported inference R8-S40R8-S39

Cards: active ETFs, alliances and wrappers.

Step Active ETFs
What happened GSAM entered European active ETFs in 2025 and extended the range in April 2026. The category is growing from a small base and is led by one competitor.
Client effect Model-portfolio builders can hold an active strategy in a wrapper that trades during the day and usually costs less than the equivalent fund share class.
Decision that changes Which wrapper the selector uses for new money, and whether a strategy they already hold should be switched.
Existing investments Money in higher-fee share classes of the same strategy may move to the cheaper wrapper.
Possible GSAM response Layer B · interpretation Lead with the wrapper the buyer's platform and process prefer.
Sales responsibility Know each buyer's platform constraints before proposing a wrapper.
Relationship management responsibility Handle switches between share class and ETF without tax or dealing surprises for the intermediary.
Risks and counterarguments A low fee leaves little margin. Switching cannibalises higher-fee assets. UK platform support for ETFs is uneven. A rival has a large lead.

5.2 Private markets for individuals, after a harder year

Layer A · verified fact Goldman Sachs Alternatives runs a "G-Series" of open-ended private-market funds for eligible investors and on 11 March 2026 added its first evergreen fund under the revised European Long-Term Investment Fund (ELTIF) rules. ✔ Verified R4-S18R4-S19R4-S20 The Bank of England's July 2026 Financial Stability Report said redemption requests had been elevated in several retail private-credit funds, with some limiting redemptions. ✔ Verified R8-S52 Blackstone's private-wealth assets still reached $330bn at 30 September 2026. ✔ Verified R8-S34

Cards: evergreen funds and ELTIF 2.0, private credit under strain.

Step Semi-liquid private funds
What happened Product launches through 2025 and March 2026. Redemption pressure in some retail funds reported July 2026.
Client effect A wealth manager can offer private assets with periodic dealing. Its clients may not be able to redeem when they want to.
Decision that changes Whether to list the product, for which clients, and at what maximum position size.
Existing investments Holdings already in semi-liquid funds need their liquidity terms re-explained to end clients.
Possible GSAM response Layer B · interpretation Lead with liquidity terms and downside cases. Say plainly who the product does not suit.
Sales responsibility Sell the product as periodic-liquidity, never as liquid. Bring a specialist.
Relationship management responsibility Make sure the intermediary's advisers understand the redemption terms before a stress, not during one.
Risks and counterarguments Liquidity mismatch. Valuations that are not market prices. Higher fees. UK retail access differs from the European Economic Area. Stress has so far been concentrated in particular funds.

Client question: "If you could not redeem for four quarters, would this allocation still be the right size for your clients?"

5.3 Who holds the buying power, and what they must prove

Layer A · verified fact UK fund managers must assess each fund's value at least once a year, and the Financial Conduct Authority's Consumer Duty adds a "price and value" outcome that distributors must also meet. ✔ Verified R4-S31R4-S32 The UK model portfolio service market was reported at about £190bn, up 32% in a year; that figure was seen only in a search result. ≈ Supported inference R4-S37 New disclosure rules for retail investment products are fully in force from 8 June 2027. ✔ Verified R4-S28

Cards: value scrutiny, model portfolios, disclosure rules, targeted support.

Layer B · interpretation The practical effect is that fewer people control more money, and they must document why each fund is worth its cost. A model-portfolio team's decision moves money for thousands of end clients in one step, in either direction.

When this is not a reason to sell. Regulatory changes such as the new disclosure regime are mostly an operations and data task. The useful act is supplying what the distributor needs on time. Treating it as a product opening would misread it.

Element View (forecasts labelled)
Base case (forecast) Buying power keeps concentrating in model-portfolio and central selection teams. Active ETFs take share of new money from a small base. Semi-liquid private funds grow, rationed by position limits.
Plausible alternatives A visible gating episode reverses private-market flows. Or cost caps in models harden and favour index funds for almost everything.
Indicators to watch European active ETF flows and issuer shares. Redemption data from the largest wealth-channel private funds. FCA findings on fair value.
Evidence that would change the view UK platforms removing ETF dealing frictions. A large distributor delisting semi-liquid funds. Selectors publishing explicit cost budgets.

6. Insurance

Level 1 · First principles

An insurer invests premiums until claims are paid. Its regulator requires it to hold capital against the risk in its investments. So an insurer does not ask "what does this yield?" It asks "what does this yield after the capital I must hold against it, and does it pay out when my liabilities fall due?"

That is why insurance is covered by specialists. A manager who cannot speak about capital, accounting and matching is not credible to an insurer's chief investment officer.

Layer A · verified fact GSAM states it manages $651bn of general-account assets for insurers as at 31 December 2025. ✔ Verified R5-S02 Insurance appears to be run as a global client vertical with London and Frankfurt seats, not as a regional team. ≈ Supported inference R5-S21 Its 2026 survey of 434 insurance investment and finance chiefs, published 25 March 2026, found 62% planning to increase private-asset allocations. ✔ Verified R5-S02R5-S03 Amended European Union Solvency II rules take effect on 30 January 2027. ✔ Verified R5-S39 In the UK the Prudential Regulation Authority consulted in April 2025 on letting annuity writers add certain assets to matching-adjustment portfolios before formal approval, within limits. ✔ Verified R5-S38 The final UK rules were not read in this research.

Cards: capital rules, insurers and private assets, and the link to pensions through buy-ins.

Step Capital rules and private assets
What happened EU changes effective 30 January 2027. UK consultation April 2025. Survey intentions published March 2026.
Client effect The ranking of assets by return after capital charge shifts. UK annuity writers receiving pension buy-in assets may be able to invest in new asset types sooner.
Decision that changes Which private and long-dated assets to add, and how fast.
Existing investments Portfolios are re-tested under the new basis. Some holdings become more capital-efficient, some less.
Possible GSAM response Layer B · interpretation Show capital-adjusted return under the client's own regulatory basis. GSAM describes capital-efficient strategies and asset and liability advice as part of its offer. ✔ Verified R5-S02
Sales responsibility Arrive with analysis on the insurer's own balance sheet, not a fund list.
Relationship management responsibility Keep the mandate inside regulatory and accounting constraints as rules change.
Risks and counterarguments The survey is run by a firm that sells these assets and measures intentions. Supervisors are wary of private-asset concentration. Recession expectations in the same survey rose.

Client question: "Where does your private-asset allocation sit against your liquidity stress test, not against your peers?"

When this is not a reason to sell. When an insurer's constraint is liquidity under stress, more illiquid credit is the wrong answer even if the capital treatment improves.

Element View (forecasts labelled)
Base case (forecast) Rules move modestly towards making long-dated and private assets easier to hold, and insurers add them selectively. Buy-in volumes keep feeding UK annuity writers' demand for matching assets.
Plausible alternatives Supervisors tighten on private-asset concentration. Or a credit event makes insurers pull back whatever the rules say.
Indicators to watch Final UK and EU rules. Supervisory letters. Reported allocations a year after the survey.
Evidence that would change the view Insurers' actual private-asset allocations falling. A regulator capping exposure.

7. Liquidity Solutions

Level 1 · First principles

A money market fund (MMF) is a pooled fund that holds very short-term, high-quality debt. Companies, funds and pension schemes use it as an alternative to a bank deposit for cash they may need tomorrow.

The client's priorities are, in order: get the money back, get it back the same day, and earn a fair yield. The manager earns a small fee on the balance. Balances move quickly and for reasons that have nothing to do with service, such as a company paying a dividend or a pension scheme meeting a collateral call.

Layer A · verified fact Goldman Sachs reports $1,051bn of liquidity products in its assets under supervision at 30 September 2026, a category that also includes private bank deposits. ✔ Verified R2-S02R2-S01 GSAM's own page says its Liquidity Solutions team oversees more than $1.2 trillion in money market and short-term assets. ✔ Verified R5-S01 The two measures differ in scope. The firm's average effective fee on liquidity products was 14 basis points in 2025, a firm-wide blend and not a price list. ✔ Verified R2-S01 Liquidity products saw a net outflow of about $14bn in the third quarter of 2026. ✔ Verified R8-S01 No public evidence was found that French is required for these roles. ∅ Not publicly established

Layer A · verified fact On 8 June 2026 the Financial Conduct Authority said the government expects to repeal the UK's inherited money market fund regulation by the end of 2026, with new rules expecting stable-value funds to hold 40% in weekly liquid assets and removing the link between liquidity thresholds and fees or gates. ✔ Verified R5-S32 Funds domiciled in the EU hold roughly 90% of sterling money market fund assets and are sold in the UK under temporary permissions. ✔ Verified R5-S34R5-S33 In July 2025 BNY and Goldman Sachs launched a way to record "mirror" tokens of money market fund shares on a Goldman ledger, aimed at using fund shares as collateral. ✔ Verified R8-S55

Cards: money market fund rules, tokenised shares, R5 and R8, rates.

Step New UK money market fund rules
What happened Timetable and direction announced 8 June 2026. Final rules not published at the cutoff.
Client effect A treasurer gets a fund that holds more cash-like assets and is less likely to restrict withdrawals in a stress, possibly for slightly less yield.
Decision that changes Treasury policies that name fees and gates as triggers need rewriting. How to split cash between fund types may change.
Existing investments Existing fund holdings continue. Continued UK access to EU-domiciled funds is expected but not yet permanent.
Possible GSAM response Layer B · interpretation Explain how each fund already sits against the new expectations, and offer segmentation: daily cash in money market funds, cash not needed for months in short-duration accounts.
Sales responsibility Speak to the treasurer's policy document and operational needs, not to yield alone.
Relationship management responsibility Operational reliability: cut-off times, same-day settlement, reporting. Tell clients about rule changes before their auditors ask.
Risks and counterarguments Balances respond far more to rates and bank deposit pricing than to regulation. Fees are thin, so small yield differences move large sums. The equivalence decision could carry conditions.

Client question: "Does your treasury policy still refer to liquidity fees and redemption gates as triggers?"

When this is not a reason to sell. Tokenised fund shares are, on the evidence, an infrastructure project about collateral. For most treasurers there is nothing to buy yet. Saying so is more credible than presenting it as a product.

Element View (forecasts labelled)
Base case (forecast) With policy rates at or above current levels, cash balances in money market funds stay large. New UK rules arrive roughly on time. EU-domiciled funds stay available.
Plausible alternatives Rates are cut and balances move to longer-dated assets. Or equivalence is delayed and UK investors face a narrower choice.
Indicators to watch Central bank decisions. The yield gap between funds and deposits. The final rules and the equivalence decision.
Evidence that would change the view Sustained outflows from stable-value funds after the rules take effect. A stress event in which a fund restricts withdrawals.

8. Middle East sovereign investors

Level 1 · First principles

A sovereign wealth fund invests a state's money, often from oil and gas revenue. The largest Gulf funds are among the biggest investors in the world. They employ their own investment teams, invest directly in companies and deals, and use outside managers selectively.

They are not buying funds from a catalogue. They ask for partnerships: a dedicated account, the right to invest alongside the manager, training for their staff and, increasingly, an office and jobs in their country.

Layer A · verified fact Goldman Sachs has offices in Dubai, Doha and Riyadh, announced an Abu Dhabi Global Market office in 2023, opened a Kuwait office in October 2025 and opened a regional headquarters in Riyadh in December 2025. ✔ Verified R5-S04R5-S28R5-S29R5-S30 These are firm-wide openings: public sources do not say which of them house asset-management client coverage. A 2027 Dubai-based Client Solutions Group student role is listed, so not all Middle East coverage sits in London. ≈ Supported inference R5-S18 In February 2024 Goldman Sachs Alternatives and Mubadala signed a $1bn separately managed account for Asia Pacific private credit (card). ✔ Verified R5-S04 In October 2026 fourteen financial firms announced plans to establish in Abu Dhabi Global Market. ✔ Verified R8-S57 Whether Arabic is required and whether the team is split by client segment were not established. ∅ Not publicly established

Cards: Goldman's Gulf presence, managers building around sovereign investors.

Step Local presence and partnership structures
What happened Office openings 2023 to December 2025. A wave of competitor arrivals announced October 2026.

Existing investments Existing relationships are re-tested against partners who are now present locally.

The Dutch pension transition, as the worked example

Level 1 · First principles

Dutch pension funds are moving from a system that promised a fixed pension to one where each member has a personal pot managed by age group. A promise needs protecting against falling interest rates, so the old funds held very large interest-rate hedges. A young member's pot does not need that protection. So as funds convert, some of that hedging is no longer needed and the growth portfolios are redesigned.

Layer A · verified fact Thirty Dutch pension funds holding about €542bn had converted by 31 March 2026, most of them on 1 January 2026. The rest must transfer accrued entitlements by 1 January 2028. ✔ Verified R5-S35R5-S36

Step Dutch pension transition
What happened Largest conversion wave on 1 January 2026 (reported April 2026). Deadline 1 January 2028.
Client effect Funds manage pots by age cohort. Hedging and return portfolios are rebuilt.
Decision that changes How much interest-rate hedging each cohort keeps, and what replaces it.
Existing investments Long-dated bonds and swaps may be reduced. Return-seeking allocations are redesigned.
Possible GSAM response Layer B · interpretation Cohort-aware fixed income and return building blocks, with analysis specific to each fund's design.
Sales responsibility Native-language coverage of funds and of the fiduciary managers many of them use.
Relationship management responsibility Keep existing mandates aligned with the fund's new design through its conversion date.
Risks and counterarguments The January 2026 wave passed calmly, so the forced-selling story may be overstated. Estimates of future hedge reduction come from interested parties. ≈ Supported inference R5-S37 Many funds delegate to a fiduciary manager, so the buyer is one step removed.
Element View (forecasts labelled)
Base case (forecast) Remaining funds convert by the deadline and hedging demand falls gradually, cohort by cohort.
Plausible alternatives Conversions are delayed. Or several large funds cut hedges at once and long-dated euro rates move sharply.
Indicators to watch The number and size of funds converting each January. The Dutch central bank's transition reporting.
Evidence that would change the view A formal extension of the deadline. Funds publishing higher post-conversion hedge ratios than expected.
