External manager selection External Investing Group: more than $528bn; relationships with over 1,000 private equity managers. ✔ Verified R8-S19 Yes: consultants, Russell, Partners Group, Hamilton Lane. It partly answers "will you only sell me your own funds?" Consultant-heritage rivals have longer public manager-research records in UK pensions. Fees layer up.
T. Rowe Price partnership Announced September 2025; up to $1bn stake. ≈ Supported inference R8-S24 Analogous alliances exist. Brings private-market content into retirement channels Goldman does not own. US-focused. 2026 status and EMEA relevance not established. ∅ Not publicly established
Risk and analytics; quantitative investing; NN IP's sustainable-credit heritage Not researched to a verifiable standard here. ∅ Not publicly established BlackRock's Aladdin is the clearest rival technology proposition. Not assessed. Do not claim these without checking a source first.

10.4 Replacing slogans with consequences

"Global platform" and "strong reputation" could be said of ten firms. A statement worth making names a capability, the evidence, and the consequence for one type of client.

Slogan A specific version The honest qualifier
"Global platform" "A UK scheme delegating its whole portfolio gets liability hedging, external manager selection and private-market access from one accountable provider, at a firm that reports over $540bn of OCIO assets." "Several rivals offer the same combination, and trustees should ask how in-house funds are chosen over external ones."
"Strong in alternatives" "A private bank can list an evergreen private-credit vehicle and an active ETF from the same coverage relationship." "Blackstone's wealth franchise is far larger, and 2026 showed these funds can limit redemptions."
"Strong reputation" "The trustees of a £23bn scheme appointed it after a competitive tender in which they were advised by an independent investment adviser." "One appointment shows it can win a tender. It does not show how the mandate has performed since."
"Leader in liquidity" "Over a trillion dollars of liquidity products firm-wide, which supports diversification and same-day dealing." "The sterling and euro fund ranking was not found, so 'leader' is not a claim to make."

Check your understanding

  • Pick one differentiator and answer all three test questions without looking.
  • A trustee says "BlackRock offers everything you do". What specific, evidenced point would you make, and what would you concede?
  • Which three competitor names have changed, and when?

11. The future of the work

This section separates what has been observed from what is a scenario. It analyses tasks, because whole roles rarely disappear and individual tasks often do.

11.1 Observed changes and scenarios, kept apart

Theme Observed (with source) Scenario (not observed)
AI in distribution 81% of institutional sales and service teams use AI for RFP content and 77% for meeting notes; far fewer for prospecting (26% to 32%). ✔ Verified R8-S41 Only 5% of managers let AI act with any autonomy on recommendations or trades. ✔ Verified R8-S42 AI choosing which clients to pursue. Client-ready material sent with no human sign-off.
Fee pressure Institutional fees falling about 3% a year; over 80% of 2025 revenue growth came from markets; costs grew faster than revenue from 2010 to 2025. ✔ Verified R8-S38 Goldman Sachs's own effective fee was 31 basis points in 2025 and it lists further decline as a risk. ✔ Verified R2-S01 Fees stabilising as mix shifts to private assets. Or a market fall exposing cost bases.
Passive investing In Europe active equity funds still held more than passive at the first quarter of 2026, but passive ETFs took about 57% of flows in the third quarter. ≈ Supported inference R8-S39 Active becoming a specialist allocation everywhere.
Private markets Goldman Sachs raised $122bn of alternatives commitments in nine months of 2026. ✔ Verified R2-S02 Retail fund redemptions were elevated. ✔ Verified R8-S52 Semi-liquid funds becoming standard in model portfolios. Or a gating episode reversing demand.
Intermediary change Model portfolios concentrating selection. ≈ Supported inference R4-S37 Consultants consolidating. ≈ Supported inference R3-S34 A handful of gatekeepers controlling most wealth flows.
Pension consolidation DC scale test legislated; LGPS down to six pools. ✔ Verified R3-S20R3-S21 A UK market with a few dozen institutional buyers that matter.
Industry structure About $53.8bn of asset-manager mergers in the year to August 2026. ≈ Supported inference R8-S54 Reported job cuts at several large managers. ≈ Supported inference R8-S47R8-S48 AI-driven cuts to entry-level client-facing hiring. No credible data on this was found. ∅ Not publicly established

11.2 Task by task

Task What is being automated (observed) What still needs a person What is uncertain Effect on junior learning Layer B · interpretation
RFP and DDQ first drafts Drafting answers and searching content libraries. ✔ Verified R8-S41 Checking every answer against approved, current content. Invented answers are the most cited barrier. ≈ Supported inference R8-S44 Whether clients respond by issuing longer questionnaires. Less writing from scratch, more verifying. The skill moves from drafting to judging accuracy.
Meeting notes Note-taking and summaries. ✔ Verified R8-S41 Deciding what was agreed, what is sensitive, who must act. Client consent and confidentiality practice. A task that taught listening is partly automated. The learning has to come from attending and being questioned afterwards.
Routine reports and emails Drafting reports and emails; 85% of UK fiduciary managers use AI mainly for this. ✔ Verified R8-S10 Reconciling numbers, attribution, and tone when performance is poor. Regulators' expectations on accountability. Less time building packs, more responsibility for checking them.
Prospecting and planning Low adoption so far. ✔ Verified R8-S41 Relationship context, suitability, whether to pursue at all. Whether adoption is low or merely early. Client research remains a junior task, with better tools.
Investment decisions AI used in at least one process at over half of managers; almost none let it decide. ✔ Verified R8-S42 Portfolio managers remain the decision-makers. Pace of change. Not a coverage task, but coverage staff must explain how AI is used.
Headcount One consultancy estimates AI could cut industry costs 25% to 35% over three to five years. That is an estimate. ✔ Verified R8-S38 Not applicable. No data links AI to entry-level distribution hiring. ∅ Not publicly established If preparation work shrinks, firms may hire fewer juniors or expect earlier client exposure. Both are scenarios.

11.3 Where people add measurable value, and where technology may do better

It would be easy to write "relationships cannot be automated". That is a slogan. A more defensible version separates the cases.

Where technology is likely to do better. Retrieving the approved answer to a standard question. Producing the first draft of a recurring report. Summarising a long document. Noticing that a client has not been contacted for six months. These are tasks where speed, recall and consistency matter and where a mistake is caught by review.

Where a person adds value that can be observed.

  • Accountability. A named person signs what is sent to a client and answers for it. One industry analyst put it as AI being "unable to replace the credibility that comes from well-crafted and verified human communication". ✔ Verified R8-S41 That is one analyst's judgement, not a law.
  • Finding out what was not written down. A request for proposal says what the trustees agreed to ask. It does not say which trustee is unconvinced or what went wrong with the last manager. That comes from conversation.
  • Deciding not to proceed. Judging that a product does not suit a client, or that a prospect is two years from buyout and should not be pursued, is a judgement with a commercial cost attached.
  • Delivering bad news. Explaining poor performance to a board that must then explain it to members.

Where it is uncertain. Whether clients will come to prefer a faster, cheaper, more automated service for routine matters and reserve people for the difficult moments. If so, the number of coverage people needed per client falls even though the value of each good one rises.

Limits and caveats: The apprenticeship problem

Layer B · interpretation Many junior tasks that are being automated (first drafts, notes, packs) were also how people learned the business. If those shrink, a junior person learns less by doing unless the firm replaces them with something else: earlier attendance at meetings, more responsibility for checking, structured questioning by seniors. A fair interview question to ask is how the team trains analysts now that drafting is assisted.

11.4 What is established about Goldman Sachs's own AI tools

The former intern said Goldman "recently restricted staff use of Claude Code". The public record is narrower and should be stated precisely.

  • Goldman Sachs launched its own "GS AI Assistant" firm-wide in June 2025, with versions for different staff groups including asset and wealth management. ✔ Verified R2-S13
  • Reuters reported on 28 April 2026 that Goldman removed its Hong Kong bankers' access to one external model on its internal platform, with other models still available. Goldman declined to comment. ✔ Verified R2-S12
  • Bloomberg News published an article on 2 November 2026 headed "Goldman Restricts Traders and Bankers From Using Some AI Tools". ✔ Verified R2-S10 The article itself was not read. Two outlets that summarised it report that internal guidance limited certain AI coding tools to engineers, removing access from bankers, traders and most other staff. ≈ Supported inference R2-S08R2-S09
  • A reported October 2025 internal memo named sales and client onboarding among processes targeted for AI-driven redesign and said headcount growth would be constrained. ≈ Supported inference R8-S45

What this does not establish: a firm-wide ban on any AI model, anything specific to asset-management client staff, or the reasons. ∅ Not publicly established The safe statement is: "Press reports say Goldman narrowed access to some AI coding tools to engineers in autumn 2026, while it runs its own internal assistant for all staff. I have not seen the firm's policy."

Check your understanding

  • Name one coverage task where technology is likely to do better than a person and one where a person adds observable value. Give the reason for each.
  • State the Goldman AI-tools finding in two sentences without overstating it.
  • What would you want to know about how a team trains analysts when drafting is assisted?

12. Using this chapter without overreaching

  • Lead with the client, not the event. "A scheme at 130% funded is choosing an endgame, and the Act changes what run-on is worth" is stronger than "the Pension Schemes Act passed".
  • Date everything. "As of the November decision, Bank Rate is 4%."
  • Offer the counterargument yourself. It shows the conclusion was tested.
  • Say what you do not know. Goldman's UK market shares, fee rates and team structures are largely not public. Saying so is more credible than guessing.
  • Do not assume a sale. For each development, be ready to say when the right response is to explain, to wait, or to help the client reduce what it holds with you.

Check your understanding

  • Choose one team. State its base case, one alternative, and the single indicator you would watch.
  • For that team, name a development that is not a reason to sell anything, and say what the right response is.
  • Which three facts in this chapter are most likely to be out of date first, and where would you check them?

Interview understanding and practice

This chapter turns the research into practice. It comes last on purpose. An answer is the visible end of an argument, and the argument rests on facts about the business and on evidence about you. If either is missing, a fluent answer will fail at the first follow-up question.

Limits and caveats: What this chapter can and cannot do

The six criteria used here are a proposed practice framework written for this project. Goldman Sachs has not published scoring criteria for this programme, and nobody outside the firm knows which questions will be asked. ∅ Not publicly established Everything in the question bank is plausible practice material, not a prediction.

This material is for preparation before an assessment. Do not use it, or any tool, during a live or recorded interview. The practice mode in the application shows a silent timer only. It records nothing and sends nothing anywhere.

No personal history has been written for you. Wherever an answer needs your own experience, the bank shows a slot in square brackets, such as "[my own example: a time I …]". Only you can fill it, and an honest "I have not tested this yet" is a valid way to fill it.

What is publicly known about the process

Keep the verified facts apart from what you have been told.

Layer A · verified fact Goldman's careers site describes a first-round video interview of about 30 minutes, which it refers to as the HireVue interview, and a final round called a Superday of typically two to five interviews with people the candidate could work with. R1-S23 ✔ Verified The summer programme runs for nine to ten weeks. R1-S22 ✔ Verified An applicant may apply to at most four business and location combinations in a recruiting year. R1-S02 ✔ Verified

Layer A · verified fact The official London listing for this programme contains no duties, team names or language requirements specific to the Client Solutions Group. Its text is programme-wide and division-wide. R1-S02 ✔ Verified

Several things the former intern said are not publicly established: that the content of a recorded answer decides which team you are sent to, that an associate reviews the video at double speed, the exact order of interviewers, and that assessment centres will ask more about AI. ? Unverified account They may be true. They are one person's experience from an earlier cycle.

Limits and caveats: Do not build tactics on unverified claims

It is tempting to mention a region or a product in a recorded answer because someone said it steers you to a team. Do not. The claim is unverified, the tactic produces an answer you cannot defend ("why the Middle East?"), and it replaces a real preference with a guess about a sorting rule. Say what you actually find interesting and why. If you have a constraint, such as speaking only English, say that too: several regional teams state a language requirement in their adverts. R1-S01 ✔ Verified

Why answers come after understanding

A memorised answer has one layer. An interviewer who wants to know whether you understand something asks a second question, and the second question is never the one you memorised.

Compare two candidates asked "Why Goldman Sachs?". The first says the firm has a global platform and a culture of excellence. The interviewer asks, "What would be different at BlackRock?" and there is nothing underneath. The second says that the asset management business serves institutions and intermediaries at scale and runs whole-portfolio mandates, gives one dated fact, and says plainly that other firms have breadth too. The same follow-up now has somewhere to go, because the candidate already knows where the claim is weak.

The difference is not vocabulary or confidence. The second candidate did three things before the interview:

  1. Learned what the business does and how it is paid (Chapter 1 and the chapters on the role, the teams and the economics).
  2. Worked out which of their own claims are supported and which are hopes (by testing each one against a real example from their own life).
  3. Practised saying it aloud, in time, to the standard below.

Level 1 · First principles

In plain terms. You are not trying to produce good sentences. You are trying to hold a position you can explain, defend and, where necessary, give ground on. The sentences follow.

Building an answer from an argument

Every substantial answer in the bank is built from the same five parts. You will not always say all five aloud, but you should have all five ready.

Part What it is The test it must pass
Claim One sentence that answers the question asked Could a listener repeat it?
Mechanism Why the claim is true: how the thing works Does it explain, or only assert?
Evidence A verified fact with its date, or a real event from your own life Could someone check it?
Limit Where the claim stops being true, or what a competitor could also say Have you said it before the interviewer does?
Personal link Why this matters to you, backed by something that happened Is it evidence or an adjective?

Illustrative example: Building "Why asset management?" from the five parts

Claim. I am drawn to how asset management is paid: a fee on assets that continues only while the client chooses to stay.

Mechanism. That makes the relationship continuous. The manager is judged every quarter against something measurable, and the client's problem (a pension paid for decades) is long-term.

Evidence. In 2025, management and other fees were $11,538m of the $16,679m net revenues of Goldman's Asset & Wealth Management segment. R2-S01 ✔ Verified

Limit. Fee revenue falls when markets fall, whatever anyone does. People in client coverage do not control the investment result. A lot of early work is preparation.

Personal link. [My own example: a long-running responsibility I stayed with, and what kept me interested.] If I have none, I say that this is a reasoned preference I am applying in order to test.

The order matters less than the completeness. In a 30-second answer you might give the claim, one piece of mechanism and the limit. In a 60 to 90-second answer you add the evidence and the personal link. The longer version is not the short one with more words. It adds reasoning that was missing.

Level 2 · Institutional mechanics

Why the limit earns more than it costs. Layer B · interpretation Stating the limit of your own claim feels like weakening it. In practice it does three things. It shows you understand the claim well enough to know its edge. It removes the interviewer's easiest follow-up. And it is direct evidence of the behaviour the job needs: telling a client where a product does not fit (Chapter 7, "Trust, translated into behaviour"). A candidate who cannot find the limit of "why this firm" is unlikely to find the limit of a strategy in front of a trustee.

Where facts go. Use at most one or two figures in a spoken answer, each with its date. Figures are there to make a claim checkable, not to show how many you have learned. If you are not sure of a number, give the order of magnitude and say so, or leave it out.

The six practice criteria

Score every practice attempt from 0 to 3 on each criterion. These are this project's proposal, chosen because each one corresponds to something the work itself requires. Confidence is deliberately not on the list.

Criterion What a 0 looks like What a 3 looks like
Accuracy A wrong fact, an invented figure, or a firm term misused ("asset management is 30% of revenue") Facts correct and dated; the firm's own terms used properly; unknowns stated as unknown
Specificity Every sentence would fit any employer or any client-facing job Names a task, a client constraint or a verified fact, and survives "a competitor could say that too"
Logic A list of assertions with no "because" Claim, mechanism, evidence and limit follow in order, with no circular step
Judgement One-sided; or gives a junior person a senior's authority States the counterargument, the trade-off and who actually decides
Clarity Jargon, hedging or running over time One idea per sentence; a listener with no notes could repeat the main point
Supported personal evidence Adjectives about yourself, or a motive borrowed from a guide A specific true example, or a plain statement that the preference is untested

Three notes on scoring yourself honestly:

  • Accuracy is pass or fail in spirit. One confident factual error in front of someone who works there outweighs a good structure. The correction from "asset management is about 30% of Goldman's revenue" to "the Asset & Wealth Management segment was 28.6% of 2025 net revenues, and Asset management inside it was 11.6%" R2-S01 ✔ Verified is the kind of precision that separates understanding from repetition.
  • A 3 for personal evidence can be an admission. "I have not done this work, so this is what I expect to like and want to test" scores higher than an unsupported story.
  • Do not average away a zero. A zero on accuracy or judgement is the thing to fix before the next attempt.

Three worked transformations

Each example starts from a realistic weak answer, diagnoses it against the criteria, and rebuilds it. Notice that the improved answer is not always longer.

1. "Why Goldman Sachs?"

Realistic conversation (illustrative): Weak version

"Goldman Sachs is the most prestigious firm on the street, with a global platform, a strong culture of excellence and the best people. I have always wanted to work here and I know I would learn from the best."

Diagnosis. Specificity 0: every clause fits any large bank. Logic 0: nothing explains why any of it matters for client coverage. Personal evidence 0: "always wanted to" cannot be checked. Accuracy is untested because there are no facts to be wrong about, which is its own problem.

What is missing. A capability, evidence for it, why it changes the work, and its limit.

Realistic conversation (illustrative): Better version (about 80 words)

"Two things, both about the work. The asset management business serves institutions and wealth intermediaries at scale, and it runs public markets, alternatives, liquidity and whole-portfolio OCIO mandates under one roof. For someone starting in client coverage, that should mean the client's problem sets the conversation instead of one product. I can't claim that is unique to Goldman. I can say it is the setting I think I would learn most in, and I'd like to test that."

Why it is better. It names capabilities that can be evidenced: long-term assets under supervision of $1,245bn institutional and $714bn third-party distributed at 30 September 2026 R2-S02 ✔ Verified, and $480bn of OCIO assets at 31 March 2026 R3-S09 ✔ Verified. It links them to what a junior would experience, and it labels that link as an inference. It concedes the limit before being asked. If pressed for proof, the BAE Systems appointment of about £23bn after a competitive tender is public. R3-S01 ✔ Verified

What it still depends on. The last sentence is a personal claim. You need a real reason why problem-led work across client types appeals to you. Full treatment: IQ-01 and IQ-02.

2. "What would you actually do as an analyst?"

Realistic conversation (illustrative): Weak version

"I'd be building relationships with clients, pitching investment solutions and helping to win new mandates for the firm from day one."

Diagnosis. Judgement 0: it gives an intern a senior's job. Accuracy 0: interns do not pitch to clients or win mandates. It also hints that the candidate will be disappointed by the real work.

Realistic conversation (illustrative): Better version (about 70 words)

"Mostly preparation and follow-through. Researching a client before a meeting and writing the briefing note. Pulling the numbers for a quarterly review pack and checking them. Drafting parts of a due-diligence response. Keeping the pipeline and client records accurate. Taking notes and chasing actions. I wouldn't be advising clients or quoting anything. The point of the work is that the senior people are properly prepared and what was promised gets done."

Why it is better. It is concrete, it is modest about decision rights, and it explains why unglamorous work matters. It should be offered with one honest caveat: the published London listing does not describe team duties R1-S02 ✔ Verified, so this list is a supported inference from team adverts R1-S01 and general practice (Chapter 6, "What each level of seniority realistically contributes"). ≈ Supported inference Saying so costs nothing and shows you know the status of your own knowledge. Full treatment: IQ-14.

3. "You have explained why the role matters. Why would you enjoy it?"

This is the example where the better answer is shorter and plainer than the weak one could have been.

Realistic conversation (illustrative): Weak version

"I'd enjoy it because I'm passionate about helping clients achieve their goals, and there's nothing more rewarding than knowing you've made a difference. I thrive in fast-paced environments, I love building relationships, and I'm excited by the chance to work at the intersection of markets and people."

Diagnosis. The question excluded "why it matters", and the answer gives it again. Personal evidence 0: five self-descriptions, no event. Specificity 0: it would suit nursing, teaching or recruitment.

Realistic conversation (illustrative): Better version

"Fair challenge. Important and enjoyable aren't the same. The parts I think I'd enjoy are specific: working out how an unfamiliar organisation makes decisions, and getting a piece of written work exactly right for someone else to use. My evidence is [my own example]. The part I expect to find hard is repetition, the fifth quarterly pack. I can't prove I'd enjoy it until I've done it, which is partly why I'm applying."

Why it is better. It accepts the distinction, names tasks, offers evidence, names a cost and admits uncertainty. It contains no adjective about the speaker. If the slot is empty, the answer still works: "I don't have strong evidence yet. Here is why I expect to, and here is what would tell me I was wrong." Full treatment: IQ-31, and the section "A valuable role is not the same as a role I would enjoy" in the Relationships page.

How to handle "I don't know"

You will be asked something you cannot answer. That is partly the point: the job involves being asked such questions by clients, and the interviewer may be more interested in what you do next than in the answer.

Level 1 · First principles

There are three situations, and each has its own honest response.

You do not know a fact. Say so, then offer what you do know and how you would find out. "I don't know the current figure. The last number I saw was the end of September, about 4.1 trillion dollars of assets under supervision. I'd check the latest earnings release."

You do not know how something works. Say so, then reason from what you understand. "I haven't come across that. From what I know about how schemes hedge, I'd guess it works like this. Is that close?" A labelled guess that shows reasoning is fine. An unlabelled guess is not.

You do not know your own mind. Say so. "I don't yet know whether I'd prefer the sales or the servicing side. Here is what draws me to each, and here is what I'd need to see to find out."

Realistic conversation (illustrative): Words that work

"I'm not sure, and I'd rather not guess."

"I know part of that. The part I'm confident about is … The part I'd need to check is …"

"I haven't thought about it from that angle. Can I take a moment?"

"I got that wrong a minute ago. What I should have said is …"

Limits and caveats: What to avoid

  • Confident invention. A made-up figure or mechanism, delivered smoothly. It is the single most damaging thing you can do, because it shows the interviewer what you would do with a client.
  • The vague retreat. "It depends on a lot of factors" with none named.
  • Changing the subject to something you prepared.
  • Over-apologising. One plain sentence is enough.

Correcting yourself is also allowed. If you realise mid-answer that you misstated something, stop and fix it. People who work with clients do this every week.

What not to do

Keyword tactics drawn from unverified recruitment claims. Covered above. If you have been told that certain words send you to certain teams, or that reviewers skim at double speed, treat it as a rumour. Optimising for a rumour makes answers worse and cannot be defended.

Confident invention. Never state a Goldman fee, team size, internal structure, client name or interview criterion you cannot source. The team structure in particular: one person's informal account contains points that public sources contradict, such as OCIO being a UK-only team. R3-S09 ⇄ Conflicting evidence "I've heard an informal description but couldn't verify it" is a strong sentence.

Borrowed motives. If a line in this bank is not true of you, do not say it. The suggested answers are written in a provisional first person so that they can be adapted. They are not meant to be adopted. A motive you cannot support with one true example will fail the question "what's your evidence?".

Naming clients you cannot source. The BAE Systems appointment is public through the manager's own press release. R3-S01 ✔ Verified A second company the former intern mentioned has no public confirmation, and scheme documents point elsewhere, so it is left out of every answer here. ∅ Not publicly established Repeating a client name described as confidential would show poor judgement about exactly the thing this job depends on.

Ranking colleagues' work. Do not call relationship management "admin", banking "brutal" or passive investing "lazy". You may be speaking to someone who does it.

Lengthening instead of improving. If an answer is weak, the fix is usually a missing mechanism or a missing limit. More words rarely help.

Reading from notes or tools in the interview. Besides being against the spirit of the assessment, it shows. The purpose of practice is that the argument is in your head.

Using the practice mode

The application's practice mode draws a question, runs a silent timer and asks you to score yourself. A routine that works:

  1. Draw a question and answer aloud before opening anything. Speaking exposes gaps that reading hides.
  2. Stop at the time limit. About 70 to 80 words fills 30 seconds. About 170 to 220 words fills 60 to 90 seconds.
  3. Score all six criteria before you reveal the reasoning. Be strict on accuracy and on personal evidence.
  4. Reveal the underlying argument and compare. Look for the part you missed: usually the limit.
  5. Try one follow-up. The follow-ups get harder. If the first one stops you, the understanding is thin, and the map below shows which chapter to reread.
  6. Record the attempt if you want a history. Saving is off unless you turn it on, and it stays in your browser.

Work through the practice cases the same way. Each gives a situation, your realistic role in it, what good looks like and the traps. Say what you would do, then compare. In every case the junior's decision rights are limited on purpose: the skill being practised is noticing, checking, escalating and following through, not deciding for the client.

Note: On the personal slots

Before practising the motivation questions, write down one real example from your own life for each claim you plan to make. A slot answered with a small true example ("I kept a weekly report accurate for ten weeks and here is what I noticed") beats one answered with a large vague one.

Map: where each kind of question is fed from

Why asset management IQ-05 to IQ-07 Foundations; Mandates and economics
Why CSG IQ-08, IQ-10 The role; Sales versus relationship management
Sales or RM IQ-11 to IQ-13 Sales versus relationship management; People and recruitment

The six practice cases draw on the same material: PC-01 and PC-02 on the economics and on Chapter 7's treatment of honesty; PC-03 on suitability and decision rights; PC-04 on admitting limits; PC-05 on responsiveness against accuracy; PC-06 on the wealth-intermediary chain.

Level 2 · Institutional mechanics

How the hard follow-ups are constructed. Layer B · interpretation Almost every difficult follow-up in the bank is one of six moves. Knowing them lets you test your own answers before anyone else does.

Move Example What it tests
Generalise "Couldn't you say that about any client-facing job?" Specificity
Compete "Why Goldman Sachs rather than a competitor with similar products?" Whether the claim survives comparison
Personalise "You have explained why the role matters. Why would you enjoy it?" Evidence about you
Concretise "What would you actually do as an analyst?" Realism about tasks and decision rights
Reverse "When would the client be right to leave?" Judgement when the firm's interest and the client's diverge
Disconfirm "What would make you decide this career is not for you?" Whether the motivation has been tested

For any answer you prepare, apply all six moves yourself. If one of them leaves you with nothing to say, that is the part to work on.

Check your understanding: Before you practise

  1. Without looking, state the five parts of an answer and the test each must pass.
  2. Which two criteria should you never average away, and why?
  3. Give the corrected version of "asset management is about 30% of Goldman's revenue", with the year.
  4. What are the three kinds of "I don't know", and what is the honest response to each?
  5. Name one thing the former intern said about the process that you should not act on, and explain why acting on it would make your answers worse.
  6. Pick any answer you have prepared and apply the six follow-up moves. Which one exposes a gap?
  7. Which slots in the question bank can you fill today with a true example, and which must you answer with "I have not tested this yet"?

Acceptance test, open questions and limits

This chapter holds the project to its own standard. It answers the nine acceptance questions from the brief, lists what is still unresolved, and shows topic by topic what was investigated and what was not.

The nine acceptance questions

Each answer says where the evidence is and where the project falls short. "Yes" is only claimed where you can check it yourself by doing the test described.

Question Honest answer How to check it yourself
Can a beginner explain the business without memorising jargon? The material is there: chapter 1 teaches each idea from first principles before any acronym is used, and the glossary defines every term in plain English. Whether you can explain it is a test only you can run Close the file and explain to someone outside finance how a pension scheme's money reaches an asset manager and how the manager is paid
Can the reader distinguish sales, relationship management and adjacent roles without oversimplifying? Yes for the general industry picture (chapters 2 and 6, role comparison). For Goldman specifically, the published evidence shows the labels overlap, and the internal split is not public Compare any two roles in the Role comparison view and say what each can decide alone
Can the reader connect a junior task to a client outcome and a commercial consequence? Yes. Every lifecycle stage lists what the junior person produces and what good execution changes, and the sample work products show the documents Pick the meeting preparation note in chapter 7 and trace it to the mandate's fee in the calculator
Are the organisational claims, people and mandates supported, not invented? Supported where sources exist, and marked where they do not. Several posts have no publicly established holder, and no mandate is attributed to a London team because no source does so Open any team, person or mandate and follow its source link
Can every statement about trust, relationships, value or passion be translated into an action, a difficult choice or a concrete preference? The Relationships page and chapter 7 do this, and chapter 7 ends with a translation table. Passion is deliberately not asserted anywhere Take any sentence containing "trust" in your own draft answers and replace it using the table
Can the motivation arguments withstand repeated questioning without becoming circular? The earlier "why-tree" exercises were removed at your request. The Relationships page now ends with concrete tasks to test yourself against, and the interview bank pushes each answer through harder follow-ups Answer each follow-up in the Practise section aloud. Note where you repeat yourself
Does the material distinguish a strong business argument from evidence of personal fit? Yes. Interpretation is labelled apart from fact, and nothing personal has been written for you. Where an answer needs your own example, it shows an empty slot Check that nothing in your answers uses "the role is valuable" as proof that you would enjoy it
Does it explain when a client should not buy, when a mandate should shrink and when a different career might fit better? Yes for the first two: the Relationships page and chapter 7 on when a relationship should end, and the withdrawal cases in chapter 5. Career comparison was part of the removed motivation chapter Find the passages and summarise each in two sentences
Do the dossier, website and PDF agree, and are their limits explicit? They are generated from the same files by one script, so they cannot drift apart. Limits are stated in chapter 0 and below Run python3 build/build.py --pdf and compare any entity ID across the three outputs

What was verified, and what stayed open

The audit of the former intern's account, claim by claim:

What the former intern saidEvidence statusWhat the research foundHow to use it
Client Solutions Group is an umbrella term inside Asset Management for everyone who speaks to clients; it is the equivalent of saying "sales".✔ VerifiedGoldman's own campus titles read "Client Solutions Group / Sales" (Frankfurt) and "Client Solutions Group (Sales)" (Tokyo), and an internal role refers to "the sales organization" R1-S04 R1-S09 R1-S14. Goldman's one-paragraph definition says the group develops client relationships and delivers investment solutions for institutional and third-party wealth clients R1-S10. Limit: not everyone who speaks to clients is in it. OCIO investment staff in Multi-Asset Solutions meet clients and sit outside the sales organisation R1-S15. R1-S04 R1-S09 R1-S14 R1-S10 R1-S15Safe to say CSG is the firm's client and sales organisation for asset management. Do not say it contains every client-facing person.
It covers three functions: sales, client relationship management and consultant relations.≈ Supported inferenceAll three functions exist in Goldman advertisements. A London CSG team does both new business and existing relationships R1-S01; consultant relations works with the regional institutional sales teams R1-S21; a job advertisement lists the channels as third party wealth, institutional, consultant, insurance and retirement R4-S09. No public source gives this exact three-way list as the group's formal structure. R1-S01 R1-S21 R4-S09Use it as a description of the kinds of work, not as an org chart.
The group is cut by coverage team (mostly regional), then by client type, then by sales versus relationship management.≈ Supported inferenceJob advertisements show country or regional teams crossed with channel: for example Institutional Sales in Frankfurt and Third Party Wealth in Paris and Dubai as named CSG sub-tracks R1-S05 R1-S06 R1-S07. That supports the first two cuts as a matrix. No source shows them as an ordered hierarchy, and no reporting lines are published. The third cut (sales versus relationship management inside each client-type team) is not shown by any public source. R1-S05 R1-S06 R1-S07Describe geography and client type as overlapping cuts. Ask how the team divides new business from existing clients; do not state it.
Most regional teams split into Third Party Wealth and Institutional, like the UK.≈ Supported inferenceConsistent with advertisements for Germany and Austria (Frankfurt institutional sales and a German third-party wealth team) R1-S05 R5-S07 and Benelux R1-S01. The Nordics are an exception on the public record: in May 2020 third-party distribution and institutional sales were merged into one Nordic organisation R5-S26. Whether that is still so in 2026 was not established. R1-S05 R5-S07 R1-S01 R5-S26Fine as a general pattern with the Nordic exception noted.
The coverage teams are UK, Middle East, Nordics, Switzerland, Benelux, Liquidity Solutions and Insurance, and that list is "everyone". Germany, France, Italy and Iberia were not mentioned.⇄ Conflicting evidenceThe list is incomplete for EMEA. Germany and Austria are covered from Frankfurt and France from Paris, both recruiting CSG analysts for 2027 with a local language R1-S05 R1-S06. Italy has a country head and Iberia a managing director whose team moved from London to Madrid in 2021 R6-S11 R6-S12 R6-S13. The likeliest reading is that he listed the teams with seats in London, which is an inference. R1-S05 R1-S06 R6-S11 R6-S12 R6-S13Do not repeat the list as complete. If asked about EMEA coverage, say continental markets are largely covered from local offices.
The UK team is the largest by far, brings in the most money and so should have the best bonus.∅ Not publicly establishedGoldman discloses no revenue, assets, flows or headcount for the UK or for any client team. The only regional figure is EMEA assets under supervision of $799bn at 30 September 2026 R2-S01 R2-S02. Nothing public supports a ranking of teams or any statement about bonuses. R2-S01 R2-S02Do not use.
The UK team is split by client type into Institutional and Third Party Wealth (and OCIO).≈ Supported inference"UK Third Party Wealth (TPW) Sales Team" is Goldman's own wording in a closed London advertisement R1-S17. A 2026-cycle London listing titled "Client Solutions Group, UK Institutional Sales" appears in search results but the page had expired R1-S31. The senior public title is EMEA-wide: "co-head of EMEA Institutional Client Coverage" R6-S02. Whether "UK Institutional" is a formal team name today is not established. R1-S17 R1-S31 R6-S02"Third Party Wealth" can be used as an official name. Say "the UK institutional business" rather than asserting a team name.
OCIO is the third client-type team inside the UK team.⇄ Conflicting evidencePublic sources place OCIO and fiduciary management in Multi-Asset Solutions, an investing group, not inside a regional sales team R1-S15 R6-S18. Its head is titled "Head of International OCIO and UK Fiduciary Management Team" R6-S04. OCIO appears to have its own client relationship managers at senior level (snippet only) R1-S33. A CSG-side sales seat for fiduciary management may still exist; that is not established either way. R1-S15 R6-S18 R6-S04 R1-S33Describe OCIO as a business delivered by the multi-asset investment group that works with sales and relationship professionals.
He is "pretty sure" OCIO exists only in the UK team.⇄ Conflicting evidenceGoldman's OCIO business is global: $480bn of OCIO assets under supervision at 31 March 2026, with large United States mandates announced in July 2026 R3-S09, a $40bn multi-country appointment in September 2025 that included Germany as well as the UK R3-S06, and an Irish fiduciary award in November 2026 R3-S11. An OCIO insurance team works across The Hague, London and New York R1-S15. What may be true is narrower: the UK is where the trustee-led "fiduciary management" market is most developed. R3-S09 R3-S06 R3-S11 R1-S15Never say OCIO is UK-only. Say the UK is one of its largest markets.
In OCIO, Goldman can bring the client's in-house investment team into the firm.✔ VerifiedTrue of the BAE Systems appointment: Goldman's press release says the schemes' in-house investment management team would join the firm R3-S01 R3-S02. It is a feature of some very large mandates, not of the model in general: no transfer is reported for smaller UK fiduciary appointments R7-S15 R7-S16. R3-S01 R3-S02 R7-S15 R7-S16Use as an example of one way a large mandate can be structured. Do not present it as how every OCIO appointment works.
OCIO is already over-hired.∅ Not publicly establishedNo public support. The only public staffing evidence points the other way: a senior hire in September 2025 R6-S01 and a statement in November 2025 that the supporting multi-asset team of more than 300 was still growing R3-S07. Neither says anything about analyst seats. R6-S01 R3-S07Do not use, and do not let it steer which business you say interests you.
Goldman recently won an OCIO award; he saw it in a LinkedIn post by a managing director.≈ Supported inferenceTwo 2026 awards fit: Fiduciary Management / OCIO at the European Pensions Awards (2 July 2026) R3-S10 and Fiduciary Management / OCIO of the Year at the Irish Pensions Awards (4 November 2026) R3-S11. Which one he saw is not established, and the managing director was not identified. Goldman did not win the fiduciary category at the 2026 UK Pensions Awards R3-S14. An industry award shows that a judging panel rated an entry; it is not evidence of client outcomes. R3-S10 R3-S11 R3-S14If you mention an award, name the awarding body and year, and do not lean on it as proof of quality.
BAE Systems is an OCIO client, and that is confidential.✔ VerifiedThe relationship is public, not confidential. Goldman's own press release of 6 September 2023 announced the appointment by the trustees of the BAE Systems pension schemes for about £23bn of defined benefit assets, after a competitive tender in which Redington advised the trustees R3-S01 R3-S02. See [the mandate entry](#M-R7-01). R3-S01 R3-S02Can be named, citing the press release. Attribute the decision to the trustees, and do not claim knowledge of the mandate beyond what was announced.
A second named company is also an OCIO client, also described as confidential.∅ Not publicly establishedNo public source links Goldman to that company's pension schemes. The schemes' own latest annual reports name a different firm as fiduciary manager R3-S17 R3-S18. The name is withheld from every output of this project. R3-S17 R3-S18Never mention it. Repeating an unconfirmed client name in an interview would itself be a judgement failure.

R1-S07 R6-S14Do not describe the team's internal structure.

Within each team the sales side is called CSG and the relationship-management side is called CCG (Client Coverage Group).⇄ Conflicting evidence"Client Coverage Group (CCG)" is a real Goldman name, defined as the group "dedicated to retaining, expanding and supporting existing client relationships" R1-S11. R6-S17 R6-S27Do not use. It should not decide which side you say you prefer.
The two sides sit opposite each other, work the same hours and operate as one team; at analyst level the work is basically the same.? Unverified accountNothing public describes seating or hours. If you refer to it, say a former intern described it that way.
Sales is seen as more prestigious; many relationship people want to move across; internal moves are bureaucratic.? Unverified accountOne person's impression of culture. A managing director posted about the OCIO award; a partner told him assessment centres are moving in person and will ask more about AI.∅ Not publicly establishedNeither person could be identified from public sources and no identity is suggested here. The first stage is a recorded video interview.✔ VerifiedGoldman's own steps page: "you will be asked to participate in a video interview, which will take approximately 30 minutes to complete", referred to as the HireVue interview R1-S23. R1-S23Prepare for a recorded format.
An associate on the team reviews the recorded video, sometimes at double speed.? Unverified accountNothing public says who reviews recordings or how. The only sensible lesson is general: make the first sentences of an answer clear. Build no tactic on it.
What you say in the recorded interview decides which team you are "drafted" to: region, client type, and sales or relationship management.? Unverified accountThe mechanism is not published. The 2027 London listing names no sub-track while Frankfurt, Paris and Dubai listings do R1-S05 R1-S06 R1-S07, so some allocation must happen after applying, but how is unknown. R1-S05 R1-S06 R1-S07Do not plant keywords to steer allocation. Talk about the client segments that actually interest you and say why.
The assessment centre is three back-to-back interviews with the team and no group task: analyst and associate together, then a vice president or similar, then the managing director who runs the team.? Unverified accountOfficially the final round ("Superday") is "between two and five interviews for campus hires, depending on the division" with "a cross-section of people whom you could possibly work with" R1-S23. Three interviews fits inside that range. The number, order, interviewers and absence of a group task are his experience of one team in one year. "Vice president or similar" fits the fact that Executive Director is the same level as Vice President in EMEA R1-S26. R1-S23 R1-S26Prepare for several one-to-one or two-to-one interviews with team members at different levels; do not rely on the exact sequence.
Assessment centres are now in person and will ask more about AI.∅ Not publicly establishedOfficial pages read are silent on both. Press coverage was not searched because the search allowance ran out, so this is "not investigated" beyond official sources. Recruiters' published guidance says questions are "situational or behavioral" and that they weigh "attitude and aptitude" R1-S24. R1-S24Be ready for either format, and have a considered view on how AI changes client work (see the commercial-awareness chapter). Confirm the format with your recruiter.
Each team hires one analyst per open seat, so a candidate competes only against others drafted to the same team.? Unverified accountNothing public describes seat numbers or how candidates are compared. No hiring probability can be inferred. Do not use.
Each team runs its own hiring timeline, so offers on one team say nothing about another.≈ Supported inferenceGoldman says it evaluates applications throughout the season and that candidates "may hear back regarding different roles at different times" R1-S23. That is about roles, not teams within one listing, so it is consistent with the claim without confirming it. R1-S23Useful for managing your own expectations only.
Asset management is about 30% of Goldman's revenue and valued for stable fee income.⇄ Conflicting evidenceThe figure matches the Asset & Wealth Management segment, which was 28.6% of firmwide net revenues in 2025. The Asset Management business on its own was 11.6% R2-S01. Management and other fees were $11,538m, 69% of the segment, which is the fee income the "stable" point refers to. Fees recur while clients stay and markets hold; they are not guaranteed. Nothing is disclosed for the Client Solutions Group. R2-S01Say "Asset & Wealth Management was about 29% of 2025 net revenues" and name the segment. Do not say asset management alone is 30%.
Goldman recently restricted staff use of Claude Code.≈ Supported inferenceBloomberg reported on 2 November 2026 that Goldman restricted traders and bankers from some AI tools; outlets relaying it say internal guidance limited Claude Code and GitHub's AI coding tools to engineers R2-S10 R2-S08 R2-S09. The Bloomberg article itself could not be read. It is one report, it concerns coding tools for non-engineers, it is not a firm-wide ban on AI, and nothing says how it applies to asset-management client staff. A separate April 2026 report concerned Hong Kong bankers' access to one model R2-S12. R2-S10 R2-S08 R2-S09 R2-S12If AI comes up, describe it accurately as a reported restriction of coding tools to engineers, citing the press. Do not call it a ban on AI.
Details about the former intern's own background, his friend's internship and a candidate he knows.? Unverified accountNot researched, by design. These are private individuals and nothing about them is needed to understand the business. Not relevant. Do not name him or rely on "someone told me" as support for any claim.
An English-only UK candidate is most likely to be sent to the UK team, with the Middle East possible if the answers mention the Middle East.? Unverified accountNo public information on allocation. See IC-36. Do not mention a region you have no real interest in to influence allocation. If the Gulf's sovereign investors do interest you, say why in terms of the clients.

Open questions worth resolving before an interview

These are the gaps most likely to matter in conversation, with the fastest way to close each.

  1. The current London listing. The exact 2027 London listing carried only programme-wide wording when it was read on a mirror, and it was no longer among the live campus listings on 14 November 2026 R1-S03. Check your own application portal for the wording and any team information it shows you.
  2. How Client Solutions Group and Client Coverage Group relate in London. Both names are real. Their reporting relationship is not published. A neutral question to ask an interviewer: "How do the sales and client coverage roles divide the work on your team?"
  3. Who leads UK institutional coverage and UK & Ireland third-party wealth today. Neither post has a publicly established current holder. A departure from the EMEA third-party wealth leadership was reported in April 2026, with no successor found in public sources.
  4. Which OCIO award the former intern saw. Two 2026 awards fit. Do not name one as fact.
  5. Analyst pay. The two figures in the starting account have no public support. Do not build any argument on them.
  6. The interview format this cycle. Goldman publishes the general shape of its process. Whether this team's final round is in person, and what it asks about AI, is not established. Prepare for both.

Limits of this project

  • It is not exhaustive. The people directory is a sample of publicly visible professionals. The mandates register holds what was found in the time and search allowance available. Neither should be described as complete.
  • It is dated. Every figure is correct to the date beside it. The rates backdrop changed in the week before the cutoff, which shows how quickly a commercial-awareness point can go stale.
  • It contains interpretation. Layer B passages are arguments. A well-informed interviewer may disagree with some of them, and a reasoned disagreement is a good conversation to have.
  • It cannot assess you. Practice scores are self-assessed against a proposed framework. Goldman Sachs has not published scoring criteria, and nobody outside the firm knows the questions.
  • It was partly written by automated research and drafting. Every claim carries a source or a label so that you can check it. Open the source for anything you intend to say aloud.

What was tested

The application and PDF were checked by an automated script and by inspecting rendered pages. The README lists every check and its result. In brief: navigation, search, filters, expandable sections, the fee calculator's arithmetic against an independent implementation, keyboard access, mobile layout, reduced-motion behaviour, and that the file makes no network requests. The PDF was rendered and its pages inspected for clipped text and broken tables.

No part of this project has been published or hosted. The HTML file is a local file. If you choose to share it, check the source register and the people directory first and decide what you are comfortable circulating.

Public professional information only. The title is what the source says. The function is our reading of it, and is marked unclear where the title does not settle it. People move: check the date.

Observed public-profile sample, not headcount

The directory holds 42 people found in public sources. Of these, 6 are classified as sales, 0 as relationship management and 36 as blended, leadership, specialist or unclear. Numerator and denominator are both this sample. Senior and externally visible people are over-represented, and titles rarely state the function, so this says nothing reliable about the real sales-to-relationship-management ratio, team sizes or hiring odds.

BAE Systems Pension Scheme and BAE Systems Executive Pension Scheme

OCIO appointment · 2023-09-06 (announced); transition expected towards end of 2023; scheme SIPs updated 11 July 2024 ✔ Verified M-R7-01

Client type
Corporate defined benefit pension schemes
Country
United Kingdom
Event date
2023-09-06 (announced); transition expected towards end of 2023; scheme SIPs updated 11 July 2024
Kind of event
OCIO appointment
Strategy
Outsourced chief investment officer for the schemes' DB assets, including liability-driven and cashflow-driven portfolios; in-house investment team (BAE Systems Pension Funds Investment Management) moved to GSAM and continues to serve the schemes
Amount as disclosed
Approximately £23 billion
What the amount measures
UK defined benefit scheme assets handed over for management at announcement. Not a fee figure and not a statement of fee-paying AUM by strategy.
Stated rationale
Sponsor: 'reducing the cost and improving the efficiency of asset management are essential'. Trustee chair credited the in-house team's stewardship and framed the move as a long-term solution. Selected after a 'highly competitive tender process'.
Consultant involvement
Redington (trustees' strategic investment adviser since 2021; advised on the deal and oversees implementation). Travers Smith (trustees' lawyers). PwC advised the sponsor. Gallagher is named as the trustee's investment adviser in the 2026 implementation statement.
Decision-makers
Trustees of both schemes (chair Andrew Gallagher); sponsor group finance director Brad Greve quoted
Public attribution to a GS team
Press release quotes Ed Francis as Head of International OCIO and UK Fiduciary Management, with David Solomon and Marc Nachmann. No source attributes the win to a sales or coverage team or to any other individual.
Notes
Described by Goldman as the largest OCIO mandate awarded in the UK to that date. Still in force: the scheme's implementation statement for the year to 31 March 2026 calls GSAM 'the Scheme's OCIO'. The trustee retains a separate investment adviser, so OCIO did not remove independent oversight. Number of staff transferred is not public.
Sources
R7-S01 R7-S02 R7-S03 R7-S04 R7-S05 R7-S06 R7-S07

Various pension entities and a captive insurance company related to Shell plc (UK, Germany, Bermuda and other locations); advisory for North American plans

OCIO appointment · 2025-09-09 (announced); transitions expected to complete later in 2025 ✔ Verified M-R7-02

Client type
Corporate pension funds and captive insurer
Country
United Kingdom / Germany / other Europe / North America (advisory)
Event date
2025-09-09 (announced); transitions expected to complete later in 2025
Kind of event
OCIO appointment
Strategy
OCIO for international pension plan assets in Europe (includes LDI and CDI); investment advisory services for North American plans
Amount as disclosed
$40 billion in total; of which about $15.6 billion (about £11.5bn) UK and $2.8 billion Germany
What the amount measures
Pension plan and captive assets covered by the mandates at announcement. The rest of the $40bn is not itemised. No asset figure is given for the North American advisory element. Not fee-paying AUM by strategy.
Stated rationale
Marc Nachmann: asset owners 'increasingly want differentiated alpha, holistic total portfolio advice and customized portfolio solutions'. Each fund 'set clear objectives and selection criteria'. Shell spokesperson: Shell acted as coordinator; decisions were made by the individual funds.
Consultant involvement
Isio (oversaw the competitive tender)
Decision-makers
Trustees of each fund, deciding separately
Public attribution to a GS team
Press release quotes Chloe Kipling, co-head of EMEA Institutional Client Coverage, and Marc Nachmann. mallowstreet reports 'some staff will move to GSAM'. No further team attribution is public.
Notes
The Dutch Shell fund (SSPF) is not part of this: it appointed BlackRock in 2024. That shows one sponsor's schemes can choose different OCIO providers. Completion of the transition has not been separately confirmed in a source read for this register.

R7-S55

What is changing for each kind of client, and what follows from it. Not every change is a reason to sell something.

Bank Rate rises to 4% and gilt yields sit above 5%

2026-11-05 ✔ Verified D-R3-01

Event date
2026-11-05
Publication date
2026-11-05
1 · What happened
The Bank of England raised Bank Rate from 3.75% to 4% on an 8–1 vote, its first rise since August 2023, citing inflation of 3.5% heading to about 5% by mid-2027 on higher energy prices. The 10-year gilt yield was about 5.15% on the day.
2 · How it affects the client
For a DB pension scheme, higher gilt yields lower the present value of promised pensions. Hedged schemes see assets and liabilities fall together; under-hedged schemes see funding improve. Schemes using leveraged LDI must hold enough collateral when yields jump. Cash and short-dated bonds now pay more, which raises the bar for every riskier asset.
3 · What decision changes
How much interest-rate and inflation risk to hedge, how much collateral to hold against LDI, whether to lock in yields with buy-and-maintain credit, and whether improved funding brings buyout or run-on forward.
4 · Implications for existing investments
Long-dated bond and LDI portfolios lose market value as yields rise (matched by lower liabilities). Growth assets look less necessary for well-funded schemes. Money market and short-duration holdings earn more.
5 · Possible GSAM response (interpretation, not a GS statement)
(Layer B, not a GS statement) Review hedge ratios and collateral waterfalls with LDI clients; show cashflow-driven credit portfolios that lock in current yields; for OCIO clients, revisit the journey plan and endgame timing.
6 · Sales responsibility
A prospect whose funding has just improved may reopen manager or OCIO selection. The useful opening is a specific observation about their hedge ratio or endgame date, not a product.
7 · Relationship-management responsibility
Existing clients need a clear account of what the move did to their own assets, liabilities and collateral, before they ask.
8 · Risks and counterarguments
The Bank said the move should not be read as the start of a long run of rises, yet also that it is unlikely to be the last unless the Middle East conflict is resolved. Yields could fall back, reversing funding gains for unhedged schemes. A rate rise driven by an energy shock can hurt growth assets and sponsor covenants at the same time.
A question to ask a client
If gilt yields moved another 100 basis points in either direction, what would happen to your funding level and your collateral position, and who would have to act?
Indicators to watch
MPC decision on 17 December 2026; CPI prints; 10- and 30-year gilt yields; PPF 7800 monthly funding ratio.
Base case
Forecast, not fact: gilt yields stay high enough that most DB schemes remain in surplus on a low-dependency basis, so trustees' main questions are endgame choice, hedge ratio and collateral, not deficit repair.
Plausible alternatives
(1) Yields fall materially and under-hedged schemes lose part of their surplus. (2) A disorderly rise in yields forces collateral calls; post-2022 buffers are tested for the first time.
Evidence that would change the view
PPF 7800 funding ratio falling for several consecutive months; regulator statements about collateral buffers being drawn on; a client's own hedge ratio turning out lower than reported.
Sources
R3-S31 R3-S32 R3-S33

DB schemes are in aggregate surplus and the buy-in market is busy but smaller in value

2026-10-31 ✔ Verified D-R3-02

Event date
2026-10-31
Publication date
2026-11-10
1 · What happened
The PPF 7800 index showed an aggregate surplus of £275.4bn and a 133.7% funding ratio at end October 2026. In 2025 a record 370 buy-ins completed, but premium fell to about £38bn from £47.8bn in 2024 as fewer multi-billion deals transacted.
2 · How it affects the client
Most trustees are no longer asking how to close a deficit. They are choosing an endgame: sell the liabilities to an insurer (buy-in then buyout), or keep running the scheme ('run-on') and decide what to do with surplus.
3 · What decision changes
Whether and when to approach insurers; how to reshape assets so an insurer will accept them; if running on, how to invest for cashflow and how surplus is shared.
4 · Implications for existing investments
Illiquid holdings become a problem for schemes heading to buyout because insurers prefer gilts, cash and investment-grade credit. Schemes that run on can keep or add contractual-income assets.
5 · Possible GSAM response (interpretation, not a GS statement)
(Layer B) For buyout-bound clients: portfolio transition and 'insurer-ready' credit. For run-on clients: cashflow-driven investing and OCIO. For the insurers receiving the assets: insurance asset management.
6 · Sales responsibility
Winning a mandate from a scheme that plans to buy out in three years means competing for assets that will leave. The time horizon has to be part of the proposal.
7 · Relationship-management responsibility
An RM may have to help a client leave well: preparing assets for transfer to an insurer is good service that shrinks the manager's own assets.
8 · Risks and counterarguments
The s179 measure is less demanding than buyout cost, so surplus on this basis does not mean every scheme can afford an insurer. Isio found fiduciary mandate numbers fell for the first time since 2008 as schemes exited through insurance.
A question to ask a client
Is your target buyout, run-on or still open, and which of your current holdings would be hardest to hand to an insurer?
Indicators to watch
Half-year bulk annuity volumes from LCP, Hymans Robertson and Aon; insurer pricing; PPF 7800.
Base case
Forecast, not fact: the number of buy-ins stays high and is dominated by small schemes, while more large, well-funded schemes actively compare run-on with buyout instead of treating buyout as the default.
Plausible alternatives
(1) Insurer pricing improves and large schemes transact quickly, shrinking the asset pool managers can serve. (2) Funding levels fall and endgame decisions are postponed.
Evidence that would change the view
Half-year bulk annuity volumes by deal size; the share of schemes telling surveys they target run-on; insurer capacity statements; movement in the PPF 7800 funding ratio.
Sources
R3-S29 R3-S30 R3-S27 R3-S28 R3-S25

Pension Schemes Act 2026: DB surplus release and superfunds

2026-04-29 ✔ Verified D-R3-03

Event date
2026-04-29
Publication date
2026-05-15
1 · What happened
The Act received Royal Assent on 29 April 2026. It lets trustees of private-sector DB schemes change rules to pay surplus to sponsors more easily (consultation 2026, regulations expected in force 2027), creates a statutory regime for DB superfunds, and provides a statutory remedy for the Virgin Media rulings.
2 · How it affects the client
Running a well-funded scheme on becomes more attractive to sponsors, because surplus need not be trapped until wind-up. Trustees keep their fiduciary duties and must decide what protection members need before agreeing any release.
3 · What decision changes
The buyout-versus-run-on choice, the level of funding at which surplus may be released, and the investment strategy that supports regular surplus payments.
4 · Implications for existing investments
A run-on scheme needs assets that generate dependable income over decades rather than a portfolio being tidied up for an insurer.
5 · Possible GSAM response (interpretation, not a GS statement)
(Layer B) Offer run-on modelling, cashflow-driven portfolios and OCIO governance for sponsors who decide to keep schemes. This is a provider's commercial interest and trustees should test it against insurer pricing.
6 · Sales responsibility
Run-on lengthens the life of the asset pool an asset manager can serve, which is why managers favour it. A credible salesperson says so and still shows the buyout comparison.
7 · Relationship-management responsibility
Explain what is law now and what waits for 2027 regulations, so trustees do not act on headlines.
8 · Risks and counterarguments
Detailed rules were not in force at the cutoff. Member representatives may resist releases. A future fall in yields or a credit event could remove the surplus after it has been paid out.
A question to ask a client
What would have to be true about funding, covenant and member protection before your trustees would agree to release any surplus?
Indicators to watch
DWP consultation and draft regulations on surplus; TPR guidance; first publicised surplus releases.
Base case
Forecast, not fact: surplus-release regulations arrive in 2027 and a minority of well-funded schemes with strong sponsors use them, with trustees asking for member protections first.
Plausible alternatives
(1) Trustees prove reluctant and release remains rare, so the Act changes little in practice. (2) Release becomes common and run-on turns into the mainstream choice for large schemes.
Evidence that would change the view
The final regulations and Pensions Regulator guidance; the first public examples of release and the conditions trustees attached; member-body or union challenges.
Sources
R3-S20

Pension Schemes Act 2026 and Mansion House Accord: DC scale and private markets

2026-04-29 ✔ Verified D-R3-04

Event date
2026-04-29
Publication date
2026-05-15
1 · What happened
The Act requires master trust and group personal pension default arrangements to reach £25bn by 2030 (or be on track by 2035), with the requirement starting no earlier than 1 January 2030, and creates a reserve power, usable 2028–2032, to require minimum private-market and UK allocations. Separately, 17 providers signed the voluntary Mansion House Accord in May 2025 to hold 10% of default funds in private markets by 2030, half of it in the UK.
2 · How it affects the client
DC providers below scale must merge or grow. The surviving providers are few and large, run tight fee budgets, and need private-market exposure in a form that fits daily-dealt default funds.
3 · What decision changes
Which providers survive; how defaults obtain private-market exposure (for example Long-Term Asset Funds); which external managers are kept as the number of buyers shrinks.
4 · Implications for existing investments
Low-cost index building blocks remain the core. Small specialist allocations are at risk when defaults are merged.
5 · Possible GSAM response (interpretation, not a GS statement)
(Layer B) Offer private-market and multi-asset components designed for DC defaults. GS's actual position in UK DC was not established in this research.
6 · Sales responsibility
Fewer, bigger buyers mean long sales cycles with investment teams and consultants, and severe price pressure.
7 · Relationship-management responsibility
A manager inside a default that is being consolidated has to re-earn its place with the acquiring provider.
8 · Risks and counterarguments
The Accord is voluntary and conditional on suitable assets. The reserve power had not been used. Higher-cost private assets must show value under the value-for-money framework. Scale targets may be met by a handful of incumbents, leaving little room for new managers.
A question to ask a client
How will you reach your private-market target inside your charge budget, and what would make you remove a manager from the default?
Indicators to watch
DWP regulations on scale and value for money; master trust mergers; LTAF launches; Accord progress reports.
Base case
Forecast, not fact: UK DC default money concentrates in a small number of very large providers that buy private-market exposure in bulk and on tight cost budgets.
Plausible alternatives
(1) The reserve power is used and allocations are mandated, which turns a voluntary target into a compliance exercise. (2) Private-market targets slip because suitable vehicles, daily-dealing mechanics or value-for-money evidence are lacking.
Evidence that would change the view
Any use of the reserve power; published progress against the Mansion House Accord; default-fund charges moving up or down; announced provider mergers.

LGPS 'Fit for the Future': six pools and delegated implementation

2026-06-30 ✔ Verified D-R3-05

Event date
2026-06-30
Publication date
2026-06-15
1 · What happened
Local Government Pension Scheme pools fell from eight to six after Brunel's and ACCESS's proposals were not accepted, with funds joining other pools from 1 April 2026. Regulations in force from 30 June 2026 require each fund to delegate implementation of its investment strategy to its pool and to take its principal investment advice from the pool. Pool companies must hold full regulatory authorisation by 30 September 2027.
2 · How it affects the client
The council pension fund still sets strategy, but the pool company chooses and manages investments. Pools are building internal management and concentrating external mandates.
3 · What decision changes
Who an asset manager must convince: the pool's investment team rather than 80-plus individual committees and their consultants.
4 · Implications for existing investments
Legacy mandates held directly by funds must move into pool vehicles; some will be merged or ended during transition.
5 · Possible GSAM response (interpretation, not a GS statement)
(Layer B) Cover the six pools as a small number of large, sophisticated accounts; offer strategies pools cannot easily run internally.
6 · Sales responsibility
A handful of very large tenders replaces many small ones. Losing one is costly and the next chance may be years away.
7 · Relationship-management responsibility
During transition the task is to protect service quality while assets are restructured, and to accept that some mandates will end for reasons unrelated to performance.
8 · Risks and counterarguments
Full asset transfer is running behind the original March 2026 target. Internal management by pools reduces the external-manager opportunity. Whether GS holds LGPS mandates was not established.
A question to ask a client
Which capabilities do you intend to build in-house over the next three years, and where will you still want an external partner?
Indicators to watch
Pool onboarding progress; 31 March 2027 investment strategy statements; 30 September 2027 authorisation deadline; pool tenders.
Base case
Forecast, not fact: the six pools become the buyers that matter in the LGPS, bring more management in-house over time and keep fewer, larger external mandates for things they cannot run themselves.
Plausible alternatives
(1) Pools stay reliant on external managers for longer than planned because building internal teams is slow. (2) Further pool mergers reduce the number of buyers again.
Evidence that would change the view
Pool business plans and hiring; the share of assets managed internally; published mandate awards and terminations; progress of asset transfers.

OCIO moves up-market while the UK fiduciary market total stays flat

2025-09-09 ✔ Verified D-R3-06

Event date
2025-09-09
Publication date
2025-11-28
1 · What happened
GSAM won the roughly £23bn BAE Systems mandate in 2023 (with the in-house team transferring) and a roughly $40bn multi-country Shell mandate in 2025, and reported $480bn of global OCIO assets under supervision at 31 March 2026. Isio's 2025 survey found UK fiduciary assets flat at £241bn and mandate numbers down 4%, with partial 'OCIO' mandates now 53% of assets.
2 · How it affects the client
Large sponsors are asking whether running an in-house pension investment team is core business, especially as schemes mature and need hedging and cashflow skills more than growth investing.
3 · What decision changes
Keep an in-house team, outsource implementation while keeping strategy, or delegate fully. Each changes who is accountable, what it costs and how easily the decision can be reversed.
4 · Implications for existing investments
On appointment the OCIO takes over manager selection and implementation; existing managers may be replaced, including by the OCIO's own funds.
5 · Possible GSAM response (interpretation, not a GS statement)
(Layer B) Compete for the small number of very large schemes, offering scale, private-market access and, where relevant, continuity for the in-house team.
6 · Sales responsibility
These are multi-year pursuits run through a regulated tender with a third-party evaluator. A few decisions move tens of billions.
7 · Relationship-management responsibility
The provider becomes responsible for outcomes it used to only advise on, under scrutiny from an independent oversight adviser and with fees benchmarked at each review.
8 · Risks and counterarguments
The pool of schemes shrinks as they buy out. Concentration risk in a few large clients. Conflict-of-interest scrutiny when an OCIO allocates to in-house products. Other providers also win awards and mandates (Shell's Dutch fund chose BlackRock; the 2026 UK Pensions Awards fiduciary category went to Van Lanschot Kempen).
A question to ask a client
Which decisions do you want to keep, which do you want to delegate, and how would you get them back if you changed your mind?
Indicators to watch
Isio's next fiduciary management survey; further large in-house teams outsourcing; mandate re-tenders.
Base case
Forecast, not fact: a small number of very large sponsors continue to outsource whole pension investment functions, and those few decisions drive most asset growth in the market.
Plausible alternatives
(1) The supply of very large schemes willing to outsource runs out and growth stalls. (2) Sponsors choose insurance buyout over OCIO once pricing allows.
Evidence that would change the view
New multi-billion appointments and who wins them; the next Isio or IC Select survey; whether in-house teams transfer or are wound down; published fee data.
