Fiduciary manager tendering rules shape every OCIO sale

2022-10-01 ✔ Verified D-R3-07

Event date
2022-10-01
Publication date
2022-08
1 · What happened
Since 1 October 2022 pensions regulations overseen by The Pensions Regulator (replacing the Competition and Markets Authority's 2019 Order) require trustees to run a competitive tender, inviting at least three unconnected providers, before fiduciary managers run 20% or more of scheme assets. Trustees must also set objectives for investment consultants.
2 · How it affects the client
Trustees cannot simply hand a mandate to their existing consultant's fiduciary arm. They normally hire a third-party evaluator to run the selection.
3 · What decision changes
The selection process: longlist, request for proposal, scorecard, site visits, and comparison of fees and performance on a common standard.
4 · Implications for existing investments
Appointments made before the rules without a qualifying tender had to be re-tendered.
5 · Possible GSAM response (interpretation, not a GS statement)
(Layer B) Maintain relationships with evaluators and consultants, and respond to formal requests for proposal with standardised performance data.
6 · Sales responsibility
The evaluator is a gatekeeper. Much of the work is written: questionnaires, fee templates, track records.
7 · Relationship-management responsibility
Incumbents are re-tested at reviews; documented objectives make underperformance visible.
8 · Risks and counterarguments
Tendering raises cost and favours providers with resources to bid. The rule is old news; its value in interview is explaining why the process looks the way it does.
A question to ask a client
Who is advising you on the selection, and what did your scorecard weight most heavily last time?
Indicators to watch
TPR guidance updates; evaluator market share.

Trustees have fewer independent advisers to choose from, and more of them belong to groups that also sell fiduciary management or insurance broking.
3 · What decision changes
Which adviser trustees regard as independent enough to oversee an OCIO or run a tender.
4 · Implications for existing investments
No direct effect; adviser changes can trigger strategy and manager reviews.
5 · Possible GSAM response (interpretation, not a GS statement)
(Layer B) Consultant-relations coverage must track which research teams and buy-lists survive each merger.
6 · Sales responsibility
A manager's rating with a merged consultant research team can decide access to many schemes at once.
7 · Relationship-management responsibility
When a client's adviser is acquired, expect a review of every manager.
8 · Risks and counterarguments
Only the Mercer–Cardano completion was confirmed on a fetched page; other details come from search-result summaries and need checking before being quoted.
A question to ask a client
Has your adviser's change of ownership altered how you think about conflicts between advice and fiduciary management?

Further deals; regulatory attention to adviser conflicts.

Active ETFs become a core wrapper for European wealth distribution

January 2025 to 24 April 2026 ✔ Verified D-R4-01

Event date
January 2025 to 24 April 2026
Publication date
2026-04-24
1 · What happened
GSAM launched its first European active UCITS ETFs in January 2025 (fixed income), an active equity range from 28 April 2025 (GQUS at 0.20% TER) and two more active fixed income ETFs on 24 April 2026. It says it launched 13 active ETFs in 2025 and has about $90bn of ETF assets globally.
2 · How it affects the client
Wealth managers and model-portfolio builders can hold an active strategy in a wrapper that trades intraday, is easy to use on platforms and typically costs less than the equivalent mutual fund share class.
3 · What decision changes
A fund selector now compares the same strategy across wrappers (SICAV share class vs ETF) and compares an active ETF against both index ETFs and traditional active funds.
4 · Implications for existing investments
Existing holdings in a mutual fund version may be switched into the ETF version, which moves assets rather than adding them and can lower the fee rate on those assets.
5 · Possible GSAM response (interpretation, not a GS statement)
Layer B: lead with the wrapper the buyer's platform and portfolio process prefer; position low-tracking-error 'enhanced' ETFs as core building blocks for model portfolios.
6 · Sales responsibility
Identify which gatekeepers have a mandate or model that can hold active ETFs, and whether the ETF is on the platforms their advisers use.
7 · Relationship-management responsibility
For clients already in the mutual fund, explain the differences honestly (cost, dealing, tax reporting, spread) and handle any switch so the client is not surprised by trading costs.
8 · Risks and counterarguments
Cannibalisation of higher-fee share classes; UK platform support for ETFs (fractional dealing, trading charges) is uneven; a low TER leaves little margin; low tracking error means outperformance, if any, is small.
A question to ask a client
Where an active ETF and a fund share class of the same strategy both exist, which would your portfolio process choose, and what on your platform decides that?
Indicators to watch
European active ETF assets and flows; number of GS UCITS ETFs and their assets; whether UK platforms add ETF model portfolio functionality; TER moves by competitors.
Base case
Forecast, not fact: active ETFs keep taking share of new money in European wealth portfolios from a small base, mainly in low-tracking-error building blocks used by model-portfolio teams.
Plausible alternatives
(1) UK platform frictions keep adoption low in the UK even as it grows on the continent. (2) Fee competition among issuers pushes charges down until the wrapper is no cheaper to run than a fund share class is worth.
Evidence that would change the view
Quarterly European active ETF asset and flow data; UK platforms changing ETF dealing terms; concentration of share among issuers; evidence of fund-to-ETF switching in the same strategy.

Evergreen private-markets funds and ELTIF 2.0 reach the wealth channel

July 2023 to 11 March 2026 ✔ Verified D-R4-02

Event date
July 2023 to 11 March 2026
Publication date
2026-03-11
1 · What happened
Goldman Sachs Alternatives built a 'G-Series' of open-ended private-markets funds for qualified investors (G-PE launched 2 April 2025) and on 11 March 2026 added an ELTIF range starting with the G-European Credit ELTIF, its first evergreen product under ELTIF 2.0. G-Series funds are sold through GS Private Wealth Management and select third-party distributors.
2 · How it affects the client
Private banks and wealth managers can offer private equity, private credit and infrastructure to eligible individuals with periodic subscriptions and limited redemptions instead of ten-year drawdown funds.
3 · What decision changes
The distributor must decide whether clients are eligible and suitable, how large an illiquid sleeve can be, and whether its systems and advisers can handle periodic dealing and redemption limits.
4 · Implications for existing investments
Clients may fund the allocation from listed equity or bond funds, some of which may be the same manager's.
5 · Possible GSAM response (interpretation, not a GS statement)
Layer B: pair the product with adviser education and clear liquidity terms; work through a dedicated alternatives-for-wealth specialist team alongside the TPW coverage person.
6 · Sales responsibility
Find distributors with an approved private-markets allocation and the operational set-up to deal in semi-liquid funds; expect a long due-diligence process.
7 · Relationship-management responsibility
Keep advisers informed on valuation, redemption queue and gating terms before stress arrives, not after.
8 · Risks and counterarguments
Liquidity mismatch if many investors redeem together; valuation opacity; higher fees; suitability risk under the Consumer Duty; UK retail access differs from the EEA (ELTIF is an EEA label).
A question to ask a client
What share of a typical client portfolio could you put in assets that can only be redeemed quarterly, and who in your firm signs that off?
Indicators to watch
G-Series assets if disclosed; redemption requests across the semi-liquid sector; FCA and ESMA statements on semi-liquid funds; number of distributors named in GS releases.
Base case
Forecast, not fact: evergreen private-market funds keep growing in the wealth channel, but gatekeepers ration them with small position limits and scrutinise liquidity terms more closely after 2026 redemption pressure.
Plausible alternatives
(1) A visible gating episode damages adviser confidence and flows reverse. (2) Regulatory change widens access and semi-liquid funds become standard in model portfolios.
Evidence that would change the view
Redemption queues or gates in large funds; regulator statements on suitability; net flows reported by the largest wealth-channel private-market managers; adoption of ELTIF 2.0 vehicles by distributors.

The FCA published final CCI rules (PS25/20) on 8 December 2025. Firms can opt in from 6 April 2026 and the regime is fully in force from 8 June 2027. It applies to manufacturers and distributors.

Advisers, platforms and investors will receive a redesigned product summary with a standardised core covering costs, risk and past performance.

Being operationally ready is a hygiene factor in due diligence; lateness can keep a fund off a platform.
7 · Relationship-management responsibility
Explain to existing distributors what changes in the documents their advisers hand to clients.
8 · Risks and counterarguments
Mostly an operational change; unlikely to win business; cross-border ranges must run UK and EU disclosure regimes side by side.
A question to ask a client
How are you planning the move to the new product summaries, and what do you need from fund managers before June 2027?

FCA implementation updates; distributor data-template standards; how overseas (OFR) funds are treated.

The FCA's PS25/22 (December 2025) set near-final rules for 'targeted support', where firms give ready-made suggestions to groups of consumers with common characteristics. The FCA expected the rules to take effect from 6 April 2026.
2 · How it affects the client
Platforms, banks and pension providers can point non-advised customers towards specific investment solutions, which may bring cash savers into funds.
3 · What decision changes
A distributor decides whether to offer targeted support and which funds or portfolios sit behind each ready-made suggestion.
4 · Implications for existing investments
Limited direct effect; over time default-style multi-asset solutions may gather a larger share of new non-advised money.
5 · Possible GSAM response (interpretation, not a GS statement)
Layer B: offer simple, low-cost building blocks or multi-asset funds that a distributor can defend as a ready-made suggestion under the Consumer Duty.
6 · Sales responsibility
Ask distributors whether they will launch targeted support and how the underlying funds will be chosen.
7 · Relationship-management responsibility
Support distributors with the evidence they need to show the suggested product offers fair value for the segment.
8 · Risks and counterarguments
Distributors may use in-house or index funds; take-up may be slow; the FCA says consumers remain responsible for their decisions, so reputational risk is real if outcomes disappoint. Commencement on 6 April 2026 was not confirmed in this research session.
A question to ask a client
Are you planning a targeted support service, and if so how will you select what sits behind each suggestion?

Which firms get the new permission; FCA data on take-up; whether suggestions favour in-house, passive or third-party funds.

The FCA's PS24/7 (July 2024) implemented the Overseas Funds Regime. EEA UCITS, except money-market funds, can apply for recognition to be marketed to UK retail investors, replacing the Temporary Marketing Permissions Regime.

UK wealth managers and platforms can keep using Luxembourg and Irish UCITS and UCITS ETFs once recognised.

Recognition status is a due-diligence item for any new UK platform listing.
7 · Relationship-management responsibility
Proactively confirm the status of each fund a client holds.
8 · Risks and counterarguments
Low-probability, high-impact operational risk; money-market funds are excluded from the first equivalence decision; the TMPR end date after any extension was not verified here.
A question to ask a client

2019-09 onward ✔ Verified D-R4-06

Event date
2019-09 onward
Publication date
2026-10-23
1 · What happened
UK authorised fund managers have had to assess each fund's value at least annually since September 2019, and the Consumer Duty adds a 'price and value' outcome that distributors must also meet.
2 · How it affects the client
Wealth managers must be able to show that the total cost a client pays, including the fund, is fair for what the client receives.
3 · What decision changes
Fund selectors weigh fees more heavily and may remove funds whose cost they cannot justify, or switch to cheaper share classes, ETFs or index funds.
4 · Implications for existing investments
Higher-fee share classes face pressure to reprice or be replaced.
5 · Possible GSAM response (interpretation, not a GS statement)
Layer B: offer institutional-priced share classes for scale, be explicit about what the active fee buys, and supply value evidence the distributor can file.
6 · Sales responsibility
A credible answer on cost is needed before investment merits are heard.
7 · Relationship-management responsibility
Help existing distributors document value each year; raise share-class conversions before the client asks.
8 · Risks and counterarguments
Fee cuts reduce revenue on assets already held; cheapest is not always best value; a manager's own value assessment is not independent evidence.
A question to ask a client
When you last reviewed value across your buy list, what made a fund fail?
Indicators to watch
FCA Consumer Duty reviews; published assessment-of-value outcomes; ETF TERs (GS active ETFs at 0.20%-0.25% are data points).
Base case
Forecast, not fact: value scrutiny remains a standing part of fund selection, so price and evidence of what a fee buys are tested at every review, not only at launch.
Plausible alternatives
(1) Scrutiny hardens into explicit cost caps in model portfolios, which favours index funds. (2) Regulatory attention moves elsewhere and practice settles into a documentation routine.
Evidence that would change the view
FCA supervisory findings on fair value; distributors publishing cost budgets; share-class repricing announcements; the share of buy-list removals attributed to value.

Not established
1 · What happened
A wealth manager's commentary reports the UK model portfolio service (MPS) market at about £190bn, up 32% year on year. More adviser money is run through centrally built model portfolios.
2 · How it affects the client
Advisers outsource fund selection to a discretionary manager's model, so one investment team's decision moves money for thousands of end clients.
3 · What decision changes
The decision moves from many individual advisers to a small number of MPS investment committees with tight cost budgets.
4 · Implications for existing investments
Funds held adviser-by-adviser can be sold when the client is moved into a model that does not hold them.
5 · Possible GSAM response (interpretation, not a GS statement)
Layer B: cover MPS providers as institutional-style buyers, with low-cost building blocks, capacity and consistent data.
6 · Sales responsibility
A single model inclusion can be worth more than many adviser meetings, but the bar on fees and due diligence is higher.
7 · Relationship-management responsibility
Inclusion can be reversed at any rebalance, so regular portfolio-manager access and honest performance explanation matter.
8 · Risks and counterarguments
The £190bn figure was seen only in a search result and its original source is unknown; MPS cost caps favour passive funds; concentration cuts both ways when a model drops a fund.
A question to ask a client
How much of your firm's new money now goes through models, and what cost budget does the model team work to?
Indicators to watch
Primary MPS market data (find and cite the original provider); share of passive in MPS; platform MPS charges.

Dutch pension funds move from defined benefit to the new contribution-based system (Wtp)

1 January 2026 (largest wave so far); deadline 1 January 2028 ✔ Verified D-R5-01

Event date
1 January 2026 (largest wave so far); deadline 1 January 2028
Publication date
2026-04-28
1 · What happened
Thirty Dutch pension funds, holding about EUR 542bn, had converted to the new system by 31 March 2026; 24 of them moved on 1 January 2026. Remaining funds must transfer accrued entitlements by 1 January 2028.
2 · How it affects the client
A fund that used to promise a fixed pension now manages personal pots by age group. Younger members can take more risk and need less interest-rate protection; older members still need stable income. The fund's hedging and return portfolios have to be redesigned around age cohorts and a solidarity reserve.
3 · What decision changes
How much interest-rate hedging to keep and for which cohorts; what goes into the return portfolio (more equities, credit, private assets); how the reserve is invested; whether the fiduciary manager and mandate structure still fit.
4 · Implications for existing investments
Long-dated swap and bond hedges can shrink for younger cohorts; existing matching mandates may be resized or re-benchmarked; reporting moves to cohort level and becomes more frequent.
5 · Possible GSAM response (interpretation, not a GS statement)
(Layer B, not a GS statement) Offer cohort-aware fixed income and return-seeking building blocks, and analysis specific to each fund's lifecycle design, rather than a generic LDI pitch. GSAM's Dutch presence since the 2022 NN IP acquisition is relevant capacity, but no public source ties a specific Wtp mandate to GSAM.
6 · Sales responsibility
For funds still to convert (2027 and 2028 waves), the opening is the portfolio redesign: asking what the new return portfolio needs that the old one lacked.
7 · Relationship-management responsibility
For existing mandates, the job is to keep the mandate fit for purpose through conversion: revised guidelines, benchmarks and reporting, and honesty if a matching mandate should shrink.
8 · Risks and counterarguments
The January 2026 wave passed calmly, so the 'forced selling' story may be overdone; estimates of future hedge reduction come from interested parties and carry wide uncertainty. Some funds keep higher hedging than the market expected. Many Dutch funds delegate to fiduciary managers, so the real buyer may be the fiduciary, not the fund.
A question to ask a client
Which of your age cohorts will hold less interest-rate hedging after conversion, and what will replace it in their return portfolio?
Indicators to watch
DNB quarterly counts of converted funds and assets; conversion dates of the largest remaining funds; long-end euro swap spreads around 1 January 2027 and 2028; insurer demand for long duration ahead of January 2027 Solvency II changes.
Base case
Forecast, not fact: the remaining Dutch funds convert on or before 1 January 2028 and hedging demand at the long end falls gradually, cohort by cohort, with return portfolios redesigned as they go.
Plausible alternatives
(1) Conversions are delayed and the old system's hedging persists longer. (2) Several large funds reduce hedges at the same time and long-dated euro rates move sharply.
Evidence that would change the view
The number and size of funds converting on 1 January 2027; the Dutch central bank's transition reporting; long-dated euro swap rates around conversion dates; funds' published lifecycle designs.
Sources
R5-S35 R5-S36 R5-S37

UK and EU money market fund rules: higher expected liquidity, no forced fees or gates

8 June 2026 (FCA update); UK regime targeted end-2026 ✔ Verified D-R5-02

Event date
8 June 2026 (FCA update); UK regime targeted end-2026
Publication date
2026-06-08
1 · What happened
The FCA said the Government expects to repeal the UK Money Market Funds Regulation by end-2026, with new FCA rules. Guidance will expect stable-NAV funds to hold 40% weekly liquid assets (20% for variable-NAV) and the link between liquidity thresholds and fees or gates will be removed. A European Commission report in 2026 pointed to the same 40%/20% levels as supervisory benchmarks without rewriting the EU regulation. EU-domiciled funds, about 90% of sterling MMF assets, stay on sale in the UK under an extended temporary regime pending an equivalence decision.
2 · How it affects the client
A treasurer using a stable-value fund gets a fund that holds more cash-like assets and is less likely to gate in a stress, at the cost of slightly lower yield. Continued UK access to EU funds is expected but not yet permanent.
3 · What decision changes
Whether to keep operating cash in LVNAV funds, move part to government-only (Public Debt CNAV) funds, or segment cash into operating, reserve and strategic buckets with short-duration strategies for the last.
4 · Implications for existing investments
Existing MMF holdings are unaffected day to day; yield may drift a little lower as funds hold more weekly liquidity; investment policies that reference old thresholds or 'fees and gates' triggers need updating.
5 · Possible GSAM response (interpretation, not a GS statement)
(Layer B, not a GS statement) Explain how each GS liquidity fund already sits against the new expectations, and offer cash segmentation: money market funds for daily cash, short-duration accounts for cash not needed for months.
6 · Sales responsibility
Lead with resilience and reporting (for example through the Mosaic portal) rather than yield alone; most treasurers already hold several providers, so the realistic aim is a larger share of balances.
7 · Relationship-management responsibility
Review each client's investment policy against the new rules before the client asks, and flag any share class or domicile changes early.
8 · Risks and counterarguments
Final FCA rules were not published at the cutoff, and the equivalence decision could attach conditions. Balances are driven far more by interest rates and bank deposit pricing than by regulation. Fees are thin, so a small yield difference moves large balances quickly in either direction.
A question to ask a client
Does your treasury policy still refer to liquidity fees and redemption gates as triggers, and how would you want your cash split if stable-value funds yield a little less?
Indicators to watch
FCA policy statement and interim guidance on weekly liquid assets; HM Treasury legislation; equivalence decision for EU MMFs (indicated for 2027); central bank rate path; industry sterling MMF assets.
Base case
Forecast, not fact: the UK replaces its inherited money market fund regulation with FCA rules on roughly the stated timetable, stable-value funds hold more weekly liquidity, and EU-domiciled funds stay available to UK investors.
Plausible alternatives
(1) The equivalence decision is delayed or conditional and UK investors face a narrower choice. (2) Higher liquidity requirements cut yields enough that treasurers move part of their cash to deposits or short-duration accounts.
Evidence that would change the view
The final FCA rules; the Treasury's equivalence decision; the yield gap between stable-value funds and bank deposits; flows between fund types reported by trade bodies.
Sources
R5-S32 R5-S33 R5-S34 R5-S01

In principle an institution could post fund shares as collateral directly instead of redeeming to cash first, keeping yield and avoiding a forced sale in stress.

Keep clients informed without overselling; note any availability limits by fund domicile.

Launch coverage was US-focused; no public evidence was found on volumes or on availability for European funds or EMEA clients. Regulators in Europe have not broadly accepted tokenised fund shares as margin.

Insurance capital rules change in 2027 (EU) and the UK loosens matching-adjustment investing

EU: 30 January 2027; UK consultation 8 April 2025 ≈ Supported inference D-R5-04

Event date
EU: 30 January 2027; UK consultation 8 April 2025
Publication date
2025-04-08
1 · What happened
Amended EU Solvency II rules (Directive (EU) 2025/2) take effect on 30 January 2027. In the UK, the PRA consulted in April 2025 on a Matching Adjustment Investment Accelerator that lets insurers add self-assessed eligible assets to matching-adjustment portfolios before formal approval, within the lower of 5% of liabilities or GBP 2bn and a 24-month regularisation window.
2 · How it affects the client
An insurer chooses assets by yield after capital charge, not by yield alone. Rule changes alter which assets are 'capital-efficient' and how quickly an annuity writer can invest in new private asset types.
3 · What decision changes
Allocation to long-dated and private credit assets; how much to outsource; which managers can structure assets to be matching-adjustment eligible.
4 · Implications for existing investments
Existing portfolios are re-tested against new capital charges; some long-duration and equity positions become cheaper or dearer to hold.
5 · Possible GSAM response (interpretation, not a GS statement)
(Layer B, not a GS statement) Show the capital-adjusted return of proposed assets under the client's own regulatory basis; GSAM describes 'capital-efficient investment strategies' and asset-liability advice as part of its insurance offer.
6 · Sales responsibility
Sales must speak the insurer's language (capital charge, book yield, liability matching) before talking about products.
7 · Relationship-management responsibility
Relationship managers coordinate regulatory reporting data and help the client evidence eligibility of assets already held.
8 · Risks and counterarguments
The final UK policy statement and the detailed EU changes were not read in this research, so details must be checked before quoting. Regulators are also wary of private-asset concentration at annuity writers. Survey intentions to raise private assets may not turn into allocations.
A question to ask a client
Which assets in your portfolio become more or less capital-efficient under the January 2027 rules?
Indicators to watch
PRA policy statement on the accelerator; EIOPA and Commission delegated acts before January 2027; insurers' reported private-asset allocations.
Base case
Forecast, not fact: capital rules in the EU and UK move modestly in the direction of making long-dated and private assets easier for insurers to hold, and insurers add them selectively.
Plausible alternatives
(1) Supervisors tighten their stance on private-asset concentration at annuity writers and allocations stall. (2) A credit event makes insurers pull back regardless of the rules.
Evidence that would change the view
The final UK policy statement and EU delegated rules; supervisory letters on private assets; insurers' reported allocations a year after survey intentions; credit losses in asset-backed finance.

Servicing involves co-investment reporting, training and secondment-type requests as much as performance reviews.

Policy rates are rising again: Bank Rate up to 4% in November 2026

2026-11-05 ✔ Verified D-R8-01

Event date
2026-11-05
Publication date
2026-11-05
1 · What happened
The Bank of England raised Bank Rate by 0.25pp to 4% (8-1; one member wanted 4.25%), its first increase since 2023, with CPI at 3.5% and projected near 5% by mid-2027. The Fed held at 3.75-4.00% on 28 Oct with two dissents for a hike; the ECB held its deposit rate at 2.50% after a September increase.
2 · How it affects the client
Higher yields lower the present value of DB liabilities and of existing bonds; cash and money market yields rise; leveraged borrowers and floating-rate private credit face higher servicing costs; inflation-linked liabilities grow.
3 · What decision changes
DB trustees: hedge ratios, collateral buffers, timing of buyout. Treasurers: how much to hold in MMFs versus term. Insurers: reinvestment yields versus credit risk. Wealth selectors: duration and cash allocations.
4 · Implications for existing investments
Mark-to-market losses on long-dated bonds; collateral calls on leveraged LDI (buffers are larger than in 2022); liquidity balances may grow.
5 · Possible GSAM response (interpretation, not a GS statement)
(Layer B, not a GS statement) Explain funding-level and collateral effects scheme by scheme; show liquidity and short-duration options; avoid presenting a rate view as certainty.
6 · Sales responsibility
A reason to open a conversation about liquidity, inflation protection or collateral resilience, not proof that a product should be bought.
7 · Relationship-management responsibility
Proactive calls to existing clients on what the move did to their portfolio and hedges, before they ask.
8 · Risks and counterarguments
The inflation projection may prove wrong and policy could reverse; schemes that are well hedged may need to do nothing; higher cash yields compete with every fee-bearing product.
A question to ask a client
How did your funding level and collateral headroom move this month, and has that changed your timetable or your liquidity needs?
Indicators to watch
17 December 2026 MPC; gilt yields and index-linked breakevens; CPI prints; any LDI collateral stress reports.
Base case
Forecast, not fact: policy rates stay at or above current levels into 2027 while UK inflation runs above target, so cash and short bonds keep paying a visible yield and every other asset is judged against that.
Plausible alternatives
(1) Inflation falls faster than the Bank projects and rates are cut again, which lowers cash yields and raises liability values. (2) A sharper rise in long gilt yields that tests LDI collateral and semi-liquid funds at the same time.
Evidence that would change the view
A Bank of England vote split moving towards cuts; UK CPI prints well below the projected path; long gilt yields falling back below 4.5%; evidence that LDI collateral buffers were drawn on.

1 · What happened

Clients pay less per pound managed and expect more service; they can credibly threaten to move to a cheaper provider.
3 · What decision changes
Fee renegotiation at review; move from active to passive or active ETF; consolidation of mandates to reach breakpoints.
4 · Implications for existing investments
Existing mandates face repricing requests even when performance is fine.
5 · Possible GSAM response (interpretation, not a GS statement)
(Layer B, not a GS statement) Defend price with evidence of value, offer breakpoints or broader relationships, and accept that sometimes the cheaper product is the right answer.
6 · Sales responsibility
Price is rarely the opening argument but must be competitive to reach the shortlist.
7 · Relationship-management responsibility
Fee conversations are an RM responsibility: prepare the value-for-money case before the client asks.
8 · Risks and counterarguments
Fees are observable and value is not, so pressure is structural; for small UK schemes fiduciary fees have actually risen, so the trend is not uniform.
A question to ask a client
When you last reviewed what you pay us, what did you compare it with, and what would you need to see to judge it good value?
Indicators to watch
Morningstar and BCG annual fee studies; UK value-for-money framework for DC; consultant fee surveys.
Base case
Forecast, not fact: average fee rates keep drifting down and revenue growth keeps depending on markets and on mix shifting towards higher-fee private assets.
Plausible alternatives
(1) A prolonged market fall exposes cost bases built in rising markets and accelerates consolidation. (2) Fee rates stabilise as product mix moves to alternatives and solutions.
Evidence that would change the view
Published average fee rates by asset class in managers' filings; fee surveys in fiduciary management and funds; industry cost-to-income ratios; the pace of mergers.
Sources
R8-S38 R8-S37 R8-S10

AI moves into RFPs, meeting notes and reporting in distribution teams

2026-02-19 ✔ Verified D-R8-05

Event date
2026-02-19
Publication date
2026-02-19
1 · What happened
Cerulli: 81% of institutional sales and service teams use AI for RFP content and 77% for meeting notes; far fewer for prospecting or sales strategy. Mercer: 73% of managers use AI for operational efficiency; only 5% let it act autonomously. Isio: 85% of UK fiduciary managers use AI, mainly to draft reports and emails.
2 · How it affects the client
Clients may receive faster, more consistent responses; they also ask how AI is governed and whether outputs are checked.
3 · What decision changes
Due-diligence questionnaires now include AI governance; clients may shorten response deadlines.
4 · Implications for existing investments
No direct portfolio effect.
5 · Possible GSAM response (interpretation, not a GS statement)
(Layer B, not a GS statement) Use the time saved for accuracy checks and client-specific analysis; be able to explain controls.
6 · Sales responsibility
Faster proposal turnaround is now expected, so it no longer differentiates on its own.
7 · Relationship-management responsibility
Automated reporting raises the bar for the human explanation that accompanies it.
8 · Risks and counterarguments
Survey figures are self-reported and partly vendor-sponsored; errors in AI-drafted answers create liability; no evidence yet on junior hiring effects; BCG's 25-35% cost-saving figure is an estimate.
A question to ask a client
What do you want to know about how we use AI in the material we send you, and where would you want a named person accountable?
Indicators to watch
Regulatory guidance on AI in client communications; Cerulli/Mercer follow-up surveys; reported headcount changes in distribution.
Base case
Forecast, not fact: AI becomes standard for first drafts of RFP answers, notes and routine reports, with a named person still accountable for what is sent to a client.
Plausible alternatives
(1) Adoption spreads to prospecting and client prioritisation, changing how coverage time is allocated. (2) An error in AI-drafted client material leads to regulatory or client pushback and tighter controls.
Evidence that would change the view
Survey data on adoption beyond drafting; regulator guidance on accountability for AI-assisted communications; firms' published policies; credible data on entry-level hiring in distribution.
Sources

Private credit under strain: elevated redemptions in retail semi-liquid funds

2026-07 ✔ Verified D-R8-06

Event date
2026-07
Publication date
2026-07
1 · What happened
The Bank of England's July 2026 Financial Stability Report said risky credit markets including private credit remain vulnerable to tighter financing conditions and that redemption requests have been elevated in several retail funds, with some limiting redemptions. Blackstone reported BCRED redemption requests stayed elevated in Q3 2026 even as private-wealth AUM reached $330bn.
2 · How it affects the client
Wealth clients in semi-liquid funds may be unable to redeem on demand; insurers and pension funds reassess valuation and liquidity assumptions; rising rates add pressure on borrowers.
3 · What decision changes
Fund selectors tighten due diligence on liquidity terms, valuation policy and leverage; some pause new allocations; insurers review capital treatment.
4 · Implications for existing investments
Holders of evergreen private credit funds face queues or gates; marks may lag.
5 · Possible GSAM response (interpretation, not a GS statement)
(Layer B, not a GS statement) Lead with liquidity terms and downside cases; do not sell semi-liquid as liquid; be explicit about who the product does not suit.
6 · Sales responsibility
Selling private markets to wealth now requires proving the client understands redemption limits.
7 · Relationship-management responsibility
Tell holders early how redemption queues work and what the fund has done; this is where trust is tested.
8 · Risks and counterarguments
Stress is concentrated in particular funds and borrowers; private wealth inflows continue (Blackstone BXPE record quarter); the BoE judges households and corporates resilient in aggregate.
A question to ask a client
If you could not redeem for four quarters, would this allocation still be the right size for your clients?
Indicators to watch
BoE December 2026 FSR; redemption data from large evergreen funds; default rates; FCA/ESMA action on semi-liquid funds.
Base case
Forecast, not fact: stress stays concentrated in particular funds and borrowers while overall flows into private credit continue, and buyers ask harder questions about liquidity and valuation.
Plausible alternatives
(1) Redemption limits spread and wealth-channel demand for semi-liquid funds falls sharply. (2) Rates stabilise, defaults stay contained and the episode is remembered as a liquidity test that the structures passed.
Evidence that would change the view
The next Bank of England Financial Stability Report; redemption request and fulfilment data from large funds; default and non-accrual rates; insurer and pension disclosures of private-credit marks.
Sources
R8-S52 R8-S34 R8-S53

UK fiduciary management: fewer mandates, larger ones, falling fees at the top

2026-04 ✔ Verified D-R8-07

Event date
2026-04
Publication date
2026-04
1 · What happened
UK fiduciary assets are above £250bn (+58% in three years) but the number of mandates fell 4% in the year to June 2025, the first fall since 2008, as schemes buy out. OCIO-style mandates are 6% by number and 53% of DB fiduciary AUM. Fees above £500m are falling; below £50m they rose. Providers are consolidating (Mercer-Cardano, Nuveen-Schroders) and Columbia Threadneedle exited.
2 · How it affects the client
Large schemes have many bidders and pricing power; small schemes have fewer bidders. About 26% of fully delegated schemes expect buyout within three years, which ends the mandate.
3 · What decision changes
Whether to delegate fully, partially or not at all; whether to run on or buy out; whether to pay for independent oversight (only one in three do).
4 · Implications for existing investments
Existing fiduciary mandates shrink or terminate at buyout: a good client outcome that removes fee revenue.
5 · Possible GSAM response (interpretation, not a GS statement)
(Layer B, not a GS statement) Compete where bespoke capability matters (£1bn+); be clear about the endgame path and what happens to fees when the scheme buys out.
6 · Sales responsibility
Few, very large, slow competitive tenders run by third-party evaluators; losing after months of work is normal.
7 · Relationship-management responsibility
Help the scheme reach its endgame even though success ends the relationship; propose oversight rather than resist it.
8 · Risks and counterarguments
Goldman's UK share is not public; consultant-heritage providers hold about half of mandates by number; run-on with surplus release could slow buyouts (scenario).
A question to ask a client
Is your endgame buyout or run-on, and how should your fiduciary manager be paid in a way that does not reward delaying it?
Indicators to watch
Isio, IC Select, XPS and Quantum annual surveys; large mandate announcements; Pension Schemes Act surplus rules (see R3).
Base case
Forecast, not fact: the UK fiduciary market keeps growing in assets and shrinking in mandate count, with fee pressure concentrated in the largest mandates and continued provider consolidation.
Plausible alternatives
(1) Surplus-release rules make run-on attractive and extend mandate lives. (2) Faster buyouts shrink the market in assets as well as mandates.
Evidence that would change the view
Mandate numbers rising again; fee surveys showing stabilisation above £500m; regulatory action on conflicts where a fiduciary manager uses in-house funds; further provider exits.
Sources
R8-S10 R8-S09 R8-S11 R8-S26

Public-private alliances and active ETFs reshape products for wealth intermediaries

2026-07-22 ≈ Supported inference D-R8-08

Event date
2026-07-22
Publication date
2026-07-22
1 · What happened
Wellington, Vanguard and Blackstone launched two public-private funds (US, July 2026); Capital Group and KKR took a public-private credit fund to Europe and Asia-Pacific via HSBC Private Bank (May 2026); Goldman agreed a T. Rowe Price partnership (Sept 2025). European active ETF assets reached about EUR 117bn at end Q3 2026, with J.P. Morgan holding about 41%; passive ETFs took about 57% of Q3 2026 European fund flows.
2 · How it affects the client
Fund selectors face more wrappers for similar exposures and must judge liquidity and layered fees; shelf space goes to firms with distribution access.
3 · What decision changes
Which vehicle (mutual fund, active ETF, evergreen fund, model portfolio) goes on the approved list; how many private-market providers to carry.
4 · Implications for existing investments
Mutual fund holdings may be switched to cheaper ETF share classes or models.
5 · Possible GSAM response (interpretation, not a GS statement)
(Layer B, not a GS statement) Offer the client's preferred wrapper where it exists; be honest where a competitor leads (for example active ETFs).
6 · Sales responsibility
Approved-list placement is the start: funded assets depend on adviser adoption afterwards.
7 · Relationship-management responsibility
Support advisers with training and reporting so listed funds are actually used and held appropriately.
8 · Risks and counterarguments
Active ETFs are still about 3.4% of European ETF assets; alliance funds are small at launch; fee levels are lower than the vehicles they replace (BCG).
A question to ask a client
Which wrapper do your advisers actually use for new money now, and what would make a fund you already list easier to hold?
Indicators to watch
Morningstar active ETF data; European launches by the alliances; platform shelf changes.

Global managers build presence around Gulf sovereign investors

2026-10-19 ✔ Verified D-R8-09

Event date
2026-10-19
Publication date
2026-10-19
1 · What happened
Fourteen firms announced plans for an Abu Dhabi Global Market presence in October 2026; managers there oversee more than $2.1tn globally; Capital Group obtained an ADGM licence. BlackRock is reported to plan up to $100bn of deployment via the region; Mubadala and ADIA are reported to partner with Apollo, Blue Owl and KKR in private credit; PIF anchors new vehicles for managers that open in Riyadh.
2 · How it affects the client
Sovereign investors can ask for local presence, co-investment, knowledge transfer and anchor terms; they are partners and competitors for deals as well as clients.
3 · What decision changes
Which managers receive mandates or anchor commitments, and on what conditions (local office, joint ventures).
4 · Implications for existing investments
Existing mandates may be consolidated into strategic partnerships.
5 · Possible GSAM response (interpretation, not a GS statement)
(Layer B, not a GS statement) Coverage needs partnership structures and senior access, not product pushing; local regulation and presence matter.
6 · Sales responsibility
Long, relationship-led cycles with bespoke terms; origination credit is shared across the firm.
7 · Relationship-management responsibility
Servicing includes training, secondments and co-investment flow, beyond reporting.
8 · Risks and counterarguments
Regional conflict in 2026 has affected sentiment (BoE refers to the Middle East conflict); headline commitment figures are not funded assets; Goldman-specific Gulf evidence is outside this stream (see R5).
A question to ask a client
Beyond returns, what do you want a manager to build with you locally?
Indicators to watch
ADGM/DIFC/Riyadh licence announcements; sovereign fund annual reports; anchor mandates.
Base case
Forecast, not fact: competition among global managers for a handful of Gulf sovereign relationships intensifies, and local presence becomes a condition of entry instead of an advantage.
Plausible alternatives
(1) Sovereign funds build more capability in-house and use fewer external managers. (2) Headline commitments are announced but funded slowly, so the commercial value arrives later than the press suggests.
Evidence that would change the view
Funded amounts against announced targets; the number of managers licensed in Abu Dhabi and Riyadh; sovereign funds' own hiring; statements about fees or terms from the funds.
Sources
R8-S57 R8-S58 R8-S52

Tokenised money market fund shares as collateral

2025-07-23 ✔ Verified D-R8-10

Event date
2025-07-23
Publication date
2026-07-13
1 · What happened
BNY and Goldman Sachs launched 'mirror' tokens of MMF shares on Goldman's digital asset platform in July 2025, with funds from BlackRock, Fidelity, Federated Hermes, BNY Dreyfus and GSAM. In July 2026 an industry group (GDF with ISDA) published sandbox work on using tokenised MMFs as collateral.
2 · How it affects the client
Treasurers and pension funds could post MMF shares as margin instead of redeeming to cash, reducing forced selling in stress.
3 · What decision changes
Whether to hold liquidity in vehicles that can be mobilised as collateral; operational readiness and legal certainty.
4 · Implications for existing investments
No change yet for most holders; adoption volumes not established.
5 · Possible GSAM response (interpretation, not a GS statement)
(Layer B, not a GS statement) Explain what is live versus pilot; keep the focus on the client's liquidity and collateral problem.
6 · Sales responsibility
A talking point with sophisticated treasury and LDI clients, not yet a mainstream product decision.
7 · Relationship-management responsibility
Help operations teams understand eligibility and custody implications.
8 · Risks and counterarguments
Legal and regulatory acceptance of tokenised collateral is incomplete; competitors participate in the same programme, so it is not exclusive; volumes may stay small.
A question to ask a client
In a margin call, how quickly can you turn your liquidity holdings into eligible collateral today?
Indicators to watch
Regulatory statements on tokenised collateral eligibility; reported volumes; UK and EU MMF reform implementation.
Sources

Who does what, and who can decide what. General industry practice, not a Goldman Sachs job structure.

Summer Analyst (intern)

≈ Supported inference ROLE-SUMMER-ANALYST

Purpose
Learn how a coverage team works by producing supervised inputs to real client work over a fixed internship.
Recurring tasks
  • Research a client or prospect from public documents
  • Draft slides or tables from approved content for a senior colleague to edit
  • Take notes in meetings attended as an observer
  • Reconcile figures in a pack to their official source
  • Complete a defined project and present it to the team
Work products
  • Prospect or client briefing
  • Draft slides
  • Meeting notes
  • Reconciled data table
  • Internship project presentation
Stakeholders
  • Supervising analyst and associate
  • Team vice presidents
  • Fellow interns
  • Occasionally specialists who supply data
Decision rights
Can decide
  • How to structure their own draft
  • Which public sources to consult
  • When to ask for help
Can recommend
  • Questions the team might ask a client
  • Improvements to a template or tracker
Needs approval
  • Anything sent outside the team
  • Any contact with a client
  • Any use of client data beyond the task given
Belongs to others
  • Client relationships
  • Fees and terms
  • Investment views and decisions
  • What is said to a client
Measures of success
  • Accuracy: figures tie to source
  • Reliability: delivered when promised
  • Judgement about when to ask
  • Curiosity shown in the questions asked
  • Whether the team would want them back
Notes
General industry practice for internships in client-facing asset management teams, not a Goldman Sachs statement. The actual content of an internship depends on the team and the supervisor.

Analyst

≈ Supported inference ROLE-ANALYST

Purpose
Own the recurring inputs that let senior colleagues spend their time with clients, and learn the clients and products in depth.
Recurring tasks
  • Prepare the briefing before each client or prospect meeting
  • Maintain the pipeline file and the CRM record
  • Build the first draft of review packs and proposals
  • Draft RFP and DDQ answers from the approved library
  • Write up minutes and track actions to completion
  • Handle routine data requests from clients and consultants
Work products
  • Meeting preparation note
  • Pipeline update
  • Review pack draft
  • RFP answer drafts
  • Minutes and action log
  • Flow and holdings reports
Stakeholders
  • Associates and vice presidents on the team
  • RFP, reporting and client service teams
  • Product specialists
  • Client operations contacts for routine matters
Decision rights
Can decide
  • Order and method of their own work
  • When a figure is not safe to send and must be escalated
  • Routine factual replies using approved material, where the team permits
Can recommend
  • Which prospects look worth a meeting
  • What a client is likely to ask
  • Process improvements
Needs approval
  • External documents
  • Non-standard data disclosures
  • Any commitment on timing made to a client
Belongs to others
  • Pricing
  • Contract terms
  • Investment content
  • Ownership of the relationship
Measures of success
  • Error rate in material produced
  • Timeliness
  • Seniors trusting drafts with less rework
  • Growing product and client knowledge
  • Being asked into client meetings
Notes
General industry practice. At analyst level the day-to-day work on the sales and relationship sides is widely described as similar; that description is plausible but team-specific.

Associate

≈ Supported inference ROLE-ASSOCIATE

Purpose
Run defined pieces of the client process with limited supervision and check the work of analysts.
Recurring tasks
  • Coordinate an RFP response or a review cycle end to end
  • Lead preparation for meetings and attend them
  • Handle day-to-day contact for smaller clients or for the working-level contacts at large ones
  • Review analysts' drafts
  • Liaise with legal, onboarding and operations on live matters
Work products
  • Completed RFP submission
  • Final review pack
  • Onboarding tracker
  • Client correspondence
  • Internal opportunity notes
Stakeholders
  • Vice presidents and the team head
  • Analysts
  • Specialist teams
  • Client investment and operations staff
  • Consultant analysts
Decision rights
Can decide
  • How a process is run and sequenced
  • Routine client replies
  • Quality sign-off on analyst inputs before senior review
Can recommend
  • Whether to enter a search
  • How to position a proposal
  • When to escalate a client issue
Needs approval
  • Fees and non-standard terms
  • Messages on performance problems or incidents
  • Commitments of portfolio-manager time
Belongs to others
  • Final commercial decisions
  • Investment decisions
  • Contract sign-off
Measures of success
  • Processes delivered on time without senior rescue
  • Client contacts choosing to call them directly
  • Quality of judgement on escalation
  • Development of analysts
Notes
General industry practice. The point at which an associate begins to carry their own client list varies widely.

Vice President or Executive Director-level coverage professional

≈ Supported inference ROLE-VP-ED

Purpose
Own a list of clients or a territory and be accountable for its commercial results.
Recurring tasks
  • Lead client and prospect meetings
  • Decide which opportunities to pursue and assemble the pitch team
  • Negotiate fees and terms within approved limits
  • Manage difficult conversations on performance and service
  • Forecast flows and report pipeline to management
  • Coach junior team members
Work products
  • Account plans
  • Pitch strategy
  • Pricing requests
  • Pipeline forecast
  • Escalation notes
Stakeholders
  • Client decision-makers and their consultants
  • Team head
  • Portfolio managers and product heads
  • Legal, compliance and pricing committees
Decision rights
Can decide
  • Whether to pursue an opportunity
  • Meeting strategy and who attends
  • Routine service matters for their clients
Can recommend
  • Fee proposals and concessions
  • Guideline changes
  • Resource allocation to a client
Needs approval
  • Pricing outside standard schedules
  • Non-standard contract terms
  • Remediation or compensation
Belongs to others
  • Investment decisions
  • Firm pricing policy
  • Product design
Measures of success
  • New assets and revenue
  • Retention and growth of the book
  • Client and consultant feedback
  • Forecast accuracy
  • Conduct and compliance record
Notes
Title usage differs by firm and region; do not assume Vice President and Executive Director are separate consecutive levels everywhere. See Chapter 4 for what public sources show.

Managing Director, team head

≈ Supported inference ROLE-MD-HEAD

Purpose
Set the strategy for a client segment or region, own its largest relationships and be accountable for the team's results and conduct.
Recurring tasks
  • Sponsor the largest clients and prospects
  • Allocate coverage and set priorities
  • Approve or escalate pricing and resource requests
  • Represent the segment's needs to product and investment leadership
  • Hire, develop and assess the team
Work products
  • Business plan for the segment
  • Budget and flow forecast
  • Coverage model
  • Senior client correspondence
Stakeholders
  • Client chief investment officers, trustee chairs and senior consultants
  • Regional and global distribution heads
  • Investment and product heads
  • Risk, compliance and legal leadership
Decision rights
Can decide
  • Team priorities and coverage allocation
  • Which searches the team enters
  • Hiring recommendations within approved headcount
Can recommend
  • New products the segment needs
  • Strategic pricing for major clients
Needs approval
  • Headcount
  • Exceptional pricing or terms
  • New product launches
Belongs to others
  • Investment decisions
  • Firm-wide strategy and risk appetite
Measures of success
  • Segment revenue, flows and retention
  • Team stability and development
  • Reputation with clients and consultants
  • Control and conduct record
Notes
General industry practice. Partner at Goldman Sachs is a separate designation, not simply the next rung for every Managing Director.

Institutional sales (business development)

≈ Supported inference ROLE-INST-SALES

Purpose
Win new mandates from institutional asset owners by matching a real client need to a capability the firm can deliver.
Recurring tasks
  • Prospect research and targeting
  • Discovery meetings
  • Proposal design with specialists
  • Coordinating RFPs and final presentations
  • Pipeline management
  • Working with consultant relations
Work products
  • Prospect briefings
  • Proposals
  • RFP submissions
  • Pitch materials
  • Pipeline reports
Stakeholders
  • Prospects' investment staff, trustees and committees
  • Investment consultants
  • Portfolio managers and product specialists
  • RFP team
  • Relationship managers who will inherit the client
Decision rights
Can decide
  • Which prospects to prioritise
  • Whether to compete in a search
  • How to frame the firm's answer
Can recommend
  • Pricing and terms
  • Which strategy and vehicle fit
Needs approval
  • Fees outside the schedule
  • Bespoke terms
  • Capacity for large mandates
Belongs to others
  • The client's decision
  • The consultant's rating
  • Investment performance
Measures of success

  • Quality of qualified pipeline
  • Mandates that are still in place several years later
Notes
The former intern's label for this side of a team is an unverified account. Titles vary by firm.

Institutional relationship management

≈ Supported inference ROLE-INST-RM

Purpose
Keep existing institutional clients accurately informed and well served so that they can make sound decisions about their mandates.
Recurring tasks
  • Overseeing reports
  • Leading review meetings
  • Handling queries and change requests
  • Managing guideline, fee and contract events
  • Escalating and resolving problems
  • Recognising new needs
Work products
  • Review packs
  • Minutes and action logs
  • Client service plans
  • Incident explanations
  • Re-tender defence packs
Stakeholders
  • Clients' investment staff, trustees, operations and finance teams
  • Consultants monitoring the mandate
  • Portfolio managers
  • Client service, reporting, legal and operations
Decision rights
Can decide
  • Meeting agendas and who attends
  • When and how to escalate
  • Routine service responses
Can recommend
  • Fee adjustments at review
  • Guideline amendments
  • Additional mandates
Needs approval
  • Fee changes
  • Contract amendments
  • Remediation after an error
Belongs to others

Measures of success

  • Timeliness and accuracy of service
  • Appropriate growth of existing relationships
  • How problems were handled
Notes
Retention is hard to attribute to one person and is not automatically a good client outcome. The former intern's label for this side of a team is an unverified account.

Third-party wealth sales

≈ Supported inference ROLE-TPW-SALES

Purpose
Get suitable funds researched, approved and adopted by wealth managers, private banks and other intermediaries who invest on behalf of their own clients.
Recurring tasks
  • Covering fund selectors and research teams
  • Supplying data in the selector's format
  • Arranging portfolio-manager access
  • Presenting to advisers and model-portfolio teams
  • Monitoring flows by intermediary
Work products
  • Selector briefings
  • Peer-group comparisons
  • Adviser presentations
  • Flow reports
  • Buy-list status tracker
Stakeholders
  • Fund selectors (gatekeepers)
  • Intermediary investment committees
  • Advisers and discretionary managers
  • Platforms
  • Investment specialists and marketing
Decision rights
Can decide
  • Which intermediaries and funds to prioritise
  • How to support adoption after approval
Can recommend
  • Share-class and fee arrangements
  • Which fund suits a selector's search
Needs approval
  • Fee terms and rebates where permitted
  • Marketing material
  • Any performance claim
Belongs to others
  • The selector's and committee's decision

Measures of success
  • Net flows by intermediary
  • Number and quality of approved-list positions
  • Adoption after approval
  • Selector feedback
Notes
An approved-list position is permission to buy, not funded assets. For funds reaching UK retail investors, Consumer Duty obligations apply across the distribution chain.

Third-party wealth relationship management

≈ Supported inference ROLE-TPW-RM

Purpose
Keep intermediaries that already hold the firm's funds informed and supported so the funds remain appropriately used.
Recurring tasks
  • Annual and triggered due-diligence updates
  • Communicating fund and team changes to all holders
  • Resolving platform, data and share-class issues
  • Monitoring holdings and watch-list status
  • Supporting advisers with material
Work products
  • Due-diligence update packs
  • Change notifications
  • Watch-list tracker
  • Holder flow analysis
Stakeholders

Consultant relations

≈ Supported inference ROLE-CONSULTANT-RELATIONS

Purpose
Make sure investment consultants' research teams understand and can fairly assess the firm's strategies, because their ratings shape which managers asset owners consider.
Recurring tasks
  • Covering consultants' manager-research teams
  • Preparing portfolio managers for research meetings
  • Supplying data to consultant databases
  • Tracking ratings and review dates
  • Briefing sales and relationship colleagues on consultant views
Work products

Stakeholders

Can recommend

Belongs to others

Product or investment specialist (client portfolio manager)

≈ Supported inference ROLE-PRODUCT-SPECIALIST

Purpose
Represent an investment team to clients in technical depth, so portfolio managers can spend more time managing money.

Client service

RFP team

How management-fee arithmetic works. Every rate is an input you choose. Nothing here is a Goldman Sachs fee, and the result is before costs and every other adjustment.

Assets
Client flows
Fee

Gross management fee over the period (illustrative)

PeriodAverage fee baseFeeEffective rateAssets at end
Month by month
MonthFlowBalance after flowFee baseFeeBalance at end
How the model works
  1. Flows land at the start of a month. A withdrawal cannot take the balance below zero.
  2. The month's fee is the yearly fee on that month's fee base, divided by twelve.
  3. The market return is applied at the end of the month.
  4. Fees are assumed to be billed separately, not taken from the assets.

Left out on purpose: performance fees, rebates, costs, minimum fees and tax.

Worked examples

£500m fixed-income mandate

£500m at 20bp, fully funded on day one ✎ Illustrative example

The base arithmetic: assets x fee rate. 1 basis point = 0.01%, so 20bp = 0.20%.

PeriodAverage fee baseGross management feeEffective annual rateAssets at period end
Year 1£500m£1m20.0bp£500m
Total over 12 months£1m

£500m at 20bp, half funded in month 1 and half in month 7 ✎ Illustrative example

Timing: an awarded mandate is not fee-paying until the money arrives. Same headline size, 25% less first-year revenue.

PeriodAverage fee baseGross management feeEffective annual rateAssets at period end
Year 1£375m£750k20.0bp£500m
Total over 12 months£750k

£500m at 20bp, markets fall 8% over the year ✎ Illustrative example

Fees follow the value of the assets, so revenue moves with markets even when no client does anything.

PeriodAverage fee baseGross management feeEffective annual rateAssets at period end
Year 1£481.391m£962.8k20.0bp£460m
Total over 12 months£962.8k

£500m, fee renegotiated from 20bp to 16bp from month 7 ✎ Illustrative example

Pricing pressure: a retained mandate can still earn less. Retained revenue is not the same as stable revenue.

PeriodAverage fee baseGross management feeEffective annual rateAssets at period end
Year 1£500m£900k18.0bp£500m
Total over 12 months£900k

£1bn client considering withdrawal

£1bn at 15bp, client stays ✎ Illustrative example

The baseline against which a withdrawal is measured. Keeping the client adds nothing new: it avoids a loss.

PeriodAverage fee baseGross management feeEffective annual rateAssets at period end
Year 1£1bn£1.5m15.0bp£1bn
Year 2£1bn£1.5m15.0bp£1bn
Total over 24 months£3m

£1bn at 15bp, client withdraws £400m in month 7 ✎ Illustrative example

A partial withdrawal: the relationship continues but the fee base shrinks from that month onwards.

PeriodAverage fee baseGross management feeEffective annual rateAssets at period end
Year 1£800m£1.2m15.0bp£600m
Year 2£600m£900k15.0bp£600m
Total over 24 months£2.1m

£1bn at 15bp, client leaves entirely in month 7 ✎ Illustrative example

Full termination. Recurring fees are recurring only while the client chooses to stay.

PeriodAverage fee baseGross management feeEffective annual rateAssets at period end
Year 1£500m£750k15.0bp£0
Year 2£0£0n/a (no fee-bearing assets)£0
Total over 24 months£750k

Relationship expanding from £300m to £600m

£300m growing to £600m in month 7, flat 22bp ✎ Illustrative example

If the fee rate is flat, doubling the assets doubles the run-rate fee from the funding month.

PeriodAverage fee baseGross management feeEffective annual rateAssets at period end
Year 1£450m£990k22.0bp£600m
Year 2£600m£1.32m22.0bp£600m
Total over 24 months£2.31m

£300m growing to £600m in month 7, tiered fee (25bp to £250m, 20bp to £500m, 15bp above) ✎ Illustrative example

Breakpoints: larger mandates pay a lower marginal rate, so doubling assets does not double fees. The client's average rate falls as they grow.

Total over 24 months£2.275m

Approval is permission to buy, not a purchase. Assets arrive adviser by adviser, so first-year revenue is small even when the listing is a real win.

The failure case that looks identical on the day of approval: listed, zero flows, zero fees.

Different business models

OCIO: £2bn scheme, tiered fee on total assets (10bp to £1bn, 6bp above) ✎ Illustrative example

An OCIO fee is typically charged on the whole portfolio for running it, at a low rate, with underlying managers' fees charged separately. The provider is paid for delegated responsibility, not for one product.

PeriodAverage fee baseGross management feeEffective annual rateAssets at period end
Year 1£2bn£1.6m8.0bp£2bn
Total over 12 months£1.6m

Liquidity: £750m in a money market fund at 10bp, £500m redeemed in month 4 ✎ Illustrative example

Cash balances are operating money. They can leave in a day for reasons that have nothing to do with service, so average balance matters more than the opening figure.

PeriodAverage fee baseGross management feeEffective annual rateAssets at period end
Year 1£375m£375k10.0bp£250m
Total over 12 months£375k

Private markets: £100m commitment, 100bp charged on committed capital ✎ Illustrative example

Many closed-end private funds charge on committed capital during the investment period, so the fee does not depend on how much has been drawn or on valuations. Always check the fund's actual fee base.

The same commitment charged on invested value earns far less in year one. Using NAV by default would misstate either structure.
