Active management

Plain English
Trying to beat a benchmark by choosing investments that differ from it.
Mechanics
Charges higher fees for uncertain outperformance. Success is judged after fees over a full cycle.
Why it matters to this role
Most of what an active house sells has to justify its fee against a cheap passive alternative.

Advisory & OCIO accounts · Advisory and outsourced chief investment officer accounts

Plain English
A GS reporting bucket that combines assets it advises on with assets where it acts as a client's outsourced investment office.
Mechanics
From Q4 2025 OCIO assets are 'reported in aggregate with advisory accounts'. In alternatives these accounts averaged $112bn in 2025 at 17 bps, against 77 bps on funds and discretionary accounts.
Why it matters to this role
Shows OCIO-type relationships carry a lower fee rate per pound than fund products, and that GS publishes no standalone OCIO total.

Sources: R2-S01 R2-S02

AIF · Alternative investment fund

Plain English
A regulated fund that is not a UCITS, typically used for private assets, property and hedge strategies.
Mechanics
Governed by the AIFMD framework in the EU and its UK equivalent. Usually for professional investors.
Why it matters to this role
The wrapper for most private-market products.

AIFMD · Alternative Investment Fund Managers Directive

Plain English
European rules for managers of funds that are not UCITS.
Mechanics
Governs marketing of private and hedge funds to professional investors across borders.
Why it matters to this role
Determines where and to whom private funds can be marketed.

ALM · Asset–liability management

Plain English
Choosing investments by looking at what you owe as well as what you own.
Mechanics
Matches the size, timing and sensitivity of assets to liabilities. Central to pensions and insurance.
Why it matters to this role
The frame for most institutional solutions conversations.

Alpha

Plain English
Return above the benchmark that comes from the manager's decisions.
Mechanics
Uncertain, hard to distinguish from luck over short periods.
Why it matters to this role
What active fees are meant to pay for.

Alternatives

Plain English
Investments outside ordinary listed shares and bonds.
Mechanics
Private equity, private credit, real estate, infrastructure, hedge funds. Higher fees, less liquidity.
Why it matters to this role
A strategic growth area for large managers and a major source of fee revenue.

AML · Anti-money laundering

Plain English
Rules and checks designed to stop criminal money entering the financial system.
Mechanics
Requires customer due diligence, monitoring and reporting of suspicious activity.
Why it matters to this role
No client can be funded until these checks pass.

Assessment centre · Also: Superday

Plain English
A final-round event where a candidate has several interviews, usually on one day.
Mechanics
Format varies by firm, team and year.
Why it matters to this role
The stage where team-specific knowledge is most likely to be tested.

Asset

Plain English
Something you own that is worth money or will pay you money.
Mechanics
Shares, bonds, cash, property, loans made to others.
Why it matters to this role
The starting vocabulary for everything else.

AUM · Assets under management

Plain English
The total amount of client money an asset manager invests.
Mechanics
Usually counts assets where the manager has discretion to buy and sell. Moves with client flows and with market prices. Definitions differ between firms, so compare like with like.
Why it matters to this role
Fees are a percentage of it, so it is the base of the firm's revenue and the usual scorecard for client coverage.

AUS · Assets under supervision

Plain English
Goldman Sachs's headline measure of client money: everything it manages for clients plus some assets it only advises on or holds as private bank deposits.
Mechanics
Per the 10-K: institutional clients' assets, assets sourced through third-party distributors and high-net-worth assets managed on a discretionary basis, plus client assets with third-party managers, private bank deposits and fee-earning advisory relationships without discretion. Excludes self-directed brokerage assets. $4,097bn at 30 Sep 2026.
Why it matters to this role
Management fees are driven by average AUS, so every flow a client team wins or loses moves this number. Do not call it AUM: AUS is wider.

Sources: R2-S01 R2-S02

Average effective management fee

Plain English
The average yearly fee GS earned per unit of client assets, shown in basis points.
Mechanics
Disclosed by asset class and excluding non-asset-based fees. 2025: alternatives 58 bps, equity 54 bps, fixed income 17 bps, liquidity products 14 bps, total 31 bps.
Why it matters to this role
Shows why product mix matters: moving a pound from equity to fixed income or liquidity lowers revenue even if the client stays. It is a firm-wide blend, not the price of any mandate.

Sources: R2-S01 R2-S02

AWM · Asset & Wealth Management

Plain English
The Goldman Sachs reporting segment that contains both Asset Management and Wealth Management.
Mechanics
One of three segments with Global Banking & Markets and Platform Solutions. Net revenues $16,679m in 2025 (28.6% of the firm), of which Asset management $6,784m and Wealth management $9,895m.
Why it matters to this role
When someone says asset management is about 30% of Goldman's revenue they are quoting AWM, which also includes private banking, lending and principal investments.

Sources: R2-S01

Beauty parade · Also: finals, pitch

Plain English
The meeting where shortlisted managers present to the client one after another.
Mechanics
Usually the last stage of a search, with the consultant present. Short, structured and scored.
Why it matters to this role
Preparing the team and materials for it is a classic coverage work product.

Benchmark

Plain English
The yardstick a portfolio is measured against.
Mechanics
Usually a market index, sometimes a cash rate plus a margin or the client's liabilities. Set in the guidelines.
Why it matters to this role
A badly chosen benchmark makes a manager look good or bad for the wrong reasons.

Beta

Plain English
The return you get simply from being exposed to a market.
Mechanics
Also a measure of how much a portfolio moves when the market moves. Cheap to obtain through index funds.
Why it matters to this role
Clients increasingly refuse to pay active fees for it.

bps · Basis points

Plain English
One hundredth of one percent. 100 bps = 1%.
Mechanics
Used for fees, yields and spreads because the numbers are small. £500m at 20 bps is £1m a year (illustrative).
Why it matters to this role
All fee arithmetic in this role is done in basis points; you should convert without thinking.

Breakpoint · Also: fee tier

Plain English
A size threshold above which a lower fee rate applies to the extra money.
Mechanics
Example: 25 bps on the first £200m, 15 bps above. Applies slice by slice, so the effective rate falls gradually (illustrative).
Why it matters to this role
Central to pricing an expansion of an existing mandate.

Bulk annuity

Plain English
The insurance contract used in a buy-in or buyout.
Mechanics
Written by a small group of specialist UK insurers, which then need assets to back the promises.
Why it matters to this role
Moves assets from pension clients to insurance clients.

Buy list · Also: approved list, recommended list

Plain English
An intermediary's list of funds its advisers and portfolio managers may use.
Mechanics
Often tiered: a wide approved list and a narrower recommended or model-portfolio list. Funds are reviewed and can be removed.
Why it matters to this role
Getting listed is a milestone; assets arrive only if advisers then choose the fund.

Buy-in

Plain English
A pension scheme buys an insurance policy that pays it the money needed to pay some or all members' pensions.
Mechanics
The policy is an asset of the scheme; trustees remain responsible. Often a step towards buyout.
Why it matters to this role
Assets used to pay the premium leave the asset manager.

Buyout

Plain English
An insurer takes over a pension scheme's promises entirely and the scheme is wound up.
Mechanics
Members become policyholders of the insurer. The scheme's assets pass to the insurer as premium.
Why it matters to this role
Ends the asset manager's relationship with the scheme, and may create a new one with the insurer.

Capital call · Also: drawdown notice

Plain English
A request from a private fund for part of the money an investor has promised.
Mechanics
Calls arrive over several years as deals are found. Investors must hold or be able to raise the cash at short notice.
Why it matters to this role
Clients need liquidity planning around calls; it links private markets to their cash management.

Carried interest

Plain English
The private-fund manager's share of profits, paid only after investors have their money back plus a minimum return.
Mechanics
Often around a fifth of profits above the hurdle (illustrative). It is realised when investments are sold, so it is lumpy and uncertain.
Why it matters to this role
In private markets it sits alongside management fees; the two behave very differently as revenue.

CCG · Client Coverage Group (reported)

Plain English
A label one former intern used for the relationship management side.
Mechanics
Not confirmed by this glossary as an official name or as meaning relationship management. Treat as an unverified account until the role chapter says otherwise.
Why it matters to this role
A reminder not to repeat informal labels in an interview as if they were official.

CDI · Cashflow-driven investment

Plain English
Building a portfolio whose income and repayments arrive when the investor needs to make payments.
Mechanics
Typically buy-and-maintain credit and private credit matched to pension payments.
Why it matters to this role
A common proposal for mature DB schemes and insurers.

CIO · Chief investment officer

Plain English
The most senior person responsible for an organisation's investments.
Mechanics
At an asset owner, the CIO leads the in-house investment staff and reports to trustees or a board.
Why it matters to this role
Often the main day-to-day counterpart at larger clients.

Client channel

Plain English
How the client reaches Goldman Sachs: directly as an institution, as one of GS's own wealth clients, or through another firm that distributes GS products.
Mechanics
GS reports long-term AUS in three channels: Institutional ($1,245bn), Wealth management ($1,087bn) and Third-party distributed ($714bn) at 30 Sep 2026. Global only; no regional split.
Why it matters to this role
The Institutional and Third-party distributed channels correspond most closely to institutional and third-party wealth client teams, but GS does not map channels to teams and gives no UK or EMEA channel figure.

Sources: R2-S01 R2-S02

Client service

Plain English
The team that handles day-to-day client requests, reporting and queries.
Mechanics
Often distinct from relationship management, which owns the overall relationship and commercial judgement.
Why it matters to this role
Where much junior work sits, and how reliability is demonstrated.

CMA · Competition and Markets Authority

Plain English
The UK's competition regulator.
Mechanics
Its 2019 Order on investment consultancy and fiduciary management introduced mandatory tendering and objective-setting for consultants.
Why it matters to this role
The origin of the tender rules that shape OCIO sales.

Sources: W1-S03

CNAV · Constant net asset value (public debt CNAV)

Plain English
A money market fund that aims to keep its share price fixed, and invests almost entirely in government debt.
Mechanics
Permitted to use amortised cost accounting because holdings are overwhelmingly public debt.
Why it matters to this role
The most conservative MMF type; favoured where policy requires government exposure.

Co-investment

Plain English
An investor puts money directly into a specific deal alongside a fund manager.
Mechanics
Usually at lower or no fees. Requires the investor to assess deals quickly.
Why it matters to this role
Something large sovereign and pension investors expect from manager relationships.

Collateral

Plain English
Assets pledged to the other side of a contract as security.
Mechanics
Topped up or returned daily as positions move. Usually cash or government bonds.
Why it matters to this role
Clients must be able to find it quickly; that is a coverage conversation as well as an investment one.

Committed capital

Plain English
The total amount an investor has promised to a private fund, paid in stages when the manager asks for it.
Mechanics
Management fees in private funds are often charged on commitments during the investment period, then on invested capital. So the fee base is not NAV.
Why it matters to this role
Using NAV to estimate private-market fees gives the wrong answer; check the fee base first.

Conflict of interest

Plain English
A situation where what benefits the firm or employee differs from what benefits the client.
Mechanics
Managed through disclosure, policies, independent oversight and, sometimes, by declining business.
Why it matters to this role
Central to honest discussion of what client coverage owes the client.

Consultant rating

Plain English
A consultant's formal opinion of an investment strategy, such as 'buy' or 'preferred'.
Mechanics
Based on research meetings with the investment team. Without a positive rating a strategy rarely reaches a shortlist.
Why it matters to this role
A precondition for much institutional business.

Consultant relations

Plain English
The team that manages an asset manager's relationships with investment consultants.
Mechanics
Keeps consultant researchers informed, supports strategy ratings and coordinates messaging across client teams.
Why it matters to this role
A consultant's rating can open or close the door to many clients at once.

Consumer Duty

Plain English
A UK rule requiring firms to act to deliver good outcomes for retail customers.
Mechanics
Set by the Financial Conduct Authority. Covers product design, price and value, understanding and support, and applies along the distribution chain.
Why it matters to this role
Shapes how funds are priced, described and sold through UK intermediaries.

Corporate titles · Analyst, Associate, Vice President, Managing Director, Partner

Plain English
The ranks used at investment banks and their asset management arms.
Mechanics
Usage differs by firm and region, and a title does not by itself tell you a person's function or team. See the role chapter for what is verified about Goldman Sachs.
Why it matters to this role
Do not infer reporting lines or teams from titles alone.

Corporate treasury

Plain English
The team in a company that manages its cash, funding and financial risks.
Mechanics
Invests operating cash under a board-approved policy that puts safety and access ahead of return.
Why it matters to this role
The core client for liquidity and money market products.

Covenant · Employer covenant

Plain English
How able and willing the employer is to support its pension scheme.
Mechanics
A strong covenant allows more investment risk and a longer horizon; a weak one pushes towards caution.
Why it matters to this role
Explains why two schemes with the same funding level can want different things.

Coverage

Plain English
Responsibility for a defined set of clients, by region, type or both.
Mechanics
A coverage team is the firm's point of accountability for those clients.
Why it matters to this role
The organising idea behind how client teams are divided.

CPM · Client portfolio manager

Plain English
A person who sits close to an investment team and explains its strategy to clients in depth. Also called a product specialist or investment specialist.
Mechanics
Represents the strategy in pitches, reviews and due-diligence meetings and answers detailed portfolio questions. Does not usually make the buy and sell decisions, which stay with the portfolio managers.
Why it matters to this role
Coverage teams bring a client portfolio manager into a meeting when the questions go beyond what a salesperson or relationship manager should answer.

Credit spread

Plain English
The extra yield a borrower pays compared with the government, to compensate for the risk it will not repay.
Mechanics
Widens when investors worry about defaults. The return source in credit strategies.
Why it matters to this role
Explains what a client earns, and risks, in a credit mandate.

CRM system · Client relationship management system

Plain English
The database where a firm records its clients, contacts, meetings and sales opportunities.
Mechanics
Salesforce is a widely used example. Quality depends on people logging accurately.
Why it matters to this role
Turns one person's knowledge into the firm's knowledge; juniors maintain much of it.

Cross-sell

Plain English
Providing an existing client with a further product or service.
Mechanics
Appropriate only when it answers a real client need; relationship breadth is not a goal in itself.
Why it matters to this role
A commercial objective that must be tested against suitability.

CSG · Client Solutions Group

Plain English
The name in the title of the Goldman Sachs Asset Management programme this project prepares for.
Mechanics
Reported by one former intern to be used both for the whole client-facing group and for its sales side. That usage is unverified; see the role chapter for what official sources establish.
Why it matters to this role
Know what the official role description says before relying on anyone's shorthand.

Custodian

Plain English
A bank that holds a client's investments safely and settles its trades.
Mechanics
Legally separates client assets from the asset manager. Uses sub-custodians in each local market.
Why it matters to this role
The reason a manager's failure should not lose a client's assets, and a key party in onboarding.

DB · Defined benefit pension

Plain English
A pension where the amount you will be paid is promised in advance, usually based on salary and years worked.
Mechanics
The employer bears investment and longevity risk. Most UK private-sector schemes are closed to new members and focused on securing benefits.
Why it matters to this role
DB schemes are the largest UK institutional client group and drive demand for LDI, credit and OCIO.

Sources: W1-S01

DC · Defined contribution pension

Plain English
A pension where what goes in is fixed and what comes out depends on how the investments perform.
Mechanics
The member bears the risk. Most money sits in a default fund chosen by the provider or trustees.
Why it matters to this role
A growing, price-sensitive market where the buyer is the default designer, not the member.

Sources: W1-S07

DDQ · Due diligence questionnaire

Plain English
A detailed questionnaire a client or consultant uses to check a manager, before hiring it or each year afterwards.
Mechanics
Covers investment, operational, compliance, cyber and ESG topics. Many are answered from a maintained library and routed to subject experts.
Why it matters to this role
Completing and tracking DDQs accurately is a routine, high-volume part of client service.

Dealing cut-off

Plain English
The time of day by which an order to buy or sell fund units must arrive to be processed that day.
Mechanics
For MMFs, late cut-offs and same-day settlement are selling points.
Why it matters to this role
A practical detail treasurers care about more than yield.

Default fund

Plain English
The investment a pension saver is put into automatically if they make no choice.
Mechanics
Holds the large majority of DC assets. Subject to a charge cap in the UK for auto-enrolment schemes.
Why it matters to this role
Winning a place inside a default strategy is the main prize in DC.

Derivative

Plain English
A contract whose value depends on something else, such as an interest rate or share index.
Mechanics
Futures, options, swaps, forwards. Used for hedging and efficient exposure. Use is limited by guidelines.
Why it matters to this role
Clients ask what derivatives are for and what could go wrong.

DFM · Discretionary fund manager

Plain English
A firm that makes investment decisions for clients without asking permission for each trade.
Mechanics
In UK wealth, DFMs run bespoke and model portfolios for advisers' clients. They are professional fund buyers.
Why it matters to this role
A major buyer group in UK third-party wealth.

Discount rate

Plain English
The interest rate used to turn future payments into a value today.
Mechanics
A lower rate makes distant liabilities worth more today. Usually tied to gilt or high-quality bond yields.
Why it matters to this role
The reason interest rates move pension liabilities.

Distribution · Also: client business, client coverage

Plain English
The part of an asset manager that finds, wins, serves and keeps clients.
Mechanics
Includes sales, relationship management, consultant relations, product specialists, RFP and client service teams. Names vary by firm.
Why it matters to this role
It is the function this project studies.

Distribution (private funds)

Plain English
Money a private fund pays back to investors when it sells an investment or receives income.
Mechanics
Not to be confused with 'distribution' meaning sales. Timing is uncertain and depends on exit markets.
Why it matters to this role
Slow distributions reduce clients' ability to make new commitments.

Drawdown

Plain English
The fall in value from a high point to the next low point.
Mechanics
Maximum drawdown is the worst such fall over a period. Also used, confusingly, for capital calls and for taking pension income.
Why it matters to this role
It is how clients experience loss.

Duration

Plain English
A measure of how much a bond's price changes when interest rates change.
Mechanics
Roughly, a bond with a duration of 15 years falls about 15% if yields rise by one percentage point. Liabilities have duration too.
Why it matters to this role
The key number for matching assets to pension liabilities.

E&F · Endowments and foundations

Plain English
Charitable pots of money invested to fund a mission over the long term.
Mechanics
Aim to preserve real value while spending a steady percentage each year. Governed by trustees or an investment committee.
Why it matters to this role
A distinct institutional segment with long horizons and mission-related constraints.

Effective fee rate

Plain English
The average fee a client actually pays across all its assets, after tiers and discounts.
Mechanics
Total annual fee divided by average assets. With tiered fees it falls as the mandate grows. At firm level it falls when the mix shifts towards cheaper products such as passive or liquidity.
Why it matters to this role
Lets you compare mandates and see why asset growth does not always mean equal revenue growth.

ELTIF · European long-term investment fund

Plain English
An EU fund type that lets a wider range of investors access long-term private assets.
Mechanics
Revised rules, often called ELTIF 2.0, loosened earlier restrictions. Used for semi-liquid private-market funds for wealth clients.
Why it matters to this role
The EU counterpart to the LTAF in private-markets-for-wealth conversations.

Endgame

Plain English
A DB scheme's intended final destination: insure the liabilities, or keep running the scheme.
Mechanics
Options include buy-in, buyout, run-on and consolidation vehicles. The choice drives asset allocation and liquidity needs.
Why it matters to this role
Determines what a scheme will and will not buy from an asset manager.

Equities

Plain English
Shares: part-ownership of companies.
Mechanics
Higher long-term expected return with larger falls along the way.
Why it matters to this role
The growth engine in DC and endowment portfolios.

ESG · Environmental, social and governance

Plain English
Considering how companies treat the environment, people and their own management when investing.
Mechanics
Ranges from exclusions to integration to impact strategies. Client requirements and regulation differ sharply by region.
Why it matters to this role
A standard section of RFPs and DDQs; clients' positions vary and must not be assumed.

ETF · Exchange-traded fund

Plain English
A fund you buy and sell on a stock exchange like a share.
Mechanics
Most track an index cheaply; active ETFs are growing. Trades throughout the day at market price, close to NAV.
Why it matters to this role
A major channel for low-cost investing and a source of fee pressure on traditional funds.

Executive Director · Working title used outside the United States for the Vice President level

Plain English
The same level of seniority as Vice President, under a different name.
Mechanics
Goldman listings titled Executive Director carry the corporate title Vice President, and the firm announces one combined Vice President and Executive Director class.
Why it matters to this role
It is one rung, not two. Do not assume an Executive Director outranks a Vice President.

Sources: R1-S26

Family office

Plain English
A private firm that manages the wealth of one very rich family, or a few.
Mechanics
Sits between institutional and wealth clients: professional staff, flexible mandate, interest in private deals.
Why it matters to this role
Coverage may sit in either an institutional or a wealth team.

FCA · Financial Conduct Authority

Plain English
The UK regulator of how financial firms behave towards customers and markets.
Mechanics
Authorises asset managers and funds; sets conduct rules including the Consumer Duty.
Why it matters to this role
Its rules shape what can be said and sold to whom.

Fiduciary duty

Plain English
A legal duty to act in someone else's best interests, not your own.
Mechanics
Trustees owe it to beneficiaries. Managers owe contractual and regulatory duties to clients. It is why trust never replaces due diligence.
Why it matters to this role
Frames what a client may properly decide and why process matters.

Fixed income

Plain English
Investments that pay set interest and return the money lent: bonds and loans.
Mechanics
Government bonds, corporate credit, securitised debt, emerging market debt. The largest asset class for pensions and insurers.
Why it matters to this role
Most institutional mandates in the UK are fixed income or liability-related.

FM · Fiduciary management

Plain English
The usual UK pensions name for OCIO.
Mechanics
Trustees must run a qualifying competitive tender, with bids from at least three unconnected providers, before fiduciary management first covers 20% or more of scheme assets.
Why it matters to this role
The regulated tender process shapes how UK OCIO business is won.

Sources: W1-S04 W1-S03

Fund of funds

Plain English
A fund that invests in other funds instead of directly in shares or bonds.
Mechanics
Its manager is a professional fund buyer. Adds a layer of fees in exchange for selection and diversification.
Why it matters to this role
Another type of intermediary buyer.

Funding level

Plain English
A scheme's assets as a percentage of the value of what it has promised to pay.
Mechanics
Depends heavily on how liabilities are valued. The same scheme has different funding levels on technical provisions, PPF and buyout measures.
Why it matters to this role
The scorecard trustees care about most.

Gatekeeper · Also: fund selector

Plain English
The person or team at an intermediary that decides which funds its advisers are allowed to use.
Mechanics
Runs research and due diligence and maintains the approved list. Approval permits purchase; it does not cause it.
Why it matters to this role
The first, but not the last, person a wholesale salesperson must convince.

General account

Plain English
The pool of an insurer's own investments that backs its promises to policyholders.
Mechanics
Distinct from unit-linked funds, where the policyholder bears the investment risk.
Why it matters to this role
The portfolio an insurance asset management team is hired to manage.

Gilt

Plain English
A bond issued by the UK government.
Mechanics
Conventional gilts pay fixed interest. Long-dated gilts are the main matching asset for UK pension liabilities.
Why it matters to this role
Gilt yields set the value of UK pension liabilities.

GMRA · Global Master Repurchase Agreement

Plain English
The standard legal contract under which repo trades are done.
Mechanics
Sets collateral eligibility, margining and what happens on default. Negotiated per counterparty.
Why it matters to this role
Clients ask about eligible collateral and margin terms under it.

Gross flows

Plain English
All the new money won in a period, before subtracting what left.
Mechanics
Gross sales can be high while net flows are negative if existing clients are withdrawing more than new clients add.
Why it matters to this role
Explains why winning new business and keeping existing business are both needed.

Hedge

Plain English
An investment made to reduce a risk you already have.
Mechanics
A good hedge loses money when the thing it protects gains. That is success, not failure.
Why it matters to this role
Explaining hedge losses in plain terms is a recurring client conversation.

High yield

Plain English
Bonds from riskier borrowers that pay more interest.
Mechanics
Rated below investment grade. Higher default risk and more equity-like behaviour.
Why it matters to this role
Often restricted or capped in institutional guidelines.

High-water mark

Plain English
A rule that the manager earns a performance fee only on gains above the fund's previous highest value.
Mechanics
Prevents a client paying twice for the same gain after a fall and recovery.
Why it matters to this role
A standard question in fee discussions for strategies with performance fees.

HireVue

Plain English
A platform for recorded video interviews where candidates answer set questions on camera.
Mechanics
Used by many large employers as an early screening stage. How any firm reviews recordings should be taken from its own official guidance.
Why it matters to this role
Likely to be the first interview stage a candidate meets.

Hurdle rate

Plain English
The minimum return investors must receive before the manager can take a share of profits.
Mechanics
In private funds often called the preferred return. Carried interest is paid only once it is cleared.
Why it matters to this role
Determines when, and whether, performance-related fees are earned.

IC · Investment committee

Plain English
The group that makes or approves investment decisions for an organisation.
Mechanics
Meets periodically; works from papers prepared by staff or advisers. Its timetable sets the pace of any sale.
Why it matters to this role
Knowing the committee calendar is basic account planning.

IFA · Independent financial adviser

Plain English
An adviser who recommends financial products from across the whole market.
Mechanics
Many now outsource investment selection to DFMs or model portfolios.
Why it matters to this role
The end of the UK advised distribution chain.

IMA · Investment management agreement

Plain English
The contract between a client and an asset manager for a segregated mandate.
Mechanics
Covers objective, guidelines, fees, reporting, liability and termination. Often terminable on short notice.
Why it matters to this role
Negotiating and then living within it is where the relationship becomes concrete.

Incentive fees

Plain English
Extra fees GS earns when a fund or account beats an agreed return or benchmark.
Mechanics
A percentage of return or of excess return, recognised only when significant reversal is not probable. Includes 'overrides' on private equity and credit funds. $489m in 2025; $882m in the first nine months of 2026.
Why it matters to this role
Lumpy and tied to realisations, so it should not be treated like recurring management fees in a worked example.

Sources: R2-S01 R2-S02

Index

Plain English
A published list of securities and weights that represents a market.
Mechanics
Built by an index provider to stated rules. The basis for passive funds and most benchmarks.
Why it matters to this role
You cannot discuss performance without naming the index.

Index-linked gilt

Plain English
A UK government bond whose payments rise with inflation.
Mechanics
Used to match pension promises that increase with inflation.
Why it matters to this role
A core LDI building block.

Information asymmetry

Plain English
When one side of a deal knows more than the other.
Mechanics
The manager knows more about its process; the client knows more about its own needs and constraints.
Why it matters to this role
Much of client coverage is reducing it honestly in both directions.

Information ratio

Plain English
Outperformance divided by tracking error: how much extra return per unit of active risk.
Mechanics
A ratio of 0.5 sustained over time is generally considered strong (illustrative rule of thumb).
Why it matters to this role
A compact way consultants compare active managers.

Infrastructure

Plain English
Investments in essential physical assets such as energy networks, transport and data centres.
Mechanics
Long-lived, often inflation-linked cash flows.
Why it matters to this role
Fits long-horizon investors and features in UK policy debates on pension investment.

Institutional investor

Plain English
An organisation that invests large sums on behalf of others, such as a pension scheme or insurer.
Mechanics
Decisions are made by committees under formal governance, often with a consultant. Mandates are large and individually negotiated.
Why it matters to this role
One of the two main client groups in client coverage, with its own sales cycle and service model.

Intermediary

Plain English
A professional firm that chooses investments for its own clients, such as a private bank or wealth manager.
Mechanics
The asset manager's customer is the intermediary; the money belongs to the intermediary's clients. Reached through wholesale or third-party distribution.
Why it matters to this role
Selling to an intermediary means winning approval and then usage.

Investment consultant

Plain English
A firm that advises asset owners on investment strategy and on which managers to hire.
Mechanics
Researches and rates strategies, runs manager searches and monitors appointed managers. Paid by the client.
Why it matters to this role
An adviser to your client and a judge of your product at the same time.

Investment grade

Plain English
Bonds from borrowers judged likely to repay.
Mechanics
Rated BBB-/Baa3 or above by the main rating agencies. Many guidelines require it.
Why it matters to this role
A common guideline boundary.

Investment guidelines

Plain English
The client's written rules for what the manager is aiming for and what it must not do.
Mechanics
Benchmark, permitted assets, limits, exclusions. Monitored by compliance systems. Breaches, even passive ones, must be reported and fixed.
Why it matters to this role
Coverage staff relay the client's intent accurately when guidelines are drafted and communicate promptly when one is breached.

Investment horizon

Plain English
How long money can stay invested before it is needed.
Mechanics
Set by the liabilities. The governance horizon is often shorter than the stated one.
Why it matters to this role
Keeps performance conversations in the right time frame.

ISDA · International Swaps and Derivatives Association (master agreement)

Plain English
The standard legal contract for trading derivatives between two parties.
Mechanics
Supplemented by a credit support annex that sets collateral terms.
Why it matters to this role
Needed before a mandate can use swaps; often on the onboarding critical path.

Journey plan · Also: flight path

Plain English
A scheme's plan for getting from its current funding level to its long-term target.
Mechanics
Sets how risk is reduced as funding improves, often with pre-agreed triggers.
Why it matters to this role
The reference point for most strategic conversations with a DB scheme.

Key-person risk

Plain English
The danger that something valuable depends on one individual.
Mechanics
Applies to portfolio managers (the strategy) and to coverage staff or client contacts (the relationship). Consultants often treat a departure as a trigger for review.
Why it matters to this role
Explains why firms want multiple contacts and written records for every client.

KYC · Know your customer

Plain English
Checks a firm must make to confirm who a client really is before doing business with it.
Mechanics
Identity, ownership and control, source of funds. Part of anti-money-laundering rules.
Why it matters to this role
A frequent cause of onboarding delay; coverage chases the documents.

LDI · Liability-driven investment

Plain English
Investing so that your assets move in step with what you owe.
Mechanics
Uses gilts, index-linked gilts, repo and swaps to hedge interest rate and inflation risk. Often leveraged, which creates collateral calls when yields rise.
Why it matters to this role
Central to UK DB relationships; the 2022 gilt episode still shapes liquidity discussions.

Sources: W1-S05

Leverage

Plain English
Using borrowed money or derivatives to get more exposure than the cash you put in.
Mechanics
Magnifies gains and losses and creates a need for collateral.
Why it matters to this role
The source of the liquidity stress in LDI in 2022.

LGPS · Local Government Pension Scheme

Plain English
The pension scheme for local government workers; unlike most public-sector schemes it holds real investments.
Mechanics
In England and Wales it is run through 86 administering authorities that invest via shared pools, which are being consolidated.
Why it matters to this role
A large UK institutional segment where the buyer is increasingly the pool.

Sources: W1-S08

LGPS pool

Plain English
A shared investment company owned by a group of LGPS funds to invest their money together.
Mechanics
Pools select and oversee external managers or manage in-house. Government reforms are reducing the number of pools and making pooling compulsory.
Why it matters to this role
Changes who an external manager must win over, and concentrates decisions.

Sources: W1-S08

Liability

Plain English
Something you owe, now or in the future.
Mechanics
For a pension scheme, the promised pensions; for an insurer, expected claims.
Why it matters to this role
Client needs are driven by liabilities more than by a wish for return.

Liquidity

Plain English
How quickly an investment can be turned into cash without a poor price.
Mechanics
Also used for the cash-management business line. Liquidity can vanish in stressed markets.
Why it matters to this role
Shapes what a client can hold and what it needs in a crisis.

Liquidity mismatch

Plain English
When a fund lets investors leave faster than it can sell its investments.
Mechanics
Can force dealing suspensions. A focus of regulators for property and credit funds.
Why it matters to this role
A risk clients and gatekeepers test for.

Liquidity products

Plain English
Cash-like holdings: money market funds and private bank deposits.
Mechanics
A GS AUS asset class. $1,051bn at 30 Sep 2026; average effective fee 13 bps for nine months 2026.
Why it matters to this role
Large balances and low fees, and flows can reverse quickly. The reported class mixes money market funds with private bank deposits, so it is not a clean measure of the Liquidity Solutions fund business.

Sources: R2-S01 R2-S02

Long-term AUS · Long-term assets under supervision

Plain English
AUS excluding cash-like liquidity products: alternatives, equity and fixed income.
Mechanics
GS reports net flows and the client-channel split (Institutional, Wealth management, Third-party distributed) on long-term AUS only. $3,046bn at 30 Sep 2026.
Why it matters to this role
When GS says 'long-term fee-based net inflows' it means flows into these assets, which carry higher fees than liquidity products.

Sources: R2-S02

LTAF · Long-term asset fund

Plain English
A UK fund type designed to hold illiquid investments such as private equity and infrastructure.
Mechanics
An open-ended authorised fund with long notice periods for withdrawals. Aimed at DC pensions and, with conditions, wealth investors.
Why it matters to this role
One route by which private markets reach UK pension savers.

LVNAV · Low volatility net asset value

Plain English
A money market fund that deals at a steady price so long as the true value of its holdings stays very close to it.
Mechanics
If the stable price deviates from market value by more than 20 basis points, dealing switches to the market-based price.
Why it matters to this role
The most widely used prime MMF structure in Europe for corporate cash.

Sources: W1-S06

Management and other fees

Plain English
The AWM revenue line for fees charged on client assets and related services.
Mechanics
Mostly asset-based fees on managed client assets, plus advisory, planning and brokerage fees for wealth clients. $11,538m in 2025, of which Asset management $4,990m and Wealth management $6,548m.
Why it matters to this role
The recurring fee line that asset gathering and retention feed. Recurring does not mean guaranteed: it moves with markets, flows and mix.

Sources: R2-S01

Management fee

Plain English
The regular fee an asset manager charges, set as a yearly percentage of the money it manages.
Mechanics
Accrues on average assets and is billed monthly or quarterly. It is gross revenue, not profit. Private market funds often charge it on committed or invested capital instead of NAV.
Why it matters to this role
It is the recurring income that client coverage helps to win and keep.

Mandate

Plain English
An instruction from a client to an asset manager to run a specific pot of money in a specific way.
Mechanics
Used loosely for any appointment. Check whether it is awarded, funded, and fee-paying: these are different stages.
Why it matters to this role
Press reports of 'mandate wins' often describe awards, not money that has arrived.

Master trust

Plain English
A single DC pension scheme used by many unrelated employers.
Mechanics
Run by a professional trustee board and authorised by TPR. Large master trusts are among the most significant DC buyers.
Why it matters to this role
A concentrated, professional buyer for DC investment capabilities.

Matching adjustment

Plain English
A rule that lets insurers value long-term promises more favourably if they hold assets with matching, predictable cash flows.
Mechanics
Central to UK annuity business. Eligibility rules determine which assets insurers want.
Why it matters to this role
Drives UK insurers' demand for long-dated and private credit.

MFN clause · Most-favoured-nation clause

Plain English
A promise that a client's fee will be at least as good as that of any similar client.
Mechanics
Usually limited to comparable strategy, size and service. One discount elsewhere can trigger repricing for MFN holders.
Why it matters to this role
Explains why a fee concession to one client can cost far more than it appears.

MiFID II · Markets in Financial Instruments Directive II

Plain English
European rules on how investment firms deal with clients and markets.
Mechanics
Covers client classification, suitability, cost disclosure, inducements and research payments. The UK has its own version.
Why it matters to this role
Underlies client categories such as professional and retail.

MMF · Money market fund

Plain English
A fund that holds very short-term, high-quality debt to keep cash safe and available.
Mechanics
An investment, not a deposit, with no deposit guarantee. Low fees, very large balances. UK and EU rules recognise three structures.
Why it matters to this role
The core product of a liquidity solutions business.

Sources: W1-S06 W1-S09

MPS · Model portfolio service

Plain English
A ready-made portfolio of funds that advisers can apply to many clients at once.
Mechanics
Run by a DFM or asset manager. One decision by the model's manager moves money for thousands of clients.
Why it matters to this role
Being selected into a model is often worth more than being on a buy list.

Multi-asset

Plain English
A portfolio that mixes shares, bonds and other investments under one manager.
Mechanics
The manager also decides the mix. Used in DC defaults, wealth portfolios and OCIO.
Why it matters to this role
A solutions product that depends on asset allocation skill.

Multi-Asset Solutions · Goldman Sachs Asset Management's multi-asset investing group

Plain English
The investment group that builds and runs whole portfolios across asset classes, including outsourced (OCIO) mandates.
Mechanics
An investing group, separate from the sales organisation. Its OCIO teams work with sales and client relationship professionals.
Why it matters to this role
OCIO clients are served by this group, so not every client-facing person sits in the Client Solutions Group.

Sources: R1-S15

NAV · Net asset value

Plain English
What a fund is worth: its assets minus what it owes. Divided by the number of units, it gives the price of one unit.
Mechanics
Calculated daily for most public funds and quarterly, by estimate, for most private funds. Dealing in a pooled fund happens at NAV per unit.
Why it matters to this role
Fund fees, performance and client statements are all based on it.

NAV-based fee

Plain English
A fee calculated as a percentage of the current value of the client's investment.
Mechanics
Standard for public-market funds and mandates. The fee rises and falls with markets as well as with flows.
Why it matters to this role
Explains why a market fall cuts revenue even when no client leaves.

Net flows

Plain English
New client money coming in minus client money going out over a period.
Mechanics
Gross inflows minus redemptions and withdrawals. Reported separately from market movements, so it shows whether clients are adding or leaving regardless of what markets did.
Why it matters to this role
It is the cleanest public measure of whether a client business is winning and keeping assets.

Non-fee-earning alternative assets

Plain English
Alternative assets GS controls or has commitments for but does not currently charge management fees on.
Mechanics
Mainly balance-sheet investments, unfunded commitments (GS's own and clients' where fees are not charged on commitments), fund credit facilities and employee funds. $207bn at 31 Dec 2025 against alternative AUS of $420bn.
Why it matters to this role
Explains why a commitment a client signs today may not produce fee revenue until capital is drawn and invested.

Sources: R2-S01

OCF · Ongoing charges figure

Plain English
The yearly cost of owning a fund, shown as a percentage.
Mechanics
Includes the management fee plus administration, custody and similar running costs. Excludes dealing costs inside the fund and any performance fee.
Why it matters to this role
The number fund selectors and advisers compare first.

OCIO · Outsourced chief investment officer

Plain English
An arrangement where an organisation hands day-to-day investment decisions for all or most of its portfolio to a specialist provider.
Mechanics
The client keeps objectives and risk appetite; the provider handles asset allocation within limits, manager selection, implementation and reporting. Measured against the client's own objective.
Why it matters to this role
A different business model from single-strategy mandates: a governance sale, a whole-portfolio relationship.

ODD · Operational due diligence

Plain English
A client's check that a manager's operations, controls and systems are sound, separate from whether its investing is good.
Mechanics
Covers valuation, trading controls, business continuity, cyber security, service providers. A failed ODD can veto an otherwise attractive strategy.
Why it matters to this role
Explains why winning a mandate involves far more people than the portfolio manager.

OEIC · Open-ended investment company

Plain English
The usual legal form for UK-based funds.
Mechanics
The UK counterpart to a SICAV. Creates and cancels shares as investors come and go.
Why it matters to this role
Appears in UK fund names and platform listings.

Official institution

Plain English
A central bank, government agency or similar public body that invests reserves.
Mechanics
Very conservative, focused on safety and liquidity, with strict eligibility rules.
Why it matters to this role
A specialist client segment often covered alongside sovereign funds.

Onboarding

Plain English
Everything that has to happen between a client saying yes and its money being invested.
Mechanics
Legal agreement, anti-money-laundering checks, custody and market account openings, guideline coding, reporting set-up, transition of assets.
Why it matters to this role
Delays here postpone revenue and shape the client's first impression.

Overrides

Plain English
GS's word for its larger share of profits on a private fund once returns pass a threshold; commonly called carried interest.
Mechanics
Defined in the 10-K as 'the increased share of the income and gains derived primarily from our private equity and credit funds when the return on a fund's investments over the life of the fund exceeds certain threshold returns'.
Why it matters to this role
Use GS's own term when discussing its disclosures; a client-side reader will usually say carried interest.

Sources: R2-S01

Passive management · Also: index tracking

Plain English
Trying to match a benchmark as closely and cheaply as possible.
Mechanics
Very low fees, huge scale. Has taken market share from active equity for many years.
Why it matters to this role
The main source of fee pressure and the default alternative a client compares you with.

Performance fee

Plain English
An extra fee paid only if the manager beats an agreed target.
Mechanics
Usually a share of returns above a benchmark or hurdle, often subject to a high-water mark. Makes revenue more variable.
Why it matters to this role
Clients ask how it is calculated and whether it rewards skill or just rising markets.

Pipeline

Plain English
The list of potential deals a sales team is working on, with their stage and likelihood.
Mechanics
Stages typically run from lead through proposal and finals to won, funded or lost.
Why it matters to this role
Pipeline reviews are a regular work product.

Platform

Plain English
An online service where advisers and investors hold and trade funds.
Mechanics
Provides custody, dealing and reporting. A fund must be available on the platforms an intermediary uses before it can be bought.
Why it matters to this role
A practical precondition for wholesale sales.

PLSA · Pensions and Lifetime Savings Association

Plain English
The main trade body for UK workplace pension schemes.
Mechanics
Runs major industry conferences and lobbies on pensions policy. The body has announced a change of name to Pensions UK; the date was not verified in this stream, so check current usage.
Why it matters to this role
Its events are where UK institutional coverage teams meet clients and consultants.

PM · Portfolio manager

Plain English
The person who decides what a portfolio buys and sells.
Mechanics
Accountable for performance within the guidelines. Their time with clients is rationed.
Why it matters to this role
Coverage decides when a client meeting justifies the PM's time.

Pooled fund

Plain English
A shared pot: many investors put money into one fund that is managed as a single portfolio.
Mechanics
Investors own units, deal at NAV and accept the fund's rules. Cheaper and quicker to enter than a segregated mandate, with no customisation.
Why it matters to this role
The standard vehicle in wealth distribution and for smaller institutions.

PPF · Pension Protection Fund

Plain English
The UK safety net that pays compensation to members of DB schemes whose employer has failed.
Mechanics
Funded by a levy and its own investments. Publishes the Purple Book, the standard data source on UK DB schemes.
Why it matters to this role
Its data is the best public picture of the UK DB market.

Sources: W1-S01

PRA · Prudential Regulation Authority

Plain English
The part of the Bank of England that supervises the financial soundness of banks and insurers.
Mechanics
Sets Solvency UK requirements for insurers.
Why it matters to this role
Its rules shape insurance clients' investment choices.

Principal–agent problem

Plain English
The difficulty that arises when one party relies on another to act for it but cannot fully check what the other does.
Mechanics
Addressed through contracts, monitoring, incentives and reputation. Runs through the whole chain from member to manager.
Why it matters to this role
Explains why reporting, due diligence and guidelines exist.

Private bank

Plain English
A bank division that manages money for wealthy individuals and families.
Mechanics
Selects third-party funds centrally and distributes them through its bankers. Often global buying decisions with local implementation.
Why it matters to this role
A core third-party wealth client type.

Private credit

Plain English
Lending directly to companies or projects instead of buying bonds in the market.
Mechanics
Offers extra yield for illiquidity and complexity. Popular with insurers and pension schemes seeking income.
Why it matters to this role
A fast-growing area in institutional and insurance conversations.

Private equity

Plain English
Buying companies that are not listed on a stock exchange, improving them and selling them.
Mechanics
Funds last around ten years; returns come mostly at exit.
Why it matters to this role
A flagship alternatives product.

Private markets

Plain English
Investments negotiated directly and not traded on an exchange.
Mechanics
Accessed through closed-end or semi-liquid funds with commitments, capital calls and long holding periods.
Why it matters to this role
Changes the fee base, the liquidity conversation and the client's due diligence.

Product specialist · Also: investment specialist, client portfolio manager (CPM)

Plain English
An investment expert who explains a strategy to clients but does not usually make the investment decisions.
Mechanics
Sits between portfolio managers and coverage. Presents at pitches and reviews so portfolio managers can stay focused on investing.
Why it matters to this role
The colleague coverage relies on for technical depth in meetings.

Public markets

Plain English
Markets where securities trade openly with visible prices.
Mechanics
Listed shares and most bonds. Daily valuation and liquidity.
Why it matters to this role
The contrast case for private markets.

Re-tender test

Plain English
Ask whether the client would choose the manager again in a fresh, fully informed competition.
Mechanics
A reasoning device used in this dossier (not an industry standard term) to separate retention that reflects value from retention that reflects inertia.
Why it matters to this role
Gives a concrete way to challenge the claim that retention proves a good relationship.

Rebate

Plain English
Part of a fund's fee paid back to a large investor or intermediary.
Mechanics
A way to deliver a negotiated price inside a pooled fund. Restricted in some markets and channels by rules on inducements.
Why it matters to this role
Comes up in wholesale and platform pricing discussions.

Repo · Repurchase agreement

Plain English
Selling a bond today with a promise to buy it back later: in effect, a short-term loan secured on the bond.
Mechanics
The main way LDI portfolios obtain leverage on gilts.
Why it matters to this role
Explains how pension schemes borrow to hedge.

Retail investor

Plain English
An individual investing their own money.
Mechanics
Has the strongest regulatory protection. Usually reached through advisers and platforms, not directly.
Why it matters to this role
The end customer behind most wealth-channel sales.

RFI · Request for information

Plain English
A shorter, earlier questionnaire used to build a long list of possible managers.
Mechanics
Often precedes an RFP. Less binding, but still a written record.
Why it matters to this role
An early signal that a search is under way.

RFP · Request for proposal

Plain English
A formal invitation to bid for a mandate, with a long list of questions the manager must answer in writing.
Mechanics
Covers firm, team, process, performance, risk, operations, fees. Answers must be accurate and consistent with every other document the firm has issued.
Why it matters to this role
Drafting and coordinating RFP responses is a core junior task in a client business.

RM · Relationship management / relationship manager

Plain English
The role focused on looking after existing clients.
Mechanics
Reviews, reporting, issue resolution, account planning, and identifying further needs. Often shares responsibility for growth.
Why it matters to this role
The other track; in practice overlaps with sales.

Run-on

Plain English
Choosing to keep a well-funded DB scheme going instead of passing it to an insurer.
Mechanics
The scheme invests to pay pensions over time and may generate surplus. Needs ongoing governance and investment management.
Why it matters to this role
Keeps assets with managers for longer and changes what trustees want.

Sales · Also: business development

Plain English
The role focused on winning new clients and new money.
Mechanics
Prospecting, discovery, proposals, RFP leadership, negotiation through to funding. Boundaries with relationship management vary by firm.
Why it matters to this role
One of the two tracks a candidate may be placed in.

SCR · Solvency capital requirement

Plain English
The amount of capital an insurer must hold to survive a severe year.
Mechanics
Calculated under Solvency II by standard formula or internal model. Riskier assets need more capital.
Why it matters to this role
Explains insurers' preference for high-quality, capital-efficient assets.

Search costs

Plain English
The time and effort needed to find and assess a suitable provider.
Mechanics
Thousands of strategies exist; consultants, ratings and coverage teams all reduce the cost of finding the right one.
Why it matters to this role
One reason distribution exists.

Segregated mandate · Also: separate account, SMA

Plain English
A private portfolio run for one client under rules written for that client.
Mechanics
Assets sit in the client's own custody account. Governed by an IMA and guidelines. Needs scale because of legal and operational set-up cost.
Why it matters to this role
The typical vehicle for larger institutional clients and the reason onboarding is a project.

SFDR · Sustainable Finance Disclosure Regulation

Plain English
EU rules on how funds must describe their sustainability characteristics.
Mechanics
Funds are commonly referred to by the article they disclose under. The regime has been under review.
Why it matters to this role
European intermediaries filter funds by it.

Share class

Plain English
A version of a fund with its own fee level, currency or minimum investment.
Mechanics
All classes own the same portfolio. Institutional and 'clean' classes carry lower charges than legacy retail classes.
Why it matters to this role
Much wholesale pricing negotiation is about which share class an intermediary can access.

SICAV · Société d'investissement à capital variable

Plain English
A common legal form for European funds, often based in Luxembourg.
Mechanics
An open-ended investment company whose share capital varies with investor flows. Many cross-border UCITS are Luxembourg SICAVs.
Why it matters to this role
You will see it in fund names and documents.

Side letter

Plain English
A separate agreement giving one investor in a fund special terms.
Mechanics
Typical contents: fee terms, extra reporting, MFN rights. Common in private funds.
Why it matters to this role
Shows how individual negotiation happens even inside pooled vehicles.

SLA · Service level agreement

Plain English
An agreed standard for service, such as how quickly reports are delivered.
Mechanics
May sit in the IMA or alongside it. Missed SLAs are tracked and reported.
Why it matters to this role
Turns 'reliability' into something measurable.

Solvency II / Solvency UK

Plain English
The rules that decide how much capital European and UK insurers must hold against their risks.
Mechanics
Each asset carries a capital charge depending on its risk. The UK's reformed version is called Solvency UK.
Why it matters to this role
Insurers judge investments on return after capital cost, not headline yield.

Sponsor · Sponsoring employer

Plain English
The company that stands behind a DB pension scheme and must fund any shortfall.
Mechanics
Its interests can differ from the trustees': it bears the cost and may share in any surplus.
Why it matters to this role
A second party whose view shapes scheme decisions.

Stewardship

Plain English
How an investor uses its ownership rights: voting and engaging with companies.
Mechanics
Clients ask for voting records and engagement examples.
Why it matters to this role
A regular reporting and due diligence topic.

Sub-advisory

Plain English
One firm hires another to manage the investments of a fund sold under the first firm's name.
Mechanics
The sub-adviser earns a negotiated fee; the brand owner keeps the client relationship.
Why it matters to this role
A way to win assets from wealth firms without selling a branded fund.

Sub-custodian

Plain English
A local bank that holds assets in a particular country on behalf of the main custodian.
Mechanics
Each market a segregated account will trade in needs an account opened through the local sub-custodian, with local documentation.
Why it matters to this role
Market account openings are a common critical path item before a mandate can trade.

Suitability

Plain English
Whether an investment fits the client's objectives, constraints and understanding.
Mechanics
A regulatory requirement when advising retail clients and a professional standard everywhere.
Why it matters to this role
The test for when not to sell.

Superday · Goldman Sachs's name for its final-round interviews

Plain English
The last stage of campus recruitment: a series of interviews with people from the business.
Mechanics
Goldman says it typically holds between two and five interviews for campus hires, depending on the division.
Why it matters to this role
It is the stage at which you meet members of a specific team.

Sources: R1-S23

Swap

Plain English
A contract to exchange one stream of payments for another, such as fixed interest for floating.
Mechanics
Interest rate and inflation swaps are used to hedge liabilities without buying bonds outright.
Why it matters to this role
A core LDI instrument.

SWF · Sovereign wealth fund

Plain English
A state-owned investment fund, often built from oil, gas or trade surpluses.
Mechanics
Very large, long-horizon, staffed by professionals. Often invests directly and through co-investments as well as through managers.
Why it matters to this role
A central client type in Middle East coverage.

Switching costs

Plain English
The cost and disruption of moving from one provider to another.
Mechanics
Transition costs, governance time, legal work, operational risk. Can keep a client in place for reasons unrelated to quality.
Why it matters to this role
Retention caused by inertia is not the same as a satisfied client.

TCFD · Task Force on Climate-related Financial Disclosures

Plain English
A framework for reporting climate-related risks.
Mechanics
Large UK pension schemes must report in line with it, so they request data from managers.
Why it matters to this role
Generates recurring client data requests.

TER · Total expense ratio

Plain English
An older name for a fund's total yearly running cost as a percentage.
Mechanics
Largely replaced by the OCF in UK and European disclosure, though still used informally and for ETFs.
Why it matters to this role
You will see both terms; they are close but not identical.

Third-party commitment

Plain English
A client's promise to provide money to a private fund when the manager calls for it.
Mechanics
GS reports commitments raised ($115bn in 2025) separately from AUS; some become fee-earning AUS only 'if and when the commitments are drawn and assets are invested'.
Why it matters to this role
Keeps a fundraising headline apart from funded, fee-paying assets.

Sources: R2-S01

Third-party distributed

Plain English
Client assets that come to GS funds through other firms, such as banks, wealth managers and platforms, and not from GS's own wealth clients.
Mechanics
One of three GS client channels for long-term AUS. $714bn at 30 Sep 2026, up from $526bn a year earlier; net inflows of $97bn in the first nine months of 2026, which include acquired ETF assets.
Why it matters to this role
This is the disclosure line closest to what a third-party wealth team works on, at global level only.

Sources: R2-S02

TPE · Third-party evaluator

Plain English
An independent adviser that helps trustees choose and then monitor a fiduciary manager.
Mechanics
Runs the tender, compares providers on a like-for-like basis and reports on ongoing performance.
Why it matters to this role
An influential gatekeeper in OCIO sales.

TPR · The Pensions Regulator

Plain English
The UK public body that protects workplace pensions.
Mechanics
Regulates trustees and employers, sets codes of practice, authorises master trusts and oversees fiduciary management tendering duties.
Why it matters to this role
Its guidance shapes what trustees ask of managers and advisers.

Sources: W1-S02

TPW · Third-party wealth

Plain English
Selling an asset manager's funds to other firms' wealth businesses, which then use them for their own clients.
Mechanics
A label used by some firms for wholesale distribution to private banks, wealth managers and advisers. The official name of any Goldman Sachs team should be checked against the teams chapter.
Why it matters to this role
One of the reported client-segment teams in the group this project studies.

Tracking error

Plain English
How differently a portfolio behaves from its benchmark.
Mechanics
The annualised standard deviation of the difference in returns. Often capped in guidelines.
Why it matters to this role
Tells a client how much active risk they are paying for.

Transition management

Plain English
A specialist service that moves a portfolio from one manager or strategy to another at controlled cost and risk.
Mechanics
Plans the trades, keeps market exposure during the move and reports the cost against a benchmark.
Why it matters to this role
Used when mandates are won, lost or restructured; the cost can decide whether a switch is worthwhile.

Trustee

Plain English
A person legally responsible for running a pension scheme or charity in the interests of its beneficiaries.
Mechanics
Must take proper advice, follow the scheme's rules and act prudently. Many are lay people; professional trustees are increasingly common.
Why it matters to this role
The decision-maker in most UK pension relationships, with limited time and personal accountability.

UCITS · Undertakings for Collective Investment in Transferable Securities

Plain English
The standard regulated investment fund sold across Europe and the UK.
Mechanics
A common rulebook on diversification, liquidity, custody and disclosure. Usually daily dealing.
Why it matters to this role
Most funds sold through wealth intermediaries are UCITS.

VNAV · Variable net asset value

Plain English
A money market fund whose share price moves with the market value of what it holds.
Mechanics
No stable price promise; can be short-term or standard.
Why it matters to this role
An alternative where stable pricing is not required.

Volatility

Plain English
How much an investment's returns bounce around.
Mechanics
Usually the annualised standard deviation of returns. Understates risk for assets that are valued infrequently.
Why it matters to this role
The most quoted risk number, and often not the one the client should care about most.

Wholesale distribution

Plain English
Selling funds to professional intermediaries instead of directly to institutions or the public.
Mechanics
Covers private banks, wealth managers, advisers, platforms and funds of funds.
Why it matters to this role
The general industry term for the third-party wealth channel.

Yield

Plain English
The annual return an investment is expected to pay, as a percentage of its price.
Mechanics
For bonds, yield moves opposite to price.
Why it matters to this role
Rates and yields drive pension funding, insurance demand and cash balances.

Research date and cutoff: 14 November 2026. 379 sources, 360 checked claims.

How to read the labels

  • ✔ Verified The supporting passage was read on a primary or credible source.
  • ≈ Supported inference Reasoned from verified facts or general industry practice; not itself a disclosed fact.
  • ? Unverified account Known only from one person's account (for example the former intern's call).
  • ✎ Illustrative example Invented to teach a mechanism. Not a real client, fee or event.
  • ⇄ Conflicting evidence Credible sources disagree, or the account conflicts with a source.
  • ∅ Not publicly established Searched for and not found in public sources.

W2-C01UK occupational pension scheme trustees must invest scheme assets in the best interests of members and beneficiaries, and in their sole interest where there is a potential conflict of interest.
“in the best interests of members and beneficiaries; and ... in the case of a potential conflict of interest, in the sole interest of members and beneficiaries”
Regulation 4 does not apply to schemes with fewer than 100 members (regulation 7, not fetched). It is a duty on trustees, not on the asset manager.

W2-C02Before investing, trustees must obtain and consider proper advice on whether the investment is satisfactory, and must decide how often to take such advice on investments they keep.
“the trustees must obtain and consider proper advice on the question whether the investment is satisfactory”
This is why an investment consultant or other adviser normally sits between the manager and the trustee decision.
✔ VerifiedW2-S02
W2-C03Trustees may delegate investment discretion to a fund manager and are not responsible for the manager's acts or defaults only if they have taken all reasonable steps to satisfy themselves about the manager's knowledge, experience and competence.
“if they have taken all such steps as are reasonable to satisfy themselves ... that he is carrying out his work competently”
The statutory protection depends on continuing checks, so a trusted manager is still monitored.

Search strings used

How to adapt the syntax. The strings in this register were written for a general web search engine. Engines differ: some ignore site:, some need OR in capitals, some drop quotation marks on long phrases, and professional-profile sites often show only a snippet. If an operator is ignored, move the site name into the query as a plain word, shorten quoted phrases to two or three words, and run one query per name instead of chaining OR. Record every string you run and whether the page itself could be opened, so that 'searched and not found' stays separate from 'not searched'. The three lines below show one query rewritten three ways.

site:linkedin.com/in/ "Goldman Sachs" "Client Solutions" London
linkedin "Goldman Sachs Asset Management" "Client Solutions Group" London
"Goldman Sachs Asset Management" "Client Solutions Group" London analyst OR associate
